claim: Use only the minimum necessary operational information in every workbook. Do not place unnecessary patient-identifying information, payer portal credentials, or sensitive documents in shared workbooks.
correct_statement: This matches the HIPAA minimum necessary standard, which is a legal duty, not a tip. The kits' own columns (patient or account reference, scheduled service date, payer) make a filled-in workbook electronic protected health information, so Security Rule access, audit and transmission safeguards apply, and any cloud host needs a business associate agreement.
practice_impact: A queue holding facility residents' account references and visit dates is protected health information; keep it on access-controlled storage covered by a business associate agreement, not emailed spreadsheets.

claim: The Control Kits are Excel workbooks. Yellow cells are for your input; teal cells calculate automatically.
correct_statement: All three kits are .xlsx files with yellow or cream input cells. Calculated cells are light blue (#DDEBF7) in the Front-End and Prior Authorization kits and pale teal only in the Denial kit. One calculated-coloured column, Suggested Clearance Status in the Pre-Service Clearance Queue, holds no formula, so the huddle's Urgent and Watch counts stay at zero.
source_title: Vendor file 03_CleanClaimRx_Front-End_Control_Kit_REBUILT.xlsx (v1.1), inspected and recalculated; kit Start Here tabs; vendor listing
practice_impact: The front-end kit will not flag urgent pre-service cases by itself; staff must type the status or add a formula before trusting the weekly huddle counts.

claim: When a case in the Pre-Service Clearance Queue needs authorization, record the Queue ID from the Front-End Control Kit on the matching record in the Authorization Tracker.
correct_statement: The Queue ID exists in the Front-End kit (column A of the queue), but the Authorization Tracker in the v1.1 Prior Authorization kit has no Queue ID column and no patient or account reference. The link can only be typed into Notes, reused as the Tracker ID, or added as a new column by the practice.
source_title: Vendor file 05_CleanClaimRx_Prior_Authorization_Control_Kit_REBUILT.xlsx (v1.1), tab 01_Authorization_Tracker, inspected directly
practice_impact: Little for a facility-based Medicare practice with few authorizations; if the kit is used, add a Queue ID column to the tracker or the promised traceability does not exist.

claim: Your purchase is a one-time purchase of Version 1.1 as described in this document. It does not include future updates or new editions. If a revised edition is released, past buyers may be offered it at a reduced price.
correct_statement: This matches the vendor's public listing, which today still says the product is a one-time purchase of Version 1.1 with future updates not included. The reduced-price offer is discretionary ('may'), not a commitment, and the listing shows no refund policy. Dated content will not be refreshed for buyers.
source_title: CleanClaimRx Gumroad listing, Clean Claim Performance System (fetched 2026-11-10)
practice_impact: No update entitlement: anything rule- or rate-dependent in the September 2026 files must be re-verified by the practice, including against the 2027 Medicare fee schedule rule.

claim: Prior Authorization Control Kit: fixed the 'Open denial/appeal cases' and 'Urgent appeal/deadline cases' counts on the Weekly Authorization Review tab, which did not calculate in the 1.0 build.
correct_statement: In the v1.1 file both counts do calculate. The 1.0 build was never released, so its defect cannot be checked. The urgent count is still unreliable: the Urgency formula excludes only Reversed cases, so Closed or Upheld cases with past deadlines stay URGENT, and cases with a blank status are not counted as open.
source_title: Vendor file 05_CleanClaimRx_Prior_Authorization_Control_Kit_REBUILT.xlsx (v1.1), tabs 05 and 06, formulas inspected and recalculated
practice_impact: Do not use the urgent appeal count as a deadline control; it inflates over time with resolved cases. Track appeal deadlines in the practice's own system.

claim: Rewrote the Start Here Guide to match the Control Kits tab by tab.
correct_statement: Every tab the guide names exists and its eight Escalation Log columns match the workbook exactly, but the guide gives instructions for only 14 of the kits' 22 working tabs. Several instructions also do not match the files: the tracker has no Queue ID field, and the guide's four huddle decisions appear in no kit.
source_title: Vendor Start Here Guide v1.1 compared with the sheet names and headers of the three v1.1 Control Kit workbooks
practice_impact: Little; expect to work out eight of the tabs without guidance and to reconcile the guide's wording with the workbooks before training staff.

claim: Administrative fee is $15 per party per dispute for disputes initiated on or after June 11, 2026 (previously $115); as of 2026 the IDR entity fee ranges about $200-$840 for single disputes and up to $1,173 for batched disputes.
correct_statement: Correct. The administrative fee is $15 per party per dispute for disputes initiated on or after June 11, 2026 ($115 from January 22, 2024 through June 10, 2026). Permitted certified IDR entity fees are $200-$840 (single) and $268-$1,173 (batched), plus $75-$250 per additional 25 line items; these ranges change only by rulemaking, not annually.
source_title: eCFR 45 CFR 149.510(d)(2)(ii) and (e)(2)(viii) (current to Nov. 5, 2026); Federal IDR Operations final rule, 91 FR 33900 (June 4, 2026); CMS IDR Administrative Fee Update notice (June 3, 2026); CMS List of certified IDR entities (modified Nov. 4, 2026)
practice_impact: Little: the practice's Medicare and Medicare Advantage claims cannot enter Federal IDR; the $15 fee matters only for rare out-of-network commercial or FEHB hospital-based claims, where a 26-50 line batch also carries the tiered add-on.

claim: The en banc Fifth Circuit decided TMA III on August 11, 2026, holding that plans may no longer include non-negotiated 'ghost rates' in QPA calculations, nor categorically exclude retrospective adjustments such as bonuses and incentive payments.
correct_statement: Correct. On August 11, 2026 the en banc Fifth Circuit (No. 23-40605) affirmed vacatur of the QPA rules that counted non-negotiated ghost rates and excluded bonus, incentive and retrospective payments; it upheld excluding single-case agreements. No implementing guidance is posted yet, and the court said agencies may let plans keep using existing QPAs meanwhile.
source_title: Texas Medical Association v. HHS, No. 23-40605 (5th Cir. Aug. 11, 2026) (en banc, per curiam), Parts I, II and IV; CMS No Surprises Act Notices, 'TMA III Statement' (Aug. 13, 2026); FAQs Part 73 (Apr. 1, 2026)
practice_impact: Little: QPAs are calculated by commercial and FEHB plans and never apply to Medicare or Medicare Advantage claims; treat the vendor's 'retroactive adjustment opportunities' as speculative until the Departments publish guidance.

claim: A final rule effective for disputes initiated on or after June 11, 2026 caps batches at 50 line items and allows cross-code-range batching for anesthesiology, radiology, pathology and laboratory services; batched claims must share the same NPI.
correct_statement: The 50-line-item cap and the anesthesiology, radiology, pathology and laboratory option are real, but they apply to disputes whose open negotiation period begins on or after November 1, 2026; June 11 is only the $15 fee date. The option covers different codes within one CPT code range, never across ranges. Batched items may share an NPI or a TIN.
source_title: eCFR 45 CFR 149.510(c)(4)(i) and (h)(4) (current to Nov. 5, 2026); CMS No Surprises Act Notices, 'Coming Soon: Changes to Batching Disputes' (Aug. 3 and Oct. 2, 2026); CMS Federal IDR Guidance, Treatment of Batched and Bundled Qualified IDR Items and Services (Oct. 29, 2026); 91 FR 33900
practice_impact: Little for a Medicare-heavy facility practice; if it ever batches commercial out-of-network claims, the new rules start with November 1, 2026 open negotiations, and one group TIN is enough even when clinicians bill under different NPIs.

claim: According to CMS Federal IDR process status reports, providers prevailed in approximately 80 percent of payment determinations in 2023, approximately 85 percent in 2024 and approximately 88 percent in the first half of 2025.
correct_statement: The figures match CMS's Supplemental Background reports: providers prevailed in 77% (first half) and 82% (second half) of 2023 payment determinations, 84% and 85% in 2024, and 88% in the first half of 2025. The newest report shows 85% for the second half of 2025, so the rate is no longer rising; 15-22% of determinations are defaults.
source_title: CMS, Supplemental Background on Federal Independent Dispute Resolution Public Use Files: Jan.-June 2023, July-Dec. 2023, Jan.-June 2024, July-Dec. 2024, Jan.-June 2025 (Jan. 21, 2026) and July-Dec. 2025 (July 22, 2026)
practice_impact: Little: these win rates come largely from high-volume emergency and radiology filers disputing commercial claims, and say nothing about Medicare or Medicare Advantage payment, which cannot be taken to Federal IDR.

claim: The Medicare allowable for the CPT code is the most broadly accepted and objectively verifiable benchmark available; start there and frame the IDR offer as a percentage of Medicare, attaching the Medicare fee schedule reference.
correct_statement: The statute bars the certified IDR entity from considering Medicare or any other public payor rate, and CMS guidance extends the bar to rates expressed as a proportion of public payor rates. Party submissions may not include prohibited-factor information. Offers should rest on the QPA and the statutory factors, such as acuity, training, market share and prior contracted rates.
source_title: 42 U.S.C. 300gg-111(c)(5)(D); eCFR 45 CFR 149.510(c)(5)(i)(B), (iii) and (v)(C) (current to Nov. 5, 2026); CMS Federal IDR Process Guidance for Disputing Parties (December 2023 update), secs. 7.4-7.6
practice_impact: Do not adopt the vendor's offer template: a percent-of-Medicare offer with the Medicare fee schedule attached puts a prohibited factor before the arbitrator and wastes the submission; relevant only to rare commercial out-of-network disputes.

claim: Eligible plans are fully insured group, individual market and FEHB plans; self-funded ERISA plans are also covered unless the plan's home state has a qualifying surprise billing law; a UnitedHealthcare Medicare Advantage claim is a different payer for batching purposes.
correct_statement: The vendor has the state-law rule backwards. Self-insured ERISA plans use Federal IDR in every state unless the plan itself opted into a state process (possible only in GA, ME, NV, NJ, VA, WA). State laws displace Federal IDR for fully insured coverage; Florida is such a bifurcated state. Medicare Advantage claims are not IDR-eligible at all.
source_title: CMS, Chart for Determining the Applicability for the Federal Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) Process (current as of Jan. 11, 2023); CMS CAA enforcement letter to Florida (Jan. 28, 2022); 45 CFR 149.30 (specified State law); 45 CFR 149.510(c)(4)(i)(B)
practice_impact: In Florida the screen is the reverse of the vendor's: self-funded employer and FEHB claims go to Federal IDR, fully insured claims generally fall under Florida's own process (physician disputes under $500 revert to Federal IDR), and Medicare Advantage claims are outside both.

claim: The open negotiation notice must be submitted through the CMS IDR portal at federalidrportal.cms.gov within 30 business days of initial payment; negotiation runs 30 business days; IDR must be initiated within four business days after it closes.
correct_statement: The three timeframes are right, but today the open negotiation notice goes directly to the plan or issuer on the Departments' standard form, by email or paper, not through a CMS portal. Portal submission becomes mandatory only 90 days after CMS announces that function, expected from spring 2027. The portal is at nsa-idr.cms.gov; the vendor's address could not be reached.
source_title: CMS Federal IDR Process Guidance for Disputing Parties (December 2023 update), secs. 3.2 and 4; eCFR 45 CFR 149.510(b) and (h)(2) (current to Nov. 5, 2026); CMS Federal IDR Operations Final Rules Implementation Timeline Guide (Aug. 7, 2026); CMS payment disputes page (modified Sept. 15, 2026)
practice_impact: Rarely relevant to a Medicare-heavy panel, but a notice 'submitted' only to a portal and never delivered to the payer would not start the 30-business-day clock, which can make a later award unenforceable.

claim: Emergency services, non-emergency services at in-network facilities, and air ambulance services are covered under the NSA's IDR process.
correct_statement: Correct as a category list. Qualified IDR items are out-of-network emergency services, non-emergency services by out-of-network providers at participating hospitals, hospital outpatient departments, critical access hospitals or ambulatory surgical centers (absent valid notice and consent), and out-of-network air ambulance services. Nursing facilities are not covered facilities, and Medicare, Medicaid and TRICARE claims are excluded.
source_title: eCFR 45 CFR 149.510(a)(2)(xi) and 45 CFR 149.30 (current to Nov. 5, 2026); CMS, Chart for Determining the Applicability for the Federal Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) Process
practice_impact: Little: visits in skilled nursing, long-term care and assisted living facilities are outside the NSA facility definition, so only hospital or ASC work for commercially insured out-of-network patients could ever qualify.

correct_statement: Per-violation ranges and the $2,190,294 figure match the HHS rule of January 28, 2026 (91 FR 3665, HIPAA rows at 3672), still current on 2026-11-10. That rule sets a $2,190,294 calendar-year cap for every tier; the lower Tier 1-3 caps are unofficial inflation-adjusted figures from OCR's 2019 enforcement-discretion notice ($25,000, $100,000, $250,000), not Federal Register amounts.
source_title: HHS, Annual Civil Monetary Penalties Inflation Adjustment, 91 FR 3665 (Jan. 28, 2026), amending 45 CFR 102.3; OCR Notification of Enforcement Discretion, 84 FR 18151 (Apr. 30, 2019)
practice_impact: Exposure figures are right for 2026, but the low annual caps are OCR policy that can be withdrawn without rulemaking; the binding cap is $2,190,294 per provision per year.

claim: As of the 2026 Unified Agenda the Security Rule proposal is not final; HHS moved it to its Long-Term Actions agenda and now targets July 2027 for final action, past the originally anticipated May 2026 date.
correct_statement: Correct. The Security Rule proposal (RIN 0945-AA22; 90 FR 898, January 6, 2025) is not final as of 2026-11-10; 45 CFR part 164 was last amended in 2024. The 2026 Unified Agenda lists it under Long-Term Actions with final action 07/2027; the Spring 2025 agenda had it at Final Rule Stage with final action 05/2026. Agenda dates are non-binding targets.
source_title: OIRA/Reginfo.gov Unified Agenda, RIN 0945-AA22, HIPAA Security Rule to Strengthen the Cybersecurity of Electronic Protected Health Information (2026 and Spring 2025 editions)
practice_impact: The existing Security Rule still governs; proposed mandates (multi-factor authentication, encryption, asset inventory, annual compliance audit) are not yet enforceable, though OCR still enforces risk analysis now.

claim: The risk analysis must be conducted at implementation of any new billing technology, on significant changes, and, under current OCR guidance and the proposed NPRM, at least annually.
correct_statement: The current Security Rule requires an accurate and thorough risk analysis, updated as needed when the environment or operations change; it sets no fixed interval, and OCR's guidance says frequency varies by entity. Only the unfinalized 2025 proposal would require review at least every 12 months. MIPS Promoting Interoperability separately requires a yearly analysis or review.
source_title: 45 CFR 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A), 164.306(e), 164.316(b)(2)(iii) (eCFR); HHS Security Rule NPRM, 90 FR 898 (Jan. 6, 2025); OCR Guidance on Risk Analysis (2010) as quoted; NIST SP 800-66r2
practice_impact: Annual review is sound practice and is needed each year for the MIPS attestation, but it is not a current HIPAA mandate; OCR penalizes absent or stale analyses, not a missed anniversary.

claim: Receive and document the BA's breach notification. Note the date of receipt, this starts the covered entity's own notification clock.
correct_statement: True only when the business associate is an independent contractor. If it acts as the practice's agent under federal common law of agency, its discovery is imputed to the practice and the 60-day clock runs from the day the business associate discovered (or should have discovered) the breach, not from receipt of its notice (45 CFR 164.404(a)(2); 78 FR 5655).
source_title: HHS Omnibus Final Rule, 78 FR 5566, 5655-5656 (Jan. 25, 2013); 45 CFR 164.404(a)(2) and 164.410 (eCFR)
practice_impact: A billing company working under the practice's direction may be an agent; if it sits on a breach for weeks, the practice's 60 days may already be running. The agreement should require notice within days.

claim: Breaches involving fewer than 500 individuals are reported to HHS annually, by March 1 of the year after discovery; the practice must keep a written log and submit it by that date.
correct_statement: Deadline right in substance: breaches under 500 individuals must be reported to HHS within 60 days after the end of the calendar year of discovery (March 1, 2027 for 2026 discoveries; February 29 in leap years such as 2028). The log is kept internally for six years, not submitted: each breach is reported individually through OCR's online breach portal.
source_title: 45 CFR 164.408(c) (eCFR); HHS Omnibus Final Rule, 78 FR 5566, 5654 (Jan. 25, 2013)
practice_impact: Misdirected statements or claim files that qualify as breaches each need their own portal entry by March 1, 2027, plus patient notice within 60 days of discovery; keep the log six years.

claim: Review each BAA: does it postdate January 25, 2013 (Omnibus Rule effective date)? A BAA that was signed before the 2013 Omnibus Rule does not meet current requirements.
correct_statement: January 25, 2013 is the Omnibus Rule's publication date, not its effective date (March 26, 2013; compliance date September 23, 2013). Agreements signed before January 25, 2013 were grandfathered only until September 22, 2014 at the latest, so an unrevised one is presumptively deficient today, but compliance turns on the agreement's content (45 CFR 164.504(e)), not its signature date.
source_title: HHS Omnibus Final Rule, 78 FR 5566 (Jan. 25, 2013); 45 CFR 164.532(d)-(e) and 164.504(e) (eCFR)
practice_impact: Audit each billing, clearinghouse and IT vendor agreement for the required terms (breach reporting, Security Rule compliance, subcontractor flow-down); a post-2013 date alone does not prove compliance.

claim: The permissible fee is a cost-based fee covering the labor to copy and the supplies used, not a flat fee or a per-page fee; $1 per page likely exceeds the limit for electronic records.
correct_statement: The patient-access fee must be reasonable and cost-based: only labor for copying, supplies, postage, and an agreed summary. A flat fee is allowed: OCR guidance accepts up to $6.50 for electronic copies of electronic records in lieu of calculating cost, and rejects per-page charges for such records. State caps such as Florida's $1 per page are only a ceiling.
source_title: 45 CFR 164.524(c)(4) (eCFR); HHS Privacy Rule NPRM, 86 FR 6446, 6469-70 (Jan. 21, 2021) describing OCR's 2016 Access Guidance; Omnibus Rule, 78 FR 5566, 5636; Fla. Admin. Code R. 64B8-10.003
practice_impact: A simple compliant policy for portal or emailed billing and chart copies is a flat fee of $6.50 or less (or free); charging Florida's $1 per page to patients for electronic records invites an OCR complaint.

claim: A covered entity must provide access within 30 days of the request, with a single 30-day extension on written notice; OCR's Right of Access Initiative, launched in 2019, has produced more than 54 enforcement actions.
correct_statement: Correct. A covered entity must act on an access request within 30 days of receipt, with one extension of up to 30 days if, within the first 30 days, it gives the individual a written statement of the reasons and a completion date (45 CFR 164.524(b)(2)). OCR's Right of Access Initiative reached its 56th enforcement action in October 2026.
source_title: 45 CFR 164.524(b)(2) (eCFR, last amended 2014); HIPAA Journal reports of OCR announcements, Aug. 28 and Oct. 9, 2026 (HHS press pages could not be fetched)
practice_impact: Requests for billing records count. A 2021 proposal to cut the deadline to 15 days is still pending at final-rule stage, and OCR's first case under the initiative was a Florida hospital.

claim: CMS released an updated Form CMS-R-131 on March 13, 2026, with OMB approval valid through March 31, 2029; it became mandatory May 12, 2026 and use of any prior version is a compliance failure.
correct_statement: CMS announced the renewed ABN (Form CMS-R-131, Exp. 03/31/2029) on March 13, 2026; OMB's own approval date was March 10, 2026. The expired 01/2026 form was allowed until May 12, 2026; an expired form used for services on or after that date makes the notice invalid.
source_title: CMS FFS ABN page and form ZIP; OMB reginfo ICR 202511-0938-004; Noridian and CGS MAC notices (March 2026)
practice_impact: Any Original Medicare ABN still printed from an old template (Exp. 01/31/2026 or earlier) is invalid for services since May 12, 2026; the redesigned form has no lettered fields, unlike the vendor's field guide.

claim: A voluntary ABN for a statutorily excluded service is not required, but without one the practice cannot bill the patient if the service is later denied; an unissued voluntary ABN is a guaranteed revenue forfeiture.
correct_statement: No ABN is needed to bill a Medicare patient for a statutorily excluded or non-benefit service. The patient is liable either way; a voluntary ABN is only a courtesy and does not change financial liability. Limitation-on-liability protection does not apply to these categorical denials, so skipping the notice forfeits nothing.
source_title: CMS MLN Booklet MLN006266, Medicare Advance Written Notices of Non-coverage (May 2025); Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch.30 §§20.2, 50.2.1 and Ch.1 §60.4.2
practice_impact: Do not write off routine foot care, hearing or other never-covered services for lack of a 'voluntary ABN'; they are patient-billable regardless (Medicaid/QMB limits aside).

claim: When a mandatory ABN is missing or invalid, the result is a billing prohibition that is permanent, non-appealable and complete; there is no administrative remedy, no reconsideration pathway and no recovery mechanism, and the denial is final.
correct_statement: Without a valid required ABN the provider generally cannot collect from the patient and must refund, but this is appealable: providers may appeal both the coverage denial and the liability finding, and Medicare pays the assigned claim if neither provider nor patient knew or could have known of non-coverage.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), Chapter 30, §§20, 30.3 and 50.9 (Rev. 12934); 42 CFR 405.924(b)(2)
practice_impact: A missing-ABN medical-necessity denial should still be reviewed for appeal (coverage and provider-knowledge grounds) rather than written off as final.

claim: Field C should hold the patient's Medicare Beneficiary Identifier (MBI), or HICN for older beneficiaries not yet transitioned to MBI; the field is optional but completing it is strongly recommended.
correct_statement: The ABN's optional identification number is for an internal number such as a medical record number. CMS instructs that MBIs and Social Security numbers should not appear on the notice. HICNs were retired (MBI-only since 2020). The current form has no lettered 'Field C'.
source_title: CMS ABN Form Instructions, Form CMS-R-131 (Exp. 03/31/2029), OMB 0938-0566
practice_impact: Following the vendor would put MBIs on ABN copies handed to patients and facilities, against CMS instructions; use the chart or account number instead.

claim: Field E consists of reason boxes, one or more of which must be checked (seven quoted reasons are listed); an ABN with an unchecked reason box is invalid.
correct_statement: The ABN has no reason check boxes. The notifier writes a plain-language reason in the 'Reason Medicare may not pay' column; at least one reason must apply to each listed item. CMS gives three example reasons, not seven. The only check boxes are the patient's three options.
source_title: CMS ABN Form Instructions and Form CMS-R-131 (Exp. 03/31/2029)
practice_impact: Staff trained to look for seven check boxes will not find them on the real form; a reason must be written (or pre-printed and marked) for every listed service.

claim: Blanket ABNs, including a single ABN issued at the start of a course of treatment or calendar year, are not valid under CMS policy; a service-specific ABN must be issued before each service for which denial is anticipated.
correct_statement: Generic, routine and blanket notices (for all claims, or naming no specific service and reason) are invalid. But CMS allows a single ABN for an extended or repetitive course of treatment if it lists all items and the duration; it stays effective while care, health status and coverage policy are unchanged.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch.30 §§40.2, 40.2.2.C and 50.8 (Rev. 12934); CMS MLN006266 (Extended Treatment; Repetitive or Continuous Non-covered Care)
practice_impact: For recurring non-covered care in facilities, one properly itemized ABN can cover the course of treatment; a new form before every visit is not required.

claim: When a voluntary ABN is issued for a service later denied, the claim should carry modifier GY to indicate the patient has been notified and may be billed; mandatory ABN situations use GA.
correct_statement: GA is correct for a mandatory ABN on file. GX, not GY, reports that a voluntary ABN was given. GY only says the service is statutorily excluded or not a Medicare benefit; it may be used with or without GX, and the patient is liable either way.
source_title: CMS MLN Booklet MLN006266 (May 2025), Table 2; CMS HCPCS Level II quarterly file (October 2026); Claims Processing Manual Ch.1 §60.4.2
practice_impact: Use GA for required ABNs, GX (with GY) for voluntary notices on excluded services, GZ when a required ABN was not obtained; GY alone does not signal notice.

claim: For dually eligible patients an ABN may still be required, and Medicaid rules in most states prohibit billing Medicaid beneficiaries for Medicare medical-necessity denials without a separate, valid financial liability agreement under Medicaid.
correct_statement: An ABN is still required for dual eligibles, under a federal CMS procedure the vendor omits: patient checks Option 1 with payment wording struck; no billing until Medicare and Medicaid both adjudicate; then charge only QMB-without-full-Medicaid, or full-Medicaid patients when Medicaid denies, subject to state law. 'Most states' is unsourced.
source_title: CMS ABN Form Instructions (Form CMS-R-131, Exp. 03/31/2029), special guidance for dually enrolled patients; Fla. Admin. Code R. 59G-1.050(2)
practice_impact: High for facility geriatrics: many nursing-home patients are dual eligible/QMB; the ABN needs the Option 1 strike-through, nothing is collected up front, and Florida Medicaid needs its own documented notice.

claim: CMS may impose civil monetary penalties of up to $10,000 per GFE violation, indexed annually for inflation under 45 CFR part 102; voluntary self-disclosure to CMS has specific procedures and potential penalty mitigation outcomes.
correct_statement: $10,000 is only the statutory base (42 U.S.C. 300gg-134(b)). The inflation-adjusted maximum in 45 CFR 102.3 is $12,123 per violation for penalties assessed on or after Jan. 28, 2026. States enforce first; CMS enforces directly in Florida. No CMS self-disclosure protocol for GFE violations was found: the SRDP covers Stark only, and the statutory penalty waiver covers balance billing only.
source_title: eCFR 45 CFR 102.3 Table 1 (current to Nov. 5, 2026), amended by HHS Annual Civil Monetary Penalties Inflation Adjustment, 91 FR 3665 (Jan. 28, 2026); 42 U.S.C. 300gg-134; CMS CAA enforcement letter to Florida (Jan. 28, 2022); CMS Self-Referral Disclosure Protocol page; Unified Agenda RIN 0938-AU61
practice_impact: The playbook's exposure worksheet uses a stale $10,000 (current cap $12,123) yet overstates real risk: a mostly Medicare panel has few qualifying encounters, CMS's enforcement reports describe complaint-driven corrective action and mention no penalties, and no CMS self-disclosure channel for GFE lapses was found, so take counsel's advice before volunteering anything.

claim: Patients covered by Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE or VA (federal or state government health programs) are exempt from the NSA GFE requirement; separate program protections apply.
correct_statement: Correct. People enrolled in a Federal health care program (Medicare including Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, VA) are not 'uninsured (or self-pay)' and are not entitled to an NSA GFE, even for a non-covered service or when they decline claim submission. Caveat: state or local government employee plans are group health plans, so members electing self-pay still get GFEs.
source_title: CMS fact sheet, What is Considered 'Health Insurance'? Determining When Uninsured (or Self-Pay) Good Faith Estimate Rules Apply (Dec. 2024); 45 CFR 149.610(a)(2)(xiii); 42 U.S.C. 300gg-136; CMS GFE FAQs Part 1, Q4
practice_impact: Decisive for geriatrics: Medicare, Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, dual-eligible, TRICARE and VA patients never trigger an NSA GFE, so the playbook applies only to the rare uninsured or commercially insured self-pay patient; Medicare's own notice rules (such as the ABN) apply instead.

claim: Scheduled 10+ business days ahead: GFE within 3 business days of scheduling; 3-9 business days ahead: within 1 business day; request without scheduling: within 3 business days; under 3 business days: no regulatory deadline.
correct_statement: Correct under 45 CFR 149.610(b)(1)(vi): scheduled at least 10 business days ahead, GFE within 3 business days of scheduling; 3-9 business days ahead, within 1 business day; on request, within 3 business days. Scheduled under 3 business days ahead, no GFE is required at all, unless the patient asks about cost, which counts as a request.
source_title: eCFR 45 CFR 149.610(b)(1)(iv) and (vi) (current to Nov. 5, 2026); CMS GFE FAQs Part 5 (Dec. 13, 2024), Q5-Q7; CMS GFE FAQs Part 2 (Apr. 5, 2022), Q5
practice_impact: Touches only the few uninsured or commercial self-pay patients; facility visits arranged under 3 business days ahead need no GFE unless the patient or representative asks about cost, and a voluntary GFE in that window is not dispute-eligible.

claim: A compliant GFE must contain 10 required content elements, the tenth being an expiration date; there is no federal standard for expiration, and best practice is 90 days for stable services, 30 days for services subject to fee changes.
correct_statement: The regulation lists ten operative content elements, but none is an expiration date. The tenth, 45 CFR 149.610(c)(1)(xi), is a disclaimer that the GFE is not a contract, missing from the vendor's ten-item list. The only federal validity limit is 12 months for recurring-service GFEs. The 90-day and 30-day 'best practice' has no traceable federal source.
source_title: eCFR 45 CFR 149.610(c)(1)(i)-(xi) and (b)(1)(x) (current to Nov. 5, 2026); CMS Model Notice: Good Faith Estimate for Health Care Items and Services (OMB 0938-1433)
practice_impact: Do not build from the vendor's ten-item list (it drops the mandatory not-a-contract disclaimer), and its template's dispute disclaimer lacks the required statement that a dispute will not affect quality of care; use the CMS model GFE, with one recurring GFE (12 months maximum) for standing visits.

claim: If the final bill exceeds the GFE by $400 or more, the patient has 120 days from the date of the bill to start a dispute; the $25 administrative fee is paid by the patient; the determination is binding.
correct_statement: Correct as of Oct. 2026. A dispute is available when one provider's or facility's billed charges are at least $400 above its GFE total; initiation within 120 calendar days of the initial bill; $25 fee paid by the patient but deducted from the amount owed if the patient prevails; determination binding absent fraud or misrepresentation, though parties may settle.
source_title: eCFR 45 CFR 149.620 (current to Nov. 5, 2026); CMS, Dispute a medical bill (page last modified Oct. 2, 2026); CMS CY 2023 PPDR fee guidance (Oct. 31, 2022)
practice_impact: Rare for a Medicare-heavy panel, but for any self-pay patient keep the bill within $399 of the GFE or reissue the GFE before service; stop collections and late fees while a dispute is pending; the federal process applies in Florida.

claim: Notice of the right to a GFE has three requirements: on the practice website (within two clicks of the homepage), posted in the office, and given at scheduling orally and always in writing; the CMS model notice satisfies them.
correct_statement: The regulation requires notice (A) written, prominently displayed and search-engine findable on the website, in the office and on-site where scheduling or cost questions occur; (B) orally at scheduling or cost questions; (C) in accessible formats and patients' languages. No two-click or individual-handout requirement exists. The model notice is good-faith compliance; oral notice and language access still apply.
source_title: eCFR 45 CFR 149.610(b)(1)(iii)(A)-(C) (current to Nov. 5, 2026); CMS Model Notice, Right to Receive a Good Faith Estimate of Expected Charges (Appendix 1); 86 FR 55980, 56016 (Oct. 7, 2021)
practice_impact: The notice duty applies even with almost no self-pay patients: post the CMS model notice on a search-findable web page and wherever scheduling happens, tell self-pay callers orally, and offer it in the languages patients speak; ignore the invented two-click test.

claim: Omitting co-provider charges is a compliance failure: a GFE must itemize expected charges of co-providers such as anesthesiologists, pathologists and assistant surgeons who bill separately, listed by name and NPI.
correct_statement: The regulation's text requires co-provider and co-facility charges (with name, NPI and TIN), but HHS has never enforced it: enforcement discretion covered 2022 and was extended on Dec. 2, 2022 'pending future rulemaking.' No such rule exists as of Nov. 2026, and CMS tells consumers a GFE lists one provider's charges. A co-provider asked directly must issue its own GFE.
source_title: CMS FAQs, Good Faith Estimates for Uninsured (or Self-Pay) Individuals, Part 3 (Dec. 2, 2022); CMS, What is a good faith estimate? (page last modified Oct. 5, 2026); 45 CFR 149.610(b)(2)(iv), (c)(1)(iii) and (v)
practice_impact: A facility-based practice is usually the co-provider, the very role under enforcement discretion, so it need not build pricing exchange with facilities now; but a self-pay patient who asks the practice directly must get the practice's own GFE within 3 business days.

claim: The uninsured and self-pay GFE, notice and dispute requirements have been enforced by CMS since January 1, 2022, while the insured-patient GFE and Advanced EOB requirement is delayed indefinitely, with a proposed rule only targeted as of early 2026.
correct_statement: Still accurate on Nov. 10, 2026. Self-pay GFE, notice and dispute rules have applied since Jan. 1, 2022; states enforce first and CMS enforces directly where they cannot, including Florida. The insured GFE and AEOB remain deferred: no proposed rule is published; the Unified Agenda's September 2026 target for CMS-9900 passed and it is not under OIRA review.
source_title: Unified Agenda, RIN 0938-AU98, Requirements Related to Advanced Explanation of Benefits (CMS-9900); FAQs About ACA and CAA 2021 Implementation Part 49 (Aug. 20, 2021); 45 CFR 149.610(g); CMS No Surprises overview of rules and fact sheets (modified Nov. 9, 2026); CMS CAA enforcement letter to Florida
practice_impact: Nothing to build for insured patients now; the Advanced EOB would reach commercial and FEHB plans, not Medicare or Medicaid, so even a final rule would touch little of a geriatrics panel. Watch for the CMS-9900 proposed rule.

claim: Once a provider has identified or should have identified an overpayment, it must be reported and returned within 60 days; 'identifies' means when the provider should have known through reasonable diligence; look-back extends up to six years.
correct_statement: The deadline is still 60 days after an overpayment is identified, and the look-back is six years from receipt. But since January 1, 2025, "identified" means knowingly receiving or retaining an overpayment (actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance or reckless disregard). CMS removed the "should have, through reasonable diligence" test; a good-faith investigation can suspend the deadline up to 180 days.
source_title: 42 CFR 401.305 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); CMS, CY 2025 Physician Fee Schedule final rule, Medicare Overpayments, 89 FR 97710, 98333-98338 (Dec. 9, 2024); the CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule final rule (91 FR 70992, Nov. 9, 2026) amends no provision of 42 CFR Part 401 or 411
practice_impact: Refund policy should cite the knowledge standard and the 180-day investigation window; the playbook also credits "courts" for a CMS test that a federal court rejected for Medicare Advantage.

claim: A medical director arrangement must meet the AKS personal services safe harbor: written agreement signed by all parties; term of at least one year; compensation set in advance at fair market value; consistent with actual services; not reflecting referral volume.
correct_statement: The safe harbor is voluntary: missing it does not make a directorship illegal, though meeting every element is the safest course. Since January 19, 2021 its elements are a signed writing covering all services, a term of at least one year, a compensation methodology set in advance at fair market value and not referral-based, and services not exceeding legitimate need.
source_title: 42 CFR 1001.952(d) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026; amended 85 FR 77684, Dec. 2, 2020); HHS-OIG General Compliance Program Guidance (Nov. 2023)
practice_impact: Nursing-home medical directorships are the practice's likeliest exposure; a facility that bills Part B therapy or lab is a Stark entity, so a Stark exception (mandatory, unlike the safe harbor) must also be met.

claim: The Stark non-monetary compensation limit was $519 per physician for calendar year 2025 and $535 for calendar year 2026, covering gifts, meals, entertainment and other non-cash benefits.
correct_statement: Correct. The Stark nonmonetary compensation limit is $519 per physician for 2025 and $535 for 2026. It covers items or services, not cash or cash equivalents, given by an entity that furnishes designated health services, and they must be unsolicited and unrelated to referrals. CMS had not posted a 2027 figure as of November 10, 2026.
source_title: CMS, Physician Self-Referral: CPI-U Updates (page last modified Feb. 19, 2026); 42 CFR 411.357(k)
practice_impact: Count gifts and meals from hospitals, labs, home health agencies and equipment suppliers against $535 per physician; drug-company gifts are generally a kickback-statute matter, not this limit.

claim: False Claims Act civil monetary penalties are up to $28,619 per false claim, the current inflation-adjusted maximum, on top of treble damages.
correct_statement: Correct as of November 2026. False Claims Act civil penalties are $14,308 minimum to $28,619 maximum per claim for penalties assessed after July 3, 2025, in addition to three times the government's damages. DOJ announced in July 2026 that there is no 2026 inflation adjustment, so the 2025 amounts remain in force.
source_title: 28 CFR 85.5 (90 FR 29447, July 3, 2025); Department of Justice, Civil Monetary Penalties Inflation Adjustments for 2026, 91 FR 43405 (July 15, 2026)
practice_impact: Figure is usable; add the $14,308 per-claim floor, which matters more than the ceiling when hundreds of small Part B claims are involved.

claim: Before the in-office ancillary services exception can apply, the referring physician must be a member of a group practice with at least two physicians; the ACA patient notice covers MRI, CT, PET, physical therapy and radiation therapy.
correct_statement: The in-office ancillary services exception is open to solo physicians as well as group practices: the referring physician may personally furnish or supervise the service and bill it. Only a "group practice" needs at least two physicians. The ACA notice rule covers MRI, CT and PET only (with a list of alternative suppliers), not physical therapy or radiation therapy.
source_title: 42 CFR 411.355(b) and 411.352 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); the CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule final rule (91 FR 70992, Nov. 9, 2026) amends no provision of 42 CFR Part 401 or 411
practice_impact: A solo geriatrician is not shut out, but the exception's same-building test rarely fits services furnished inside nursing homes; the home-visit rule covers assisted living, not nursing facilities.

claim: Per-click or usage-based equipment rental fees paid to a referring physician can be structured to comply with the Stark rental exception if documented as consistent with fair market value.
correct_statement: No. The Stark equipment-rental exception bars per-unit-of-service ("per-click") rent to the extent it reflects services to patients the lessor referred to the lessee, and bars percentage-of-revenue rent. A per-click fee paid to a physician who refers the patients fails the exception however well fair market value is documented. Per-click rent is allowed only when the lessor does not refer.
source_title: 42 CFR 411.357(b)(4)(ii) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); CMS, CY 2017 Physician Fee Schedule final rule, 81 FR 80170, 80525-80526 (Nov. 15, 2016); the CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule final rule (91 FR 70992, Nov. 9, 2026) amends no provision of 42 CFR Part 401 or 411
practice_impact: Never take per-test rent for equipment the practice or its physicians lease to an entity they refer patients to (portable imaging, lab analyzers); use rent fixed in advance.

claim: Under the Stark recruitment exception, remuneration must be paid directly to the recruited physician (or the physician's new employer), not through a pre-existing practice the physician is joining; any income guarantee must rest on a reasonable income estimate.
correct_statement: The Stark recruitment exception expressly allows a hospital to pay recruitment money through the existing practice the physician joins, if the practice passes it through (less actual recruiting costs), allocates only incremental costs under an income guarantee, keeps records six years and does not unreasonably restrict the recruit's practice. There is no "reasonable income estimate" or "new employer" element.
source_title: 42 CFR 411.357(e) Physician recruitment (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); the CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule final rule (91 FR 70992, Nov. 9, 2026) amends no provision of 42 CFR Part 401 or 411
practice_impact: If a hospital helps recruit a physician into the practice, the practice may receive the funds but must document pass-through and incremental-cost accounting and sign the agreement if it keeps any amount.

claim: CMS's 2020 Stark final rule (effective January 2021) addressed physician compensation plans where productivity exceeds the 75th percentile relative to benchmarks, noting these could receive greater scrutiny.
correct_statement: The 2020 final rule (effective January 19, 2021) says the opposite. CMS declined to adopt percentile-based presumptions and stated it is not CMS policy that compensation above the 75th percentile of a salary survey is suspect. Fair market value turns on each arrangement's facts; surveys are a starting point, and exceeding a percentile does not by itself fail the test.
source_title: CMS, Medicare Program; Modernizing and Clarifying the Physician Self-Referral Regulations, final rule, 85 FR 77492, 77557-77558 (Dec. 2, 2020)
practice_impact: No federal 75th-percentile trigger exists; document fair market value from the physician's actual duties and local market, and keep pay tied to personally performed work, not referrals.

claim: To diagnose front-end failures, filter denials for CO-4 (service inconsistent with modifier), CO-16 (information missing), CO-22 (coordination of benefits), CO-27 (expenses after coverage terminated) and PR-27 (expenses incurred prior to coverage date).
correct_statement: Four descriptors are close to X12 wording (4, 16, 22, 27). 'PR-27' is wrong: code 27 always means expenses incurred after coverage terminated; 'prior to coverage' is code 26. Code 4 is a modifier (coding) error, not a registration error, and the list omits the missing-authorization code, 197. The 30% trigger is given without a source.
source_title: X12 External Code Source 139, Claim Adjustment Reason Codes (retrieved Nov. 10, 2026); First Coast Service Options, 'Tips to prevent RUC CO4' (Sept. 16, 2026)
practice_impact: A denial filter built on this list would miss prior-to-coverage denials (code 26) and authorization denials (197), and would count modifier errors as registration failures.

claim: Clearinghouse rejections: if ANSI error codes 004 (subscriber not eligible), 005 (invalid subscriber ID), or 021 (missing required information) exceed 40% of rejection volume, you have a registration accuracy problem.
correct_statement: No ANSI X12 code set gives 004 or 005 those meanings. As interchange (TA1) codes, 004, 005 and 021 are file-format errors. As claim status codes, 4 and 5 were retired in 2008 and 21 is 'Missing or invalid information'. Subscriber rejections use status codes such as 33, 88, 109 or 164. The 40% threshold is given without a source.
source_title: X12 External Code Source 508, Claim Status Codes, and Claim Status Category Codes (retrieved Nov. 10, 2026); Indiana Health Coverage Programs TA1/999 5010 Companion Guide v1.8; First Coast 5010 reject code lookup help guide (June 26, 2025); CGS Medicare 277CA edit documentation
practice_impact: Staff sorting a rejection report by these numbers would mislabel rejections; Florida Medicare rejections arrive as category, status and entity codes (for example A7:164:IL for a bad Medicare number), and clearinghouse numbers are vendor-specific.

claim: Medicare Advantage prior authorization requirements that exceed clinical guidelines and medical necessity criteria that differ from published LCDs are payer design choices; cross-payer denial comparisons support a complaint to the state insurance commissioner.
correct_statement: Since 2024 Medicare Advantage plans must follow national and local coverage determinations and may add criteria only where Medicare's are not fully established; prior authorization may only confirm diagnoses or medical necessity. State insurance regulators have no authority over these complaints: federal law preempts them. Providers complain to CMS through its online form, opened December 22, 2025.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.101, 422.138 and 422.402 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); CMS HPMS memo, 'Complaints Tracking Module Updates for Managing Provider Complaints' (Dec. 22, 2025) and CMS Provider Complaints Form page (modified Feb. 18, 2026); Florida DFS Division of Consumer Services
practice_impact: High: for a Florida geriatrics practice with Medicare Advantage residents, a state complaint goes nowhere, while plan criteria stricter than the local coverage determination are a federal violation reportable to CMS.

claim: Contracted payment terms for most commercial payers are 30 days for electronic claims; a payer consistently exceeding them can be escalated, and state insurance commissioners take timely payment violations seriously.
correct_statement: Thirty days is common, not universal. Florida law gives state-regulated insurers and HMOs 20 days to pay, deny or contest an electronic claim, with 12% interest when overdue, and contracts cannot waive it. State regulators cannot act on self-funded employer plans (71% of covered workers), Medicare or Medicare Advantage. Three sampled Florida compliance reports list no prompt-pay fines.
source_title: Fla. Stat. 627.6131 and 641.3155 (2026); 42 CFR 422.520 and 422.402 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); KFF 2026 Employer Health Benefits Survey, section 10; Florida DFS Division of Consumer Services; Florida OIR Insurer Compliance Reports (July 2024, Oct. 2025, Apr. 2026)
practice_impact: Limited where the payer mix is Medicare and Medicare Advantage: late Medicare Advantage payment is a CMS or contract matter, not one for the Florida regulator; the 20-day rule helps only on state-regulated commercial claims.

claim: Quarterly write-off audits can recover timely filing write-offs where the payer may accept a late filing with documentation of prior submission attempts; recovery rates on audited write-offs typically run 10 to 20 percent.
correct_statement: Commercial and Medicare Advantage plans (UnitedHealthcare, for one) reverse timely-filing denials only on proof the claim was received and accepted within the limit; rejected submissions do not count. Original Medicare extends its one-year deadline only under four regulatory exceptions, such as contractor error, and treats unprocessable claims as never filed. The 10-20% recovery figure has no traceable published source.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.44 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); First Coast Service Options timely filing FAQ; 2026 UnitedHealthcare Care Provider Administrative Guide, ch. 10 'Proof of claim timely filing'
practice_impact: For Florida Medicare claims a timely-filing write-off is almost never recoverable; budget no 10-20% recovery, and keep payer acceptance reports for Medicare Advantage claims.

claim: Current published data (2024-2025) puts the national average patient collection rate at about 34% to 48%; 45-50% or better is strong, target-level performance and 80% or more is top-quartile.
correct_statement: The 34-48% range matches Kodiak Solutions' hospital and health-system data, not a national average for physician practices: insured patients paid 34.5% of balances in 2024 on one measure, and 45.1% (2024) and 42.4% (2025) on another. No published benchmark makes 45-50% a target or 80% the top quartile; physician-office balances, being smaller, are collected at higher rates.
source_title: Kodiak Solutions, 'State of the healthcare revenue cycle' (Mar. 2026) and RCA benchmarking analysis (Feb. 2025); Ippolito et al., JAMA Health Forum 2025;6(8):e252284 (via PubMed, doi:10.1001/jamahealthforum.2025.2284); Chernew and Bush, Health Affairs Forefront (May 4, 2017)
practice_impact: Hospital figures are a poor yardstick for a nursing-facility practice, where patient balances are mainly Part B coinsurance often covered by Medigap or Medicaid; the tiers are vendor labels, not benchmarks.

claim: Cost-to-collect benchmarks for independent practices range from 3% to 8%; a best-in-class range of roughly 2% to 4% is commonly cited by HFMA for the most efficient revenue cycle operations.
correct_statement: No published benchmark sets 3-8% for independent practices. An AAFP estimate from MGMA survey data put billing costs at 4% to 8.9% of net revenue; billing companies charge roughly 4-10% of collections; a JAMA study measured 14.5% for primary care visits. HFMA's figures (2% best practice, about 3.5-3.7% average) are hospital benchmarks using a narrower cost definition.
source_title: HFMA, 'Ask the Expert Answer: Calculating Cost-to-Collect' (updated Nov. 29, 2022); HFMA MAP Keys FM-6; Ask FPM, Fam Pract Manag 2004;11(7):63; Physicians Practice, 'Outsourcing Your Billing' (Feb. 1, 2010); Tseng et al., JAMA 2018;319(7):691-697 (via PubMed, doi:10.1001/jama.2017.19148); TechTarget on HFMA survey (Sept. 15, 2022)
practice_impact: A small Medicare practice landing above 4% is not failing against a real benchmark; the 2-4% stretch target is a hospital figure that omits coding and IT costs.

claim: Without a formal charge reconciliation process, the gap between encounters and charges is typically 1% to 3% of total encounter volume.
correct_statement: No published study or benchmark gives a 1-3% encounter-to-charge gap; the figure has no traceable origin. Reference points: a 2018 MD Anderson internal audit of clinics lacking full reconciliation found unbilled open encounters under 1% of annual encounters; HFMA consultants put hospital charge-capture loss at up to 1% of net revenue; a 2008 trade article claimed 3-5% of practice revenue.
source_title: No traceable source for the 1-3% figure. UT MD Anderson Cancer Center Internal Audit 17-101, 'Charge Capture - Houston Area Locations' (Feb. 8, 2018); HFMA, 'Capturing All Charges: the Operational Reality' (Sept. 20, 2019); Physicians Practice, 'Billing Problems? Consider Your Charge Ticket' (Nov. 1, 2008)
practice_impact: Reconciling facility visit logs against charges is worthwhile for nursing-home rounding, but measure the practice's own gap; do not plan revenue recovery around an unsourced 1-3%.

claim: Medicare allows retroactive claims submission for dates of service during the enrollment period under specific conditions.
correct_statement: Correct. For physicians and non-physician practitioners, billing privileges begin on the later of the date the contractor received an application it later approved or the date services began at the location, and billing may reach back up to 30 days earlier (90 for a declared disaster). Earlier services are unpayable; claims are due within one year. Unchanged for 2027.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.520, 424.521 and 424.44 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); First Coast Service Options, 'Determining your Medicare effective date' (Feb. 18, 2026); CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule final rule, 91 FR 70992 (Nov. 9, 2026) (no amendment to these sections)
practice_impact: A new clinician's nursing-facility visits are payable only from the application receipt date (or 30 days before); file the application before or on the first day of rounds and hold claims until approval.

claim: Even if the practice uses a locum tenens or billing-under-supervision arrangement during the credentialing period... Billing under a supervising physician's NPI is appropriate in some circumstances and inappropriate in others.
correct_statement: Medicare's fee-for-time (locum) rule covers only a substitute for an unavailable regular physician (or certain physical therapists), up to 60 continuous days; it is no bridge for a new hire awaiting enrollment. Billing under a supervising physician is allowed only as incident-to (non-institutional setting, physician-initiated treatment, direct supervision), never for hospital or skilled nursing patients.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) ch. 1 s.30.2.11 (Rev. 13725) and ch. 12 s.30.6.13.E (Rev. 13753); 42 CFR 410.26 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); Medicare Benefit Policy Manual ch. 15 s.60.2; First Coast, 'Reciprocal billing and fee-for-time compensation arrangements' (Oct. 29, 2024)
practice_impact: High: nursing-facility visits are not payable incident-to, so billing an unenrolled clinician's facility visits under another physician's number misstates who rendered them and creates overpayment and false-claims exposure.

claim: Medicare through PECOS, when complete and error-free, typically processes in 30 to 45 days.
correct_statement: The 45-day figure was CMS's 2009 standard. Contractors must now process 95% of PECOS initial applications that need no development, site visit or fingerprinting within 15 calendar days, and all within 50; applications needing development, 95% within 50 days and all within 85. First Coast publishes the same timeframes for Florida.
source_title: CMS Medicare Program Integrity Manual (Pub. 100-08) ch. 10 s.10.5 (Rev. 13717, issued July 8, 2026); First Coast Service Options, 'CMS-855 enrollment application processing timeframes' (Feb. 18, 2026); CMS, Internet-based PECOS organization overview (June 1, 2009)
practice_impact: A clean online application should clear First Coast in about two weeks; a 45-day benchmark hides avoidable development requests. The effective date still runs from receipt, not approval.

claim: practices with documented, standardized prior authorization submission processes achieve first-submission approval rates of 82% to 90%... consistent with the range KFF has reported for 2025 approval rates
correct_statement: KFF's 82-90% is real but is the 2025 average approval rate for all providers at the largest insurers: Medicare Advantage 88% of standard and 90% of expedited requests, Medicaid managed care 86-88%, Marketplace 82-84%. It is not a rate earned by practices with standardized processes; nothing supports that link or the 60-75% contrast, and KFF reports no specialty breakdown.
source_title: KFF, 'Prior Authorization Metrics Provide New Insights into Insurer Practices, but Gaps Remain' (Aug. 13, 2026); KFF, 'Medicare Advantage Insurers Made Nearly 53 Million Prior Authorization Determinations in 2024' (Jan. 28, 2026)
practice_impact: An 82-90% approval rate is the Medicare Advantage market average, not proof of a good process; compare each plan against its own published rate (5% to 17% denied).

claim: Auth Turnaround Time: benchmark < 3 days; > 5 days for urgent cases requires escalation pathway.
correct_statement: The 5-day trigger is too late. Federal rules require urgent (expedited) decisions within 72 hours for Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care and employer group plans; a missed Medicare Advantage deadline is itself an appealable denial. Standard Medicare Advantage requests must be decided within 7 calendar days since January 1, 2026. Insurers' median 2025 response was about one day.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.568, 422.572 and 438.210(d) and 29 CFR 2560.503-1(f)(2) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); KFF, 'Prior Authorization Metrics Provide New Insights into Insurer Practices, but Gaps Remain' (Aug. 13, 2026)
practice_impact: For Medicare Advantage residents, escalate an urgent request at 72 hours and a standard request at 7 calendar days, then appeal the silence as a denial; waiting 5 days forfeits two days.

claim: When a payer's prior authorization denial rate for a specific service type is materially above the rate for other payers... that is grounds for a formal complaint to your state insurance commissioner.
correct_statement: A higher denial rate than other payers is evidence, not a legal violation. Florida's regulator acts only on state-regulated insurers and HMOs, cannot make medical judgments, and cannot compel payment absent a breach of law, rule or policy. Medicare Advantage complaints go to CMS's provider complaint form, self-funded employer plans to the Labor Department, Medicaid plans to AHCA.
source_title: Florida Department of Financial Services, Division of Consumer Services, 'Need Our Help?' (accessed Nov. 10, 2026); 42 CFR 422.402 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); CMS HPMS memo on provider complaints (Dec. 22, 2025) and CMS Provider Complaints Form page
practice_impact: For a Medicare Advantage-heavy geriatrics practice the state commissioner is the wrong door; send documented denial patterns to CMS through cms.gov's provider complaint form.

claim: Calculate the percentage of office visits billed at each level, 99202 through 99205 for new patients, 99211 through 99215 for established patients... The benchmark data is publicly available through CMS and through specialty society publications.
correct_statement: Correct. Office visit codes are 99202-99205 (new; 99201 was deleted in 2021) and 99211-99215 (established). CMS publishes free annual 'E&M Codes by Specialty' reports, latest for calendar year 2025, with allowed services per code and specialty. They cover Medicare fee-for-service only, are not adjusted for patient mix, and also include nursing facility codes 99304-99310.
source_title: CMS, 'Evaluation and Management (E&M) Codes by Specialty Reports' (Medicare Utilization for Part B), CY 2025 file, Medicare Part B Physician/Supplier National Data
practice_impact: Usable now, but a facility-based practice should benchmark nursing facility codes 99304-99310, not office codes; the national geriatric-medicine mix for 2025 is in the same CMS file.

claim: <1% is best-in-class (aspirational)... MGMA/HFMA guidance treats roughly <3-5% of net revenue as the standard benchmark band for most independent practices.
correct_statement: The figures trace to Conifer Health sponsored content published through HFMA (sponsored article) and MGMA (white paper), not to either body's own benchmarks: under 5% of total service revenue is 'commonly considered' good, 3% a goal, 1% reached by many Conifer clients. HFMA's own metric divides bad debt by gross revenue and sets no target; MGMA reports dollars per physician.
source_title: HFMA, '7 KPIs providers should be tracking' (sponsored by Conifer Health Solutions; Apr. 6, 2023, updated Sept. 11, 2024); Conifer Health Solutions, 'Top KPIs Physician Practices Should be Monitoring' (2023, hosted by MGMA); HFMA MAP Keys AR-7 (2023 ed.); MGMA DataDive Glossary (2025)
practice_impact: Little: bad debt is small where Medigap or Medicaid pays the coinsurance, and dual-eligible (QMB) balances cannot be billed at all; treat 3-5% as a vendor guideline, not a standard.

claim: Medicare Advantage plans have the authority to impose prior authorization requirements that exceed traditional Medicare's, to apply medical necessity criteria that differ from published LCDs, and to conduct post-payment audits using criteria not in the original coverage policy.
correct_statement: Only the first part holds: MA plans may require prior authorization where Traditional Medicare does not. Since 2024 they must follow NCDs and LCDs, may add public, evidence-based criteria only where Medicare's are not fully established, may not deny basic benefits on other criteria, and may not later deny an authorized service for medical necessity, absent fraud or good cause.
source_title: eCFR 42 CFR 422.101(b)-(c), 422.138 and 422.616(e) (current to Nov. 6, 2026); CY 2024 Medicare Advantage final rule, 88 FR 22120 (Apr. 12, 2023); CY 2026 final rule amendments, 90 FR 15910-15911 (Apr. 15, 2025); CY 2027 final rule, 91 FR 17384 (Apr. 6, 2026), which left these provisions unchanged
practice_impact: High for a Medicare Advantage-heavy panel: appeal by citing the NCD or First Coast LCD plus 422.101(c)(1)(i)(A), and contest any clawback of a pre-authorized service under 422.138(c), rather than accepting plan-specific criteria as lawful.

claim: CMS data analyzed by KFF shows that 80.7% of appealed Medicare Advantage prior-authorization denials were overturned in full or in part in 2024 (above 80% every year 2019-2024), yet only about one in ten denials is ever appealed.
correct_statement: Correct. KFF's analysis of CMS data shows 80.7% of appealed Medicare Advantage prior authorization denials were partially or fully overturned in 2024, more than eight in ten in every year 2019-2024, while only 11.5% of the 4.1 million denials were appealed. These are plan-level reconsiderations of pre-service requests, not post-service claim or payment denials.
source_title: KFF, Medicare Advantage Insurers Made Nearly 53 Million Prior Authorization Determinations in 2024 (Biniek, Sroczynski, Freed and Neuman; published Jan. 28, 2026)
practice_impact: Modest: nursing-facility visits rarely need prior authorization, so the statistic supports appealing the occasional authorization denial but does not predict success on Medicare Advantage claim or payment denials.

claim: Modifier 25 denials require documentation that the E&M was for a separately identifiable problem not related to the procedure.
correct_statement: The record must show a significant, separately identifiable E/M service beyond the procedure's usual pre- and post-service work. It need not concern a separate or unrelated problem: different diagnoses are not required. New from January 1, 2027: Medicare pays 80% for all but the highest-valued service when an office E/M with modifier 25 accompanies a 0-day global procedure.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) ch. 12, sec. 30.6.6.B (Rev. 13753, issued May 7, 2026); Medicare NCCI Policy Manual ch. I, secs. D and E.1.b (revision date Jan. 1, 2026); CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule final rule, 91 FR 70992 (Nov. 9, 2026) and CMS fact sheet (Nov. 4, 2026)
practice_impact: The vendor's 'unrelated problem' test would make staff drop or lose valid same-day visit-plus-procedure claims; the 2027 20% reduction covers only office codes 99202-99215, not the practice's nursing-facility or home visit codes.

claim: An NCCI edit with a modifier indicator of '1' can be separately billed when a modifier appropriately documents distinct services; if the modifier indicator is '0,' the services cannot be unbundled regardless of circumstances.
correct_statement: Correct for Medicare NCCI procedure-to-procedure edits billed by the same provider for the same patient and date. Indicator 1 means an NCCI-associated modifier may bypass the edit only when clinical circumstances justify it; indicator 0 means no modifier bypasses it; indicator 9 marks deleted edits. Commercial payers may apply their own edits.
source_title: CMS, Medicare National Correct Coding Initiative Policy Manual, Chapter I, General Correct Coding Policies, sec. E, Modifiers and Modifier Indicators (effective Jan. 1, 2026)
practice_impact: Useful as stated: check the indicator in the quarterly CMS edit file before appealing a bundled facility-visit procedure; an indicator-0 pair is not worth appealing, and a modifier added only to bypass an edit is an audit risk.

claim: Payment variance of more than 3% on any code warrants a payer inquiry; a variance consistent over multiple months warrants a formal underpayment dispute and, if unresolved, a state insurance commissioner complaint.
correct_statement: The 3% trigger is unsourced; MGMA's audit guidance sets no threshold. In Florida, DFS reviews only prompt-pay violations by state-regulated insurers and HMOs, and refers disputes over payment amount to the AHCA claim dispute resolution program (s. 408.7057). Neither reaches self-funded ERISA or FEHB plans, and DFS cannot assist with Medicare Advantage. Underpayment claims expire after 12 months.
source_title: Florida Department of Financial Services, Division of Consumer Services, 'Medical Providers' and 'Need Our Help?' pages (fetched Nov. 10, 2026); AHCA, Statewide Provider and Health Plan Claim Dispute Resolution Program FAQ; Fla. Stat. 627.6131(19) and 408.7057 (2026); 42 CFR 422.402; CMS Provider Complaints Form page (modified Feb. 18, 2026); MGMA Stat (Feb. 11, 2025)
practice_impact: For a Medicare and Medicare Advantage panel the commissioner step does not exist: use the plan's contract dispute process and CMS's Medicare Advantage provider complaint form; for Florida-regulated commercial plans, underpayment disputes of $500 or more go to the voluntary Capitol Bridge program within 12 months.

claim: Modifier AS: Assistant surgeon (PA/NP/CRNA); high risk in surgical specialties, credentialing and payer policy dependent.
correct_statement: HCPCS modifier AS identifies assistant-at-surgery services by a physician assistant, nurse practitioner or clinical nurse specialist, not a CRNA. Medicare pays these at 85% of the 16% assistant fee (13.6% of the surgical fee schedule amount), and only for procedures whose fee schedule indicator permits an assistant. The 'high risk' rating is the vendor's opinion.
source_title: CMS HCPCS Level II quarterly file, October 2026 (alpha-numeric modifiers); Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) ch. 12, secs. 20.4.3, 110.2 and 120.1
practice_impact: Little: a facility-based geriatrics practice does not bill assistant-at-surgery services; the CRNA error matters only to surgical groups.

claim: A physician spending three to five hours per week on authorization-related activities is generating $3,000 to $12,000 per week in lost clinical revenue in most specialty practices.
correct_statement: The vendor cites no source and none was found. It assumes $1,000 to $2,400 of revenue per physician hour, about three to six times what MGMA's medians imply (roughly $330 to $440 an hour, or $1,000 to $2,200 for three to five hours). The AMA reports 13 hours a week for physicians and staff combined, not physician hours alone.
source_title: No traceable origin for the statistic; context from MGMA, 2025 Financials and Operations Data Report (Sept. 4, 2025) and 2025 AMA prior authorization physician survey (published May 2026)
practice_impact: Do not use the vendor's range in a business case: nursing-facility visits seldom need prior authorization, and the practice should multiply its own measured physician hours by its own collections per clinical hour.

claim: Medical necessity denials are the most common denial type in specialty billing, and medical necessity, bundling and modifier disputes account for the majority of specialty claim denial volume in most practices.
correct_statement: No data located support this, and the vendor cites none. Available rankings put eligibility and missing-information problems first; medical necessity is 6% of hospital denials (Change Healthcare, 2022), 5% of marketplace in-network denials (KFF, 2024) and the top reason for 7.1% of billing companies (HBMA, 2024). First Coast's most frequent Florida Part B denials are NCCI, duplicate and bundling codes.
source_title: HBMA RCM Advisor, Data Science Committee Denials Survey Results (Q2 2024); Optum, 'Actionable Insights & Strategies From the Change Healthcare 2022 Denial Index' (HFMA Texas, May 2023); KFF, 'Claims Denials and Appeals in ACA Marketplace Plans in 2024' (Mar. 24, 2026); First Coast, 'Using web tools to handle top denied claims in your practice' (July 28, 2026)
practice_impact: Rank denials from the practice's own remittance codes before adopting the vendor's three-pattern framework; for facility visits billed to Medicare in Florida, eligibility, Medicare Advantage enrollment, hospice, duplicate and NCCI edits are likelier leaders than medical necessity.

claim: Collaborative care codes 99492 (first month), 99493 (subsequent months) and 99494 (add-on) pay the psychiatric consulting practitioner for their time; a consultant with a 50-patient caseload can generate $8,000 to $15,000 per month in CoCM billing.
correct_statement: Medicare pays 99492, 99493 and 99494 to the treating (billing) practitioner, usually primary care, for a month of behavioral health care manager time (70, 60 and each added 30 minutes). The psychiatric consultant cannot bill them and is paid by contract with that practice. Fifty patients yield the billing practice about $7,200-$8,000 a month before add-ons in 2026.
source_title: CMS MLN Booklet 'Behavioral Health Integration Services' (MLN909432, January 2026); CY 2026 PFS relative value file RVU26D; CY 2027 PFS final rule Addendum B
practice_impact: If the geriatrics practice is the treating practitioner, it (not the psychiatrist) bills CoCM and must fund the care manager and consultant; with place of service 31 (skilled nursing facility) the lower facility rate applies (99493: $89.51 in 2026, $107.02 in 2027).

claim: When a psychotherapy add-on (90833, 90836, 90838) is billed with an E/M, the E/M level should be supported by medical decision making or total time, exactly as for any other E/M visit.
correct_statement: When 90833, 90836 or 90838 is billed with an E/M visit, the E/M level must be chosen on medical decision making only. CPT bars using time to select the E/M level in that case, bars prolonged-service codes, and E/M time cannot count toward psychotherapy time (16-37, 38-52, 53+ minutes), which must be documented separately.
source_title: Noridian Healthcare Solutions, 'Billing Tips for Psychotherapy with Evaluation & Management (E/M)' (updated Nov. 27, 2024); First Coast Service Options Billing and Coding Article A57520 (ver. 48, effective Oct. 1, 2026)
practice_impact: Any clinician billing a nursing-facility or office E/M plus a psychotherapy add-on must level the E/M on decision making; leveling by total time while also billing timed psychotherapy double-counts minutes and will not survive review.

claim: Medicare requires HCPCS G0396 and G0397 instead of 99408/99409 for SBIRT; Medicare pays approximately $29 for G0396; the codes are billable in addition to the primary visit code by any provider who performs them.
correct_statement: Medicare does not pay 99408/99409 and uses G2011 (5-14 minutes), G0396 (15-30) and G0397 (over 30). G0396 pays $37.07 nationally in 2026 ($29.06 facility rate) and $41.44 in 2027. Only listed practitioner types may bill, and only for reasonable and necessary assessment and intervention in patients with signs or symptoms, not routine screening.
source_title: CMS MLN Booklet 'SBIRT Services' (MLN904084, May 2025); CY 2026 PFS relative value file RVU26D; CY 2027 PFS final rule Addendum B
practice_impact: Adding G0396 to every Medicare visit as a screening add-on invites denial and recoupment; bill it only with 15+ documented minutes, a validated tool, a symptomatic patient and a separately identifiable visit.

claim: MHPAEA requires payers to apply prior authorization to behavioral health services no more restrictively than to analogous medical/surgical services; complaints go to the state insurance commissioner (fully insured) or the U.S. Department of Labor EBSA (ERISA self-funded).
correct_statement: The parity standard and both complaint routes are right, but only for group health plans and insurers. MHPAEA does not apply to traditional Medicare, Medicare Advantage or TRICARE. The test compares processes within a benefit classification, not session-for-session rules. Self-funded state and local government plans go to CMS. The 2024 rule's new provisions have gone unenforced since May 15, 2025.
source_title: CMS, 'The Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act (MHPAEA)' page; 45 CFR 146.136(c)(4); Tri-agency enforcement statement of May 15, 2025; DoD TRICARE final rule, 81 FR 61068 (Sept. 2, 2016)
practice_impact: Parity complaints give a Medicare-heavy geriatrics practice no leverage over Medicare Advantage authorization denials; those go through the plan's organization-determination and appeal process instead.

claim: A majority of commercial payers now require prior authorization for initial behavioral health evaluations, with concurrent review every 4-8 sessions; TRICARE requires authorization for specialty mental health and typically a PCM referral; traditional Medicare requires none for outpatient psychotherapy.
correct_statement: No source supports a commercial 'majority'. The only national plan survey (2010 data) found 4.7% of products requiring authorization to start outpatient behavioral care, and Aetna's list omits routine outpatient therapy. TRICARE Prime enrollees need no primary care manager referral for network outpatient mental health visits; active-duty members do need referral and authorization. Traditional Medicare requiring none is correct.
source_title: TRICARE.mil 'Referrals and Pre-Authorizations' (updated Oct. 7, 2026); Quinn AE et al., Psychiatr Serv 2017;68(9):931-937, doi:10.1176/appi.ps.201600081 (via PubMed); Aetna behavioral health precertification list
practice_impact: Check each plan's own authorization list rather than assume one is needed. For the practice's mix the real gatekeeper is Medicare Advantage, plan by plan; TRICARE For Life patients follow Medicare rules.

claim: Audio-only telehealth billed with modifier 95 is an error; the correct modifier is 93 for audio-only where covered; claims need place-of-service code 02 (telehealth) or 10 (telehealth in patient's home).
correct_statement: Correct for Medicare: audio-only telehealth takes modifier 93 (95 means audio-video), and telehealth claims carry place of service 02 (paid at the facility rate) or 10 (patient's home, non-facility rate). Medicare covers audio-only only for a patient at home who cannot or will not use video. From January 1, 2027 modifiers BB and BC are also required in some cases.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Chapter 26, section 10.5 (Rev. 14466, May 27, 2026); 42 CFR 410.78(a)(3); CY 2027 PFS final rule, 91 FR 71024 (modifiers BB and BC)
practice_impact: Telehealth to a skilled nursing facility resident is place of service 02, and an audio-only call to someone not at home is a coverage risk; Medicare Advantage risk scores exclude audio-only diagnoses from payment year 2027.

claim: If more than 60% of individual psychotherapy claims are at 90834 with fewer than 20% at 90837, you likely have a time-documentation gap; the 90834 to 90837 difference is typically $40 to $60 per session.
correct_statement: The $40-$60 gap is about right at 2026 Medicare rates ($53 non-facility, $43 facility). The 60%/20% test has no published source. The code must follow actual psychotherapy minutes: 38-52 is 90834, 53 or more is 90837. In 2024 Medicare data 90837 was 55% of individual psychotherapy overall but only 18% in facility-rate settings (hospital, skilled nursing), where 90832 leads.
source_title: CMS, Medicare Physician & Other Practitioners - by Geography and Service (2024 data, released May 2026); CY 2026 PFS relative value file RVU26D; First Coast Billing and Coding Article A57520 and LCD L33252
practice_impact: In facility-rate settings such as skilled nursing facilities short sessions are the Medicare norm, and First Coast denies psychotherapy for residents too cognitively impaired to take part; steering clinicians toward 90837 to hit a code-mix target creates audit exposure, not revenue.

claim: Group psychotherapy (90853) is reimbursed at approximately 50% to 60% of individual psychotherapy rates; psychological testing codes pay $150 to $300 or more per hour at Medicare rates, $900 to $2,400 for a full evaluation.
correct_statement: At 2026 Medicare rates group psychotherapy (90853) pays $30.39 per patient, which is 18% of a 60-minute, 27% of a 45-minute and 35% of a 30-minute individual session, not 50-60%. Psychological testing pays about $71-$124 per hour, and a 6-8 hour evaluation totals roughly $510-$675 (about $810 at most), not $900-$2,400. 2027 rates are similar.
source_title: CMS CY 2026 PFS relative value file RVU26D (October 2026 release, nonqualifying APM conversion factor $33.4009); CY 2027 PFS final rule Addendum B; First Coast LCD L33252
practice_impact: Group therapy and testing revenue for Medicare residents would be roughly half or less of what the guide projects, and First Coast does not cover group or individual psychotherapy for residents whose dementia prevents meaningful participation.
