CPT requires permanently recorded images plus a description of the localization, which may sit inside the procedure note. Guidance must also be medically necessary.
source_title: CMS Medicare NCCI Procedure-to-Procedure (PTP) Edits, Practitioner, v32.3 (Oct 2026); NCCI Policy Manual 2026 ch. 4; CPT ultrasound guidance guideline as quoted by AAPC
practice_impact: Adding 76942 to bedside joint injections in nursing facilities would be denied or, if forced through with a modifier, recouped on audit; the only legitimate change is 20610 to 20611 when real-time guidance is used, needed and recorded.

claim: The difference between 20610 (major joint injection, no imaging) and 20611 (with ultrasound guidance) is $60 to $100 per procedure at Medicare rates; 30 guided injections a week at $80 yields $124,800 a year.
correct_statement: At 2026 Medicare rates 20611 pays about $35 more than 20610 at the non-facility rate (national $104.21 vs $68.81; Florida locality 99 $103.76 vs $69.29) and about $10 more at the facility rate. 2027 final rule: about $34. Thirty a week is roughly $54,000-$55,000 allowed a year, not $124,800.
source_title: CMS PFS Relative Value File RVU26D; First Coast Service Options Florida Locality 99 fee schedule (1/1/2026); CY2027 PFS final rule Addendum B (91 FR 70992)
practice_impact: The projected gain is overstated about 2.3-fold at the non-facility rate (office and POS 32 nursing facility) and about 8-fold at the facility rate (POS 31 skilled nursing facility, hospital outpatient), where the difference is about $10 per injection.

claim: Rituximab (J9312): billed per 100mg. Belimumab IV, Benlysta (J0490): billed per mg.
correct_statement: Both units are wrong. J9312 is "Injection, rituximab, 10 mg" (the per-100 mg code J9310 ended 12/31/2018), so a 1,000 mg dose is 100 units. J0490 is "Injection, belimumab, 10 mg", so an 800 mg dose is 80 units, not 800.
source_title: CMS HCPCS Quarterly Update, October 2026 Alpha-Numeric HCPCS File
practice_impact: Following the guide would bill rituximab at one tenth of the correct units and belimumab at ten times the correct units (an overpayment and false-claim exposure); little direct use in facility-based geriatrics unless infusions are billed.

claim: Methylprednisolone IV (J1020-J1040): dose-dependent J-code; document dose and indication.
correct_statement: J1020, J1030 and J1040 were methylprednisolone acetate (Depo-Medrol, an IM/intra-articular depot product), not IV, and were deleted 3/31/2024. IV methylprednisolone sodium succinate is J2919 (per 5 mg) since 4/1/2024, replacing J2920/J2930; acetate is J1010 (per 1 mg).
source_title: CMS HCPCS Quarterly Update, October 2026 Alpha-Numeric HCPCS File
practice_impact: Claims with J1020-J1040 reject as invalid codes for dates of service after 3/31/2024; steroid injections in nursing-facility patients must use J1010 or J2919 with units counted per mg / per 5 mg.

claim: Rheumatology infusion visits are billable E&M encounters in addition to the drug and administration codes; the assessment supports 99213 or 99214 at minimum for virtually every infusion patient, and 80 percent is a conservative estimate.
correct_statement: An E/M is payable with an infusion only when the physician or NPP personally performs a significant, separately identifiable E/M beyond the usual pre- and post-infusion work, billed with modifier 25. Screening, treatment-plan affirmation and supervision are inside the administration codes; 99211 is never billable with them. No source supports 80 percent.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Pub. 100-04, ch. 12 s.30.5; NCCI Policy Manual for Medicare Services 2026, ch. 1 and ch. 11
practice_impact: Attaching a modifier-25 E/M to every infusion or injection claim by template is a classic audit and overpayment pattern (OIG found 35% of modifier-25 claims failed program requirements); the same rule governs E/M billed with any procedure in facility-based geriatrics.

claim: The CCM revenue for a practice with 200 enrolled patients, billing at the standard 99490 rate of $62 per month: $12,400 per month, $148,800 per year.
correct_statement: $62 was roughly the 2024 national rate ($62.58). 99490 pays $66.13 nationally in 2026 ($65.97 Florida locality 99; $43.76 at the facility rate) and $63.63 under the 2027 final rule. $148,800 is a gross ceiling: it assumes 20 documented minutes for all 200 patients every month and includes 20% coinsurance.
source_title: CMS PFS Relative Value Files (RVU24B, RVU25A, RVU26D); First Coast Florida Locality 99 fee schedule; CY2027 PFS final rule Addendum B (91 FR 70992, Nov 9, 2026)
practice_impact: CCM pays about $66 with an office or POS 32 nursing-facility place of service and about $44 at the facility rate (POS 31 skilled nursing facility, hospital outpatient); only one practitioner per patient per month can bill, so the vendor's figure is not a usable forecast.

claim: Every patient with RA, SLE, PsA, or AS has at minimum two chronic conditions when the cardiovascular comorbidity burden is considered, and that burden is universal; the panel qualifies overwhelmingly for CCM.
correct_statement: CCM needs two or more diagnosed chronic conditions expected to last 12+ months that pose significant risk, plus consent, a comprehensive care plan and 20 minutes a month. Elevated cardiovascular risk is not a second condition. In a US commercial-claims cohort only 57.4% of RA patients had any other chronic condition. One practitioner per patient per month may bill.
source_title: CMS MLN Booklet MLN909188 Chronic Care Management Services (June 2025); England BR et al., Ann Rheum Dis 2021;80:286-292; Dougados M et al. (COMORA), Ann Rheum Dis 2014;73:62-68
practice_impact: Enrolling patients in CCM on a presumed comorbidity rather than documented diagnoses, or while another clinician already bills CCM for that patient that month, produces denials and repayments; geriatric panels qualify on real diagnoses, not on a specialty-wide assumption.

claim: MDM elements that rheumatology visits routinely generate include independent interpretation of laboratory results (CBC, metabolic panel, anti-dsDNA, complement levels, drug levels); the majority of established visits support 99214 or 99215.
correct_statement: Under AMA guidelines results-only lab tests (CBC, metabolic panel, anti-dsDNA, complement, drug levels) never count as independent interpretation; each unique test ordered or reviewed counts once as data. Medicare data do show rheumatologists billing 99214 (73.6%) or 99215 (10.2%) for most established visits, so the specialty is not broadly undercoded; each visit must still meet two of three MDM elements.
source_title: AMA, CPT Evaluation and Management (E/M) Code and Guideline Changes (effective January 1, 2023); CMS, CY 2025 Evaluation & Management Codes by Specialty (Medicare Part B national data)
practice_impact: Counting routine lab review as 'independent interpretation' inflates the data element and can push visits to a level the record does not support; the same MDM table governs nursing-facility visit codes 99307-99310.

claim: CARC 16 (claim lacks information) or CARC 252 (referring/ordering provider not found): missing NPI, missing authorization number, or incomplete claim data. This is a claim completion problem, usually a practice management system configuration issue.
correct_statement: CARC 16 is right: 'Claim/service lacks information or has submission/billing error(s).' CARC 252 is wrong: X12 defines it as 'An attachment/other documentation is required to adjudicate this claim/service.' Missing NPI is CARC 206-208; an ineligible referring or ordering provider is 183/184. Medicare reports missing referring/ordering names or NPIs as CO-16 with remark codes N264/N265/N285/N286.
source_title: X12 External Code Source 139, Claim Adjustment Reason Codes (retrieved Nov. 10, 2026); CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) ch. 1 §§80.3.1-80.3.2.1.2 (Rev. 13725, Apr. 10, 2026)
practice_impact: A CARC 252 denial means the payer wants records or an attachment, so send documentation instead of changing PM settings; Medicare CO-16 returns flagged unprocessable (alert N211) cannot be appealed and must be corrected and resubmitted within one year of service.

claim: CARC 96 (non-covered charge) or CARC 167 (this diagnosis is not covered) is a front-end coverage verification failure or a diagnosis code problem; CARC 96, 167 and 272 are grouped as 'coverage and eligibility' front-end denial patterns.
correct_statement: The descriptors for CARC 96 and 167 match X12, and CARC 272 is 'Coverage/program guidelines were not met.' All three are coverage codes; none is an eligibility code. Eligibility and wrong-payer denials carry CARC 26, 27, 31, 177, 109, 22 or 24. In Florida Medicare, CARC 96 mostly marks statutorily excluded services, which eligibility checks cannot prevent.
source_title: X12 Claim Adjustment Reason Codes (retrieved Nov. 10, 2026); First Coast Service Options, 'Top claim errors' (Aug. 14, 2026), 'Tips to prevent CARC PR 96' (Feb. 16, 2026), 'Tips to prevent RUC CO 24' (June 29, 2026) and 'RUC CO 109' (Mar. 12, 2025)
practice_impact: Same-day eligibility checks will not cut CARC 96/167/272 denials; they prevent CO-24 (Medicare Advantage enrollment), CO-109 (Part A skilled nursing stay or wrong contractor), CO-22 (Medicare secondary) and B9 (hospice), which the vendor's list omits.

claim: CARC 50 (non-covered services because this is not deemed a 'medical necessity' by the payer) is a documentation or medical-necessity-criteria problem, not a prior-authorization problem.
correct_statement: The CARC 50 wording matches X12, and missing authorization has its own codes (197, 198, 284, 39). Two caveats: Florida's Medicare contractor issues CO/PR-50 when the billed diagnosis is not covered under an LCD or NCD, so it is usually a diagnosis-to-policy mismatch; and a Medicare Advantage plan may not deny for medical necessity a service it prior-authorized.
source_title: X12 Claim Adjustment Reason Codes (retrieved Nov. 10, 2026); First Coast Service Options, 'Tips to prevent CARC CO 50/PR 50' (Feb. 21, 2025); eCFR 42 CFR 422.138 (current as of Nov. 6, 2026); Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 30 §50
practice_impact: For Medicare visits, check the diagnosis against First Coast LCDs and NCDs and obtain a signed ABN when denial is expected, because without proper notice the patient cannot be billed; for Medicare Advantage, cite any prior-authorization approval in the appeal.

claim: CARC 197 (precertification/authorization/notification absent): the claim was submitted without an authorization that this payer requires; either a workflow failure or a policy change making authorization newly required.
correct_statement: CARC 197 is the no-authorization code. Its current X12 wording, since May 1, 2018, is 'Precertification/authorization/notification/pre-treatment absent.' Related codes the vendor omits: 198 (authorization exceeded), 284 (number valid but does not apply to the billed services) and 39 (denied when authorization was requested). Old CARC 15 was retired May 1, 2018.
source_title: X12 External Code Source 139, Claim Adjustment Reason Codes (retrieved Nov. 10, 2026)
practice_impact: Usable as written for Medicare Advantage and commercial plans; Original Medicare requires no prior authorization for nursing-facility or office visits, so CARC 197 should appear only on plan claims. Track 198 and 284 with it.

claim: CARC 18 (duplicate claim) or CARC 97 (payment included in another service): your billing team is submitting the same claim twice, or the payer considers a billed service bundled into another.
correct_statement: Both descriptors match X12 in substance: CARC 18 is 'Exact duplicate claim/service' and CARC 97 means the benefit is included in the payment for another adjudicated service. They ranked first and second among First Coast's Part B denials for April-June 2026. Duplicates also come from repeat services lacking modifiers and refiled whole claims; Medicare reports NCCI bundling under CARC 236.
source_title: X12 Claim Adjustment Reason Codes (retrieved Nov. 10, 2026); First Coast Service Options, 'Top claim errors' (Aug. 14, 2026), 'Tips to prevent CARC OA18' (June 29, 2026), 'Tips on how to avoid billing a duplicate claim' (Nov. 1, 2024); Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 1 §120
practice_impact: Directly relevant: these were First Coast's two most common Part B denials in April-June 2026. Resubmit only corrected lines or use a SPOT clerical reopening, let the first claim finish processing before rebilling, and add repeat-service modifiers for same-day repeat services.

claim: CARC 29 (the time limit for filing has expired): the claim was submitted after the payer's timely filing deadline. This is a charge entry lag problem.
correct_statement: CARC 29 is quoted correctly. Charge-entry lag is only one cause: rejected or corrected claims resubmitted late, wrong-payer billing and late secondary claims also trigger it. Original Medicare allows one calendar year from the service date; Florida law gives six months for state-regulated insurers and HMOs (90 days after the primary's determination for secondary claims).
source_title: X12 Claim Adjustment Reason Codes; eCFR 42 CFR 424.44 (current as of Nov. 6, 2026); First Coast, 'Tips to prevent RUC CO 16' (Mar. 12, 2025); Fla. Stat. 627.6131(3)(b) and 641.3155(2)(b) (2026); Marting R, 'The Cure for Claims Denials,' Fam Pract Manag 2015;22(2):7-10
practice_impact: With a one-year Medicare limit, CARC 29 in a mostly Medicare practice more likely means rejected claims never resubmitted or services first billed to the wrong payer than slow charge entry; work the rejection queue, and watch the shorter plan deadlines.

claim: In a typical practice with eight to twelve contracted payers, the top two denial-generating payers account for 60 to 70 percent of total denial volume.
correct_statement: No published source gives this figure; it reads as a vendor rule of thumb. Public denial data report denial rates by payer, not a practice's top-two share. That share mostly tracks claim volume: in a Medicare-heavy practice the largest payer leads denial counts even with a low rate. Rank payers by denial rate against their share of claims instead.
source_title: KFF, 'Claims Denials and Appeals in ACA Marketplace Plans in 2024' (Mar. 24, 2026); searches of MGMA, HFMA, HBMA, AAPC and trade press, Nov. 10, 2026
practice_impact: Little: do not treat 60-70% as a benchmark. A geriatrics practice billing mainly Original Medicare and a few Medicare Advantage plans should expect its top two payers to produce most denials simply because they produce most claims.

claim: Ten re-worked denials per biller per day is sustainable. Fifty is not.
correct_statement: No industry standard sets these numbers. HFMA's expert panel says productivity should be built from measured time per task; one hospital CFO there reports a follow-up goal of 50-63 accounts worked per day. A DecisionHealth survey found practice coders, alongside other duties, appeal about 4 denials a day (9 in primary care). Set the quota from your own time study.
source_title: HFMA, 'Ask the Experts: Billing Staff Metrics' (Oct. 7, 2015; updated Nov. 29, 2022); DecisionHealth, 'Today's Medical Practice Coding Productivity Benchmarks' white paper (survey data through 2016); ACDIS, 'Q&A: Measuring productivity for denials specialists' (Oct. 15, 2020)
practice_impact: Little: use it only as a starting guess. A clerical correction in First Coast's SPOT portal and a written appeal with records take very different amounts of time, so a single per-day quota misleads; time both task types and set separate targets.

claim: Clean claim rate measures the percentage of claims that pass through your clearinghouse and are accepted by the payer on the first submission: no rejections, no missing information, no edit failures.
correct_statement: There is no single definition. HFMA's standard (MAP Key CL-1) counts claims that pass claim-scrubber edits with no manual intervention, measured before submission, not payer acceptance. HBMA separates clearinghouse first-pass acceptance from claims paid on first submission. Medicare's own "clean claim" is a prompt-payment term: a claim needing no external investigation or development.
source_title: HFMA MAP Keys, Clean Claim Rate (CL-1); HBMA RCM Advisor Q1 2024 Data Science Committee survey; CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 1 §80.2; 42 CFR 422.500
practice_impact: Benchmarks swing with the definition (a 2026 Kansas MGMA conference deck cites an 85% MGMA family-medicine median alongside a 97% national average from another benchmark set), so the vendor's unsourced 95% "best-in-class" cut-off cannot be applied to a clearinghouse report as is.

claim: A rejection happens before adjudication: the clearinghouse or payer finds a technical or structural problem and returns the claim without processing it. A denial happens after adjudication.
correct_statement: Correct. In Medicare, a claim with missing or invalid required data is "returned as unprocessable": it is not an initial determination, is not denied and carries no appeal rights, so it must be corrected and resubmitted as a new claim. X12 status category A3 likewise means rejected and not entered into the adjudication system. Denials follow adjudication and are appealable.
source_title: CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) ch. 1 §80.3.1-80.3.2 (Rev. 13725, 04-10-26); First Coast, What you should do with claims returned as unprocessable (2025); X12 Claim Status Category Codes
practice_impact: First Coast returns defective Part B claims with remark MA130; appealing them wastes up to 60 days and risks the one-year filing limit, so correct and refile as new claims.

claim: Authorization failures generate a specific and highly visible rejection class that is entirely preventable when the authorization workflow is functioning correctly.
correct_statement: Authorization problems are a distinct, visible category, but X12 codes them mainly as adjudicated denials on the remittance (CARC 197 absent, 198 exceeded, 284/296 number does not apply, 302 expired, 288 referral absent); a front-end rejection arises only where a required number is missing or malformed. They are largely, not entirely, preventable: pre-approved claims are still denied.
source_title: X12 Claim Adjustment Reason Codes and Claim Status Codes (status reviewed 11/1/2026); HBMA RCM Advisor Q2 2024 denials survey; Premier claims adjudication survey (Feb. 24, 2025); 42 CFR 422.138
practice_impact: Original Medicare requires no prior authorization for facility visits (the WISeR model excludes Florida), so exposure sits with Medicare Advantage plans; these arrive as denials to reopen or appeal and will not appear in a rejection-based clean claim rate.

claim: Invalid diagnosis code: the ICD-10 code is missing a required digit, is an invalid code for the date of service, or is a header code that cannot be used on a claim.
correct_statement: Correct. A diagnosis code is invalid unless carried to the full number of characters its category requires, including any 7th character (characters, not only digits). CMS flags category and subcategory "headers" as not valid for HIPAA transactions, and the code must be in effect on the date of service; the FY2027 set applies to encounters from October 1, 2026.
source_title: ICD-10-CM Official Guidelines for Coding and Reporting FY 2027 (CMS/NCHS); CMS 2027 ICD-10-CM Code Descriptions in Tabular Order (order file and layout)
practice_impact: Geriatric staples such as F03 (dementia), G30 (Alzheimer's) and E11 (type 2 diabetes) are headers that reject; on October 1, 2026, Z68.1 (BMI 19.9 or less) became a header, replaced by Z68.18 and Z68.19 (190 codes added, 30 deleted for FY2027).

claim: Every rendering provider, billing provider, and referring provider in the system should have an NPI that matches the CMS NPPES database and the enrollment records at each contracted payer.
correct_statement: Sound. HIPAA requires each provider's NPI on standard transactions and NPPES updates within 30 days. Medicare rejects claims missing a required NPI, requires NPPES and PECOS legal names to match exactly, and denies ordered lab, imaging, DMEPOS, home health and hospice claims unless the orderer is Medicare-enrolled or validly opted out. Referring clinicians need not enroll with commercial plans.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.506 and 424.507; 45 CFR 162.410; CMS Medicare Program Integrity Manual ch. 10 §10.6.3 (Rev. 13717, 07-08-26); First Coast Top claim errors (Aug. 14, 2026)
practice_impact: First Coast's third most common rejection in April-June 2026 was CO-16/N290: rendering NPI missing, invalid or not associated with the billing group, so each clinician's reassignment to the group must be on file in PECOS.

claim: Re-submitting a rejected claim with the same error generates a second rejection and, at some payers, triggers a duplicate claim flag that complicates the eventual correct submission.
correct_statement: Resubmitting an uncorrected claim just repeats the rejection. Duplicate flags arise when an identical claim or line is already pending or paid (First Coast, UnitedHealthcare) or is re-sent within a clearinghouse's short window, not because a claim was rejected: Noridian, a Medicare contractor, states refiling an unprocessable claim does not cause a duplicate denial. Correct, then refile as new.
source_title: First Coast: Top claim errors (Aug. 14, 2026), Using web tools to handle top denied claims (July 28, 2026), Tips to prevent RUC CO 16 (Mar. 12, 2025); Noridian, Reminder - Unprocessable (Return/Reject) Claims Must Be Resubmitted; UnitedHealthcare, Avoid claim rejections and denials (Feb. 17, 2025); MacPractice HelpDesk, Common Rejections - Duplicate Claims (2025); CMS Claims Processing Manual ch. 1 §80.3.1 and §120; Fla. Stat. 627.6131(3); HFMA Ask the Expert: Rebilling Denials (2015)
practice_impact: Exact duplicate (CARC 18) was First Coast's top Part B denial in April-June 2026: check status in SPOT and refile only rejected lines. Do not hold rejected claims for long as the vendor suggests: HFMA experts advise rebilling within days, and rejections do not stop Medicare's 12-month clock or Florida insurers' 6-month window.

claim: If your practice management system is reporting a clean claim rate above 95% but your denial rate is above 8%, those two numbers are in conflict.
correct_statement: Not inherently in conflict. Under HFMA's standard definitions, clean claim rate (CL-1) is measured at the claim scrubber before submission and denial rate (AR-5) on adjudicated remittances, so a high clean rate and a denial rate above 8% routinely coexist. They conflict only if "clean" is defined as paid on first submission. Reconciling definitions is sound advice.
source_title: HFMA MAP Keys (CL-1, AR-5); HBMA RCM Advisor Q1 2024 survey; Kodiak Solutions State of the healthcare revenue cycle (March 2026); Premier claims adjudication survey (Feb. 2025)
practice_impact: Hospice-enrollment (B9), bundling, duplicate and medical-necessity denials hit technically clean Medicare claims, so track rejections and denials separately instead of treating a gap between them as a data error.

claim: Clean claim rate predicts the other metrics 30 to 60 days in advance. A clean claim rate that drops in January will show up as elevated Days in AR in February and elevated denial rate in March.
correct_statement: No study or benchmark source establishes a 30-to-60-day lead. Rejections do delay payment, so a falling clean claim rate plausibly raises days in A/R, but Medicare pays electronic clean claims between day 14 and day 30, so the effect appears within weeks. Rejections are not denials; they become denials mainly through missed filing deadlines.
source_title: No traceable origin for the statistic; context from CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 1 §80.2.1.1-80.2.1.2 and 42 CFR 424.44
practice_impact: Reviewing rejections first is a reasonable habit, but do not plan cash around a fixed lag: with Medicare paying clean electronic claims in 14-30 days, a rejection spike reaches A/R within the same month.

claim: Medicare typically pays within 14 days of a clean claim.
correct_statement: Fourteen days is Medicare's floor, not its ceiling. A clean electronic claim cannot be paid before the 14th day after receipt (paper: 29th day) and must be paid within 30 days, after which interest accrues (4.75% for July-December 2026). Physician Medicare fee-for-service claims averaged 18.9 days to payment in 2015 remittance data.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), Ch. 1, ss. 80.2.1.1-80.2.1.2 (Rev. 13725, issued 04-10-26); First Coast Service Options FAQ on the payment floor; 42 CFR 405.922; Treasury prompt payment rate (July-Dec. 2026); Gottlieb, Shapiro & Dunn, Health Affairs 2018;37(4):619-626, doi:10.1377/hlthaff.2017.1325
practice_impact: Medicare Part B is the core payer: expect electronic First Coast payments from day 14, treat any clean claim unpaid at day 30 as an exception with interest due, and avoid paper claims (29-day floor).

claim: Some Medicare Advantage plans take 30 to 45 days [to pay a clean claim].
correct_statement: Some Medicare Advantage claims do take 30-45 days, but no rule entitles plans to it. Plans must pay 95% of non-contract clean claims within 30 days, with interest after; contracted claims follow the contract's prompt-pay clause. UnitedHealthcare says most claims adjudicate within 15 days, up to 45. In 2015 data MA averaged 14.3 days.
source_title: MGMA Stat, 'Strategic improvements in your RCM to reduce your practice's claim denials' (Mar. 6, 2024); 42 CFR 422.520 and 422.402 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide; Gottlieb, Shapiro & Dunn, Health Affairs 2018;37(4):619-626, doi:10.1377/hlthaff.2017.1325; S. 2879/H.R. 5454 bill status (still in committee as of Sept. 2026 data)
practice_impact: MA covers a large share of Florida seniors: read each MA contract's prompt-pay clause, pursue non-contract clean claims unpaid at day 30 (interest is owed) and do not accept 45 days as a given; state prompt-pay law is generally preempted for MA.

claim: Some Medicaid programs take 60 or more [days]; these are structural delays that cannot be fixed by the practice.
correct_statement: Medicaid is the slowest payer class (2015 means: 39 days fee-for-service, 27 managed care, 19 Medicare), but 60-plus days breaches the standard. Federal rules require 90% of clean practitioner claims paid within 30 days and 99% within 90; Florida Medicaid plans must pay, deny or contest electronic claims within 20 days, with 12% interest on overdue payments.
source_title: 42 CFR 447.45 and 447.46 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); Fla. Stat. 409.967(2)(j) and 641.3155 (2026 Florida Statutes); Gottlieb, Shapiro & Dunn, 'The Complexity of Billing and Paying for Physician Care', Health Affairs 2018;37(4):619-626, doi:10.1377/hlthaff.2017.1325 (author manuscript on bea.gov)
practice_impact: Dual-eligible crossover claims are this practice's Medicaid exposure (Medicaid as secondary payer averaged 51.8 days in the same study); age them separately and escalate Florida Medicaid plan claims past 20 days, since unpaid claims become an uncontestable obligation at 120 days.

claim: Aged AR that is not resolved within 90 to 120 days of service typically becomes uncollectable (filing window closed, appeal deadline passed, or account sent to collections).
correct_statement: There is no general 90-120-day cliff. Medicare allows one calendar year from service to file and 120 days from the denial notice to request redetermination; Florida-regulated insurers and HMOs have a 6-month filing period; Medicaid fee-for-service allows 12 months. The short clocks are 90-day contract filing limits, Florida's 90-day secondary-claim deadline and MA non-contract 60-day appeals.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.44, 405.942, 447.45(d)(1), 422.582 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); Fla. Stat. 627.6131(3)(b) and 641.3155(2)(b) (2026 Florida Statutes); UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide and MA non-contracted provider dispute notice
practice_impact: For a Medicare-heavy practice, treating AR as dead at 90-120 days would abandon collectible money; key each account to its payer's actual clock, counted from the denial notice, and send secondary claims within 90 days of Medicare's determination (the Florida statutory and common contract limit).

claim: Any denial past the appeal window is not workable - it should be written off and documented as a process failure.
correct_statement: A missed appeal window does not end a Medicare claim. The contractor may accept a late redetermination request for good cause, and a party may request a (discretionary) reopening within 1 year of the initial determination for any reason, within 4 years for good cause, or at any time to correct a clerical error. MA reconsiderations also allow good-cause extensions.
source_title: 42 CFR 405.942(b), 405.980(c), 405.986, 422.582(c) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Ch. 34 (Reopening and Revision of Claim Determinations and Decisions); Fla. Stat. 408.7057(2)(d) (2026)
practice_impact: Before writing off a First Coast denial older than 120 days, test it for a clerical-error reopening, a one-year reopening or a good-cause late appeal; the vendor's rule would discard recoverable Medicare money.

claim: Every claim that fails on first submission adds 20 to 45 days to its AR age.
correct_statement: No published source gives a 20-45 day penalty per failed claim; none was found in MGMA, HFMA, AAPC or peer-reviewed literature. Delay depends on failure type and correction speed: front-end rejections return on 999/277CA acknowledgment reports (Florida plans must acknowledge e-claims within 24 hours after the next business day begins), and Medicare restarts its 14-day payment floor on resubmission.
source_title: No traceable source for the statistic; Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Ch. 1, s. 80.2.1 (Rev. 13725, issued 04-10-26); Fla. Stat. 627.6131(4)(a) (2026 Florida Statutes)
practice_impact: Measure the practice's own rejection-to-resubmission lag from clearinghouse and 277CA reports rather than assuming 20-45 days; for Medicare the unavoidable cost of a rejection is a fresh 14-day floor.

claim: Raising clean claim rate from 87 to 94 percent 'will see days in AR drop by 5 to 8 days within 60 days without any other intervention'.
correct_statement: No published source supports a 5-8 day drop, and the vendor's own inputs give far less. Moving 7 percentage points of claims from a 45-60 day cycle to 14-21 days saves 24-46 days on 7% of claims, about 1.7-3.2 days of average AR. A 5-8 day drop would need each fixed claim to save 71-114 days.
source_title: No traceable source for the statistic; calculation from the vendor's own figures (KPI 03, Section 3); HFMA MAP Keys, 2023 edition (metric definitions only)
practice_impact: Do not forecast a 5-8 day AR improvement from clean-claim work alone; the vendor's own numbers support about 2-3 days.

claim: A contract paying 5 percent above market rate on a 45-day cycle 'may generate less actual cash per quarter' than one paying market rate on a 21-day cycle.
correct_statement: In steady state, cash per quarter follows the rate, not the lag: the 5%-higher contract pays 5% more every quarter. A 24-day slower cycle lowers cash only in the first quarter (cumulative cash catches up in about 17 months) and costs about 0.5% of revenue a year to finance at the 7% prime rate.
source_title: Arithmetic check; Federal Reserve H.15 Selected Interest Rates (release of Nov. 9, 2026); Fla. Stat. 627.6131 and 641.3155 (2026 Florida Statutes); 42 CFR 422.520(b)
practice_impact: Do not trade fee-schedule rate for faster payment on this logic: a 5% rate premium is worth roughly ten times the carrying cost of 24 days. Seek prompt-pay terms in MA contracts as an addition, not a swap.

claim: For most commercial payers, the appeal deadline is 90 to 180 days from service date.
correct_statement: Commercial appeal deadlines run from the remittance or denial date, not the service date, and are mostly longer: UnitedHealthcare 12 months from the original EOB/PRA; Aetna and Cigna 180 calendar days from the initial decision; Florida Blue one year from the remittance advice. ERISA gives claimants at least 180 days after the denial notice.
source_title: UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide (effective Apr. 1, 2026); Aetna 'Disputes and appeals overview' and Cigna 'Appeals and Disputes' (read Nov. 10, 2026); Florida Blue, 'Provider Appeal Changes' (June 2025); 29 CFR 2560.503-1(h)(3)(i); Fla. Stat. 627.6131(19)
practice_impact: Commercial and employer-plan claims are a small share here, but dating appeals from the service date (with the vendor's write-off rule) would wrongly retire appealable claims; load each payer's clock from the remittance date.

claim: Clean claims submitted to most payers will pay or deny within 14 to 30 days.
correct_statement: Broadly right for electronic clean claims. Medicare pays between day 14 and day 30; Florida-regulated insurers, HMOs and Medicaid plans must pay, deny or contest within 20 days (40 for paper); ERISA plans must decide post-service claims within 30 days. Mean time to payment in 2015 data: private 13.7 days, MA 14.3, Medicare 18.9, Medicaid 26.5-39.2.
source_title: Fla. Stat. 627.6131 and 641.3155 (2026 Florida Statutes); Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Ch. 1, s. 80.2.1 (Rev. 13725); 29 CFR 2560.503-1(f)(2)(iii)(B); UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide; Gottlieb, Shapiro & Dunn, Health Affairs 2018;37(4):619-626, doi:10.1377/hlthaff.2017.1325
practice_impact: Usable rule of thumb: an electronic claim with no payment or denial by day 30 (day 20 for Florida-regulated plans) needs a status check rather than more waiting.

claim: Payers with 365-day timely filing windows have claims that are genuinely recoverable at 150 or 180 days.
correct_statement: Correct for filing: Medicare allows one calendar year from the date of service, Medicaid fee-for-service 12 months, and UnitedHealthcare says MA plans must give non-contract providers 365 days, so an unfiled or rejected claim is still billable at day 150-180. A denied Medicare claim instead needs redetermination within 120 days of the notice, or a reopening.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.44(a)(1), 447.45(d)(1), 405.942, 405.980 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide
practice_impact: Medicare fee-for-service claims, the core of a geriatrics payer mix, stay fileable for a year, so aged Medicare AR deserves a worked queue; check the 120-day appeal clock on denied claims, and note secondary claims to Florida-regulated plans are due 90 days after the primary's determination.

claim: For 0-30 day claims, verification that the claim was received and is in process 'can be batch-checked via ERA rather than individually worked'.
correct_statement: An ERA (X12 835) reports only finalized claims, so it cannot confirm that a pending claim was received. Receipt is confirmed by the 999 and 277CA acknowledgment reports; in-process status comes from the 276/277 claim status transaction or the payer portal, which can be run in batch. Claims rejected at the front end never produce an ERA.
source_title: CMS, 'Health Care Payment and Remittance Advice' and 'Claim Status Request and Response' (pages last modified 09/10/2024); Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Ch. 24, s. 50.3.1 (Rev. 13954, issued 09-29-26); 45 CFR 162.1401-162.1402 and 162.1601-162.1602
practice_impact: A claim rejected at the front end never appears on an ERA; if 0-30 day claims are 'verified' by ERA, rejections sit unseen until they age. Reconcile every batch against 999/277CA reports daily.

claim: Historical recovery rate for the 120-plus day bucket is 'typically 30 to 50 percent for most independent practices'.
correct_statement: No published benchmark gives a 30-50% recovery rate for AR older than 120 days. The only figures found are unsourced: Physicians Practice says about 10 cents on the dollar past 120 days, and MGMA cites 10-20% for collection-agency recoveries. The vendor's own KPI 03 says AR unresolved at 90-120 days 'typically becomes uncollectable'. Use the practice's own recovery history.
source_title: No traceable source for the statistic; MGMA, 'A structured approach to collecting patient A/R' (Dec. 7, 2022); Physicians Practice, 'Claim denials, patient collections and the revenue cycle' (Mar. 6, 2026)
practice_impact: This rate drives the vendor's write-off forecast; replace it with the practice's own 12-month recovery rate for the 120-plus bucket, by payer.

claim: Most practices use $100 minimum for collections referral.
correct_statement: No survey reports the dollar minimum practices use for collections referral. MGMA's poll covers timing only (42% refer at 91-120 days, 32% after 120, 10% never). Examples vary widely: MGMA advises in-house calls only above $100, and a Physicians Practice Q&A describes an agency refusing accounts under $500. Credit bureaus removed medical collections under $500 in 2023.
source_title: No traceable source for the statistic; MGMA, 'A structured approach to collecting patient A/R' (Dec. 7, 2022); CFPB, 'Have medical debt? Anything already paid or under $500 should no longer be on your credit report' (May 8, 2023, archived page)
practice_impact: Little: set the threshold from the agency contract. The real exposure is referring Medicare cost-sharing of QMB dual eligibles, which federal law forbids billing at all.

claim: When an account is referred to collections or written off, 'the documented contact history is the compliance record that demonstrates due diligence'.
correct_statement: A contact log helps but is not 'the compliance record'. OIG expects a good-faith effort to collect Medicare cost-sharing; write-offs need documented financial need or reasonable collection efforts and must not be routine. QMB patients cannot be billed Medicare cost-sharing at all, and Florida bars patient collection while a contested claim is pending. Medicare bad-debt documentation rules exclude fee-schedule services.
source_title: 42 CFR 1003.110 ('Remuneration') and 413.89(i)(1) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); OIG Special Fraud Alert, 59 FR 65372 (Dec. 19, 1994); CMS Qualified Medicare Beneficiary Program page (modified 03/16/2026); Fla. Stat. 627.6131(9) and 559.72 (2026); IRS Topic 453
practice_impact: Nursing-facility patients are often dual eligibles with QMB protection: screen QMB status before any statement or referral, and keep hardship determinations and a written, uniformly applied write-off policy alongside the contact log.

claim: A new provider whose claims concentrate in the 61-plus day buckets within their first 60 days has a credentialing gap (NPI not active with a payer, wrong taxonomy codes, or fee schedule not loaded).
correct_statement: Enrollment gaps are a common cause, but the test fails as written: aged from date of service, no claim can be 61-plus days old in a provider's first 60 days. For Medicare, billing privileges start on the later of the application filing date or first service date, with 30 days of retrospective billing, so late filing forfeits earlier claims.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.520(d), 424.521(a), 424.522(a) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); HFMA MAP Keys, 2023 edition (AR-1 aging definition)
practice_impact: File each new clinician's PECOS enrollment and reassignment before the first facility visit; Medicare reaches back only 30 days before the filing date, so monitor held-claim counts weekly instead of waiting for a 61-plus bucket.

claim: Research across independent practices consistently shows the probability of collecting a patient balance in full drops from about 95% at time of service to 70-80% after a first statement, 50-60% after a second, and 30-40% in collections.
correct_statement: No study with this curve was found; similar ladders appear only in unsourced vendor blogs that disagree with one another. Measured data differ: practices collected about 90% (2019) and 56% (2022) of copays at time of service, hospital-system datasets show 42-54% of insured patient balances collected, and surveyed medical collection agencies report median recovery near 10-15%, not 30-40%.
source_title: MGMA Stat, 'Patient balance collection: What's moving the numbers and how to get ahead' (Oct. 22, 2025); CFPB Regulation V final rule preamble, 90 FR 3276, 3320-3324 (Jan. 14, 2025); Ippolito et al., JAMA Health Forum 2025;6(8):e252284 (PubMed PMID 40779258); Kodiak Solutions KPI Benchmarking Report (Mar. 2026)
practice_impact: Do not model cash on this curve: nursing-facility Part B coinsurance is billed after adjudication, mostly to Medigap or Medicaid, so the 95% time-of-service tier does not exist here.

claim: A copay collection rate below 95% means the front desk is not collecting money the practice has an absolute right to collect at every visit.
correct_statement: There is no absolute right. Federal law bars every Medicare provider, including in Medicare Advantage, from collecting Medicare deductibles, coinsurance or copays from QMBs. Florida Medicaid exempts institutional residents from copays and Medicaid payment is payment in full. Original Medicare Part B carries 20% coinsurance, not visit copays, and First Coast recommends not collecting it before Medicare pays.
source_title: CMS MLN Fact Sheet MLN7936176, Prohibition on Billing Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries (Sept. 2025); CMS QMB Program page (modified 03/16/2026); 42 U.S.C. 1396a(n)(3)(B); 42 CFR 422.504(g)(1)(iii); Fla. Stat. 409.9081, 409.907(3)(j) (2026); First Coast, 'When not to show patient paid amounts on claims' (Oct. 29, 2024)
practice_impact: Dual-eligible/QMB facility residents cannot be charged Medicare cost sharing; knowingly billing duals outside assignment carries penalties up to $19,940 per violation (45 CFR 102.3) plus refunds, so a 95% copay KPI is the wrong yardstick.

claim: A POS collection rate above 90% is best practice, is achievable, and should be the target for every independent practice.
correct_statement: No MGMA or HFMA benchmark was found that sets 90% for a blended point-of-service rate. MGMA data show practices collected about 90% of copays at time of service in 2019 but 56% in 2022, and only 15%-39% of patient-due balances. Kodiak's standard metric, POS cash as a share of patient payments, has a median near 16%. Not a universal target.
source_title: MGMA Stat, 'Patient balance collection: What's moving the numbers and how to get ahead' (Oct. 22, 2025); Kodiak Solutions KPI Benchmarking Report (Mar. 2026); HFMA, 'Patient POS collections pose a growing problem for RCM departments' (June 8, 2026)
practice_impact: Facility visits have no check-in desk and Medicare coinsurance is unknown until adjudication, so a 90% POS target is inapplicable; measure post-adjudication patient and secondary collection instead.

claim: A $200 balance sent through two statements and a collections referral yields $60 to $80 gross; after a typical 25 to 40 percent agency fee the net recovery is $36 to $60.
correct_statement: The arithmetic is right and 25-40% contingency fees match trade reports, but a 30-40% gross recovery is well above documented medical collection results: an ACA International member survey found median rates of 14.5% in 2022 falling to 9.6% in late 2023, and CFPB put the baseline below 25%. A $200 referral more plausibly nets about $12-$37.
source_title: CFPB, Prohibition on Creditors and Consumer Reporting Agencies Concerning Medical Information (Regulation V), final rule preamble, 90 FR 3276, 3320 and 3324 (Jan. 14, 2025; rule vacated July 2025); AAPC Practice Management Alert, 'Six Tips for Hiring a Collection Agency' (Sept. 2001)
practice_impact: Budget on roughly 10-20% gross agency recovery, not 30-40%; QMB and Medicaid-covered coinsurance can never be placed with an agency.

claim: Every patient with a known balance (copay, prior balance, or estimated deductible) is told the amount and asked for payment before they are roomed.
correct_statement: Not lawful or advisable for every patient. QMBs may not be asked to pay Medicare cost sharing; providers generally may not deny Medicaid services over an unpaid copay, and institutional residents owe none. For Original Medicare, First Coast recommends collecting no deductible or coinsurance until Part B pays, because over-collection is program abuse. The rule fits commercial copays only.
source_title: First Coast Service Options, 'When not to show patient paid amounts on claims' (Oct. 29, 2024); Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 1 §30.3.1.1 and §30.3.3 (chapter as of Rev. 13725, 04-10-26); CMS MLN7936176 (Sept. 2025); 42 CFR 447.52(e), 447.56(a)(1)(viii); Fla. Stat. 409.9081(3)(c) (2026)
practice_impact: Nursing-facility and ALF visits have no check-in or rooming step; bill coinsurance after the Medicare remittance, report any pre-collected amount on the claim, and screen every account for QMB/Medicaid status first.

claim: For balances above $200 the front desk immediately offers a payment plan, such as $50 per month, with automated monthly charges to the card on file.
correct_statement: Payment plans are lawful, but conditions are missing. A written agreement payable in more than four installments (any balance above $200 at $50 a month) makes a practice that does this more than 25 times a year a Regulation Z creditor owing Truth in Lending disclosures. Recurring debit-card or bank-account charges need signed written authorization under Regulation E.
source_title: 12 CFR 1026.2(a)(14), (a)(17) and Supplement I comment 2(a)(17)(i)-1 (Regulation Z); 12 CFR 1005.10(b), (d) (Regulation E); eCFR current as of Nov. 6, 2026
practice_impact: Point-of-visit plans rarely arise in facility-based care, but any written plan program needs TILA-compliant forms and signed card authorizations, and must exclude QMB/dual-eligible cost sharing, which cannot be billed.

claim: Collectible means the patient is not on a payment plan, financial assistance program, or hardship waiver that legitimately defers collection; a written charity care policy with income thresholds lets the practice keep a firm standard.
correct_statement: OIG permits waiving Medicare cost sharing for financial need only if the waiver is not routine, not advertised, and follows a good-faith individualized assessment under uniform, documented, objective guidelines. The definition also omits balances uncollectible by law (QMB cost sharing, Medicaid payment-in-full), and Florida treats a general business practice of waiving insureds' copays or deductibles as insurance fraud.
source_title: 42 CFR 1003.110 (definition of 'Remuneration'); OIG Supplemental Compliance Program Guidance for Hospitals, 70 FR 4858, 4871 (Jan. 31, 2005); OIG Special Fraud Alert on routine waiver of copayments, 59 FR 65372 (Dec. 19, 1994); Fla. Stat. 817.234(7)(a) (2026)
practice_impact: Use a written hardship policy with documented per-patient determinations, never advertise it, and code QMB/Medicaid adjustments separately from hardship write-offs; beneficiary-inducement penalties reach $25,595 per item or service.

claim: Without active management, most practices' POS collection rate settles between 60 and 70 percent, and a team trained to 90 percent can fall to 65 percent within 60 days of one experienced staff departure.
correct_statement: No survey or study was found for a 60-70% resting rate or for a drop from 90% to 65% within 60 days of one departure; both appear to be vendor assertions. MGMA benchmarking shows time-of-service copay collection of about 90% in 2019 and 56% in 2022, a different measure that says nothing about turnover effects.
source_title: MGMA Stat, 'Patient balance collection: What's moving the numbers and how to get ahead' (Oct. 22, 2025)
practice_impact: little (a facility-based practice has no front-desk point-of-service collection)

claim: In many independent practices, patient responsibility now represents 20 to 35 percent of total revenue.
correct_statement: Only the low end has support, and as a share of allowed amounts for insured patients: AMA's 2013 report card found nearly one-quarter and Kodiak about 23% in early 2026. Nationally, out-of-pocket payments were 8.5% of physician and clinical services spending in 2024; Kodiak put insured patient responsibility at 7.3% of net revenue for 2025. Nothing supports 35%.
source_title: CMS National Health Expenditure Accounts, Table 8 (2024 data) and NHE Fact Sheet (modified 06/24/2026); Kodiak Solutions KPI Benchmarking Reports (Mar. and June 2026); Medical Economics on AMA National Health Insurer Report Card (July 10, 2013); KFF, 'A Snapshot of Sources of Coverage Among Medicare Beneficiaries' (Dec. 19, 2025)
practice_impact: For a Medicare/Medicaid nursing-facility panel the patient-paid share should be far below 20%: coinsurance goes to Medigap or Medicaid crossover, and Florida Medicaid often pays $0 on dual-eligible coinsurance (s. 409.908(13)(b)) that cannot be billed to the patient.

claim: Research consistently shows statements received within 30 days of service produce payment rates 25 to 35 percentage points higher than those received after 60 days.
correct_statement: No study quantifying a 25-35 point payment-rate gap between statements received within 30 days and after 60 days was found; similar figures appear only in unsourced vendor material. Measured data address bill size and elapsed time generally: across 1,348 practices, 93.8% of small balances but 66.7% of balances over $200 were collected within 12 months.
source_title: Chernew M, Bush J, 'As Patients Take On More Costs, Will Providers Shoulder The Burden?', Health Affairs Forefront (May 4, 2017), as quoted by PNHP (original page returned HTTP 403)
practice_impact: Send statements promptly after the Medicare remittance, but do not expect a proven 25-35 point lift; most balances here belong to secondary payers rather than patients.

claim: Every dollar that passes through the statement cycle costs $8 to $15 to collect and recovers at a fraction of face value.
correct_statement: As written it is a unit error: a dollar cannot cost $8-$15 to collect. The vendor's own Front-End RCM Playbook says $8-$14 per statement, and no MGMA, HFMA or CAQH source was found for that either. Published statement-mailing fees run about $1 per statement (Elation Billing charges $0.95) before staff time.
source_title: Elation Health Help Center, 'What are the delivery charges for sending patient statements in Elation Billing' (accessed Nov. 10, 2026); 2025 CAQH Index Executive Report; vendor Front-End RCM Playbook (internal inconsistency)
practice_impact: Compute the practice's own cost per statement (vendor fee, postage, staff minutes); do not carry $8-$15 into cost-to-collect models.

claim: The collections agency recovers 20 to 35 cents on the dollar on average; recovery rates below 20 percent should prompt consideration of a different agency.
correct_statement: Overstated. The best public data put medical collection agency recovery well below this: an ACA International member survey showed median rates of 14.5% in 2022 falling to 9.6% in late 2023, and CFPB concluded the baseline is under 25%. Older trade sources cite 15-19% averages. A 20% floor would flag typical agency performance, not poor performance.
source_title: CFPB, Prohibition on Creditors and Consumer Reporting Agencies Concerning Medical Information (Regulation V), final rule preamble, 90 FR 3276, 3320 and 3324 (Jan. 14, 2025; rule vacated July 2025); AAPC Practice Management Alert, 'Six Tips for Hiring a Collection Agency' (Sept. 2001); Physicians Practice Q&A (June 2004)
practice_impact: Expect roughly 10-20 cents on the dollar gross, less a 25-40% fee, on the few truly patient-owed balances; never refer QMB or Medicaid-covered balances, and confirm the agency is registered in Florida (s. 559.553).

claim: Every account that meets the referral criteria (minimum balance, days from service, completed statement series, no active payment plan) is referred to collections without exception.
correct_statement: Law requires exceptions the listed criteria omit. QMB cost-sharing balances may never be billed or sent to collections; Florida Medicaid payment is payment in full; HMO subscribers cannot be pursued for amounts the HMO owes; bills in federal patient-provider dispute resolution cannot go to collections; and bankruptcy stays collection. Uniform policy is sound only after these screens.
practice_impact: A no-exceptions rule would send dual-eligible/QMB coinsurance to an agency, a federal violation; add QMB, Medicaid, HMO-liability, dispute and bankruptcy holds to the referral checklist before any account is released.

claim: A patient collection rate above 90% is best practice and is still achievable in a high-deductible environment; below 60% is structural failure.
correct_statement: No MGMA, HFMA or AAPC benchmark with these tiers was found. Measured results are lower: across 1,348 practices, 93.8% of balances of $35 or less but only 66.7% of balances over $200 were collected within 12 months (2015), and Kodiak reports insured patients paid 42.4% of what they owed in 2025. Above 90% is documented only for small, copay-size balances.
source_title: Kodiak Solutions KPI Benchmarking Report (Mar. 2026); Chernew and Bush, Health Affairs Forefront (May 4, 2017), as quoted by PNHP; Ippolito et al., JAMA Health Forum 2025;6(8):e252284 (PubMed PMID 40779258, doi:10.1001/jamahealthforum.2025.2284)
practice_impact: Benchmark only truly patient-owed balances after excluding QMB, Medicaid and secondary-payer amounts; otherwise legally required write-offs will make the practice look like a 'structural failure'.

claim: A written payment plan policy sets minimum payment, maximum duration and whether interest is charged; most practices charge no interest for plans under 12 months, with automatic monthly charges to a card on file.
correct_statement: A written policy is sound, but conditions are missing. A written plan payable in more than four installments (even at 0%), or any plan with interest, makes a practice doing this more than 25 times a year a Regulation Z creditor owing Truth in Lending disclosures. Florida caps interest at 18% simple. No data support 'most practices charge no interest.'
source_title: 12 CFR 1026.2(a)(17) and Official Interpretation comment 2(a)(17)(i)-1 (Regulation Z, CFPB); 12 CFR 1005.10(b) (Regulation E); Fla. Stat. 687.02(1) (2026)
practice_impact: If more than 25 written plans a year are signed, give closed-end TILA disclosures and keep signed card authorizations; apply plans only to balances patients legally owe, never QMB or Medicaid cost sharing.

claim: ERA enrollment is free and is the single most impactful administrative change most practices have not completed.
correct_statement: Payer ERA enrollment generally carries no charge: Medicare's is free with free CMS viewing software, and plans must send standard ERAs on request. But clearinghouses and payment vendors often charge fees, and ERA is already the norm: CAQH's 2025 Index shows 87% of medical-plan remittance advice fully electronic. 'Single most impactful' is unsupported.
source_title: 2025 CAQH Index Executive Report; Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 24 §40.2.4.4 (chapter as of Rev. 13954, 09-29-26); First Coast, 'Electronic remittance advice -- what you need to know' (Aug. 11, 2026); 45 CFR 162.925(a); CMS Guidance Letter GL-2022-04 (Mar. 22, 2022); AMA, 'Physicians protected from health plan credit card fees'
practice_impact: Confirm 835 enrollment with First Coast, each Medicare Advantage plan and Florida Medicaid, and check what the clearinghouse charges per ERA; this is routine hygiene, not a breakthrough.

claim: For write-offs coded 'denial appeal expired' or 'timely filing', the quarterly recovery review asks: 'Is there a balance transfer to patient responsibility that was never executed?'
correct_statement: A missed filing or appeal deadline cannot be shifted to the patient. Medicare: the provider 'may not charge the beneficiary' beyond the deductible and coinsurance otherwise due. Medicare Advantage enrollees may not be held liable beyond plan cost sharing, plan contracts say the same, and Medicaid requires payment in full. Only amounts remittances code as patient responsibility (PR) are billable.
source_title: CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) ch. 1 §§30.3, 60.5, 70.4 (Rev. 13725, Apr. 10, 2026); Medicare Managed Care Manual ch. 4 §170; eCFR 42 CFR 422.504(g) and 447.15 (current as of Nov. 6, 2026); Fla. Stat. 641.3154 (2026); 2026 UnitedHealthcare Care Provider Administrative Guide; Marting R, Fam Pract Manag 2015;22(2):7-10
practice_impact: High: billing Medicare, Medicare Advantage or dual-eligible nursing-facility patients for claims the practice filed or appealed late can violate the assignment agreement and plan contracts and require refunds; limit this review step to PR-coded deductible, coinsurance, valid-ABN and excluded-service balances.

claim: Rejected claims, claims returned before adjudication, restart their AR clock when resubmitted, but the original service date governs the timely filing deadline.
correct_statement: Correct on the deadline. A Medicare claim returned as unprocessable is not considered filed, cannot be appealed, and must be resubmitted within one calendar year of the service date; UnitedHealthcare likewise applies its filing limit to corrected claims. Whether the A/R clock restarts is a software setting, not a rule: HFMA ages physician receivables from the date of service.
source_title: CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 1 §§70.2.3, 80.3.1 (Rev. 13725, Apr. 10, 2026); eCFR 42 CFR 424.44 and 405.926(s); First Coast, 'Tips to prevent RUC CO 16' (Mar. 12, 2025); 2026 UnitedHealthcare Care Provider Administrative Guide; HFMA MAP Keys (2023 ed.)
practice_impact: Useful: work First Coast unprocessable returns (CO-16, CO-24, CO-109) promptly and age A/R from the service date so they stay visible. The vendor's 90-day example fits some plan contracts, not Medicare's one-year limit.

claim: Every denial that is categorized as appealable must have an appeal filed within 30 days of receipt ... A filed appeal stops the clock on the appeal deadline.
correct_statement: Thirty days is an internal target, not law, and filing does not freeze every clock. Medicare allows 120 days from receipt of the determination for a redetermination, then 180 days for reconsideration; Medicare Advantage non-contract providers get 65 days from the remittance date. UnitedHealthcare gives 12 months total for both steps. Medicare's unprocessable and timely-filing denials cannot be appealed.
source_title: eCFR 42 CFR 405.926, 405.942, 405.952, 405.962, 405.980, 422.582 (current as of Nov. 6, 2026); CMS, 'Parts C & D Enrollee Grievances, Organization/Coverage Determinations, and Appeals Guidance' (effective July 6, 2026); 2026 UnitedHealthcare Care Provider Administrative Guide (effective Apr. 1, 2026)
practice_impact: A 30-day target sits inside the main deadlines here, but calendar each appeal level separately, send clerical errors and duplicate denials to First Coast as reopenings, and correct and resubmit unprocessable claims, since an 'appeal' on those is dismissed while the filing limit keeps running.

claim: Accounts written off as 'denial appeal expired' may have a secondary recovery path, including 'a small claims or arbitration option for large amounts'.
correct_statement: Rarely, and not for Medicare. Medicare denials can be challenged only through the administrative appeals process; a missed deadline is cured only by a good-cause extension or a reopening request. Plan contracts typically make timely internal appeals a precondition to arbitration. Florida small claims court is capped at $8,000, so it is not a forum for large amounts.
source_title: 42 U.S.C. 405(h) and 1395ii; eCFR 42 CFR 405.942(b), 405.980, 405.1136 (current as of Nov. 6, 2026); 2026 UnitedHealthcare Care Provider Administrative Guide ch. 10; Florida Small Claims Rules (Florida Bar, July 1, 2026); Fla. Stat. 408.7057 (2026); Federal Register notices 2025-21879 and 2026-19016
practice_impact: For a Medicare-heavy practice the real second chances are a good-cause late redetermination request or a reopening request (one year for any reason, four for good cause); federal court requires a Council decision and $1,960 in controversy ($2,000 from 2027). Florida-regulated plans: the state claim dispute program, within 12 months of the plan's final determination.

claim: Any timely filing write-off is a 100% preventable revenue loss, the claim was never denied for clinical or coverage reasons.
correct_statement: Mostly preventable, not always. Medicare itself recognizes late filings outside the provider's control (contractor error, retroactive entitlement, retroactive Medicaid or Medicare Advantage recoupment) and extends the deadline for them. Florida's six-month clock starts only once the provider has the correct insurer. And a claim never adjudicated was never found payable, so the full amount is not certain lost revenue.
source_title: eCFR 42 CFR 424.44(b) and 405.926(n) (current as of Nov. 6, 2026); CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 1 §§70.4, 70.7 (Rev. 13725); Fla. Stat. 627.6131(3)(b) (2026); New York State Comptroller, Report 2016-S-50, SUNY Upstate Medical University Billing Practices (Feb. 17, 2017)
practice_impact: Before writing off a Medicare timely-filing denial, check for a 424.44(b) exception (relevant to dual-eligible and plan-switching patients) and for proof the original claim was accepted in time; do not count these write-offs as revenue that was certain.

claim: Bad debt (uncollected patient): below 3% of net revenue is acceptable; 3% to 5% is a warning zone; above 5% of net revenue is the action threshold.
correct_statement: These bands echo old consultant rules of thumb, not a published benchmark. A 2003 trade article put bad debt at 3-5% with alarm above 5%; a 2014 university audit cited an HFMA target under 2-3% of revenue. Denominators differ (HFMA's metric divides by gross revenue; MGMA's analyses use dollars per physician). Kodiak's 2025 median, hospital-centred, was 1.3%.
source_title: Part B Insider (Multispecialty) Coding Alert, 'How to Benchmark Your A/R' (Oct. 6, 2003); UT Southwestern Office of Internal Audit, Report 14:10A (Nov. 19, 2014); HFMA MAP Keys AR-7 (2023 ed.); MGMA, 'Data Mine: Predicting bad debt with key revenue cycle metrics'; Kodiak Solutions release (Mar. 31, 2026)
practice_impact: Use 3% and 5% only as loose alarms. Many nursing-facility patients are dual eligible, and Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries cannot be billed Medicare cost sharing at all, so those balances are not bad debt; the practice's own trend is the better yardstick.

claim: Timely filing write-offs above 0.5% of gross charges and expired-appeal denial write-offs above 1% of gross charges are action thresholds; preventable write-offs should be less than 5 percent of total write-offs.
correct_statement: No published benchmark sets these figures; an HFMA 'Ask the Experts' respondent knew of no industry standard for timely-filing losses. Traceable references use net revenue, not gross charges: an HFMA standard of 1-2% of net patient service revenue for uncollectible write-offs (per a 2017 state audit), a best-practice denial write-off rate under 0.5%, and Kodiak's 2025 median final-denial rate, 2.7%.
source_title: HFMA, 'Ask the Experts: Timely filing measurement' (May 14, 2019; updated Nov. 29, 2022); New York State Comptroller Report 2016-S-50 (Feb. 17, 2017); UT Southwestern Office of Internal Audit Report 14:10A (Nov. 19, 2014); HFMA MAP Keys AR-6 (2023 ed.); Kodiak Solutions release (Mar. 31, 2026)
practice_impact: Treat the cut-offs as the vendor's opinion. They also conflict: a practice sitting at both action thresholds (1.5% of gross charges) still passes the 'under 5% of total write-offs' test whenever total write-offs exceed 30% of charges. Track denial write-offs against net revenue instead.

claim: The recovery rate from these retrospective reviews is typically 10 to 15 percent of the dollar amount reviewed.
correct_statement: No published study or benchmark supports a typical 10-15% recovery from retrospective write-off reviews; searches found only vendor marketing. For Medicare, the main payer here, prospects are narrow: untimely-filing denials cannot be appealed, an expired appeal needs a good-cause extension or a discretionary reopening, and the balance cannot be moved to the patient.
source_title: eCFR 42 CFR 405.926, 405.942(b), 405.980, 424.44(b) (current as of Nov. 6, 2026); searches of HFMA, MGMA, AAPC and trade press, Nov. 10, 2026
practice_impact: Do not budget on 10-15%. In a Medicare-heavy book, recoveries come mainly from clerical-error reopenings, 424.44(b) filing exceptions, proof of timely filing sent to plans and secondary payers never billed; measure one quarter's actual yield before committing staff time.

claim: Net Collection Rate = (Payments Received) / (Charges Billed minus Contractual Adjustments).
correct_statement: The formula matches AAFP and MGMA: payments net of refunds and credits, divided by charges net of approved contractual adjustments, times 100, ideally over a 12-month window. MGMA's denominator also removes charity and courtesy adjustments. AAFP's floor is 95%, with top performers at 99% or more; the vendor's 97% best-practice label is its own.
source_title: AAFP, Managing practice finances (Adjusted collection rate), fetched Nov. 10, 2026; MGMA DataDive Definitions Glossary (2025), 'Adjusted Fee-for-Service Collection Percentage'
practice_impact: Formula is safe to use; net out refunds, match payments to the same service period, and never post timely-filing or denial write-offs as contractual, or the rate is flattered.

claim: A 5 percent improvement in clean claim rate typically produces a 1 to 2 percent improvement in net collection rate with a 60-day lag.
correct_statement: No MGMA, HFMA or peer-reviewed source links a 5-point clean-claim gain to a 1-2 point net-collection gain or a 60-day lag; the figure has no traceable origin. It assumes 20-40% of non-clean claims are never collected. HFMA's clean claim rate counts claims passing edits before submission, and failed edits are normally fixed, not lost.
source_title: No traceable source for the statistic; HFMA MAP Keys, Clean Claim Rate (CL-1) (hfma.org, fetched Nov. 10, 2026); Premier Inc., 'Claims Adjudication Costs Providers $25.7 Billion' (Feb. 24, 2025)
practice_impact: Do not budget revenue from this ratio; measure the practice's own unpaid-after-denial dollars by payer instead.

claim: Patient responsibility is commonly estimated at roughly 20 to 35 percent of net collectible revenue for most practices ... A patient collection rate of 75 percent means ... a direct 5 to 9 percent drag on net collection rate.
correct_statement: The arithmetic follows from its premise, but the premise is inflated. Patients paid 8.5% of U.S. physician and clinical services spending out of pocket in 2024. Measured patient-responsibility shares for insured patients reach about 23-25% of allowed amounts at most; nothing supports 35% or 'most practices'. At realistic shares, 75% patient collection costs roughly 2-6 points.
source_title: CMS National Health Expenditure Accounts, Table 8, Physician and Clinical Services Expenditures by Source of Funds (2024 data; nhe-tables.zip downloaded Nov. 10, 2026); Kodiak Solutions benchmarking reports (Mar. and June 2026); Medical Economics on the AMA National Health Insurer Report Card (July 10, 2013); KFF, 'A Snapshot of Sources of Coverage Among Medicare Beneficiaries' (Dec. 19, 2025)
practice_impact: Overstated for facility geriatrics: 87% of traditional Medicare beneficiaries had supplemental coverage in 2023 (KFF) and dual-eligible QMB patients cannot be billed, so patient-pay is a small share of revenue.

claim: A practice with a net collection rate of 97 percent ... commands a higher valuation multiple than a peer practice at 89 percent with the same clinical volume.
correct_statement: No transaction data or valuation standard ties net collection rate to the multiple. Appraisers set the earnings multiple from comparable deals, practice attributes, market factors and perceived risk. Some M&A advisers claim strong revenue-cycle metrics earn a premium multiple but cite no data; buyers also say they pay more for revenue-cycle upside. Higher collections do raise the earnings being valued.
source_title: Medical Economics, 'Selling a medical practice: Planning tips for physicians' (Apr. 10, 2026); SovDoc, 'Essential revenue cycle KPIs for healthcare practice owners' (Oct. 23, 2025; adviser marketing, no data); VMG Health, 'How Post-Transaction Physician Compensation Structure Affects Fair Market Value of Physician Practices' (Feb. 22, 2024; copy saved earlier this session, re-fetch returned 403). No reliable source found for the multiple claim.
practice_impact: Higher collections raise the earnings a buyer capitalizes; a premium multiple on top is an adviser's sales claim, not a documented market fact, so do not model one.

claim: A primary care practice with 45 percent Medicaid volume will have a structurally lower achievable net collection rate ... because Medicaid's lower rates and higher administrative burden create a different collection environment.
correct_statement: Half right. Billing friction does make Medicaid harder to collect: physicians lose an estimated 18% of Medicaid revenue to billing problems versus 4.7% for Medicare and 2.4% for commercial insurers. Lower Medicaid rates are not a reason: net collection rate is measured after contractual adjustments, so fee levels drop out. No benchmark quantifies a 45%-Medicaid ceiling.
source_title: Dunn, Gottlieb, Shapiro, Sonnenstuhl & Tebaldi, 'A Denial a Day Keeps the Doctor Away', NBER Working Paper 29010 (rev. Jan. 2023; Quarterly Journal of Economics 2024;139(1):187-233); Gottlieb, Shapiro & Dunn, Health Affairs 2018;37(4):619-626, https://doi.org/10.1377/hlthaff.2017.1325 (PubMed PMID 29608348); AAFP, Managing practice finances
practice_impact: Medicaid matters here as the secondary payer for dual eligibles: Florida Medicaid often pays nothing on the Medicare coinsurance (s. 409.908(13)) and QMB patients cannot be billed, so how that write-off is coded moves the rate.

claim: The percentage of AR over 120 days is the most predictive leading indicator of net collection rate. [Unworked aged AR] will become write-offs within one to two quarters.
correct_statement: A/R over 120 days is a recognized collectability indicator (AAFP, HFMA, MGMA), but no source ranks it 'most predictive', and no rule turns aged balances into write-offs in one to two quarters. Medicare claims can be filed for one year after service and denials appealed within 120 days of the notice; Florida-regulated insurers must be billed within six months.
source_title: AAFP, Managing practice finances (fetched Nov. 10, 2026); HFMA MAP Keys, Aged A/R (AR-1); MGMA Stat, 'Days in A/R holds steady for most practices, but payer pressure persists in 2026' (July 30, 2026); 42 CFR 424.44 and 405.942; Fla. Stat. 627.6131. No source found for 'most predictive' or the one-to-two-quarter horizon.
practice_impact: Track the over-120 share by payer, but with Medicare's one-year filing window an old balance is often still collectible; work it before writing it off.

claim: The decomposition in Section 2 will almost always reveal one component that contributes 40 to 60 percent of the total collection gap.
correct_statement: No MGMA, HFMA or published study supports a 40-60% share for one component; the figure has no traceable origin and reads as a rule of thumb. The nearest data is opinion polling: 48% of medical group leaders named denials and appeals as their largest source of revenue leakage and 23% front-end issues, which says nothing about dollar shares.
source_title: No traceable source for the statistic; MGMA Stat, 'Days in A/R holds steady for most practices, but payer pressure persists in 2026' (July 30, 2026), citing the Jan. 6, 2026 MGMA Stat poll
practice_impact: Little: run the decomposition on the practice's own write-off and adjustment codes and rank the components by dollars, without expecting one to dominate.

claim: Every payer has a timely filing deadline - typically 90 days, 180 days, or one year from service date, depending on the payer.
correct_statement: Broadly right, but several limits are set by law, not the payer. Medicare fee-for-service: one calendar year from the date of service. Medicaid: 12 months. Florida-regulated insurers and HMOs: six months by statute, secondary claims 90 days after the primary's determination, not waivable by contract. Contracted Medicare Advantage and commercial limits are commonly 90 or 180 days.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.44 and 447.45 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); Fla. Stat. 627.6131 and 641.3155 (2026); First Coast timely filing FAQ; Cigna 'When to File Your Claims' (fetched Nov. 10, 2026); UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide; Humana 2026 Provider Manual; Fla. Admin. Code r. 59G-1.052(15)
practice_impact: Medicare allows one year and Florida Medicaid crossover claims at least 12 months; the short clocks sit in contracted Medicare Advantage agreements (often 90 to 180 days), so read each contract.

claim: some Medicare Advantage plans require submission within 90 days, some commercial payers within 60 days
correct_statement: True for some plans. Wellpoint Medicare Advantage gives participating providers 90 days and nonparticipating providers 12 months; Humana's Medicare default is one year. Sixty-day commercial limits exist but are rare (Magellan's behavioral-health standard); Cigna's participating-provider limit is 90 days. Claims to Florida-regulated insurers and HMOs are due within six months, and a contract cannot shorten that.
source_title: Wellpoint Medicare Advantage Reimbursement Policy G-06050, Claims Timely Filing (approved 06/03/2025; April 2026 print); Magellan Health, Claims Filing Procedures (fetched Nov. 10, 2026); Fla. Stat. 627.6131 and 641.3155 (2026); UnitedHealthcare 2026 Administrative Guide; Humana 2026 Provider Manual
practice_impact: Florida statute gives six months for state-regulated insurers and HMOs (self-funded and Medicare Advantage plans are outside it); the real exposure is 90-day clauses in contracted Medicare Advantage agreements.

claim: For any service within 30 days of its timely filing deadline: enter the charge immediately and submit the claim the same day, regardless of documentation completeness; most payers allow medical record submissions to support pending claims.
correct_statement: Federal guidance and Florida Medicaid law say the opposite: document, then bill. Medicare expects services documented when rendered; OIG says submit claims only when documentation supports them; Florida Medicaid claims must rest on records made at the time of service. Payers accept records on pended claims (Medicare 45 days, Florida insurers 35), but these must already support the codes billed.
source_title: OIG Compliance Program Guidance for Third-Party Medical Billing Companies, 63 FR 70138 (Dec. 18, 1998) and for Individual and Small Group Physician Practices, 65 FR 59434 (Oct. 5, 2000); Medicare Program Integrity Manual (PIM) Ch. 3 s.3.3.2.5 (Rev. 13971); Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 12 s.30.6.1.A; 42 U.S.C. 1395l(e); Fla. Stat. 409.913(7)(f) and 627.6131(4)(c) (2026); First Coast, Responding to ADRs (Sept. 22, 2026)
practice_impact: Dangerous for a Medicare-heavy facility practice: billing nursing-facility or hospital visits before the note is complete invites denial, repayment and possible False Claims Act exposure. Finish the note, then file.

claim: A claim that misses the timely filing deadline because someone was waiting for a complete note is not recoverable at any documentation quality level.
correct_statement: Correct for Medicare: a late-filing denial is not an initial determination and cannot be appealed, and the four extensions (Medicare error, retroactive entitlement, Medicaid recoupment, retroactive Medicare Advantage disenrollment) do not cover a provider's own delay. The patient can be charged only the usual deductible and coinsurance. Commercial plans generally reconsider only with proof of timely submission or extraordinary circumstances.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) Ch. 1 ss.70.4, 70.7 (Rev. 12909; chapter Rev. 13725, 04-10-26); 42 CFR 424.44(b) and 405.926(n) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); First Coast timely filing FAQ; Cigna 'When to File Your Claims'; UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide
practice_impact: A late Medicare claim forfeits the Medicare payment and cannot be shifted to the patient; the fix is same-week notes, not filing claims on unfinished documentation.

claim: Same day or next day (0-1 days) is best practice; 1-2 days acceptable; 3-5 days is the action threshold; above 5 days is a significant problem.
correct_statement: No MGMA or HFMA standard sets these tiers; they are the vendor's. MGMA (July 2026) advises closing encounters within 72 hours and posting charges within two days, against a three- to seven-day lag across the sector. HFMA counts a charge as late when posted more than 3 days after service. Same-day entry is a stretch goal.
source_title: MGMA Stat, 'Days in A/R holds steady for most practices, but payer pressure persists in 2026' (July 30, 2026); HFMA MAP Keys, Total Charge Lag Days (PB-4) and Late Charges as a Percentage of Total Charges (CL-2) (hfma.org, fetched Nov. 10, 2026); MGMA DataDive Practice Operations Data Report (Aug. 2023)
practice_impact: Facility rounding charges usually lag office charges; MGMA's 72-hour note plus two-day posting standard is defensible, and missing the vendor's 0-1 day tier is not evidence of failure.

claim: A practice with a 4-day average charge lag has every claim starting its AR clock 4 days late. The practice reports 42 days in AR. The effective AR age - from service date to payment - is 46 days.
correct_statement: The arithmetic holds for the standard ratio: MGMA counts a charge in A/R only once it is invoiced, so days in A/R exclude pre-posting lag. Aging reports run from date of service already include it. MGMA calls a three- to seven-day lag the sector norm, so a 4-day lag does not put the practice behind benchmark peers.
source_title: MGMA DataDive Definitions Glossary (2025), Accounts Receivable and Days in A/R definitions; HFMA MAP Keys (AR-1, PB-4, FM-1) (fetched Nov. 10, 2026); MGMA Stat, 'Days in A/R holds steady for most practices, but payer pressure persists in 2026' (July 30, 2026)
practice_impact: Check whether the billing system ages A/R from service date or posting date before adding lag to days in A/R; do not add it twice.

claim: hospital progress notes completed within 24 hours of the encounter, operative notes completed and dictated within 24 hours of the procedure, discharge summaries completed within 24 hours of discharge
correct_statement: Reasonable internal targets, not legal standards. Medicare hospital rules require the operative report written or dictated immediately after surgery, so 24 hours is too loose; records must be promptly completed and finished within 30 days of discharge.
