Nursing-facility physicians must write, sign and date a progress note at each visit. Medicare billing guidance says document 'as soon as practicable'.
source_title: 42 CFR 482.24, 482.51 and 483.30 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 12 s.30.6.1.A (chapter Rev. 13753, 05-07-26); Fla. Admin. Code r. 64B8-9.003(5) (late entries); MGMA Stat (July 30, 2026)
practice_impact: For nursing-facility rounding the binding rule is a signed, dated progress note at each visit (42 CFR 483.30(b)); Florida requires late entries to be labeled, dated and timed.

claim: The monthly surgical charge reconciliation shows a discrepancy rate below 2 percent... A reconciliation discrepancy rate above 5 percent means the intraoperative charge capture workflow is not functioning consistently.
correct_statement: No published benchmark sets 2% or 5% thresholds for surgical charge reconciliation; the figures have no traceable origin. HFMA recommends reconciling charges but gives no target rate; the nearest published figure is a consultant estimate that hospitals lose as much as 1% of net revenue to charge-capture problems. Treat the thresholds as the vendor's own rule of thumb.
source_title: No traceable source for the thresholds; HFMA, 'Capturing All Charges: the Operational Reality' (Sept. 20, 2019, updated Nov. 7, 2022); HFMA MAP Keys (no reconciliation-rate key)
practice_impact: Little for a non-surgical practice; the useful analogue is reconciling each facility's rounding list or census against entered charges every day.

claim: Collections agency commissions: variable by contract terms, typically around 1 percent of collections referred.
correct_statement: Collection agencies are paid a contingency share of what they recover, not about 1 percent. Published physician-practice sources put the fee at roughly 20 to 50 percent of amounts collected (flat per-account fees also exist). Because agencies recover only about 10 to 30 percent of dollars referred, fees equal several percent of referred balances.
source_title: Dillon K, Getting Off the Collections Treadmill, FPM 2006;13(6):51-54 (AAFP); Medical Economics, Q&A: Referring accounts to collections (Feb. 5, 2009) and Getting paid (Apr. 17, 2015); MGMA Stat, A structured approach to collecting patient A/R; HFMA MAP Key FM-6
practice_impact: Budget agency fees at a quarter to half of whatever is recovered, not 1 percent; on small facility-visit coinsurance balances little is left, and Qualified Medicare Beneficiary balances may not be billed or referred at all.

claim: Industry benchmarks for claims per FTE per month range from 750 to 1,200 for outpatient practices depending on complexity.
correct_statement: HFMA has said no industry standard exists for claims worked per collector, and MGMA's data glossary has no claims-per-FTE measure. Published figures are dated trade rules of thumb: a median of 6,700 claims per biller a year (about 560 a month) and a recommended 10.45 billing FTEs per 100,000 claims (about 800 a month). The 1,200 upper bound is unsourced.
source_title: Physicians Practice, Biller Benchmarks (Apr. 1, 2008) and Billing Benchmarks (July 1, 2005); HFMA Ask the Expert: Insurance Claim Standards (Oct. 25, 2012); MGMA DataDive Definitions Glossary (2025); Medical Economics, How to measure your biller's productivity (Jan. 10, 2013)
practice_impact: Do not read 400-750 claims per FTE as proof of inefficiency: the one published median is about 560 a month and counts depend on which staff are included; track the practice's own trend for its simple, high-volume facility-visit claims.

claim: A rejected claim that must be corrected and resubmitted costs approximately three to five times as much in billing staff time as a clean claim... A denied claim that requires an appeal costs five to ten times as much.
correct_statement: The multipliers have no traceable source. HFMA's own expert answer calls the added cost of a rebill "difficult to calculate" and cites $25 per rebill as the most quoted figure; MGMA puts rework at $25.20 a claim, against about $3 to $6 of provider labor to submit a claim (CAQH). Direction is right; the ratios are unconfirmed.
source_title: HFMA Ask the Experts Answer: Cost-to-Collect Calculations (Oct. 25, 2012; updated Nov. 29, 2022); MGMA Stat, 6 keys to addressing denials in your medical practice's revenue cycle (2021 poll); 2024 CAQH Index report (released 2025); Premier, Claims adjudication costs providers $25.7 billion (Feb. 24, 2025)
practice_impact: The direction is sound (rework is far dearer than a clean claim), but do not build staffing or savings estimates on the 3-5x and 5-10x figures; time the practice's own rework on First Coast rejections instead.

claim: Staff cost (salaries + benefits + management overhead): typically 70 to 80 percent of total billing cost in in-house operations... Technology cost (PMS, clearinghouse, eligibility tools, patient portal): typically 10 to 15 percent.
correct_statement: No published benchmark gives these shares for in-house practice billing. Labor clearly dominates: a JAMA costing study attributed 63 to 77 percent of billing costs to labor with the rest allocated overhead, and Premier's hospital survey attributed 90 percent of claims-processing expense to labor. No traceable source supports a typical 10 to 15 percent technology share.
source_title: Tseng P, Kaplan RS, Richman BD, et al. Administrative Costs Associated With Physician Billing and Insurance-Related Activities at an Academic Health Care System. JAMA 2018;319(7):691-697 (PubMed PMID 29466590); Premier claims adjudication survey (2025)
practice_impact: Little: split the practice's own ledger rather than testing it against these bands; a small facility-based practice with bundled software or a billing vendor will not resemble them.

claim: Establish a small balance write-off threshold... balances below the threshold [$25 or $50] receive one automated statement and are written off if not paid within 30 days, without any manual follow-up.
correct_statement: Small-balance write-offs are lawful only within limits the vendor omits. Medicare cost sharing may not be routinely waived: a write-off must follow a genuine collection effort matching that for non-Medicare patients, or an individual hardship finding. Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries may not be billed cost sharing. Florida treats a business practice of not intending to collect copayments as insurance fraud.
source_title: CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 23 §80.8.1 (Rev. 13701, 06-16-26); 42 CFR 1003.110 and 1003.1010; 45 CFR 102.3 (91 FR 3666, Jan. 28, 2026); OIG Special Fraud Alert, 59 FR 65372 (1994); CMS QMB program page; Fla. Stat. 817.234(7)(a) (2026)
practice_impact: Coinsurance on Florida nursing-facility visits (99307-99310) is about $7-$33 in 2026, slightly less after the 2027 conversion factor cut, so a $25-$50 threshold would forgive nearly all Medicare coinsurance after one statement; apply any threshold to every payer alike, document it, and never bill QMBs.

claim: In a well-managed billing operation, rework activities should consume no more than 25 to 30 percent of total billing staff time.
correct_statement: No published benchmark sets a 25 to 30 percent ceiling on rework time; it is a vendor rule of thumb. For context, a dated Physicians Practice staffing guide puts 3.1 of 10.45 billing FTEs per 100,000 claims (about 30 percent) on insurance denial and follow-up, and an MGMA article reports only about 40 percent of claims are paid untouched.
source_title: No traceable origin for the statistic; context from Physicians Practice, Billing Benchmarks (July 1, 2005) and MGMA, Beyond days in A/R: Building RCM reporting around human effort (2025)
practice_impact: Little: run a short time study for the practice's own baseline; the vendor counts routine A/R follow-up and collections referrals as rework, so its ceiling is not comparable with other definitions.

claim: Cost to collect should include all direct and allocated costs of the revenue cycle function: billing staff salaries and benefits, management overhead, clearinghouse fees, statement costs, practice management system fees, collections agency commissions, and outsourced billing fees.
correct_statement: Right in principle, and each item listed is in HFMA's cost-to-collect definition (MAP Key FM-6, updated August 2025). But HFMA's numerator is wider than the billing office: it also counts patient access and registration, coding and health information management, revenue integrity, revenue-cycle IT support, legal fees and record storage. The denominator is patient service cash collected, net of refunds.
source_title: HFMA MAP Keys, Cost to Collect (FM-6) and Cost to Collect by Functional Area (FM-7), definition updated August 2025; HFMA Guide to Better Practices in Measuring Cost-to-Collect (Sept. 2025); HFMA Ask the Experts Answer: Cost-to-Collect Calculations (2012, updated 2022)
practice_impact: Counting only billing-office costs will flatter the figure against any HFMA-based number; decide whether front-desk eligibility work, coding and vendor fees are in before comparing. The MAP Key sets no target (an HFMA column cited 2-3% as hospital best practice in 2012).

claim: Many practices that outsource billing do so at a higher cost to collect than their internal operation
correct_statement: No survey or study quantifies how many outsourcing practices pay more than their in-house cost; only conflicting billing-vendor claims were found. Published fee ranges for billing companies run about 4 to 10 percent of collections, higher for primary care, and are usually all-inclusive, so the comparison depends on a practice's own fully loaded in-house cost.
source_title: Physicians Practice, Outsourcing Your Billing (Feb. 1, 2010); Medical Economics, Practice Pointers: Outsource billing? Here's how (May 23, 2003); MGMA Stat poll on outsourcing and automating RCM (Nov. 19, 2024)
practice_impact: Low-dollar, high-volume facility visits sit at the costly end of percentage-of-collections pricing; compare any vendor quote with the practice's full in-house cost and net collection rate rather than assuming either direction.

claim: Our coders and providers are current on the 2021 E&M guideline changes and correctly apply the medical decision-making pathway.
correct_statement: The 2021 revisions covered only office and outpatient visits (99202-99215). Since January 1, 2023 nursing facility, home or residence and hospital visits are also leveled by medical decision making or total time; history and exam no longer set the level. Later changes include G2211 for home visits (2026) and its replacement by modifier B1 on January 1, 2027.
source_title: First Coast Service Options, 'Nursing facility E/M services' (June 26, 2026); CMS MLN Booklet MLN006764, Evaluation and Management Services (May 2026); AMA, CPT E/M Code and Guideline Changes effective January 1, 2023, and CPT Evaluation and Management page; CMS fact sheet, CY 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule (Nov. 4, 2026; 91 FR 70992, Nov. 9, 2026)
practice_impact: Nearly all facility-practice visits use nursing facility (99304-99310) and home or residence (99341-99350) codes the 2021 rules never covered; staff current only to 2021 miss the 2023 rules, prolonged codes G0317/G0318 and the January 2027 modifier B1 change.

claim: Copays are collected at check-in, before the patient is roomed, at every visit, with no exceptions.
correct_statement: Exceptions are required by law. Providers may not collect Medicare deductibles, coinsurance or copays from Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries, in Original Medicare or Medicare Advantage. Florida Medicaid exempts institutional residents and managed-care enrollees from copays. Medicare pays annual wellness visits at 100%. First Coast recommends not collecting Part B deductible or coinsurance until Medicare has paid.
source_title: CMS MLN Fact Sheet MLN7936176, Prohibition on Billing Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries (Sept. 2025); 42 CFR 422.504(g)(1)(iii), 447.56(a)(1)(viii)-(ix), 447.52(e), 410.152(l) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); Fla. Stat. 409.9081(3) and 409.907(3)(j) (2026); First Coast, 'When not to show patient paid amounts on claims' (Oct. 29, 2024); Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Ch. 2, s. 10.4
practice_impact: Facility rounds have no check-in desk, Original Medicare carries coinsurance rather than copays, and QMB or institutional Medicaid residents cannot be charged at all; a no-exceptions rule would produce prohibited collections, refunds and possible sanctions.

claim: Patient responsibility now represents 25 to 35 percent of revenue in most independent practices, and that percentage is growing as high-deductible plans continue to dominate the market.
correct_statement: No source supports 25-35%. CMS national accounts show patients paid 8.5% of physician and clinical spending out of pocket in 2024, unchanged since 2022. The highest measure found, Kodiak's hospital-system data, is about 23% of allowed amounts in first-quarter 2026, flat from 2025, with roughly 30% collected. PPOs cover 50% of covered workers; HSA-qualified high-deductible plans 29%.
source_title: CMS National Health Expenditure Accounts, Table 8, Physician and Clinical Services Expenditures by Source of Funds (2024 data; page updated Jan. 14, 2026); Kodiak Solutions, 'Untangling the patient financial responsibility web' (June 2026) and 'State of the healthcare revenue cycle' (Mar. 2026); KFF 2026 Employer Health Benefits Survey (Oct. 22, 2026)
practice_impact: Inapplicable to a Medicare facility practice: high-deductible plans are irrelevant, cost sharing is the 20% Part B coinsurance, billed first to any Medigap or Medicaid secondary coverage, and QMB balances cannot be collected; secondary and crossover billing matters more than patient pay.

claim: Total score 31, 46 (AT RISK): 'Likely costing $50,000, $150,000 annually in preventable revenue loss.' Total score 47, 61 (MODERATE): 'Likely $20K, $50K recoverable annually.'
correct_statement: No study, survey or published method links this vendor's 77-point yes/no self-assessment to dollar losses, and the guide gives none. The bands are fixed amounts that ignore practice size. Measured leakage is reported as rates, not flat dollars: Kodiak's 2025 medians were a 2.7% final denial rate and a 1.3% bad debt rate.
source_title: No source found for the claim. Comparator: Kodiak Solutions, 'State of the healthcare revenue cycle' (Mar. 2026). Vendor text checked: Scoring Interpretation Guide (pp. 7-8) and Overall Practice Rating (pp. 36-37)
practice_impact: Do not budget or justify purchases from these dollar bands; size any opportunity from the practice's own denial, write-off and underpayment data as a percentage of its revenue.

claim: Our overall patient collection rate is at or above 90% of patient responsibility billed.
correct_statement: No MGMA or HFMA benchmark setting 90% for overall patient collections was found. Measured rates are far lower: across 1,348 practices, 93.8% of balances of $35 or less but 66.7% of balances over $200 were paid within a year (2015); insured patients paid 42.4% of what they owed in 2025; hospital-system yield was about 30% in early 2026.
source_title: Ippolito B, Trish E, Duffy EL, Vabson B, 'Patient Repayment of US Hospital Bills From 2018 to 2024', JAMA Health Forum 2025;6(8):e252284 (PubMed PMID 40779258, doi:10.1001/jamahealthforum.2025.2284); Chernew M, Bush J, Health Affairs Blog (May 4, 2017), as reproduced by PNHP; Kodiak Solutions reports (Mar. and June 2026); MGMA Stat (Oct. 22, 2025); HFMA MAP Keys (2026)
practice_impact: QMB and Medicaid balances are uncollectible by law and must leave the denominator; track secondary and crossover payments and non-QMB coinsurance separately, and do not treat a rate under 90% on larger balances as failure.

claim: We offer structured payment plans with automatic payment required, not open-ended 'send us what you can' arrangements.
correct_statement: Written payment plans are lawful, but mandatory autopay carries conditions the guide omits. Federal law bars conditioning credit on repayment by preauthorized electronic fund transfers, so a non-debit option should exist. Recurring bank or debit-card charges need signed authorization with a copy to the patient. Written plans over four installments can trigger Truth in Lending disclosures.
source_title: Electronic Fund Transfer Act, 15 U.S.C. 1693k; Regulation E, 12 CFR 1005.10(b)-(e) and Supplement I comment 10(e)(1)-1; Regulation Z, 12 CFR 1026.2(a)(17)(i), (v) and comment 2(a)(17)(i)-1 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026). No agency ruling found applying the compulsory-use ban specifically to interest-free medical payment plans
practice_impact: Residents' bills are often paid by relatives or representatives: get the account holder's own signed authorization, offer a credit-card or non-automatic option, and never place QMB or Medicaid cost sharing on a plan.

claim: Our patient payment portal allows a patient to click a link, see their balance, and complete payment in under two minutes, without requiring a username, password, or portal login.
correct_statement: HIPAA does not prescribe usernames or passwords, but a named patient's balance is protected health information and the Security Rule requires verifying that the person seeking access is the one claimed. A login-free payment link is acceptable only if it still verifies the recipient, for example by date of birth or one-time code. HHS's 2025 multi-factor proposal is not final.
source_title: HIPAA Security Rule, 45 CFR 164.312(a), (d); Privacy Rule, 45 CFR 160.103, 164.510(b), 164.514(h) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); Unified Agenda 2026, RIN 0945-AA22 (reginfo.gov); FCC rule 47 CFR 64.1200(a)(9)(iv)(D). No OCR guidance found that addresses login-free payment links specifically
practice_impact: Statements for facility residents often go to relatives or representatives; an unverified link can show a resident's balance to the wrong person, and texted billing links fall outside the TCPA health care message exemption, so prior consent is needed.

claim: Our charge lag standard is defined in writing (target: ≤48 hours for office encounters, ≤5 business days for hospital and procedure encounters) and monitored by provider.
correct_statement: No MGMA, HFMA or Medicare rule sets these targets. HFMA's MAP Keys treat charges posted more than 3 days after service as late in any setting, and MGMA's median service-to-claim lag was 3 days (2018 data). A 48-hour office target is consistent; 5 business days for hospital work is looser. Medicare allows one year to file.
source_title: HFMA MAP Keys, Total Charge Lag Days (PB-4) and Late Charges as a Percentage of Total Charges (CL-2) (hfma.org, 2026); MGMA letter to Senate HELP and House Energy and Commerce leaders (Dec. 9, 2019); MGMA Practice Operations Glossary; 42 CFR 424.44(a)(1); CMS MLN006764 (May 2026)
practice_impact: Nursing facility and assisted living rounds are neither 'office' nor 'hospital' encounters; write a standard for them (3 days matches HFMA and MGMA), monitor it by provider, and bill only after the note is complete and signed.

claim: Industry benchmarks from MGMA and HFMA: median days in AR 45, 55 vs top quartile 30, 38; median clean claim rate 85, 90% vs >96%; median initial denial rate 8, 12% vs <5%.
correct_statement: These are not published MGMA or HFMA quartiles. MGMA family medicine medians cited at a 2026 MGMA chapter conference: clean claims 85.0%, first-submission denials 7.08%, and 69.81 net days in A/R, roughly 35 on gross charges by my estimate. MGMA says under 5% denials is achievable. HFMA publishes definitions, not free quartiles; its clean-claim measure counts scrubber edits.
source_title: MGMA Stat, 'Days in A/R holds steady for most practices, but payer pressure persists in 2026' (July 30, 2026); Forvis Mazars, 'Know Your KPIs, Cash Flow and Claims Optimization', Kansas MGMA Annual Conference (Apr. 22, 2026), citing MGMA DataDive 2025 Financials and Operations and 2024 Practice Operations; HFMA MAP Keys (2026); AAFP, 'Managing practice finances' (2026); Kodiak Solutions, 'State of the healthcare revenue cycle' (Mar. 2026)
practice_impact: Benchmark against MGMA specialty medians and the practice's own trend, and fix one days-in-A/R basis first: net-charge and gross-charge versions differ about twofold, so the vendor's 45-55 'median' can make a normal practice look fast or slow.

claim: For a practice billing $4 million annually, the difference between median and top-quartile performance on these three metrics 'can represent $200,000 to $400,000 in additional annual collections'; called 'the documented revenue gap.'
correct_statement: No MGMA, HFMA or other study documents a $200,000-$400,000 gap for a $4 million practice. The figure is the vendor's own arithmetic, which double-counts clean-claim and denial gains and treats faster payment as new revenue. Kodiak's 2025 data put the median-to-top-quartile gap at about 1.6% of net revenue (final denials plus bad debt): roughly $64,000 on $4 million.
source_title: No source found for the claim (searched MGMA, HFMA, AAFP, Kodiak and trade press). Comparators: Kodiak Solutions, 'State of the healthcare revenue cycle' (Mar. 2026); Forvis Mazars at Kansas MGMA (Apr. 22, 2026), citing MGMA DataDive 2025 Financials and Operations; AAFP, 'Managing practice finances' (2026)
practice_impact: Do not size a billing budget or justify a vendor fee on this figure; the practice's own denial write-offs and bad debt set the real ceiling on recoverable revenue, and that is likely a small fraction of the claimed amount.

claim: Benchmark targets by practice size: small (<3 providers) days in AR 35, 45, clean claim 90, 93%, denial 7, 10%, net collection 94, 96%, AR over 90 days <20%; large (10+) days in AR 40, 52, net collection 96, 98%.
correct_statement: No MGMA, HFMA or other published benchmark stratifies these five measures by provider count; the table has no traceable source. MGMA family medicine medians cited at a 2026 MGMA chapter conference differ: net collection 97.13%, A/R over 90 days 27.86% (worse than every vendor band), clean claims 85.0%, first-pass denials 7.08%. MGMA's standard ageing benchmark is A/R over 120 days.
source_title: No source found for the table. Comparators: Forvis Mazars, 'Know Your KPIs, Cash Flow and Claims Optimization', Kansas MGMA Annual Conference (Apr. 22, 2026), citing MGMA DataDive 2025 Financials and Operations (2024 data) and 2024 Practice Operations (2023 data); AAFP, 'Managing practice finances' (2026); MGMA, 'Understanding cost and revenue data'
practice_impact: A small practice using this table could accept a net collection rate at or below the MGMA median and AAFP's 95% floor, yet be told its A/R ageing is a 'crisis' at a level the median family practice reports.

claim: Clean claim rate: the percentage of claims submitted that are accepted by the payer on first pass without rejection, denial, or request for additional information.
correct_statement: No single standard exists. HFMA's MAP Key counts claims that pass claim-scrubber edits with no manual intervention before submission; it does not measure payer denials. The vendor's version is closer to a first-pass payment rate. Medicare's 'clean claim' needs no outside development and can still be denied. Benchmarks differ accordingly: MGMA family medicine median 85%, HFMA-style about 97%.
source_title: HFMA MAP Keys, Clean Claim Rate (CL-1) (hfma.org, copyright 2026); Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Ch. 1, s. 80.2 (Rev. 13725); Forvis Mazars, 'Know Your KPIs, Cash Flow and Claims Optimization', Kansas MGMA Annual Conference (Apr. 22, 2026), citing MGMA DataDive 2024 Practice Operations and HBI Professional Benchmarks 2024
practice_impact: A billing vendor can report a 97% clean claim rate on scrubber edits while payers still deny 7% or more of claims; write one definition into any billing contract and track first-pass denials separately.

claim: Each payer has timely filing limits, and denials based on timely filing are almost never overturned.
correct_statement: Limits exist but differ: Medicare allows one calendar year from the date of service; Florida-regulated insurers and HMOs must allow 6 months by statute; others follow contract. Medicare timely-filing denials cannot be appealed, though four regulatory exceptions extend the deadline. Commercial and Medicare Advantage plans reverse them on proof of timely submission. No data support 'almost never'.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.44 and 405.926(n) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); First Coast Service Options timely filing FAQ; Fla. Stat. 627.6131(3)(b) and (10) and 641.3155(2)(b) (2026 Florida Statutes); UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide, 'Proof of claim timely filing'
practice_impact: Most of a geriatrics practice's claims are Medicare with a one-year window, so timely-filing losses are avoidable; keep clearinghouse acceptance reports, the proof that reverses Medicare Advantage and commercial timely-filing denials.

claim: CARC (Claim Adjustment Reason Code) and RARC (Remittance Advice Remark Code) on every denial explanation of benefits 'tell you exactly why the claim was denied.'
correct_statement: Every adjustment on a HIPAA electronic remittance (835) carries a group code and a claim adjustment reason code. Remark codes are supplemental: required with some reason codes, absent on many denials. Many reason codes are generic (16, 96), giving a category, not an exact cause. The code sets are mandated for electronic remittances, not for every paper explanation of benefits.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Ch. 22 Remittance Advice, ss. 60.2, 60.3, 80.2 (Rev. 11427); X12 Claim Adjustment Reason Codes list; 45 CFR 162.1602 and 162.1603 (eCFR current to Nov. 5, 2026), adopting the CORE 360 Uniform Use of CARCs and RARCs (835) Rule
practice_impact: Categorising denials by group code, reason code and remark code works for First Coast and Medicare Advantage 835s, but generic codes such as CO-16 still need the remark code or a payer call before a root cause is assigned.

claim: For 1, 2 providers: 1, 2 billing staff covering all functions, or outsourced. Full outsourcing is often more cost-effective at this size.
correct_statement: No MGMA, HFMA, AMA or peer-reviewed data show full outsourcing is 'often more cost-effective' for one- or two-provider practices. Trade guidance gives a rule of thumb of one in-house billing person per two providers, outsourcing fees of roughly 4-10% of collections (higher for primary care), and warns outsourcing may cost as much as in-house. It is a break-even calculation.
source_title: No authoritative source found (searched MGMA, AAFP, AMA, HFMA, PubMed). Comparators: Physicians Practice, 'How many staff members does my practice actually need?' (Mar. 13, 2026) and 'Outsourcing Your Billing' (2010); Medical Economics, 'Practice Pointers: Outsource billing? Here's how' (May 23, 2003); MGMA Stat, 'Automating and outsourcing medical practice revenue cycle management' (Nov. 2024)
practice_impact: Compare a vendor's percentage fee on the practice's actual collections with the loaded cost of its billing staff; front-end work such as facility census and face-sheet capture stays with the practice either way.

claim: A denial that must be appealed costs 25, 45 minutes of staff time and delays payment 30, 60 days; every dollar invested in denial prevention typically returns 3, 5x in avoided denial management cost.
correct_statement: No published source gives 25-45 minutes per appealed denial or a 3-5x return on prevention; the vendor itself calls the multiplier its own observation. Published figures: about $25 to rework a claim (MGMA, 2021); $57.23 per denied claim fought, with about three review rounds of 45-60 days each (Premier, 2023 hospital data). Medicare redeterminations are decided within 60 days.
source_title: No source found for the minutes or the multiplier. Comparators: MGMA Stat, '6 keys to addressing denials in your medical practice's revenue cycle' (Mar. 2021); Premier Inc., 'Claims Adjudication Costs Providers $25.7 Billion' (Feb. 2025); 42 CFR 405.950 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026)
practice_impact: Little: prevention is still cheaper than appeals, but staffing and return-on-investment plans should use the practice's own denial counts; a Medicare appeal can add up to 60 days at each level.

claim: Medicare's deadline is one year from the date of service. Most commercial payers range from 90 to 180 days, and some managed care contracts impose 60-day windows.
correct_statement: Medicare fee-for-service claims must reach the contractor within 1 calendar year after the date of service (Part B: 'From' date); rejected, unprocessable claims do not count as filed. Commercial windows are contractual, commonly 90 to 180 days; Medicare Advantage follows each plan contract. Florida law sets a non-waivable 6-month period for state-regulated insurers and HMOs. 60-day windows were not confirmed.
source_title: eCFR 42 CFR 424.44 (current to Nov. 6, 2026); Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 1 s.70 (Rev. 13725); First Coast Service Options timely filing FAQ; Fla. Stat. 627.6131 and 641.3155 (2026); Florida Blue Manual for Physicians and Providers, claims section (Sept. 2026); Cigna 'When to File Your Claims'; UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide
practice_impact: Calendar First Coast claims at 12 months from the 'From' date, but work to each Medicare Advantage contract's own window (the Florida statute does not reach those plans); fix rejected claims at once because First Coast does not count them as filed.

claim: Payers may deny for late filing and, 'absent a documented administrative error exception, those denials are final'; 'A timely filing denial is not an appeals opportunity. It is a forfeiture.'
correct_statement: Medicare timely-filing denials are not initial determinations and cannot be appealed, but four regulatory exceptions extend the deadline: administrative error, retroactive Medicare entitlement, Medicaid recoupment after retroactive entitlement, and retroactive Medicare Advantage or PACE disenrollment. Commercial and Medicare Advantage timely-filing denials can be reconsidered or appealed with proof of timely submission, so they are not automatically final.
source_title: eCFR 42 CFR 405.926(n) and 424.44(b) (current to Nov. 6, 2026); Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 1 s.70.4-70.7 (Rev. 13725); Florida Blue Manual for Physicians and Providers, appeals section (Sept. 2026); UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide, Ch. 10 'Proof of claim timely filing'; Cigna 'When to File Your Claims'
practice_impact: Do not write these off unread: nursing-home patients often have retroactive Medicare, Medicaid or Medicare Advantage changes that reopen the Medicare window for about six months, and plan denials can be reversed with proof such as an EDI acceptance report.

claim: Review denials for timely filing reason codes - CO-29 on Medicare remits, or equivalent commercial denial codes.
correct_statement: Correct for Part B. First Coast lists 'CO 29' as its timely-filing denial code (Part A uses reject reason code 39011), commonly paired with remark code N211, 'You may not appeal this decision.' Reason code 29 is the national HIPAA code, so commercial and Medicare Advantage electronic remittances carry the same code 29 rather than a different equivalent.
source_title: First Coast Service Options, 'What is the claim timely filing guideline?' (FAQ); X12 Claim Adjustment Reason Codes; Noridian JE Part B 'Timely Filing' reason code guidance (updated Apr. 30, 2025); Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 22 s.60.1; 45 CFR 162.1603
practice_impact: Filter every payer's remittances on reason code 29; the CO group code means a write-off that cannot be billed to the patient, and a rejected claim shows no code 29 until its late resubmission is denied.

claim: HFMA-aligned industry estimate: 1 to 5 percent of collectible revenue is lost to charge capture failure. On $2 million in collections, that is $20,000 to $100,000 per year.
correct_statement: HFMA articles put charge-capture loss at 'as much as 1 percent' of hospital net revenue, based on consultant experience, not a survey. HFMA's 3-5 percent figure covers all hospital revenue leakage, including denials and underpayments, and cites a blog post. No HFMA or MGMA figure for physician practices was found. On $2 million, HFMA's charge-capture figure caps at $20,000.
source_title: HFMA, 'Capturing All Charges: the Operational Reality' (Sept. 20, 2019); HFMA, 'Avoiding the High Cost of High-Capture Leakage' (Aug. 23, 2017); HFMA hfm, 'Why AI is such a promising tool for eliminating a hospital's revenue leakage' (Jan. 30, 2026)
practice_impact: Do not size the opportunity at $20,000-$100,000 per $2 million from this figure; measure the practice's own gap by reconciling facility census and rounding lists to billed charges.

claim: A gastroenterologist performs a colonoscopy with polyp removal - the primary procedure is billed, the polypectomy add-on is missed.
correct_statement: Colonoscopy with polypectomy is not a primary code plus an add-on. It is one stand-alone code (for example 45385, snare removal) that includes and replaces the diagnostic colonoscopy 45378. No colonoscopy code is on CMS's add-on code list. Billing 45378 together with 45385 is unbundling that Medicare's edits deny with no modifier allowed.
source_title: CMS, Medicare NCCI Policy Manual 2026, Ch. VI (rev. 1/1/2026); NCCI Practitioner PTP Edits v323r0 (effective Oct. 1, 2026); CMS Add-on Code Edits file AOC_V2026Q4 (effective Oct. 1, 2026); CMS PFS Relative Value File RVU26D (released Aug. 26, 2026)
practice_impact: Little directly (no endoscopy), but the vendor misdefines add-ons; the real ones here are prolonged-service codes G0317 (nursing facility), G0316 (hospital) and G0318 (home), 99498 (extra advance care planning time) and, since January 1, 2026, G2211 on home or assisted-living visits (not nursing-facility visits).

claim: Office 'injectable medications, diagnostic supplies, or procedure kits' are 'items that have specific HCPCS codes and separate reimbursement'; unbilled supplies and implants are costs 'your payer contracts allow you to recover'.
correct_statement: Only part holds. In the office, Medicare pays separately for physician-purchased injectable drugs and diagnostic imaging agents, but routine supplies, surgical trays and procedure kits are bundled into the procedure payment. In hospitals and nursing facilities the physician generally cannot bill supplies or implants, and drugs and incident-to services for Part A skilled nursing residents belong on the facility's bill.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 12 s.20.4.2 and 20.4.4 (Rev. 13753); Medicare Benefit Policy Manual Ch. 15 s.50.3 and 60.1 (Rev. 13889); CMS PFS Relative Value File RVU26D; CMS SNF Consolidated Billing page (modified Mar. 3, 2026); UnitedHealthcare Supply Policy, Professional, 2026R0006I
practice_impact: For rounding in hospitals, skilled nursing and nursing facilities there is almost nothing to recover here; supplies and Part A residents' drugs belong on the facility's bill, so billing them risks denials and refunds.

claim: 'For a statistically meaningful sample, pull 25 to 30 encounters per provider being audited', chosen from highest-revenue service types, then 'extrapolate to annual volume to estimate the full-year revenue impact'.
correct_statement: A 25-30 chart review is a reasonable internal probe, in line with OIG's guide of five to ten records per physician and CMS's 20-40-claim probe reviews. It is not statistically valid for extrapolation: validity requires random (probability) selection, not picking the highest-revenue services, and OIG requires at least 100 randomly sampled items to estimate damages in self-disclosures.
source_title: CMS Medicare Program Integrity Manual Ch. 8 s.8.4.2 and 8.4.4.3 (Rev. 13762); OIG Compliance Program Guidance for Individual and Small Group Physician Practices, 65 FR 59434 (Oct. 5, 2000); OIG Health Care Fraud Self-Disclosure Protocol (updated Oct. 15, 2026; copy downloaded earlier this session, live re-fetch failed); CMS Targeted Probe and Educate page; 42 CFR 401.305
practice_impact: Fine as a monthly screen, but treat the extrapolated dollar figure as a rough guess; if the review instead finds overbilling, the 60-day report-and-refund rule applies and any sampling must be statistically valid.

claim: The charge master 'should be reviewed at minimum annually' to confirm 'All CPT and HCPCS codes are current - codes are added, deleted, and revised annually'.
correct_statement: Annual review matches only the CPT cycle. The AMA republishes CPT each year, but CMS updates HCPCS Level II codes quarterly (January, April, July, October), the AMA releases Category III codes three times a year and laboratory PLA codes quarterly, and Medicare's add-on code and correct-coding edit files also change quarterly. A charge master with HCPCS codes needs quarterly checks.
source_title: CMS, HCPCS Quarterly Update (modified Sept. 23, 2026) and HCPCS general information; AMA, Category III Codes and CPT PLA Codes pages (updated Oct. 2026); Florida Blue Manual for Physicians and Providers, claims section (Sept. 2026); CMS, Medicare NCCI Procedure to Procedure Edits page
practice_impact: Small: this practice bills few drug or supply codes, but load each January's visit and G-code changes on time and scan the quarterly HCPCS and coding-edit updates.

correct_statement: Those ranges were the 2021-2023 new-patient times only. Established-patient codes are lower: 99212 10, 99213 20, 99214 30, 99215 40 minutes. Since January 1, 2024 CPT uses minimums that 'must be met or exceeded', not ranges: new patient 99202 15, 99203 30, 99204 45, 99205 60. Nursing facility and home visit codes have their own thresholds.
source_title: AMA, CPT E/M Office or Other Outpatient (99202-99215) Code and Guideline Changes (effective Jan. 1, 2021); AAFP, 'Time and medical decision making levels for E/M CPT codes' (page copyright 2026); CMS, 2025 Medicare Fee-for-Service Supplemental Improper Payment Data, Tables K1-K2 (posted Jan. 2026); CMS MLN Booklet MLN006764 (May 2026), Table 3; AAPC, 'CPT 2024: Prep For These E/M Descriptor Revisions' (Oct. 19, 2023)
practice_impact: Following the table would undercode time-based established visits (30 minutes is 99214, not 99213); the practice's nursing facility (99304-99310) and home or residence (99341-99350) codes use different thresholds the table omits, e.g. 99309 30 and 99310 45 minutes.

claim: E&M MDM Score Key: 0, 2 pts = Level 2 | 3, 4 pts = Level 3 | 5, 7 pts = Level 4 | 8, 9 pts = Level 5.
correct_statement: CPT has no additive point scale: the MDM level is the one that two of the three elements meet or exceed, as the playbook's own footnote concedes. The summed key gives a different level in 18 of 64 combinations (12 too low, 6 too high); moderate problems plus moderate risk with no data scores 4, 'Level 3', but is moderate.
source_title: AMA, CPT E/M Code and Guideline Changes effective January 1, 2023, Table 1 'Levels of Medical Decision Making' (still the current revision per AMA's CPT E/M page, Nov. 2026); First Coast Service Options, 'Medical Decision Making and the Impact of Prescription Drug Management' (Sept. 23, 2026)
practice_impact: The commonest geriatric pattern (two stable chronic illnesses, prescription drug management, little data) is moderate MDM (99309, 99349) but scores as low on this key, so an audit built on it would report false coding errors in both directions.

claim: Rubric criteria: Risk 'Low (prescription drug management, minor surgery with identified risk)'; Data 'Extensive (independent interpretation of results OR discussion of management with external provider)'; Problems 'High (... new problem with uncertain prognosis ...)'.
correct_statement: All three are wrong under the CPT MDM table. Prescription drug management and minor surgery with identified risk factors are moderate risk, not low. Independent interpretation of a test or discussion with an external clinician each meets only moderate data; extensive data needs two of three categories. One undiagnosed new problem with uncertain prognosis is a moderate problem, not high.
source_title: AMA, CPT E/M Code and Guideline Changes effective January 1, 2023, Table 1 'Levels of Medical Decision Making'; AMA, Table 2 CPT E/M Office Revisions, Level of Medical Decision Making (effective Jan. 1, 2021)
practice_impact: The rubric under-scores risk on nearly every medication-managed geriatric visit and over-scores data and problems, so it would mislabel correct nursing facility and home visit codes as errors and could justify unsupported high-level codes.

claim: Listed as an undercoding pattern: 'Failing to capture the complexity of prescription drug management, particularly controlled substances, as a high-risk MDM element.'
correct_statement: Prescription drug management, including prescribing oral controlled substances, is a moderate-risk example in the CPT MDM table, not high. The high-risk drug examples are drug therapy requiring intensive monitoring for toxicity and parenteral controlled substances. Risk is one of three elements and cannot set the level alone. The playbook's own rubric scores prescription drug management as low.
source_title: AMA, CPT E/M Code and Guideline Changes effective January 1, 2023, Table 1 'Levels of Medical Decision Making'; First Coast Service Options, 'Medical Decision Making and the Impact of Prescription Drug Management' (Sept. 23, 2026)
practice_impact: Treating routine opioid or benzodiazepine prescribing as high risk would push nursing facility visits toward 99310 and home visits toward 99350 without support: an overcoding and repayment exposure with Florida's Medicare contractor, not recovered revenue.

claim: 'New patient codes require higher MDM thresholds but are consistently coded at lower levels out of unfamiliarity.'
correct_statement: New and established office codes use identical MDM thresholds at each level (99203/99213 low, 99204/99214 moderate, 99205/99215 high); only time thresholds are higher for new patients. Medicare data show no systematic undercoding: in 2025, 64% of new-patient office visits were billed at level 4 or 5 versus 62% of established, and audits find upcoding far exceeds downcoding.
source_title: AMA, Table 2 CPT E/M Office Revisions, Level of Medical Decision Making (effective Jan. 1, 2021); CMS, CY 2025 Evaluation & Management (E&M) Codes by Specialty (Medicare Part B national data; my calculation); CMS, 2025 Medicare Fee-for-Service Supplemental Improper Payment Data, Tables F5 and K3 (posted Jan. 2026)
practice_impact: Little direct revenue: the practice bills nursing facility and home codes, not office new-patient codes. The risk runs the other way: CERT 2025 found improper payment rates of 25.5% on 99306 and 24.6% on 99310, mostly incorrect coding.

claim: 'OIG's own published guidance for physician practices suggests a 5, 10 record minimum per payer'; a sample of 25-30 records is said to give 'a stronger statistical base' for a comprehensive internal audit.
correct_statement: OIG's 2000 guidance for individual and small group physician practices, still listed as its physician guidance, suggests five or more records per federal payer or five to ten per physician, and says there is no set formula. Twenty-five to 30 risk-selected charts is a reasonable probe, not a statistical base; OIG requires at least 100 randomly sampled items for damages.
source_title: OIG Compliance Program Guidance for Individual and Small Group Physician Practices, 65 FR 59434, 59437 (Oct. 5, 2000), still listed on OIG's Compliance Guidance page (Nov. 2026); OIG General Compliance Program Guidance (Nov. 2023), small entities 'should conduct at least an annual audit', no sample size given; HHS-OIG Health Care Fraud Self-Disclosure Protocol (updated Oct. 15, 2026); 42 CFR 401.305(d)(1) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); CMS Targeted Probe and Educate page (20-40 claims per round)
practice_impact: A small facility-based group can meet OIG's guide with five to ten charts per clinician a year; any repayment figure must rest on a statistically valid random sample, not on 25 to 30 hand-picked high-risk charts.

claim: False Claims Act (31 U.S.C. §§ 3729-3733) imposes civil liability of up to three times the amount of the false claim plus penalties per claim; 'knowingly' includes reckless disregard.
correct_statement: The Act imposes three times the government's damages, not three times the claim amount (reducible to two times for self-disclosure within 30 days with cooperation), plus a civil penalty of $14,308 to $28,619 per claim for penalties assessed after July 3, 2025, unchanged for 2026. 'Knowingly' covers actual knowledge, deliberate ignorance or reckless disregard; specific intent is not required.
source_title: 31 U.S.C. 3729(a)(1)-(2), (b)(1) (Cornell LII copy opened Nov. 10, 2026; also quoted in 28 CFR 85.5 Table 1, footnote 3); 28 CFR 85.5, Table 1 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); DOJ notice, Civil Monetary Penalties Inflation Adjustments for 2026, 91 FR 43405 (July 15, 2026); Mintz summary of U.S. ex rel. Zafirov v. Florida Medical Associates (11th Cir. Sept. 1, 2026)
practice_impact: For low-dollar visit codes the per-claim penalty dominates: 100 knowingly upcoded nursing facility visits carry $1.43 million to $2.86 million in penalties plus trebled overpayments. Whistleblower suits remain available in Florida after the Eleventh Circuit's September 1, 2026 Zafirov ruling.

claim: OIG's Self-Disclosure Protocol 'provides a mechanism for practices to voluntarily report and repay overpayments, typically at a reduced multiplier' compared with a government-initiated investigation.
correct_statement: OIG's protocol (updated October 15, 2026) is for potential fraud, not plain overpayments or errors; those must be reported and returned to the Medicare contractor within 60 days of identification, with up to 180 days to investigate. Inside the protocol OIG generally requires at least 1.5 times single damages, a $20,000 minimum settlement and a 100-item sample.
source_title: HHS-OIG Health Care Fraud Self-Disclosure Protocol (updated Oct. 15, 2026), sections 1.B, 2.C, 3.B and 8; 42 CFR 401.305 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026; amended 89 FR 98553); First Coast Service Options, 'Overpayment request submission reminders' (Oct. 12, 2026)
practice_impact: Ordinary audit findings are refunded to First Coast at single damages with its voluntary refund form (six-year lookback); the OIG protocol costs at least $20,000 and is for conduct that may be fraud, so counsel should pick the channel before the 60-day clock runs.

claim: Medicare requires submission within one year of the date of service; Medicare Part B redetermination: 120 days from date of denial; reconsideration (Level 2): 180 days from date of redetermination decision; QIC reconsideration 'takes 60 days to resolve.'
correct_statement: Part B claims must be filed within 1 calendar year after the date of service. Redetermination: 120 calendar days from receipt of the initial determination notice (receipt presumed 5 days after the notice date). Reconsideration: 180 calendar days from receipt of the redetermination notice. The QIC decides within 60 calendar days, extended up to 14 days per later evidence submission.
source_title: eCFR: 42 CFR 424.44, 405.942, 405.962, 405.970 (current as of Nov. 6, 2026); First Coast Service Options, 'New provider roadmap: Appeals' (Oct. 20, 2025)
practice_impact: Safe to calendar as written (the vendor's wording is about 5 days conservative); but ignore the playbook's nearby line that the one-year limit still runs during an appeal, and note Medicare untimely-filing denials are not appealable (Claims Processing Manual ch. 1, sec. 70.4).

claim: A Medicare Advantage plan 'is required by 42 CFR 422.101 to provide coverage at least as generous as traditional Medicare for all Part A and Part B services'; denying such a claim 'violates that requirement.'
correct_statement: 42 CFR 422.101(a)-(c) requires MA plans to cover all Part A and B services except hospice and kidney acquisition costs, follow NCDs, LCDs and Traditional Medicare coverage rules, and not deny on other criteria. Plans may still require prior authorization, use networks, and apply public internal criteria where Medicare's are not fully established; a denial is not automatically a violation.
practice_impact: A real lever for MA medical-necessity denials if the appeal cites 422.101(b)-(c) plus the specific NCD/LCD; it does not defeat prior-authorization, network or contract denials, and the practice's Part B claims for MA enrollees who have elected hospice go to Original Medicare (First Coast), not the plan.

claim: Medicare Advantage denials: the escalation pathway runs through the MA plan's internal appeal process first, then to an Independent Review Entity designated by CMS, [then] the same multi-level Medicare appeal system that applies to traditional Medicare.
correct_statement: For enrollees and non-contract providers (who must waive enrollee liability), the path is plan reconsideration (request within 60 days), automatic IRE review (C2C since May 1, 2026), then ALJ ($200 threshold in 2026), Appeals Council and federal court ($1,960). A contracted provider's payment denial with no enrollee liability is outside this process; the provider contract's dispute terms govern.
source_title: eCFR: 42 CFR 422.562, 422.582, 422.592, 422.600-422.612 (current as of Nov. 6, 2026); CMS, 'Parts C & D Enrollee Grievances, Organization/Coverage Determinations, and Appeals Guidance' (effective July 6, 2026); 90 FR 55869 (2026 amount-in-controversy thresholds)
practice_impact: High: for in-network MA claims the IRE/ALJ ladder is not available to the practice; use each plan's contractual dispute process and deadlines, and reserve the Subpart M route for pre-service requests on the patient's behalf or out-of-network claims with a waiver of liability.

claim: QIC reversal rates for well-supported clinical denials are materially higher than MAC redetermination reversal rates.
correct_statement: CMS data show the opposite in aggregate. For Part B in 2025, 45% of decided MAC redeterminations were fully favorable (3% partially) versus 24% of QIC reconsiderations (1% partially); in 2024 it was 43% versus 20%. Only DME shows a higher QIC rate. CMS publishes no rates for 'well-supported clinical denials,' so that qualifier cannot be tested.
source_title: CMS, 'Original Medicare Claim Appeals Data - 2025' and '- 2024' (Appeals Fact Sheets ZIP on the 'Second Level of Appeal: Reconsideration by a QIC' page, modified Sept. 30, 2026)
practice_impact: Do not expect better odds at the QIC for physician claims; put the full record into the redetermination, and file everything by reconsideration because evidence first offered after the QIC level can be excluded.

claim: The ACA established the right to independent external review for most commercial insurance denials that have exhausted the internal appeal process... IRO decisions are binding on the payer in most states.
correct_statement: The ACA (PHS Act 2719) gives enrollees in non-grandfathered plans external review, but only for denials involving medical judgment, rescissions, or No Surprises Act compliance, not most denials. The IRO decision binds the plan under every compliant state process and under the federal process. Florida has no qualifying state process; its issuers use the HHS-administered or accredited-IRO federal process.
source_title: eCFR: 45 CFR 147.136 (current as of Nov. 6, 2026); 42 U.S.C. 300gg-19; CMS/CCIIO external appeals page with state-by-state process list
practice_impact: Little: external review does not reach Medicare, Medicare Advantage or Medicaid; for the few commercial patients it is the patient's request (practice as authorized representative), due within four months, through the federal process rather than a Florida state program.

claim: [MHPAEA] requires that commercial health plans apply the same coverage standards, prior authorization requirements, treatment limitations, and reimbursement rates to [behavioral health] services as they apply to comparable medical and surgical services.
correct_statement: MHPAEA bars financial requirements and treatment limits on mental health/substance use benefits that are more restrictive than the predominant ones applied to substantially all medical/surgical benefits in a classification; prior authorization and rate-setting processes must be comparable and no more stringently applied. It does not require equal reimbursement rates or any behavioral coverage, and does not apply to Medicare.
source_title: eCFR: 45 CFR 146.136 (current as of Nov. 6, 2026); 78 FR 68240 (Nov. 13, 2013) preamble; CMS MHPAEA page (modified Mar. 13, 2026); Departments' statement of non-enforcement of the 2024 rule's new provisions (May 15, 2025)
practice_impact: Little: parity is a commercial-plan (and Medicaid managed care) tool and does not apply to Medicare, the practice's dominant payer; where it does apply, argue that the limitation is not comparable, never that rates must be equal.

claim: A claim that is denied, appealed, and reversed costs an average of $25 to $118 in staff time to manage ... and is collected 30 to 90 days later
correct_statement: The endpoints are two unrelated, dated estimates: about $25 to rework a claim (MGMA figure cited since at least 2015; $25.20 in a 2021 MGMA article) and $118 per appealed claim (Change Healthcare, 2016 hospital data). Premier's hospital surveys report $43.84 (2022) and $57.23 (2023) per denied claim. No source supports a 30-to-90-day delay.
source_title: MGMA, '4 keys to driving down denials' (Dec. 19, 2018) and MGMA Stat (Mar. 18, 2021); AAFP FPM 2015;22(2):7-10; Premier Inc., 'Claims Adjudication Costs Providers $25.7 Billion' (Feb. 2025)
practice_impact: Fine as a rough argument that prevention beats rework, but do not put $25-$118 or 30-90 days into ROI math; time the practice's own appeals and track days from denial to payment by payer.

claim: Typical % of total denials: Administrative / front-end errors 37, 38%; Medical necessity 22, 23%; Coding and billing errors 17, 18%; Coverage / non-covered service 11, 12%; Coordination of benefits 6, 8%; Timely filing exceeded 4, 5%.
correct_statement: No published source gives this distribution. The closest benchmark, Change Healthcare's 2022 index of hospital claims, shows registration/eligibility 22%, missing or invalid claim data 16%, documentation requests 14%, authorization 13%, service not covered 11%, medical necessity 6%, coding 5%, untimely filing 4%. KFF's 2024 marketplace data put medical necessity at 5% of in-network denials.
source_title: Optum, 'Actionable Insights & Strategies From the Change Healthcare 2022 Denial Index' (HFMA Texas, May 2023); KFF, 'Claims Denials and Appeals in ACA Marketplace Plans in 2024' (Mar. 24, 2026); Massachusetts Health Policy Commission DataPoints on 2024 claim denials
practice_impact: Do not benchmark against this table: its medical-necessity share (22-23%) is about four times published figures and none of the data are physician- or Medicare-specific; build the practice's own mix from remittance CARC/RARC codes by payer.

claim: CY2026 conversion factors are $33.57 (qualifying APM) and $33.40 (non-qualifying APM).
correct_statement: Correct for CY2026: $33.5675 (qualifying APM participants) and $33.4009 (all other clinicians), in force through Dec. 31, 2026. CMS's CY2027 final rule (published Nov. 9, 2026) lowers them to $32.95 and $32.63 on Jan. 1, 2027 (-1.83% and -2.31%) because the one-year 2.5% increase expires.
source_title: CMS Fact Sheet: Calendar Year (CY) 2026 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule (CMS-1832-F), Oct. 31, 2025; CY2027 figures from CMS Fact Sheet: CY 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule (CMS-1848-F), Nov. 2026
practice_impact: Benchmark at $33.40 unless clinicians are Qualifying APM Participants; on Jan. 1, 2027 the non-QP factor drops to $32.63, so the fee schedule and every Medicare benchmark must be rebuilt for 2027.

claim: The increase reflects a temporary 2.5% payment bump enacted by Congress through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, a small MACRA statutory update, and a positive budget-neutrality adjustment.
correct_statement: Correct. The CY2026 factors combine MACRA updates of +0.75% (qualifying APM) or +0.25% (others), a one-year +2.5% increase under Public Law 119-21 sec. 71202 (popularly the One Big Beautiful Bill Act; CMS says Working Families Tax Cut legislation) and a +0.49% budget-neutrality adjustment. The 2.5% covers 2026 services only; no enacted extension found as of Nov. 10, 2026.
source_title: CMS Fact Sheet: CY 2026 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule (CMS-1832-F); Public Law 119-21, sec. 71202 (govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-119publ21/html/PLAW-119publ21.htm); CY 2026 PFS final rule, 90 FR 49960-49961
practice_impact: The 2.5% bump ends Dec. 31, 2026; unless Congress acts, 2027 Medicare payment per RVU falls about 2.3% for non-QP clinicians, which belongs in the 2027 budget.

claim: For Original Medicare, the correct position is to bill above the Medicare allowed amount at the chosen multiplier... if the billed charge is below the Medicare allowed amount, the payment is limited to the billed charge.
correct_statement: Medicare bases payment on the lesser of the actual charge or the fee schedule amount, so a charge below the allowance forfeits money. Participating providers may bill any higher charge. But nonparticipating providers on unassigned claims may not charge above the limiting charge, 115% of the nonpar amount (109.25% of par), so a 200-250% multiplier is unlawful there.
source_title: 42 CFR 414.21 and 414.48 (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026); First Coast Service Options, 'Fee schedule par, nonpar, and limiting charge explanation' and 2026 Florida locality 99 fee schedule; Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 12 sec. 20
practice_impact: A participating practice loses nothing by charging above the fee schedule; any nonparticipating clinician must cap unassigned Medicare charges at the limiting charge or risk civil penalties up to $19,940 per knowing violation (latest HHS inflation adjustment, 45 CFR 102.3) and exclusion.

claim: The Medicare fee schedule has separate rates for facility settings (hospital outpatient, ASC) and non-facility settings (physician office). The non-facility rate is higher because it includes the practice expense component covering office overhead.
correct_statement: Some PFS codes have separate facility and non-facility rates, set by place-of-service code. Both include practice expense; facility PE RVUs are smaller because the facility bears most direct costs and, since 2026, CMS halves work-based indirect PE. Facility includes hospitals, ASCs and SNF Part A stays (POS 31); nursing facility (POS 32), assisted living and home are non-facility.
source_title: CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule, 91 FR 70992 at 71018-71020 (Nov. 9, 2026), citing Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 12 sec. 20.4.2 (cms.gov/Regulations-and-Guidance/Guidance/Manuals/Downloads/clm104c12.pdf); 42 CFR 414.22(b)(5); CMS 2026 relative value file RVU26D
practice_impact: Nursing-home visits split by POS: in 2026 CPT 99309 is allowed $114.90 in POS 32 but $99.58 in POS 31 (Rest of Florida locality); CMS equalizes 99304-99310 and 99315-99316 on Jan. 1, 2027, so benchmark charges to the higher non-facility rate.

claim: Payment = (Work RVU + Practice Expense RVU + Malpractice RVU) × Geographic Practice Cost Index × Conversion Factor
correct_statement: There is no single GPCI. Payment = [(Work RVU x Work GPCI) + (PE RVU x PE GPCI) + (MP RVU x MP GPCI)] x CF. Each component has its own locality index; 2026 Florida GPCIs (work/PE/MP) are Miami 1.000/1.041/2.529, Fort Lauderdale 1.000/1.013/1.808, Rest of Florida 1.000/0.956/1.503.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), Chapter 12, sec. 20.1 Method for Computing Fee Schedule Amount; 42 CFR 414.26(d); CMS CY 2026 GPCI file (Addendum E, RVU26D release)
practice_impact: Florida's malpractice GPCI (1.50-2.53) dwarfs its work and PE indices, so use First Coast's locality fee schedule, not a one-index shortcut; the 1.0 work GPCI floor lapses Jan. 1, 2027 (Rest of Florida 0.977) unless Congress extends it.

claim: Increasing billed charges does not violate payer contracts, practices are generally free to set and adjust their own charges.
correct_statement: Practices generally set their own charges; fee-schedule contracts usually pay the lesser of billed charge or contracted rate, so a uniform increase normally breaches nothing. That is contract-specific (some cap increases or require notice), and law limits charges: Medicare's nonparticipating limiting charge, OIG exclusion authority for Medicare/Medicaid charges substantially above usual charges, and Florida PIP's reasonable-charge rule.
source_title: 42 CFR 1001.701 (OIG permissive exclusion, excessive charges); Fla. Stat. sec. 627.736(5)(a) (2026); 42 CFR 414.48; ECG Management Consultants, 'Capture Every Dollar: Chargemaster Maintenance Strategies for ASC Revenue Growth' (June 5, 2026)
practice_impact: Raise charges uniformly for all payers, read each Medicare Advantage and commercial agreement for charge-related clauses first, and expect no added Medicare revenue: gains arise only where a charge sat below a payer's allowed amount, and non-contracted Medicare Advantage claims stay capped at Original Medicare amounts (42 CFR 422.214).

claim: Contact each major payer's provider relations department and request the current contracted rate schedule. This data is available, payers are contractually required to provide it.
correct_statement: No universal contractual duty exists; access depends on each contract and on state law. Florida requires HMOs, by statute, to disclose the complete schedule of reimbursements to contracted physicians (confidentially); no parallel insurer mandate was found. Commercial plans' in-network rates are public under the federal Transparency in Coverage rule. Medicare Advantage contracts may fall outside both.
source_title: Fla. Stat. sec. 641.315(4)(d) (2026 Florida Statutes); 45 CFR 147.212(b) (Transparency in Coverage); 42 CFR 422.402 (Medicare Advantage preemption); American Medical News, July 31, 2009
practice_impact: Cite s. 641.315(4)(d) when asking HMOs for the full schedule; for other payers rely on the contract, the portal or public machine-readable files, and confirm each Medicare Advantage contract's stated percentage of Medicare.

claim: For most specialties, commercial contracted rates run between 120% and 180% of Medicare.
correct_statement: National averages fit the band: KFF's review found 143% of Medicare (studies ranged 118-179%); MedPAC reports 147% for 2024. But it is not a per-specialty rule: primary care and E/M run about 110-124%, three of 17 studied specialties exceed 180%, and states vary widely (Milliman 2024: 119-243%; HCCI 2017: Florida near 105-110%). The document cites no source.
source_title: MedPAC, Report to the Congress: Medicare Payment Policy (March 2026), Ch. 4; KFF, 'How Much More Than Medicare Do Private Insurers Pay? A Review of the Literature' (2020); Urban Institute (Oct. 2021); HCCI (Aug. 2020); Milliman (June 2024)
practice_impact: Geriatrics is paid mostly by Medicare and Medicare Advantage (MA physician rates ran about 91-102% of traditional Medicare in a 2017 JAMA Internal Medicine study), so few contracts will approach 120-180%; verify actual rates before choosing a multiplier.

claim: Redetermination: the MA plan itself, 60 days to file, plan has 60 days to decide. Reconsideration: Independent Review Entity, 60 days to file after redetermination. ALJ hearing: $190+ claim threshold (2025). Federal Court: $1,900+ threshold (2025).
correct_statement: Part C level 1 is a plan 'reconsideration': file within 65 days of the denial notice; the plan decides in 30 days (pre-service) or 60 days (payment). Adverse decisions go to the IRE automatically. ALJ threshold is $200 for 2026 and 2027; federal court $1,960 for 2026, $2,000 for 2027. Contracted-provider payment disputes follow the contract instead.
source_title: CMS Managed Care Appeals pages (plan reconsideration, IRE, ALJ hearing, federal court; updated 11/03/2026); 42 CFR 422.582, 422.590, 422.600, 422.612; 91 FR 58681 (Sept. 16, 2026); CMS Parts C & D Appeals Guidance (eff. July 6, 2026)
practice_impact: A contracted practice cannot take an MA payment denial to the IRE or an ALJ; it must use the contract's dispute process, and enrollee-side appeals now have a 65-day window.

claim: Common codes like hypertension (I10) carry HCC weight; elevated blood pressure (R03.0) does not.
correct_statement: Essential hypertension (I10) maps to no CMS-HCC payment category in V22, V24 or V28, so it adds nothing to the Part C risk score; it maps only to RxHCC 187 in the Part D drug model. R03.0 maps to no model. Only hypertensive heart-failure or stage 5 CKD combination codes (such as I11.0, I12.0) map to V28 HCCs.
source_title: CMS 2026 Midyear/Final ICD-10-CM Mappings (2026 Model Software/ICD-10 Mappings); identical in 2027 Initial Mappings; 2025 Midyear/Final Mappings for the V24 column
practice_impact: Recapturing I10 on nursing-facility visits will not raise the Part C risk score (only a small Part D RxHCC weight); treating it as an HCC gap misdirects coding audits and shared-savings forecasts.

claim: Type 2 diabetes with diabetic chronic kidney disease (E11.65) has a much higher RAF impact than Type 2 diabetes uncomplicated (E11.9).
correct_statement: E11.65 is type 2 diabetes with hyperglycemia; diabetic CKD is E11.22. Under the V28 model used for all 2026 and 2027 payment, E11.9 and E11.65 both map to HCC 38, and HCCs 36, 37 and 38 share one coefficient (0.166 community non-dual aged, 0.280 institutional). Extra weight requires separately coding the CKD stage (N18.30 to N18.6).
source_title: CMS 2026 Midyear/Final ICD-10-CM Mappings and CMS-HCC V28 model software (relative factors); CY 2026 and CY 2027 Rate Announcements
practice_impact: Diabetes complication specificity alone no longer moves RAF; for long-stay residents the documentable gain is the CKD stage, heart-failure and other separately mapped conditions.

claim: MA plans ... may approve and pay a claim, then months later audit the medical record and recoup payment if the documentation does not support medical necessity - even if the authorization was obtained prospectively.
correct_statement: Since 2024, 42 CFR 422.138(c) bars an MA coordinated care plan that approved a service by prior authorization, pre-service or concurrent determination from later denying coverage for lack of medical necessity. It may reopen only for good cause or reliable evidence of fraud or similar fault; for approved inpatient admissions, later-gathered clinical information cannot supply good cause.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.138(c) Prior authorization and 42 CFR 422.616(e) (eCFR, current to 11/06/2026; 88 FR 22331, amended 90 FR 15910)
practice_impact: Matters only where the practice's services need plan authorization: a later medical-necessity clawback of an authorized service can be disputed under 422.138(c); documentation still matters for coding and fraud audits.

claim: MA plans deny claims on medical necessity grounds ... using proprietary clinical criteria that may differ from CMS national coverage determinations ... the InterQual criteria, the MCG guidelines, or the plan's own proprietary policy.
correct_statement: Plans do cite InterQual, MCG or their own policies, but since 2024 42 CFR 422.101(b)-(c) binds them to NCDs, LCDs and Traditional Medicare coverage rules. Internal criteria are allowed only where Medicare criteria are not fully established, must rest on published evidence and be publicly posted, and may not otherwise be used to deny basic benefits.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.101(b)(6) and (c)(1) (eCFR, current to 11/06/2026); KFF, Medicare Advantage Insurers Made Nearly 53 Million Prior Authorization Determinations in 2024 (Jan. 28, 2026)
practice_impact: Appeals should argue the service meets the NCD, LCD or Medicare rule and that proprietary criteria cannot override it, rather than only rebutting InterQual or MCG point by point.

claim: HCC diagnoses must be submitted at least once per calendar year for each patient to be included in that year's risk score calculation ... based on the ICD-10 diagnosis codes submitted on claims from all providers.
correct_statement: Annual recapture is real, but timing and scope are misstated. The model is prospective: diagnoses from 2026 dates of service set 2027 payment. Only diagnoses from face-to-face (or audio-video) encounters with physicians and other accepted practitioners, hospital inpatient or hospital outpatient providers count; for 2027 payment CMS also excludes audio-only visits and unlinked chart reviews.
source_title: CMS, Announcement of CY 2027 Medicare Advantage Capitation Rates and Part C and Part D Payment Policies (April 6, 2026); Medicare Managed Care Manual ch. 7; CY2026 Risk Adjustment Eligible CPT/HCPCS list
practice_impact: Your own nursing-facility visit claims (99304-99310 are risk-adjustment eligible) carry diagnoses into next year's payment; SNF facility claims, audio-only visits and plan chart reviews do not.

claim: Price transparency MRF data includes MA contracted rates alongside commercial rates.
correct_statement: Only hospital machine-readable files must list rates negotiated with Medicare Advantage plans. Payer Transparency in Coverage files, the ones holding physician-practice rates, cover non-grandfathered group and individual commercial coverage; the October 2026 final rule says MA is beyond its scope. A practice cannot benchmark its MA professional rates from payer files.
source_title: Transparency in Coverage final rule, 91 FR 63748 (Oct. 6, 2026); 45 CFR 147.212; CMS Hospital Price Transparency FAQs (current as of June 26, 2026)
practice_impact: Payer files will not show what MA plans pay other physician groups for facility visits; only hospital files (hospital-employed clinicians) carry MA rates, so benchmark against the Medicare fee schedule.

claim: HEDIS measures most relevant to physician practices include Transitions of Care (follow-up within 7/30 days post-discharge), Annual Wellness Visit (AWV completed in calendar year) and Medication Adherence (PDC > 80%).
correct_statement: Of the three, only Transitions of Care is a HEDIS measure, and its windows are 2 days for admission and discharge notices and 30 days for patient engagement and medication reconciliation, not 7/30. Medication adherence is a PQA Part D Star measure (PDC of 80% or higher). The Annual Wellness Visit is neither a HEDIS nor a Star Ratings measure.
source_title: CMS Medicare 2027 Part C & D Star Ratings Technical Notes (updated 11/04/2026); NCQA, Transitions of Care (TRC)
practice_impact: AWV bonuses are plan-contract incentives, not HEDIS; most HEDIS screening and diabetes measures exclude members 66+ in I-SNPs or long-term institutional care, so TRC and readmissions matter more.

claim: Milliman's 2025 Health Cost Guidelines research: commercial payers reimburse professional services at an average of 148 percent of Medicare fee-for-service rates; overall commercial rates average 196 percent; state-level range runs from 143 to 294 percent of Medicare.
correct_statement: Milliman's July 2025 white paper, the latest edition on its site, estimates 2025 commercial payment at 148% of Medicare for professional services and 196% overall. The 143%-294% state range (Alabama, Alaska) covers all services including hospital care; for professional services alone states run from 123% (Kentucky) to 255% (Wisconsin). Figures are group commercial plans, not Medicare Advantage.
source_title: Milliman white paper, 'Commercial reimbursement benchmarking 2025: Commercial payment rates for medical services as a percentage of Medicare fee-for-service rates' (Marshall, Zhou, Mills; July 24, 2025)
practice_impact: Little: a facility-based geriatrics practice is paid mainly by Medicare and Medicare Advantage, which this benchmark excludes; for any commercial contract use the professional range (123%-255%), not 143%-294%.

claim: A 2025 analysis by Aroris found that practices using structured data in their negotiations achieved average rate increases of 15.5 percent, compared to the industry average of 2 to 4 percent.
correct_statement: The 15.5% figure is not a study. Aroris Health, a firm that sells payer-contract negotiation services, advertises a 15.5% average reimbursement increase across its own signed engagements, with no method, sample or comparison group; it advertised 13.8% in March 2025. The '2 to 4 percent industry average' has no traceable source; Milliman estimates commercial professional prices rose 1.4%-2.7% a year.
source_title: Aroris Health, Contract Negotiation service page and Insights listing (vendor marketing, read Nov. 10, 2026); Milliman, 'Commercial reimbursement benchmarking 2025' (July 24, 2025), Figure 2
practice_impact: Do not budget on a 15.5% lift: it is a vendor's self-selected result for commercial contracts, and this practice's revenue is mostly Medicare and Medicare Advantage.

claim: The No Surprises Act's price transparency requirements, effective since 2022, require payers to publish Machine-Readable Files (MRFs) containing their contracted rates with every provider in their network.
correct_statement: The files are required by the 2020 Transparency in Coverage rules under the Affordable Care Act, not the No Surprises Act; enforcement began July 1, 2022. They cover non-grandfathered commercial group and individual plans only, not Medicare Advantage or Medicaid. From March 6, 2027, payers post quarterly, per network, and must omit provider-service pairs unlikely to be paid.
source_title: 45 CFR 147.212 (eCFR, with amendment at 91 FR 63864); Transparency in Coverage final rules, 85 FR 72158 (Nov. 12, 2020) and 91 FR 63748 (Oct. 6, 2026, effective Dec. 7, 2026); Departments' FAQs About ACA and CAA 2021 Implementation Part 49 (Aug. 20, 2021)
practice_impact: Payer files hold no Medicare Advantage rates, so a geriatrics practice paid mostly by Medicare and MA plans cannot benchmark those contracts from them; useful only for commercial plans.

claim: Prompt payment terms: Penalties for late payment (typically 1.5-2 percent per month after the required payment period).
correct_statement: State prompt-pay interest most often runs 10% to 18% a year (about 0.8% to 1.5% a month); only a few statutes, such as Maryland's, reach 2% a month. Florida sets 12% simple interest a year on overdue insurer and HMO claims and bars waiving it by contract. Medicare pays the Treasury rate, 4.75% a year for July-December 2026.
source_title: Fla. Stat. 627.6131 and 641.3155 (2026); Ohio R.C. 3901.389; N.C. Gen. Stat. 58-3-225(e); Md. Code, Ins. 15-1005(g) (all read Nov. 10, 2026); Texans for Lawsuit Reform Foundation, 'An Interstate Comparison of Healthcare Prompt-Pay Laws' (Jan. 31, 2016); Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 1 s. 80.2.2; 42 CFR 422.520; Treasury Bureau of the Fiscal Service, Prompt Payment interest rates (updated June 30, 2026)
practice_impact: Florida's 12% statutory interest already applies to state-regulated plans and cannot be bargained away; Medicare's rate is fixed. A contract clause only matters for Medicare Advantage and self-funded plans.

claim: If Humana is a significant commercial payer for your practice... Key strategic considerations for Humana commercial: Humana is generally willing to negotiate. Their provider relations team is accessible.
correct_statement: Humana no longer has a commercial medical business. It announced on February 23, 2023 that it would exit all fully insured, self-funded and federal-employee medical plans within 18 to 24 months; that business produced $551 million of revenue in 2024 and none in 2025. Humana now contracts for Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, TRICARE and specialty plans. 'Willing to negotiate' is unsourced.
source_title: Humana Inc. press release, 'Humana to Exit Employer Group Commercial Medical Products Business' (Feb. 23, 2023); Humana Fourth Quarter 2025 results (Feb. 11, 2026) and Third Quarter 2026 results (Nov. 6, 2026); Humana group benefits page (read Nov. 10, 2026)
practice_impact: For a Florida geriatrics practice Humana is a Medicare Advantage payer, not a commercial one; this section's commercial advice has nothing to apply to.

claim: The Medicare Physician Fee Schedule is recalculated annually and has experienced a pattern of flat or declining conversion factor updates in recent years; any contract that pegs rates to Medicare participates in those declines automatically.
correct_statement: The conversion factor fell every year from 2021 to 2025 ($36.09 in 2020 to $32.35), rose in 2026 to $33.40 ($33.57 for qualifying APM participants), and falls again on January 1, 2027 to $32.63 and $32.95. A Medicare-pegged contract follows those changes only if it references the then-current schedule; contracts fixed to a named year do not move.
source_title: CMS Fact Sheet, CY 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule (CMS-1848-F; rule published 91 FR 70992, Nov. 9, 2026); CMS Fact Sheet, CY 2026 PFS Final Rule (Oct. 31, 2025); AMA, History of Medicare Conversion Factors; AMA Payor Contracting 101 (2021)
practice_impact: High: Medicare-priced revenue drops about 2.3% on January 1, 2027 (1.8% for qualifying APM participants), and any Medicare Advantage contract tied to current Medicare rates drops with it.

claim: In most commercial contracts the renewal date is specified, typically with a 60 to 90 day termination notice requirement (Section 4); most commercial contracts require 90 to 180 days notice (Section 9).
correct_statement: The playbook gives two conflicting 'typical' notice periods (60-90 and 90-180 days) and no source for either. Notice periods are contract-specific; the AMA's examples are 30 to 90 days. Legal floors apply: Florida HMO contracts require 60 days' advance written notice of cancellation, and Medicare Advantage contracts require at least 60 days for termination without cause.
source_title: AMA Private Practice Toolkit, Payor Contracting 101 (2021); Fla. Stat. 641.315 (2026); 42 CFR 422.202(d)(4) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026)
practice_impact: Read each contract's own notice and renewal window; the practice's Medicare Advantage and Florida HMO agreements carry a 60-day legal minimum, so a 90-180 day assumption could miss or misstate a deadline.

claim: Each major payer publishes a Table of Contents file listing MRF downloads: UnitedHealth Group transparency-in-coverage.uhc.com; Anthem anthem.com/machine-readable-file; Aetna aetna.com/transparency; Cigna cigna.com/legal/compliance/machine-readable-files; Humana humanatransparency.com.
correct_statement: Three of the five addresses work today: UnitedHealthcare, Anthem and Cigna. aetna.com/transparency returns 'File Not Found', and humanatransparency.com could not be reached; Humana has in any case left commercial medical insurance. Anthem's page covers Anthem plans only: Florida's Blue plan, Florida Blue, posts its own files on floridablue.com.
source_title: Direct retrieval of each address on Nov. 10, 2026: UnitedHealthcare, Anthem, Aetna, Cigna, Humana and Florida Blue machine-readable-file pages
