practice_impact: Little: these files show commercial rates only. For Florida use Florida Blue's page (floridablue.com/members/tools-resources/transparency/machine-readable-files), and expect none of this practice's Medicare Advantage rates.

claim: National range for physician conversion factors is roughly $45 to $65 per wRVU; a primary care conversion factor of $48 is below the market median, $58 is on the high end, and a surgical $62 is competitive.
correct_statement: No source is cited and MGMA percentile tables are paywalled. Public data put primary care medians at about $48-$56 per wRVU, so $48 is at or just below median and $58 above it. $62 equals the self-reported general surgery contract median but trails orthopedics ($70-$79), and hematology-oncology runs $90-$100, so $65 is not the ceiling.
source_title: AMGA 2026 Medical Group Compensation and Productivity Survey: Selected Data (June 2026; 2025 data, 451 groups, about 188,000 providers; all-in compensation per wRVU); Marit Health, wRVUs and $ per wRVU by Specialty (Oct. 21, 2026; self-reported contract rates, https://www.marithealth.com/posts/wrvus-by-specialty-and-per-wrvu)
practice_impact: Geriatrics is paid like primary care: expect roughly $48-$56 per wRVU, and check a current survey rather than this unsourced band before setting or accepting a rate.

claim: FMV (Fair Market Value): the value in arm's-length transactions consistent with general market value - the standard used by Stark Law to evaluate physician compensation; MGMA benchmarks are used as the primary FMV reference.
correct_statement: The definition matches 42 CFR 411.351, but fair market value is one of three tests in the Stark employment exception, with no payment for referral volume or value and commercial reasonableness. No rule makes MGMA the primary reference: CMS repealed its survey-based safe harbor in 2007, calls surveys a starting point, and recommends multiple independent surveys.
source_title: 42 CFR 411.351 and 411.357(c) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); CMS, Modernizing and Clarifying the Physician Self-Referral Regulations, 85 FR 77492, 77557-77558 (Dec. 2, 2020); Stark Phase III final rule, 72 FR 51012, 51015 (Sept. 5, 2007); Phase II interim final rule, 69 FR 16054, 16128 (Mar. 26, 2004)
practice_impact: A practice paying or receiving physician compensation tied to designated health services should document fair market value from more than one survey plus its own facts, not an MGMA percentile alone.

claim: The MGMA Physician Compensation and Production Report, published annually, shows compensation at the 25th, 50th, 75th and 90th percentiles; the MGMA benchmark figures represent total compensation - base salary plus all incentives and bonuses.
correct_statement: Correct in substance. MGMA releases the data each May, now as the paid DataDive Provider Compensation data set, reporting the 10th through 90th percentiles. Its total compensation is reported W-2 or K-1 pay: base salary, incentives or bonuses, on-call and directorship pay. It excludes employer-paid benefits and retirement contributions. Guaranteed starting salaries are a separate data set.
source_title: MGMA, Frequently Asked Questions: Data Solutions (mgma.com/faq, fetched Nov. 10, 2026); MGMA DataDive Definitions Glossary (2025), Total Compensation; MGMA, Provider Compensation Data (fetched Nov. 10, 2026)
practice_impact: Compare offers to MGMA total compensation without adding benefits, since MGMA excludes them; the percentile tables need a paid DataDive subscription, so the guide's look-it-up advice is not free to follow.

claim: Some states - California is the most notable example - largely do not enforce physician non-competes on public policy grounds. Other states enforce them strictly. Many states evaluate non-competes on a reasonableness standard.
correct_statement: Accurate as a general map. California voids employment non-competes by statute. Florida enforces reasonable ones firmly: courts must ignore individual hardship and presume irreparable injury, and its 2025 high-earner law excludes health care practitioners. No federal ban exists; the FTC removed its rule in February 2026. Since 2025 Arkansas, Montana and Wyoming voided physician non-competes; Texas and Maryland restricted them.
source_title: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code 16600 (as amended eff. Jan. 1, 2024; text via california.public.law, accessed Nov. 2026); Fla. Stat. 542.335, 542.336 and 542.43(3) (2026 Florida Statutes); FTC final rule, 91 FR 6507 (Feb. 12, 2026); Maynard Nexsen, Recent Developments in Physician Non-Compete Agreements (June 29, 2026)
practice_impact: Florida sits on the strict side: patient relationships are a protectable interest, restraints up to 6 months are presumed reasonable and over 2 years unreasonable, with a carve-out where one employer has every specialist in a county.

claim: Courts in many states will interpret ambiguous non-compete terms against the employer who drafted them, but reaching that resolution requires litigation.
correct_statement: True in some states only. Reading ambiguity against the drafter is a general contract rule, and courts such as Virginia's resolve non-compete ambiguities for the employee. Florida law says the opposite: courts must construe a restrictive covenant to protect the employer's legitimate interests, may not construe it against the drafter, and must narrow an overbroad restraint, not void it.
source_title: Fla. Stat. 542.335(1)(c) and (1)(h) (2026 Florida Statutes); Omniplex World Services Corp. v. US Investigations Services, Inc., 270 Va. 246 (Va. Sept. 16, 2005) (vacourts.gov); Cornell Legal Information Institute, Wex: contra proferentem (reviewed Aug. 2025)
practice_impact: In Florida a vague or overbroad non-compete is not read against the employer; a court trims it and enforces the rest, so fix radius and duration in writing before signing.

claim: Tail coverage can cost one to three times your annual malpractice premium. For high-risk specialties that can be $30,000 to $100,000 or more. For a primary care physician, it might be $8,000 to $20,000.
correct_statement: The multiple is about right: the AMA's insurance agency puts a purchased tail at about 200% of the final-year premium and ACP at 1.5 to 2 times. The dollar examples are unsourced and low for Florida, where $1M/$3M family practice premiums ran $19,255-$52,967 and obstetrics $107,837-$237,215, implying tails near $38,000-$106,000 and $215,000-$474,000.
source_title: AMA, Medical liability insurance: What final-year residents should know (June 16, 2026; AMA Insurance Agency); ACP, Claims-Made vs. Occurrence Malpractice Insurance; The Doctors Company, Extended Reporting Period (Tail) Coverage (2024); Florida Office of Insurance Regulation, Medical Malpractice Financial Information Annual Report (Oct. 1, 2025), Appendix A (https://www.floir.gov/docs-sf/default-source/property-and-casualty/medical-malpractice-closed-claim-database-and-rate-filing-annual-report/2025-med-mal-report---final.pdf) and Annual Report (Oct. 1, 2026)
practice_impact: A Florida primary care or geriatrics physician on a $1M/$3M claims-made policy should budget several times the guide's $8,000-$20,000 figure; lower limits cost less, and Florida rates rose a further 5.4% on average in 2025.

claim: Some agreements treat the signing bonus as taxable income at receipt but require repayment of the gross amount; you could pay taxes on $30,000, net $21,000, and then owe $30,000 back if you leave in month 18.
correct_statement: The mechanics are right: a bonus is taxed when paid by law (22% federal withholding plus 7.65% payroll tax leaves about $21,100 of $30,000), and a later-year repayment is of the gross. But the tax is not lost: a repayment over $3,000 earns a claim-of-right deduction or credit that year, and the employer can recover Social Security and Medicare tax.
source_title: IRS Publication 15 (Circular E), Employer's Tax Guide (2026), sec. 7 Supplemental Wages and sec. 13 Wage Repayments; IRS Publication 525 (2025), Taxable and Nontaxable Income, Repayments (https://www.irs.gov/publications/p525); 26 U.S.C. 1341
practice_impact: Florida has no state income tax, so a gross clawback is mostly a timing cost: federal income tax comes back through the claim-of-right credit or deduction on the repayment-year return, and same-year repayments are netted in payroll.

claim: The practice collects typically 85% to 95% of allowed/collectible charges (the net collection rate) in a well-run practice; measured against billed charges (gross collection rate), the figure is commonly in the 50% to 80% range.
correct_statement: The concept is right but both ranges miss published benchmarks. A well-run practice collects at least 95% of allowed amounts (AAFP); MGMA's family medicine median is 97.13%, so 85-90% signals a collection problem, not good performance. Gross collection rates are lower than stated: MGMA's family medicine median is 49.05% and billing-company survey means are 54-65%.
source_title: AAFP, Managing practice finances: Adjusted collection rate (fetched Nov. 10, 2026); Forvis Mazars, Know Your KPIs, Cash Flow and Claims Optimization, Kansas MGMA Annual Conference (Apr. 2026), citing MGMA DataDive 2025 Financials and Operations (2024 data) (https://s3.amazonaws.com/amo_hub_content/Association1992/files/KS%20MGMA%20Annual%20Conference%20-%20Know%20Your%20KPIs%2C%20Cash%20Flow%20and%20Claims%20Optimization%20-%20April%202026%20(1).pdf); HBMA RCM Advisor Q1 2024, Data Science Committee Survey Results (37 responses)
practice_impact: With mostly Medicare fee-schedule revenue, a geriatrics practice should hold net collections at 95% or better; treating 85% as well-run would hide about a tenth of collectible revenue and understate collections-based pay.

claim: E/M up-coding (systematic): Repayment + 3x penalties under FCA; ~$14K-$28K per claim (2024-25 inflation-adjusted)
correct_statement: FCA liability is three times the government's damages plus a per-claim civil penalty, and only for 'knowing' false claims; it is not repayment plus 3x. The penalty is $14,308 to $28,619 per claim for penalties assessed after July 3, 2025; DOJ announced no increase for 2026, so that range still applies today.
source_title: 28 CFR 85.5, Table 1 (eCFR current to 2026-11-06; last amended 90 FR 29447, July 3, 2025). Also: DOJ notice 'Civil Monetary Penalties Inflation Adjustments for 2026', 91 FR 43405, July 15, 2026 (https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/07/15/2026-14236/civil-monetary-penalties-inflation-adjustments-for-2026); 31 U.S.C. 3729(a)(1), (b)(1) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/31/3729)
practice_impact: Nursing-facility E/M levels (99304-99310) billed to Medicare/MA are the exposure: knowing or reckless upcoding risks treble damages plus up to $28,619 per claim, while honest errors still require refund within 60 days of identification (42 U.S.C. 1320a-7k(d)).

claim: Stark Law violations: $15K-$100K per violation; False Claims Act exposure
correct_statement: $15,000 and $100,000 are the unadjusted statutory amounts. Today the Stark civil monetary penalties are up to $31,670 per prohibited claim or service and up to $211,146 per circumvention arrangement or scheme, plus denial or refund of payment, assessments up to three times the amount claimed, possible exclusion, and False Claims Act exposure. HHS made no 2026 increase.
source_title: 45 CFR 102.3, Table 1 (eCFR current to 2026-11-06; last amended 91 FR 3665, Jan. 28, 2026: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/01/28/2026-01688/annual-civil-monetary-penalties-inflation-adjustment). Also: HHS notice 'No Adjustment to HHS Civil Monetary Penalty Amounts for 2026', 91 FR 66566 (https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/21/2026-21524/no-adjustment-to-hhs-civil-monetary-penalty-amounts-for-2026); 42 U.S.C. 1395nn(g)(3)-(4); 42 CFR 1003.310; Fla. Stat. 456.053(5)(e)-(f)
practice_impact: Financial relationships with labs, therapy, DME, home-health or facility entities the physicians refer to (including medical-director pay) are the Stark-sensitive areas; per-claim exposure is about double the vendor's figure, and Florida's Patient Self-Referral Act (s. 456.053) adds $15,000/$100,000 state penalties across all payers.

claim: HIPAA breach - unsecured PHI: $100-$50,000 per violation; up to $1.9M per category/year
correct_statement: Current HIPAA penalties per violation run from $145-$73,011 (no knowledge) to $73,011-$2,190,294 (uncorrected willful neglect), with a $2,190,294 calendar-year cap per identical provision; OCR applies lower annual caps to lower tiers under its 2019 enforcement discretion. $100-$50,000 is the unadjusted statute and $1.9M was the 2022 cap. HHS made no 2026 increase.
source_title: 45 CFR 102.3, Table 1, rows for 42 U.S.C. 1320d-5 / 45 CFR 160.404 (eCFR current to 2026-11-06; last amended 91 FR 3665, Jan. 28, 2026). Also: HHS notice 91 FR 66566, Oct. 21, 2026 (no 2026 adjustment); Notification of Enforcement Discretion Regarding HIPAA Civil Money Penalties, 84 FR 18151, Apr. 30, 2019 (https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2019/04/30/2019-08530/notification-of-enforcement-discretion-regarding-hipaa-civil-money-penalties); Fla. Stat. 501.171
practice_impact: Unencrypted laptops or phones used on facility rounds are the obvious unsecured-PHI risk; per-violation ceilings are about 46% above the vendor's figure, and Florida's FIPA (s. 501.171) separately requires notice within 30 days with penalties up to $500,000.

claim: Timely filing failure: 100% denial; no appeal pathway. Prevention: Submission within 72 hours of encounter
correct_statement: Late claims are denied, but deadlines and remedies differ by payer. Medicare: one calendar year from date of service; the denial is not appealable, though 42 CFR 424.44(b) grants four exceptions. Florida insurers and HMOs: six months (secondary 90 days), with statutory dispute resolution. Medicaid: 12 months. Submission within 72 hours is a vendor target, not a rule.
source_title: CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), Chapter 1, ss. 70, 70.4, 70.6, 70.7 (Rev. 12909, issued 10-24-24). Also: 42 CFR 424.44; First Coast Service Options, 'What is the claim timely filing guideline?' (https://medicare.fcso.com/node/5026); Fla. Stat. 627.6131(3)(b), (8) and 641.3155(2)(b) (2026) (https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2026/627.6131); Fla. Stat. 408.7057; 42 CFR 447.45(d)(1)
practice_impact: First Coast denies Part B claims received more than 12 months after the date of service (CO-29), and claims rejected as unprocessable do not count as filed; Florida commercial/HMO claims have only six months and secondary claims 90 days after the primary's determination.

claim: Typical reimbursement vs. Medicare: Medicare Advantage 85-110% of Medicare; Medicaid 50-80% of Medicare (state-dependent)
correct_statement: MA physician prices cluster near 100% of Medicare: studies of 2007-2014 claims found 91%-102% across common physician services (97% for 99213), and non-contracted providers receive the Original Medicare amount. Medicaid fees averaged 75% of Medicare nationally in 2024, ranging 52%-132% by state, with 27 of 50 programs above 80%. Florida: 64% overall, 56% primary care.
source_title: KFF State Health Facts, Medicaid-to-Medicare Fee Index (2024 and 2019), sourced to Skopec, Pugazhendhi, Zuckerman, Health Affairs 2025;44(5):531-538 (https://doi.org/10.1377/hlthaff.2024.01530). According to PubMed: Trish et al., JAMA Intern Med 2017;177(9):1287-1295 (https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2017.2679); Pelech, Med Care Res Rev 2020;77(3):236-248 (https://doi.org/10.1177/1077558718780604). Also: 42 CFR 422.214; Fla. Stat. 409.908(13)(b) (https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2026/409.908); CMS QMB billing protections (https://www.cms.gov/medicare/medicaid-coordination/qualified-medicare-beneficiary-program)
practice_impact: For dual-eligible residents Florida Medicaid pays nothing toward Medicare coinsurance when Medicare's payment already meets the Medicaid rate (s. 409.908(13)(b)) and QMBs cannot be billed, so those visits collect only Medicare's 80% share; check each MA contract's actual percent of Medicare.

claim: For independent physician practices, multiples typically range from 2x to 6x [EBITDA]; Primary care: 3-5x. Revenue multiples for physician practices typically range from 0.5x to 1.5x net revenue
correct_statement: No authoritative dataset was found supporting these ranges. MedPAC (2021, citing Casalino 2019) reports 8-12x EBITDA for large platform practices and 2-4x or less for small add-on practices, with EBITDA typically created by cutting owner-physician pay about 30%. The primary care 3-5x and 0.5-1.5x revenue figures have no traceable source; treat them as broker rules of thumb.
source_title: MedPAC, Report to the Congress: Medicare and the Health Care Delivery System, June 2021, Chapter 3 'Congressional request: Private equity and Medicare' (text and endnote 32, citing Casalino et al. 2019 and Helm 2019). Context only, no numeric ranges: Physicians Practice, 'Medical practice valuations', May 29, 2024 (https://www.physicianspractice.com/view/medical-practice-valuations)
practice_impact: A small physician-owned geriatrics practice that pays out its profit as physician compensation has little normalized EBITDA, so a multiple may produce a low value; a sale to a hospital or other referral recipient must be at appraised fair market value under Stark/AKS.

claim: Family Medicine median updated to ~5,200 wRVUs/year per recent MGMA-derived benchmark data; 75th percentile 6,100. Internal Medicine median 4,000; 75th percentile 4,900
correct_statement: MGMA specialty percentile tables are paywalled, so 5,200 and 6,100 cannot be confirmed exactly; MGMA's public charts show 2024 primary care median wRVUs of about 5,200 (physician-owned) and 5,550 (hospital-owned). A 4,000 internal medicine median is well below published benchmarks: AMGA's 2026 survey reports medians of 6,505 for family medicine and 6,390 for internal medicine.
source_title: AMGA 2026 Medical Group Compensation and Productivity Survey: Selected Data (June 2026; 2025 data). Also: MGMA, 'Key Insights: 2025 Provider Compensation and Productivity Trends and Benchmarks' with median work RVU charts (2024 data) (https://www.mgma.com/2025-provider-compensation); MGMA 2024 Provider Compensation Data Report (2023 data) (https://www.mgma.com/getkaiasset/252744ee-c63b-4a96-9211-8a5d6b908b39/MGMA-2024-Provider-Compensation-Data-Report.pdf)
practice_impact: Office-based family/internal medicine medians are the wrong yardstick for nursing-facility geriatrics, and a 4,000 'median' would understate targets by roughly a quarter to a third; license the MGMA or AMGA geriatrics line before benchmarking productivity or setting compensation.

claim: Set your fee schedule at a minimum of 200-250% of Medicare. Anything lower is a structural leak.
correct_statement: No CMS, AMA or MGMA standard was found setting a 200-250% floor; it is a rule of thumb. Payers pay the lesser of charge or allowable, so charges need only exceed the highest allowable per code. In Florida the top statutory allowables are PIP at 200% of Medicare and workers' compensation at 175% (210% surgical), so about 200-210% is defensible.
source_title: Fla. Stat. 627.736(5)(a) (2026 Florida Statutes). Also: Fla. Stat. 440.13(12)(f)-(g) (https://www.flsenate.gov/Laws/Statutes/2026/440.13); 42 U.S.C. 1395w-4(a)(1) (Medicare pays the lesser of actual charge or fee schedule amount) and 1395w-4(g) limiting charge (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/42/1395w-4); 42 U.S.C. 1320a-7(b)(6)(A); AAPC member forum threads stating there is no rule or regulation for setting fees (https://www.aapc.com/discuss/threads/determining-how-much-to-set-your-fee-schedule.193884/)
practice_impact: Medicare, MA and Medicaid pay fixed allowables, so higher charges add nothing from them; the level matters only for auto/PIP, workers' comp, out-of-network and self-pay accounts, and one uniform schedule is needed because charging Medicare substantially more than usual charges risks exclusion (42 U.S.C. 1320a-7(b)(6)).

claim: Stark exceptions require that compensation arrangements be set in advance, in writing, for a period of at least one year. They must be signed by all parties. Oral arrangements do not qualify.
correct_statement: Only some Stark exceptions require this. Personal service arrangements and office or equipment leases must be written, signed and last at least one year. Bona fide employment (42 CFR 411.357(c)) and group-practice pay need no writing, signature or term; the fair-market-value exception has no minimum term; limited remuneration (up to $6,237 in 2026) needs no writing.
source_title: 42 CFR 411.357(c), (d), (l), (z) and 411.354(e) (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026; last amended 2023); CMS Phase II interim final rule, 69 FR 16054, 16067-68 (Mar. 26, 2004); CMS Physician Self-Referral CPI-U Updates page (CY 2026 limited remuneration limit $6,237)
practice_impact: Employed physicians need no one-year written Stark contract (written agreements remain prudent); the writing, signature and one-year rules bite on independent-contractor and medical-director agreements with SNFs, hospices, home health agencies, hospitals and labs.

claim: Arrangements that have lapsed, where the written agreement has expired but the arrangement continues, lose their Stark exception protection until a new agreement is executed.
correct_statement: Since Jan. 1, 2016, an expired lease or personal service agreement of at least one year stays protected indefinitely as a holdover if it continues on the same terms and still meets every exception requirement, including fair market value. Protection is lost only if terms change or a requirement fails. Employment arrangements never needed a writing.
source_title: 42 CFR 411.357(a)(7), (b)(6), (d)(1)(vii), (l)(2) (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026); CY 2016 Physician Fee Schedule final rule, 80 FR 70886, 71318-71320 (Nov. 16, 2015), effective Jan. 1, 2016 (govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2015-11-16/html/2015-28005.htm)
practice_impact: Medical-director or contractor agreements with SNFs, hospices or home health agencies that expired but continued unchanged are likely still protected if records show identical terms; do not refund or self-disclose on the vendor's reading without counsel, and re-paper before changing pay or duties.

claim: Compensation under a Stark exception cannot be determined in a manner that takes into account the volume or value of referrals. This prohibition is absolute. A productivity bonus based partly on referral volume, even indirectly, violates Stark.
correct_statement: Most compensation exceptions bar pay that takes referral volume or value into account, but not absolutely. Since 2021 the test is met only if referrals are a variable in the formula. Group practices may pay profit shares indirectly reflecting designated health services and bonuses on personally performed and incident-to services; value-based and physician-incentive-plan exceptions carry no such bar.
source_title: 42 CFR 411.354(d)(5), 411.352(g) and (i), 411.357(c)(4), (d)(2), (aa) (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026); Modernizing and Clarifying the Physician Self-Referral Regulations, final rule, 85 FR 77492, 77537-38 and 77559 (Dec. 2, 2020)
practice_impact: wRVU bonuses on personally performed facility visits are expressly permitted; never put home health, lab, therapy, DME or hospital referrals into a pay formula. Florida's all-payer kickback and patient-brokering laws (ss. 456.054, 817.505) also reach referral-based pay.

claim: A physician-owner earning $600,000 per year in a market where the FMV for their specialty and productivity is $350,000 has a $250,000 annual exposure that does not disappear because the physician holds an ownership stake.
correct_statement: Stark imposes no fair-market-value test on what a physician-owned group practice pays its owners. Their in-practice referrals rest on the in-office ancillary services exception and group-practice rules, which bar only pay tied directly to referral volume or value. Stark liability is refund of tainted designated-health-service claims plus penalties up to $31,670 per service, not the pay gap.
source_title: CMS Phase II interim final rule, 69 FR 16054, 16067-68 (Mar. 26, 2004); 42 CFR 411.351, 411.352, 411.353, 411.355(a)-(b) (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026); 45 CFR 102.3 (as amended at 91 FR 3666, Jan. 28, 2026); IRS, S corporation compensation and medical insurance issues (reviewed Mar. 3, 2026)
practice_impact: A practice billing only visits and care management (no lab, imaging, therapy, DME) furnishes no designated health services, so Stark does not police owner pay, and Florida s. 817.505(3)(b) likewise exempts payments within a group practice; owner pay is a tax, anti-kickback and buyer-diligence question.

claim: The FMV standard is met when compensation falls within the range supported by objective, commercially reasonable evidence, typically benchmark survey data from recognized sources such as MGMA or AMGA.
correct_statement: Stark defines fair market value as the value in an arm's-length transaction consistent with general market value: what well-informed parties not positioned to generate business for each other would pay. CMS calls salary surveys an appropriate starting point, sometimes sufficient, but rejects any percentile safe harbor. Commercial reasonableness is a separate requirement, not the evidentiary standard for FMV.
source_title: Modernizing and Clarifying the Physician Self-Referral Regulations, final rule, 85 FR 77492, 77555-58 (Dec. 2, 2020); 42 CFR 411.351 definitions of fair market value, general market value and commercially reasonable (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026)
practice_impact: Matching an MGMA or AMGA percentile is not a safe harbor; medical-director stipends and facility-based geriatric pay need documented duties, hours and local market facts, using geriatrics-specific survey cuts rather than generic primary care medians.

claim: Nationally, conversion factors generally range from approximately $45 to $65 per wRVU... A primary care physician may have a conversion factor in the $45 to $55 range. A proceduralist may command $55 to $65 or higher.
correct_statement: The $45-$65 national band has no cited source. AMGA's 2026 survey (2025 data) reports median compensation-per-wRVU ratios of $50.52-$55.62 in primary care (family medicine $52.61), consistent with the claim, but $68.79 cardiology, $72.28 gastroenterology, $74.48 general surgery and $78.94 orthopedics, above the stated range. These are all-in pay ratios, not contract rates.
source_title: AMGA 2026 Medical Group Compensation and Productivity Survey: Selected Data (June 2026; 2025 data from 451 groups, about 188,000 providers). Practice-impact figures computed from CMS RVU26D relative value and GPCI files (released Aug. 26, 2026) and Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 12, sec. 20.4.2
practice_impact: Medicare's 2026 Florida allowed amount is only about $51-$56 per wRVU for SNF visits 99308-99310 (POS 31) and $59-$65 in POS 32, before sequestration and overhead; a $45-$55 conversion factor could consume nearly all visit revenue.

claim: Typical primary care (illustrative): 25th percentile ~3,500 wRVUs/year and ~$157,500; median ~4,500 and ~$220,500; 75th ~5,500 and ~$286,000; 90th ~6,500 and ~$357,500 total comp.
correct_statement: The table is not survey data: each pay figure is wRVUs times an assumed $45-$55, and it sits far below current benchmarks. AMGA's 2026 survey (2025 data) reports medians of 6,505 wRVUs and $342,411 for family medicine and 6,390 and $361,426 for internal medicine. MedPAC reports $308,000 median primary care compensation for 2024. Percentile tables are paywalled.
source_title: AMGA 2026 Medical Group Compensation and Productivity Survey: Selected Data (June 2026); MedPAC, March 2026 Report to the Congress, ch. 4, pp. 128-129 (SullivanCotter 2025 survey, 2024 pay; medpac.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Mar26_Ch4_MedPAC_Report_To_Congress_SEC.pdf); MGMA, Key Insights: 2025 Provider Compensation and Productivity Trends and Benchmarks (mgma.com/2025-provider-compensation)
practice_impact: Benchmarking against this table would understate market pay by roughly a third and label a median producer as 90th percentile; buy geriatrics-specific MGMA or AMGA cuts, since public medians reflect general primary care, not nursing-facility practice.

claim: wRVUs do not reflect administrative work, care coordination, supervision of mid-levels, teaching, committee participation, or any non-clinical contribution a physician makes to the practice.
correct_statement: Unbilled administrative, committee and teaching time earns no wRVUs, but care coordination does when billed: in 2026 Medicare assigns 1.00 wRVU to chronic care management (99490), 2.78-3.79 to transitional care management, 1.50 to advance care planning and 1.73 to care plan oversight. Incident-to and split/shared services by nurse practitioners can also bill under the physician.
source_title: CMS, 2026 National Physician Fee Schedule Relative Value File, October release (RVU26D, released Aug. 26, 2026); CMS, Frequently Asked Questions About Practitioner Billing for Chronic Care Management Services (updated Aug. 16, 2022); 42 CFR 410.26 and 415.140 (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026)
practice_impact: Care management, transitional care, advance care planning and cognitive assessment are core geriatrics revenue, and CMS says CCM is billable for SNF, nursing facility and assisted living patients; the comp plan must state who gets that wRVU credit.

claim: The contract may limit how you export [your patient data], charge fees for data extraction, or restrict the format in which data is returned if you leave.
correct_statement: Such terms exist, but federal law limits them. HIPAA bars a business associate from blocking the practice's access to its patient data and requires return in a usable format when the agreement says so. Developers of ONC-certified health IT must supply a full patient-data export in a documented format and risk information-blocking penalties for charging export fees to switch systems.
source_title: 45 CFR 171.302, 170.315(b)(10), 170.402 and 164.504(e)(2)(ii)(J) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); ONC blog quoting HHS OCR HIPAA FAQ 2074 (Nov. 1, 2016); ONC final rule 91 FR 67916 (Oct. 28, 2026) retaining the export criterion
practice_impact: Ask whether the product is ONC-certified (export rights then exist by rule); for billing-only or clearinghouse vendors the protection is the business associate agreement, so write export terms there.

claim: Patient responsibility now represents 25 to 35 percent of independent practice revenue.
correct_statement: No traceable source gives 25-35%, and the vendor cites none. CMS national accounts put patients' out-of-pocket payments at 8.5% of physician and clinical services spending in 2024, unchanged since 2022 and down from 10.9% in 2000. Kodiak's data from 2,300 hospitals and 350,000 physicians put insured patient responsibility at 7.3% of net revenue in 2025.
source_title: CMS National Health Expenditure Accounts, Table 8, Physician and Clinical Services Expenditures by Source of Funds, 1970-2024 (tables dated Dec. 2025); Kodiak Solutions KPI Benchmarking Report (Mar. 2026); Kroll, Healthcare IT Services Insights (Jan. 2018)
practice_impact: Do not size patient-payment tools on 25-35%: Part B patients owe 20% coinsurance that Medigap or Medicaid usually pays and QMB patients cannot be billed, so the practice's patient-paid share is likely single digits (inference; confirm in its ledger).

claim: Vendor liability is typically capped at the amount paid in the prior month or quarter.
correct_statement: Liability caps tied to fees paid are standard, but the period varies. Published terms checked November 2026 use the prior 2 months (Veradigm Payerpath clearinghouse), 3 months (DrChrono), 6 months (Tebra) and 12 months (Inbox Health). ONC's contract guide and a 2023 law-firm survey of SaaS terms (about 75%) show 12 months as the most common vendor position.
source_title: ONC, EHR Contracts Untangled (2016), secs. 7.4-7.5; Herzog, What's Market in SaaS (2023 survey); public terms of DrChrono, Tebra, Veradigm Payerpath and Inbox Health (retrieved Nov. 10, 2026)
practice_impact: Read the actual cap: small-practice vendors do publish 2- to 6-month caps, so the playbook's 12-month target is a fair floor; also seek carve-outs for data breach and HIPAA indemnity.

claim: A clearinghouse with a 3% lower first-pass acceptance rate, at 500 claims per month, produces 180 additional denied claims annually, each needing follow-up and often only partial recovery.
correct_statement: The arithmetic holds: 3% of 500 claims a month is 15 a month, 180 a year. But claims that fail first-pass acceptance are rejections, not denials: they never reach adjudication, carry no appeal rights, and are corrected and resubmitted for full payment if otherwise payable. The cost is rework and delay, plus timely-filing risk, not partial recovery.
source_title: CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), ch. 1 §80.3.1 (Rev. 13725, issued Apr. 10, 2026)
practice_impact: Track clearinghouse rejections separately from payer denials; rejected Part B claims are refiled as new claims, so the risk is delay and the one-year filing limit, not lost revenue per claim.

claim: Minimum standard: a live real-time eligibility check should return copay, deductible, and auth requirements, not just active coverage, with alerts for authorization requirements and benefit limitations.
correct_statement: Copay, coinsurance and deductible (base and remaining) are federally mandated content of the eligibility response for required service types. Authorization requirements and benefit limits are not: they sit in an updated CAQH CORE rule that HHS has not adopted, so results vary by payer. Medicare's system returns Part B deductible, coinsurance and a prior-authorization flag for submitted procedure codes.
source_title: 45 CFR 162.1203 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); CAQH CORE Phase I 154 Data Content Rule v1.1.0; CAQH CORE Proposed Operating Rules summary (Nov. 2022); CMS HETS 270/271 Companion Guide v15-1 (May 2026)
practice_impact: For a Medicare nursing-facility practice the fields that matter are Medicare Advantage enrollment, hospice election, QMB status and Part A facility stays; test those in the demo rather than copays.

claim: Data migration ranges from $5,000 to $50,000+ depending on data volume and complexity.
correct_statement: No authoritative cost range was found and the playbook cites none. ONC says only that data transfer and conversion fees "vary widely." Published examples run from free (eClinicalWorks migrates existing EHR data at no charge) to vendor-blog estimates of $20,000-$50,000 for a small practice, none backed by data. For ONC-certified systems, export-to-switch fees fall outside the information-blocking fees exception.
source_title: ONC, EHR Contracts Untangled: Selecting Wisely, Negotiating Terms, and Understanding the Fine Print (2016), sec. 9.2-9.3; eClinicalWorks pricing page (retrieved Nov. 10, 2026); 45 CFR 171.302(b)(3)-(4)
practice_impact: Budget from written quotes, not this range: get the outgoing vendor's export terms and the incoming vendor's conversion fee in writing; for a small billing database the fee may be zero.

claim: A portal that converts 85% of statement recipients into payers versus one that converts 60% is a gap entirely attributable to friction in the payment process; 90-day target: payment completion rate above 70%.
correct_statement: No published benchmark supports 85%, 60% or a 70% payment-completion target; the playbook cites none. Whether patients pay depends heavily on balance size and finances, not only portal design: in data from 1,348 practices, 93.8% of small balances (up to $35) was paid within a year versus 66.7% above $200, and insured patients paid 42.4% of amounts owed in 2025.
source_title: Chernew M, Bush J, As Patients Take On More Costs, Will Providers Shoulder The Burden?, Health Affairs Blog (May 4, 2017; read via PNHP reprint); Kodiak Solutions KPI Benchmarking Report (Mar. 2026); MGMA Stat, Patient balance collection (Oct. 2025)
practice_impact: Likely little for a nursing-facility practice: balances are mainly Part B coinsurance, usually billed to secondary insurers or family, and QMB balances cannot be billed (inference); do not adopt 70% as a target.

claim: A system transition typically brings 30 to 90 days of reduced efficiency, and 60 to 90 days before staff reach pre-transition efficiency; buffer with a cash reserve equal to 2 months of expenses.
correct_statement: A temporary dip is real, but these durations have no traceable source and measured data run longer. In an AHRQ-funded study of 26 primary care practices, productivity was 8% lower for six months after an EHR go-live and visits were still 4.5% lower at 12 months. Expert commentary says about two months. No source was found for the two-month reserve.
source_title: Fleming NS et al., AHRQ Grant Final Report R03HS018220 (2011), published as Health Serv Res 2014;49(1 Pt 2):405-420, doi:10.1111/1475-6773.12133 (PubMed PMID 24359533); Bates DW et al., J Gen Intern Med 2023;38(Suppl 4):946-948, doi:10.1007/s11606-023-08329-7
practice_impact: Evidence is for clinical record systems, not billing software; plan for a dip that may last months, size the reserve from the practice's own days in A/R, and keep the old system readable.

claim: Claims submitted during a Medicare deactivation period are not retroactively compensable after billing privileges are reactivated; the gap is a permanent revenue loss, not a delay.
correct_statement: Correct in substance. Medicare pays nothing for items or services furnished while billing privileges are deactivated (42 CFR 424.540(e), 424.555(b)); reactivation takes effect only on the date the contractor receives the reactivation application it later approves (424.540(d)(2)). The bar turns on date of service, not claim submission date; deactivation may be backdated to the date non-compliance began (424.540(d)(1)(ii)).
source_title: 42 CFR 424.540 Deactivation of Medicare billing privileges (eCFR, current through 2026-11-06); CMS Revalidations (Renewing Your Enrollment)
practice_impact: A missed revalidation or unanswered First Coast request leaves facility visits unpaid from the deactivation date until a complete reactivation application is received; patients cannot be billed for them.

claim: Medicare sets the effective date as the later of the application filing date or the date services first began at the enrolled location; retroactive billing is permitted up to 30 days prior when circumstances precluded advance enrollment.
correct_statement: Correct for physicians, non-physician practitioners and their groups. Effective date is the later of the filing date of an application the contractor subsequently approves or the date services first began at a new practice location (42 CFR 424.520(d)). Retrospective billing reaches back 30 days if circumstances precluded earlier enrollment, or 90 days for a Presidentially declared disaster (424.521(a)).
source_title: 42 CFR 424.520 Effective date of Medicare billing privileges; 42 CFR 424.521 Request for payment by certain provider and supplier types (eCFR, current through 2026-11-06)
practice_impact: For a new physician or nurse practitioner, visits more than 30 days before the Medicare effective date are unpayable; a rejected or returned application resets the filing date.

claim: Start commercial payer credentialing a minimum of 120 days before a new provider is scheduled to see patients. Start Medicare enrollment 90 days out. [Onboarding table: submit Medicare PECOS enrollment 120 days before start.]
correct_statement: The 120-day commercial lead time is an industry rule of thumb, not a rule. The Medicare advice is wrong and self-contradictory (90 versus 120 days): a contractor may return, without appeal rights, a physician or practitioner application received more than 60 days before the effective date listed on it (42 CFR 424.526(a)(2)). File Medicare within 60 days of start.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.526 Return of a provider's or supplier's enrollment application (eCFR, current through 2026-11-06); First Coast, CMS-855 enrollment application processing timeframes (Feb. 18, 2026)
practice_impact: Following the playbook's 120-day table gets a new clinician's CMS-855I and reassignment returned by First Coast; the 60-day window plus 30-day retrospective billing is the real Medicare timeline.

claim: Most providers revalidate Medicare enrollment every five years (DMEPOS suppliers every three); due dates are published on the Medicare Revalidation List at data.cms.gov and are updated seven months before the deadline.
correct_statement: Correct. Providers and suppliers other than DMEPOS revalidate every 5 years (42 CFR 424.515); DMEPOS suppliers every 3 years (424.57(g)); CMS may require off-cycle revalidation. CMS posts due dates on the Medicare Revalidation List (data.cms.gov/revalidation) seven months in advance; revalidations filed more than 7 months early are returned; contractor notices arrive about 3-4 months before the due date.
source_title: CMS, Revalidations (Renewing Your Enrollment), page last modified 07/29/2025; 42 CFR 424.515, 424.57(g), 424.526(a)(8)
practice_impact: Each clinician and the group should be looked up on the Revalidation List; due dates more than seven months out are not yet posted, so the lookup should be repeated quarterly.

claim: CMS launched PECOS 2.0 in late 2025, replacing the legacy enrollment portal; legacy PECOS credentials and workflows do not transfer automatically and the transition requires account re-configuration.
correct_statement: No CMS source shows PECOS 2.0 replacing legacy PECOS in late 2025. On 2026-11-10 the provider login at pecos.cms.hhs.gov is still the legacy application (version 7.59), and CMS's July 2026 enrollment manual still treats PECOS 2.0 as awaiting implementation. CMS's own PECOS 2.0 FAQ says logins (I&A user ID and password), connections and existing records will carry over.
source_title: CMS, PECOS 2.0 FAQs (PDF, modified June 2025); Medicare Program Integrity Manual ch. 10 (Rev. 13717, 07-08-26) sec. 10.3; live PECOS login page fetched 2026-11-10
practice_impact: No account re-configuration project is needed; keep each clinician's I&A login, surrogacy connections and the authorized official current and keep using the existing PECOS site.

claim: CAQH ProView requires re-attestation every 120 days; a profile not attested within 120 days moves to Expired status. Illinois operates on a 180-day window, the only state with a different standard.
correct_statement: Correct on the rule. Profiles must be re-attested every 120 days, every 180 days for Illinois providers, the only exception CAQH names; a profile not attested in time moves to Expired (Expired Attestation) status. The product name is out of date: ProView became the CAQH Provider Data Portal in 2023, and CAQH now operates as DataSpring.
source_title: DataSpring (CAQH) Resources FAQs, fetched 2026-11-10; CAQH Provider Data Portal Provider User Guide v43 (08/22/2023), sections 8.2-8.3
practice_impact: Florida clinicians are on the 120-day cycle; a lapsed attestation stalls commercial and Medicare Advantage credentialing and recredentialing files.

claim: Medicare allows billing under the supervising physician's NPI for locum arrangements that meet the Q6 modifier requirements.
correct_statement: Medicare lets the absent regular physician (or the group, under that physician's NPI), not a "supervising" physician, bill a substitute physician's visits with modifier Q6 if the regular physician is unavailable and pays the substitute per diem, for no more than 60 continuous days. Physicians only (plus physical therapists in shortage or rural areas), not nurse practitioners or physician assistants.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) ch. 1 sec. 30.2.11 (chapter Rev. 13725, 04-10-26); First Coast, Reciprocal billing and fee-for-time compensation arrangements (Oct. 29, 2024)
practice_impact: Q6 cannot cover a nurse practitioner or physician assistant, a new hire awaiting enrollment, or coverage beyond 60 days; misuse is a false certification that risks revocation of billing privileges.

claim: Medicaid does not grant retroactive effective dates in most circumstances; unlike Medicare, there is generally no retroactive billing right for services before the enrollment effective date.
correct_statement: This is state-specific, so the generalization fails. Florida sets the Medicaid enrollment effective date at the date AHCA receives the application, not the approval date, and backdates to the date of service only for emergency services and out-of-state providers. Several other states do allow retroactive enrollment before the application date, up to one year in Ohio and Oregon.
source_title: Florida Statutes s. 409.907(9)(a) (2026); Florida Medicaid Provider Enrollment Policy (Feb. 2026) sec. 2.14; MACPAC June 2026 Report to Congress, ch. 7
practice_impact: For Florida Medicaid and dual-eligible crossover claims, payment runs from the day AHCA receives the application, so file before a new clinician's first visit; there is no 30-day look-back.

claim: File as early as legally possible, which is 30 days before the practice opens.
correct_statement: The limit is 60 days, not 30. A MAC may return a physician or group practice application received more than 60 days before the effective date listed on it, so filing up to 60 days before opening is allowed. The 30-day figure matches the separate retrospective-billing window and a superseded mid-2000s carrier practice.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.526(a)(2) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); First Coast Service Options, Top reasons for immediate returns of enrollment applications (Feb. 13, 2026); Medicare Program Integrity Manual ch. 10 §10.4.1.4.2 (Rev. 13415, eff. 10-20-25); CMS Transmittal 415, CR 7797 (Apr. 13, 2012); AAPC Part B Insider (Feb. 27, 2007) for the old 30-day First Coast practice
practice_impact: When onboarding a physician or NP, file the CMS-855I up to 60 days before the start date, not 30; the playbook's other advice to file Medicare 90 days ahead risks having the application returned. CMS standards cited by First Coast: 95% of clean web applications within 15 days, 50 days if development is needed.

claim: Medicare enrollment for a new practice requires two applications, the CMS-855I ... and the CMS-855B ... Submit CMS-855B first, the organizational enrollment must be in process before the individual reassignment (CMS-855R) ... can be submitted
correct_statement: The CMS-855R was discontinued in 2023; reassignment is reported in CMS-855I Section 4F or CMS-855B Section 4H. A group files a CMS-855B plus a CMS-855I per clinician, and these may be filed concurrently; no rule requires the CMS-855B first. A physician who solely owns the PC/PA/LLC can enroll on a CMS-855I alone. Paper applications are still accepted.
source_title: Medicare Program Integrity Manual ch. 10 §§10.1.4, 10.3.1.3.4(G), 10.4.1.2(C), 10.6.2(C) (Rev. 13717, issued 07-08-26); Form CMS-855I (05/23) and Form CMS-855B (12/2025); CMS, Consolidated CMS-855I/CMS-855R Enrollment Applications bulletin (2023); First Coast, Provider enrollment decision tree (Feb. 10, 2026)
practice_impact: Staff following the playbook will look for a retired form and hold back the clinician's CMS-855I; a group application that arrives without the clinicians' CMS-855Is draws a development request, and a reassignment package still incomplete after 30 days can be rejected (42 CFR 424.525(a)(1)(ix)), resetting the effective date.

claim: The Medicare effective date cannot precede the date of the application ... Do not see Medicare patients until enrollment is confirmed, billing Medicare for services rendered before the effective enrollment date is a compliance violation
correct_statement: For physicians, NPs, PAs and group practices the effective date is the later of the application filing date or the date services began at the location, and billing may reach back up to 30 more days if requirements were met. Services from that date may be furnished before approval and billed afterward, within one year. Earlier services are not payable.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.520(d), 424.521(a), 424.44(a)(1) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026; not amended by the CY 2027 PFS or HH PPS final rules published Nov. 9, 2026); Medicare Program Integrity Manual ch. 10 §10.6.2 (Rev. 13717, issued 07-08-26); First Coast, Determining your Medicare effective date (Feb. 18, 2026)
practice_impact: Waiting for the approval letter before a new clinician rounds forfeits weeks of billable nursing-facility visits; file first, hold the claims, bill after approval. Visits more than 30 days before the filing date are a write-off, and a rejected application resets that date.

claim: Non-enrolled payers cannot be billed at all ... Revenue generated in months 1, 3 from unenrolled payers cannot be recovered retroactively in most cases.
correct_statement: It depends on the payer. Medicare pays from the application filing date, or up to 30 days earlier, with one year to file claims. Florida Medicaid's effective date is the date AHCA receives the application. Medicare Advantage plans pay non-contract providers Original Medicare amounts for covered out-of-network care. Commercial plans set their own effective dates, usually without backdating.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.520(d), 424.521(a), 424.44(a), 422.100(b), 422.214, 422.520 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); Fla. Stat. § 409.907(9)(a) (2026); Florida Senate bill histories, SB 1236 and HB 1109 (2025). No primary source located for commercial-plan backdating practice; that part rests on trade knowledge.
practice_impact: For a Medicare-heavy facility practice the playbook overstates the loss: traditional Medicare and Florida Medicaid visits after the filing date are billable once approved. The real exposure is mainly Medicare Advantage HMO and commercial patients seen before the contract effective date.

claim: Medicare enrollment applications require active management and response to information requests within 30 days or the application is rejected
correct_statement: A MAC may reject an application if complete information is not furnished within 30 calendar days of its request; CMS may extend the period for applicants actively working on it. Rejection carries no appeal rights and requires a new application, which resets the filing date. In PECOS, an application opened for corrections is deleted if not resubmitted within 20 days.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.525 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); First Coast, Life cycle of an enrollment application (Feb. 17, 2026); CMS, PECOS Inactivity Deletion Policy (PECOS notice 07/09/2026); Form CMS-855I (05/23) instructions
practice_impact: A missed First Coast development request kills the application and its filing date, so visits made more than 30 days before the replacement filing become unbillable; name one person to watch the application's contact email and PECOS status and to answer within days.

claim: Set a calendar reminder to re-attest every 120 days, CAQH profiles expire and an expired profile will pause enrollment applications mid-process
correct_statement: Correct for Florida: re-attestation is required every 120 days (180 days for Illinois providers), and the day after it lapses the provider's status becomes Expired. The product is now the CAQH Provider Data Portal, branded DataSpring, still at proview.caqh.org. How a payer treats an expired attestation varies by plan. Traditional Medicare enrollment (PECOS) does not use CAQH.
source_title: DataSpring | CAQH Provider Data Portal, Provider User Guide v46.0 (last updated 6/15/2026); Florida Blue, Keep Your Information Up to Date in CAQH (Feb. 2024)
practice_impact: Matters for Medicare Advantage and commercial credentialing of each physician and NP (Florida Blue marks a non-current profile a 'non-responder' at recredentialing and says the agreement could be affected); no bearing on traditional Medicare enrollment.

claim: Financial hardship policy, define the income threshold (typically based on federal poverty guidelines) ... The policy must be applied consistently to avoid HIPAA and anti-discrimination exposure.
correct_statement: Poverty-guideline thresholds are common but not prescribed ($15,960 for one person in 2026). The risk is not HIPAA: waiving Medicare cost-sharing is protected only if unadvertised, not routine, and based on a good-faith finding of financial need. Otherwise it risks beneficiary-inducement penalties (up to $25,595 per item), kickback and Florida insurance-fraud exposure. Civil-rights law bars unequal application by protected class.
source_title: 42 CFR 1003.110, 1003.1000, 1003.1010 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); 45 CFR 102.3 (as amended 91 FR 3666, Jan. 28, 2026); OIG Special Fraud Alert, Routine Waiver of Copayments or Deductibles Under Medicare Part B (FR Doc. 94-31157, Dec. 19, 1994); Fla. Stat. § 817.234(7)(a) (2026); 45 CFR 92.101; HHS 2026 Poverty Guidelines. oig.hhs.gov was unreachable from this session, so OIG's own guidance pages were not opened.
practice_impact: Nursing-facility patients are mostly Medicare or dual-eligible, so the live risk is routine write-off of the 20% coinsurance: document need patient by patient, never advertise or blanket-waive, and note that QMB dual-eligibles cannot be billed Medicare cost-sharing at all.

claim: set list-price fees in the range of 200 to 250 percent of Medicare allowables ... you can never collect more than your billed charge, even if the contracted rate is higher
correct_statement: Medicare pays the lesser of the actual charge or the fee schedule amount, and commercial contracts typically contain similar 'lesser of' language, so undercharging costs revenue. The 200-250% range is the vendor's own observation with no traceable source; MedPAC puts 2024 commercial PPO rates at 147% of Medicare on average (124% for care-management visits, 213% for CT scans).
source_title: MedPAC, Report to the Congress: Medicare Payment Policy, March 2026, ch. 4, p. 129; 42 CFR 414.21 and 414.48 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); Physicians Practice, Setting Charges (July 1, 2007) and Who Cares What You Charge? You Should (May 15, 2002)
practice_impact: Little for Medicare-paid facility visits: Medicare pays its fee schedule whatever the charge, so only Medicare Advantage and commercial contracts can be capped by a low charge. A non-participating practice could not charge Medicare patients 200-250%: unassigned claims are capped at the limiting charge, 115% of the non-par amount.

claim: In most independent practices, a substantial and growing share of total revenue - commonly cited in the range of 25 to 35 percent - comes directly from patients.
correct_statement: No traceable source supports 25-35%, and the vendor cites none. CMS national accounts show patients paid 8.5% of physician and clinical services spending out of pocket in 2024, flat since 2022 and down from 10.9% in 2000. The highest measure found, Kodiak's first-quarter 2026 data, puts patient responsibility near 23% of allowed amounts, with about 30% of it collected.
source_title: CMS National Health Expenditure Accounts, Table 8, Physician and Clinical Services Expenditures by Source of Funds, 1970-2024 (tables dated Dec. 23, 2025; downloaded Nov. 10, 2026); Kodiak Solutions, 'Untangling the patient financial responsibility web' (June 2026) and 'State of the healthcare revenue cycle' (Mar. 2026)
practice_impact: A Medicare-heavy geriatrics practice collects far less than 25% from patients: Part B coinsurance is usually covered by Medigap, retiree plans or Medicaid (KFF: 87% of traditional Medicare enrollees had supplemental coverage in 2023). Do not size staffing or forecasts on this figure.

claim: By the time an account reaches a third-party collector, practices typically recover roughly 20 to 30 cents on the dollar, and pay a percentage of that to the collection agency.
correct_statement: Directionally right, but 20-30 cents is the optimistic end and no rigorous dataset exists. The CFPB treated 25% as a high-side estimate of recovery on all medical debt, with accounts placed with collectors recovering less; trade sources cite 15-19% for medical accounts. Agencies then keep a contingency fee, often 30-40% and up to 50%, leaving roughly 10-15 cents.
source_title: CFPB final rule preamble (Regulation V, medical information), 90 FR 3276, 3324 (Jan. 14, 2025), cited only for its recovery-rate analysis; the rule itself was struck down by a federal court in July 2025; Physicians Practice, 'Reviewing Collectors' (June 1, 2004); Medical Economics, 'Getting paid: Strategies and best practices' (Apr. 17, 2015)
practice_impact: Little: balances are mostly small Part B coinsurance amounts, and Qualified Medicare Beneficiary balances may not be billed or sent to collections at all.

claim: Copay is collected before the patient is roomed, every visit, no exceptions. Outstanding balances are addressed at check-in, not deferred to statements.
correct_statement: 'No exceptions' is unlawful for much of a geriatrics panel. Providers may never collect Medicare deductibles, coinsurance or copays from Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries, in Original Medicare or Medicare Advantage. Florida Medicaid exempts institutional residents and managed-care enrollees from copays. Original Medicare has 20% coinsurance, not visit copays, and First Coast recommends not collecting it until Medicare has paid.
source_title: CMS MLN Fact Sheet MLN7936176, Prohibition on Billing Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries (Sept. 2025); First Coast Service Options, 'When not to show patient paid amounts on claims' (Oct. 29, 2024); Fla. Stat. 409.9081 (2026); 42 CFR 422.504(g)(1)(iii)
practice_impact: High: many nursing-facility and assisted-living patients are dual eligibles or QMBs; collecting from them means refunds and possible Medicare sanctions. Facility visits also have no check-in point.

claim: It does not have to be exact - estimates are standard and expected; confirm your state's estimate-disclosure and good-faith-estimate requirements with counsel.
correct_statement: For insured patients an estimate need not be exact; no federal rule yet governs it. But the binding good-faith-estimate rule is federal, not state: uninsured and self-pay patients must get a written estimate, and a bill $400 or more above it can be disputed. Florida also requires estimates on request. Medicare and Medicaid patients fall outside the federal rule.
source_title: 45 CFR 149.610 and 149.620 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); CMS fact sheet, 'What is Considered Health Insurance? Determining When Uninsured (or Self-Pay) Good Faith Estimate Rules Apply'; Fla. Stat. 381.026(4)(c) and 456.0575(2) (2026); CMS ABN form instructions (CMS-R-131)
practice_impact: Nearly all patients are Medicare or Medicaid enrollees, so federal estimates rarely apply; use ABNs with a reasonable cost estimate for likely non-covered services and give an estimate whenever a patient or family asks (Fla. Stat. 381.026).

claim: Automatic payment required: the patient provides a credit card, debit card, or bank account for automatic monthly drafts. Written terms: the patient signs (or digitally acknowledges) the payment plan terms, including the monthly amount and payment dates.
correct_statement: Signed written authorization, with a copy to the patient, is a federal requirement for recurring bank or debit-card drafts. But Regulation E bars conditioning credit on repayment by preauthorized electronic transfers, so mandatory autopay is a legal risk; offer it as an option. A practice with over 25 written plans a year exceeding four installments owes Truth in Lending disclosures.
source_title: Regulation E, 12 CFR 1005.10(b), (d), (e)(1) and Official Interpretation 10(e)(1)-1 and -4; Regulation Z, 12 CFR 1026.2(a)(14), (17) and Official Interpretation 2(a)(17)(i)-1 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026; CFPB interpretations pages)
practice_impact: If the practice offers installment plans: keep a non-autopay route, give patients a copy of the authorization, check Regulation Z once written plans pass 25 a year, and never put Qualified Medicare Beneficiary or Medicaid balances on a plan.

claim: Proactive hardship identification converts what would become a write-off into either a reduced-fee arrangement (which is collectible) or a formal charity designation.
correct_statement: Need-based reductions are lawful only within limits the playbook omits. A waiver of Medicare cost sharing must be unadvertised, not routine, and follow an individual good-faith finding of financial need; OIG says hardship waivers should be occasional. Otherwise the practice risks penalties up to $25,595 per item. Florida treats a general practice of waiving insureds' copays as insurance fraud.
source_title: 42 CFR 1003.110 (definition of 'remuneration'), 1003.1010 and 45 CFR 102.3 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026; penalty table amended 91 FR 3666, Jan. 28, 2026); OIG Special Fraud Alert, Routine Waiver of Copayments or Deductibles Under Medicare Part B, 59 FR 65372 (Dec. 19, 1994; FR Doc. 94-31157, govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-1994-12-19/html/94-31157.htm); Fla. Stat. 817.234(7)(a) (2026)
practice_impact: High: almost every balance here is Medicare cost sharing. Use written, uniform income criteria and document each decision; Qualified Medicare Beneficiary and Medicaid balances are not hardship cases, they may not be billed at all.

claim: A formal charity designation is appropriately written off and potentially tax-advantaged.
correct_statement: A for-profit practice gets no federal tax advantage from labelling a balance charity care. Donated services are not a deductible charitable contribution, and a cash-method practice cannot deduct fees it never collected as bad debt, because they were never included in income. Whether the write-off itself is proper depends on the OIG financial-need waiver conditions.
source_title: IRS Tax Topic No. 453, Bad debt deduction (page last reviewed Nov. 9, 2026); 26 CFR 1.166-1(e) and 1.170A-1(g) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026)
practice_impact: Expect no tax benefit from charity write-offs; they are simply revenue never collected and never taxed. Confirm treatment with the practice's CPA before adopting any charity-care policy on tax grounds.

claim: A practice with a well-functioning point-of-service collection system and effective statement cycle should collect 90 cents or more of every patient-responsibility dollar. Practices without front-end collection processes typically land in the 60-75% range.
correct_statement: Neither figure has a traceable source; the vendor calls 60-75% its own observation, and no 90% overall benchmark was found in MGMA or HFMA material. Measured results are lower: across 1,348 practices, 93.8% of small balances but 66.7% of balances over $200 were collected within a year (2015); Kodiak's hospital and physician clients collected 42.4% from insured patients in 2025.
source_title: Ippolito B, Trish E, Duffy EL, Vabson B, 'Patient Repayment of US Hospital Bills From 2018 to 2024', JAMA Health Forum 2025;6(8):e252284 (PubMed PMID 40779258); Chernew M, Bush J, Health Affairs Blog (May 4, 2017), as reproduced at pnhp.org/news/physicians-shouldering-more-of-patients-cost-sharing (original returned HTTP 403); Kodiak Solutions, 'State of the healthcare revenue cycle' (Mar. 2026); MGMA Stat (Oct. 22, 2025)
practice_impact: Do not adopt 90% as a staff target or count the claimed $45,000-$90,000 gap as expected gain; measure collection only on balances patients legally owe, excluding Qualified Medicare Beneficiary and Medicaid amounts.

claim: Medicare participation does not transfer in an asset acquisition, the acquiring entity must enroll in Medicare under its own NPI and PTAN, and the acquired providers must be enrolled under the new entity's NPI and group in PECOS.
correct_statement: Correct for physician practices. A supplier may not sell its Medicare billing number or let another entity use it, and an ownership change that changes the tax ID requires a new enrollment by the buyer. Each clinician then reassigns benefits to the buyer on Form CMS-855I. A buyer already enrolled adds the location and reassignments instead.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.550 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); Medicare Program Integrity Manual ch. 10, sec. 10.3.1.2.1 and 10.6.1.1.3.2 (Rev. 13717, July 8, 2026); Form CMS-855B (12/2025)
practice_impact: If the practice is bought or sold as assets, the buyer's enrollment and every clinician's reassignment must be filed anew with First Coast; the seller's Medicare number cannot be carried over.

claim: This process takes 30 to 60 days from completed application submission. During the Medicare enrollment gap, claims submitted to Medicare under the new entity will be rejected.
correct_statement: CMS requires contractors to finish 95% of clean online applications within 15 days and all within 50 (50 and 85 days when follow-up is needed), so 30 to 60 days is an estimate. Claims must wait but are not lost: billing privileges start on the filing date or first service date, whichever is later, with 30 days' retrospective billing.
source_title: Medicare Program Integrity Manual ch. 10, sec. 10.5 and 10.6.2 (Rev. 13717, July 8, 2026); 42 CFR 424.520(d) and 424.521(a); First Coast Service Options, 'CMS-855 enrollment application processing timeframes' (Feb. 18, 2026)
practice_impact: In a Florida asset purchase the buyer should file with First Coast by closing, hold Medicare claims until approval, then bill back to the effective date; the gap is a cash-flow delay, not lost revenue.

claim: The right path: begin PECOS enrollment 90+ days before close; target enrollment approval at or before close.
correct_statement: Filing that early gets a physician-group application returned. Florida's Medicare contractor says it must immediately return an application received more than 60 days before its listed effective date (90 days before the sale for institutional ownership changes), with no appeal rights. File within 60 days of closing; late approval still pays back to the later of closing or filing.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.526 and 424.510(d)(6) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); First Coast Service Options, 'Top reasons for immediate returns of enrollment applications' (Feb. 13, 2026); Medicare Program Integrity Manual ch. 10, sec. 10.4.1.4.2
practice_impact: A 90-day lead would get a First Coast application returned and force refiling, resetting the date Medicare starts paying. Florida Medicaid is the opposite: the buyer's application is due at least 60 days before the change (Fla. Stat. 409.907(6)(b)).

claim: NEVER attempt to bill Medicare under the acquired practice's legacy credentials after the ownership change has occurred, this creates False Claims Act exposure for the acquirer.
correct_statement: Correct for asset purchases: the seller may not let the buyer use its Medicare billing number, CMS may revoke enrollment for it, and knowingly false claims carry False Claims Act liability of triple damages plus $14,308 to $28,619 per claim. In a stock purchase the entity is unchanged, keeps its number and reports the ownership change within 30 days.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.550(a), 424.535(a)(7), 424.516(d)(1)(i) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); 28 CFR 85.5 and DOJ notice, 91 FR 43405 (July 15, 2026); Form CMS-855B (12/2025), section 14; CY 2027 home health final rule, 91 FR 72022 (Nov. 9, 2026)
practice_impact: After an asset sale closes, Medicare claims for the buyer's services must wait for the buyer's own First Coast enrollment; billing them under the seller's number risks revocation and fraud liability.

claim: Compliance issues from the pre-close period can become the acquirer's problem in an asset acquisition if not identified and addressed in the deal structure.
correct_statement: Correct as a risk statement. An asset buyer does not automatically escape the seller's billing history: OIG expressly recognizes successor liability from buying another entity, Florida Medicaid makes the transferee liable for overpayments identified before a change of ownership, and a buyer that accepts assignment of a Medicare provider agreement takes the seller's Medicare debt.
source_title: HHS-OIG Health Care Fraud Self-Disclosure Protocol (updated Oct. 15, 2026); Fla. Stat. 409.907(6) and 409.901(5) (2026); Form CMS-855B (12/2025); 42 CFR 489.18(c)-(d)
practice_impact: In a Florida deal, missing the Medicaid 60-day notice makes buyer and seller jointly liable for all Medicaid overpayments; a pre-close coding audit, disclosure warranties and indemnity are the minimum, as the playbook says.

claim: A standard AR quality adjustment applies collection probability by age bucket: 0, 30 days 95, 98 percent, 31, 60 days 85, 90 percent, 61, 90 days 70, 80 percent, 91, 120 days 50, 65 percent, 120-plus days 20, 40 percent.
correct_statement: No published standard sets these percentages; no MGMA, HFMA or valuation-body source for them was found, and vendor figures for older buckets disagree widely. Published guidance values receivables at expected reimbursement after contractual allowances, using the practice's own collection history by payer, and gives no value to accounts in collections or inactive for six months.
source_title: Medical Economics, 'How much is your medical practice worth?' (Sept. 10, 2010); Urology Times, 'Accounts receivable in your practice: Four common myths debunked' (Apr. 1, 2008); searches of MGMA, HFMA and trade sources on Nov. 10, 2026
practice_impact: Applying 95-98% to current receivables at face value would overstate a geriatrics practice's AR if balances are carried at gross charges; price AR from the practice's own payer-level collection history instead.

claim: Average revenue disruption in an unmanaged practice acquisition transition: 15, 25% of monthly collections for 60, 90 days post-close ... can be reduced to less than 5% and resolved within 30 days.
correct_statement: The document cites no source, and searches of MGMA, HFMA, trade and PubMed-indexed literature found no study measuring collections lost after a practice acquisition, managed or unmanaged. The mechanism is real, but with timely filing Medicare's share is a delay, not a loss: billing privileges start on the later of the filing date or first service date.
source_title: Searches on Nov. 10, 2026 (MGMA, HFMA, AMA, trade press, PubMed); Singh et al., JAMA Health Forum 2022;3(9):e222886, via PubMed (https://doi.org/10.1001/jamahealthforum.2022.2886); 42 CFR 424.520(d) and 424.521(a)
practice_impact: Do not use the 15-25% figure to price a deal or to judge the playbook's value; model the gap from the practice's own payer mix and each payer's effective-date rule.

claim: Most PE-backed physician practice acquisitions use a Management Services Organization (MSO) structure ... The physician entity remains the billing entity ... payer contracts are in the physician entity's name, and revenue belongs to the physician entity.
correct_statement: Accurate where states restrict the corporate practice of medicine: the investor typically owns a management company, and a clinician-owned professional entity employs the physicians and pays it a management fee. Florida law also allows another route: a practice not wholly owned by licensed practitioners generally needs a state health care clinic license, and referral fee-splitting is prohibited.
source_title: MedPAC, Report to the Congress: Medicare and the Health Care Delivery System (June 2021), ch. 3, 'Congressional request: Private equity and Medicare'; Fla. Stat. 400.9905(4)(g) and 458.331(1)(i) (2026); 42 CFR 424.80(b)
practice_impact: A Florida practice approached by an investor should know the management-company structure is a choice rather than a state mandate, and that investor ownership brings clinic licensure and fee-splitting review.

claim: Medicare withdrawal must be completed within 90 days of the decision to retire or close, through PECOS; DMEPOS suppliers have 30 days. The clock starts when the decision is made, not when the last patient is seen.
correct_statement: CMS says a clinician who retires, surrenders a license or leaves Medicare must withdraw within 90 days (DMEPOS suppliers 30), via PECOS or a paper CMS-855. No rule starts the clock at the decision: deadlines run from when the change occurs. Deleting a practice location must be reported within 30 days. Payment stops for services after the withdrawal date.
source_title: CMS, Manage Your Enrollment: Withdraw From Medicare (page last modified Mar. 4, 2026); 42 CFR 424.516(d), 424.540(a)(7), (d)(1)(ii)(D), (e) and 424.57(c)(2) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); Medicare Program Integrity Manual ch. 10 sec. 10.4.3(B), 10.4.4(B) (Rev. 13717, July 8, 2026); First Coast, How do I voluntarily terminate or deactivate my Medicare enrollment? (June 26, 2026)
practice_impact: Filing a First Coast withdrawal 90 days after merely deciding to close would end billing before the last facility visits; date it to the actual last service and report the location closure within 30 days.

claim: Medicare Fee-for-Service providers must retain all documentation supporting Medicare claims for a minimum of six years from creation or the date last in effect, whichever is later; the requirement is grounded in HIPAA's administrative simplification rules (45 CFR 164.316).
correct_statement: The Medicare rule is seven years, not six: 42 CFR 424.516(f) requires documentation of ordered, certified, referred or prescribed Part A or B services, and related payment requests, to be kept 7 years from the date of service. 45 CFR 164.316 covers only HIPAA security policies and compliance records. The six-year wording repeats 2010 CMS education material.
source_title: CMS MLN Fact Sheet MLN4840534, Medical Record Maintenance & Access Requirements (January 2026); 42 CFR 424.516(f) and 424.535(a)(10) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); 45 CFR 164.316(b) (eCFR current to Nov. 5, 2026); CMS MLN podcast, Medical Record Retention and Media Format for Medical Records (Sept. 2010, source of the six-year wording; MLN Matters SE1022 now returns 404)
practice_impact: A geriatrics practice ordering labs, DME, home health and drugs for facility patients must keep those records 7 years from service (failure is a revocation ground), longer than Florida's 5-year board rule.

claim: Medicare managed care and Medicare Advantage providers face a longer retention requirement: patient records must be kept for a minimum of ten years, regardless of the shorter six-year federal FFS standard.
correct_statement: The ten-year figure is right for Medicare Advantage: plan contracts must give HHS audit access to a contracted provider's medical records through 10 years from the final date of the contract period, or completion of any audit, whichever is later. So the clock is not the date of service. The fee-for-service comparator is seven years, not six.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.504(d), (e)(4) and (i)(2) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); 42 CFR 424.516(f); CMS MLN podcast, Medical Record Retention and Media Format for Medical Records (Sept. 2010)
practice_impact: For Medicare Advantage patients, facility visit notes must stay retrievable for plan and CMS risk-adjustment audits for 10 years after each contract year ends, well past the closing date.

claim: State medical record retention example for Florida: 5 years from the date of last patient contact.
correct_statement: Correct for Florida medical doctors: Board of Medicine Rule 64B8-10.002(2) requires the records owner to keep patient records at least five years from the last patient contact. The rule warns this may be too short to protect the physician, and Medicare's 7-year and Medicare Advantage's 10-year rules run longer. A closing physician must also publish newspaper notice for four weeks.
source_title: Florida Administrative Code Rule 64B8-10.002, Medical Records of Physicians Relocating or Terminating Practice; Retention, Disposition, Time Limitations (Board of Medicine; latest version effective Aug. 28, 2018; fetched Nov. 10, 2026)
practice_impact: Five years is only the Florida licensing floor; for a Medicare-heavy geriatrics practice the federal 7-year and 10-year periods control, and the Board must get a copy of the closure notice within one month.

claim: A practice with primarily commercial payers that pay in 30 to 45 days can stop new patients closer to closing; high Medicare and Medicaid volume, where payment cycles can run 60 to 90 days, needs more lead time.
correct_statement: Backwards for Medicare. Fee-for-service Medicare is the fastest payer: a clean electronic claim cannot be paid before day 14 and must be paid or denied within 30 days, with interest after that. Medicaid programs must pay 90% of clean practitioner claims within 30 days and 99% within 90. Florida insurers must pay or contest electronic claims within 20 days.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) ch. 1 sec. 80.2.1.1-80.2.1.2 (Rev. 13725, Apr. 10, 2026); First Coast Service Options, New provider roadmap: Claims submission (Jan. 21, 2026); 42 CFR 447.45(d) and 422.520 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); Fla. Stat. 627.6131(4)
practice_impact: A Medicare-heavy geriatrics practice collects clean claims in roughly two to four weeks, so a long pre-closure intake freeze justified by slow Medicare payment would forgo revenue for no reason; denials and Medicaid crossovers are the slow tail.

claim: If the final audit finds overpayment risk, the physician has three choices: remediate before submitting final claims, self-disclose identified overpayments to CMS (via the CMS Self-Referral Disclosure Protocol or OIG's self-disclosure protocol), or accept the post-closure audit risk.
correct_statement: Keeping an identified Medicare overpayment is not a choice, and deliberate ignorance of audit findings counts as knowledge. It must be reported and returned within 60 days (paused up to 180 days for a good-faith investigation), looking back 6 years, or it becomes False Claims Act liability. Coding overpayments go to the Medicare contractor; CMS's SRDP takes only Stark violations.
source_title: 42 CFR 401.305 (as amended 89 FR 98553, Dec. 9, 2024; eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); 31 U.S.C. 3729(b)(1)(A); HHS-OIG Health Care Fraud Self-Disclosure Protocol (updated Oct. 15, 2026), sec. 2.C and 8 (https://oig.hhs.gov/documents/self-disclosure-info/11951/hhs-oig-self-disclosure-protocol.pdf); CMS, Self-Referral Disclosure Protocol page (last modified Sept. 23, 2026)
practice_impact: E/M or modifier overpayments found in a closing audit must be refunded to First Coast within the 60-day rule; closing the practice does not end the duty, and OIG's protocol carries a $20,000 minimum settlement.

claim: Medicare and Medicaid receivables cannot be directly assigned to third parties; factoring companies use sweep account structures where the account remains in the practice's name and the factoring company receives funds as payers remit.
correct_statement: Correct. Medicare will not pay a provider's or supplier's money to anyone else under an assignment or power of attorney, and Medicaid may not pay to or through a factor. Financiers therefore sweep funds from an account held solely in the practice's name. CMS adds that the practice may revoke the sweep anytime and financiers cannot purchase Medicare receivables.
