source_title: 42 CFR 424.73, 424.80 and 447.10 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) ch. 1 sec. 30.2.5 Payment to Bank (Rev. 13725, Apr. 10, 2026); Duane Morris, Health Care Finance Transactions: Security Interests in Commercial and Governmental Receivables (Jan. 2017)
practice_impact: With mostly Medicare and Medicaid receivables, a true sale of the practice's AR is not available; any advance depends on a revocable sweep from the practice's own account, so buyers discount it heavily.

claim: The final audit should test whether documented E&M visit levels are supported by the clinical documentation, 'using the current 2021 AMA/CMS E&M guidelines.'
correct_statement: The 2021 revision covered only office and outpatient visits (99202-99215). The current rules are the CPT E/M guidelines as revised January 1, 2023, which CMS adopted for nursing facility (99304-99310), home or residence (99341-99350) and hospital visits, with level set by medical decision making or time. An audit applies the rules in force on each date of service.
source_title: CMS Fact Sheet, Calendar Year (CY) 2023 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule (Nov. 1, 2022); CMS MLN Booklet MLN006764, Evaluation and Management Services (May 2026); AMA, CPT Evaluation and Management (E/M) Code and Guideline Changes effective January 1, 2023
practice_impact: A facility-based geriatrics practice bills almost entirely nursing facility and home or residence codes, which the 2021 office-visit guidelines never governed; auditing against them would misjudge every visit level.

claim: E&M code distribution, the count and percentage of visits billed at each level (99211, 99215 for established patients, 99201, 99205 for new patients)
correct_statement: CPT 99201 was deleted effective January 1, 2021. New-patient office visits are 99202-99205; established-patient visits are 99211-99215. Those are office/outpatient codes: a facility-based practice's distribution screen should use the nursing facility family (99304-99306 initial, 99307-99310 subsequent, 99315-99316 discharge; 99318 was deleted in 2023).
source_title: AMA, CPT E/M Office or Other Outpatient (99202-99215) and Prolonged Services Code and Guideline Changes (effective Jan. 1, 2021); CMS 2026 National Physician Fee Schedule Relative Value File, October release; CY 2027 PFS final rule (CMS-1848-F) Addendum B
practice_impact: The template's code set is nearly six years stale and office-based; a nursing-facility geriatrics practice must profile 99304-99310 against CMS specialty data, or the pre-sale coding screen measures the wrong codes.

claim: The False Claims Act creates civil liability for submitting false or fraudulent claims to government healthcare programs ... with treble damages and program exclusion as potential penalties.
correct_statement: The Act imposes three times the government's damages plus a civil penalty for every false claim, currently $14,308 to $28,619 each (no 2026 increase), which the claim omits. Exclusion is not a False Claims Act penalty: it is a separate HHS-OIG administrative remedy under Social Security Act section 1128(b)(7), which OIG may impose, reserve or release when a case settles.
source_title: 28 CFR 85.5 (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026); 31 U.S.C. 3729; DOJ notice, Civil Monetary Penalties Inflation Adjustments for 2026, 91 FR 43405 (July 15, 2026); HHS-OIG, Criteria for implementing section 1128(b)(7) exclusion authority (Apr. 18, 2016); 42 CFR 1001.901
practice_impact: Per-claim penalties scale with claim count, so a high-volume nursing-facility visit practice faces exposure far above the overpaid dollars; exclusion, though a separate OIG action, would end Medicare and Medicaid billing.

claim: Voluntary self-disclosure to CMS or other agencies may be appropriate for significant Medicare overpayments, a legal decision requiring healthcare M&A counsel
correct_statement: Returning an identified Medicare overpayment is mandatory, whatever its size: report and return within 60 days of identification (deadline suspended up to 180 days for a timely good-faith investigation), six-year lookback. Plain errors are refunded to the contractor (First Coast). CMS's protocol covers only Stark violations; potential fraud goes to OIG's protocol or DOJ's 2026 pilot.
source_title: 42 CFR 401.305 (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026); HHS-OIG Health Care Fraud Self-Disclosure Protocol (updated Oct. 15, 2026); CMS Self-Referral Disclosure Protocol page; DOJ press release 26-1218, Healthcare FCA Self-Disclosure Pilot Program (Oct. 22, 2026)
practice_impact: A pre-sale coding audit that finds overpaid Medicare claims starts a 60-day federal clock; treating repayment as optional turns a billing error into False Claims Act liability a buyer will price or refuse.

claim: in an asset sale, the seller typically retains the pre-close AR; in a stock sale, the AR stays with the entity.
correct_statement: Broadly right, but negotiable. In physician-practice asset sales receivables are usually an excluded asset the seller keeps; Medicare will not pay a seller's receivables to a buyer. Some deals instead price on a working-capital target that includes them. In a stock sale the entity keeps its receivables and liabilities, so the buyer benefits unless the price adjusts.
source_title: American Osteopathic Association, Selling a Solo Medical Practice; Morgan Lewis, A "Friendly" Guide to Private Equity Acquisitions of Physician Practices (Health Law Handbook, Sept. 2023); Gordon Feinblatt, Sale to Private Equity Part 3 (2021); 42 CFR 424.80
practice_impact: Where receivables are mostly Medicare, which cannot be paid to a buyer, the owner should expect to keep and collect pre-close AR in an asset deal, and must negotiate price credit for it in a stock deal.

claim: Stark Law and Anti-Kickback: are all physician compensation arrangements, space and equipment leases, and referral relationships structured within applicable safe harbors?
correct_statement: The review is necessary but the legal test is misdescribed. Stark has exceptions, not safe harbors; it is strict liability, so a compensation arrangement or lease tied to designated-health-service referrals must meet every element of an exception (42 CFR 411.355-411.357). Anti-kickback safe harbors (42 CFR 1001.952) are voluntary; missing one is not automatically illegal.
source_title: 42 CFR 411.353 and 411.357; 42 CFR 1001.952 (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026); HHS-OIG General Compliance Program Guidance (Nov. 2023), sections on the Federal anti-kickback statute and Physician Self-Referral Law
practice_impact: Medical-director contracts and any payments between the practice and nursing facilities, home health agencies, labs or therapy vendors must be tested under the right standard; a checklist asking only about safe harbors misses Stark's all-elements exception test.

claim: private equity completing 79 physician practice deals in Q1 2025 alone ... (FOCUS Investment Banking; Sofer Advisors) ... the median healthcare services EV/EBITDA multiple compressed to roughly 11.5x in 2025 from 14.5x in 2024
correct_statement: Neither figure holds against primary trackers. LevinPro counted 66 private-equity physician-group deals in Q1 2025, with dental dominating practice-management deals. PitchBook/StepStone put the median private-equity entry multiple for healthcare services at 13.5x in 2024 and 13.6x in 2025; the 11.5x/14.5x pair appears to be FOCUS's public-company median. Practice-management deal flow roughly halved in 2026.
source_title: PitchBook, Q2 2026 Healthcare Services Report (Aug. 14, 2026), PE benchmarking from SPI by StepStone; LevinPro HC Q1 2025 data reported by ABF Journal (Apr. 17, 2025); Bass, Berry & Sims, Healthcare Trends & Transactions Q1 2025; STAT (Aug. 17, 2026). The vendor's wording tracks a business-broker blog (Iconic, June 26, 2026) that attributes the figures to Sofer Advisors and FOCUS.
practice_impact: The market backdrop is copied from marketing blogs and describes large platforms or public companies; it says nothing reliable about a small nursing-facility geriatrics practice, and buyer demand in 2026 is weaker than the text implies.

claim: Primary care, small/solo: typical EBITDA multiple 3, 5x; primary care, scaled/platform: 6, 10x+, with value-based care outperformers reaching double-digit multiples.
correct_statement: These are advisor rules of thumb, not transaction data. Published advisor ranges are similar (small practices 3-6x EBITDA, mid-size groups 5-10x, value-based platforms 10-20x), but EBITDA means earnings after a market-rate physician salary, often near zero in a solo practice. One-to-four-provider clinics typically sell for about 1.5-3.1x owner cash flow, or asset value to hospital buyers.
source_title: Scope Research, Primary Care Physician Practice Valuation Multiples and M&A Trends 2025; Coker, practice valuation in physician-hospital transactions (2017); ECG Management Consultants / AHLA, Determining the True Value of Primary Care Practices (Feb. 2023)
practice_impact: A small fee-for-service Medicare geriatrics group sits in the bottom band; applying 3-5x to owner take-home instead of EBITDA after market physician pay would overstate the practice's value severalfold.

claim: Industry standards suggest that AR over 120 days is collectible at roughly 50 cents on the dollar; over 180 days, 20 to 30 cents; over 360 days, essentially a write-off.
correct_statement: No industry standard for these recovery values could be found: MGMA, HFMA and AAFP material gives aging-bucket benchmarks, not a cents-on-the-dollar schedule, and the vendor's own documents give different figures for the same buckets. The nearest published curve covers commercial trade debt, not insurance claims: 68.9% collectable at 90 days past due, 51.3% at six months, 21.4% at one year.
source_title: No traceable source for the claimed schedule (searched MGMA, HFMA MAP Keys, AAFP and the web). Nearest published data: Commercial Collection Agencies of America, Collectability of Delinquent Commercial Debts at Time Intervals After the Due Date
practice_impact: Medicare accepts claims for a year after service, so a Medicare-heavy facility practice's aged A/R should be valued from its own payer-level collection history, not a blanket 50-cent haircut at 120 days.

claim: During the credentialing period, claims can often be submitted under a supervising provider's NPI, but this requires explicit verification with each payer [and documented supervision].
correct_statement: Not a general workaround. Medicare allows billing under a supervising physician's NPI only as incident-to services: physician-initiated care, direct supervision, noninstitutional setting, never for hospital or SNF patients. Substitute-physician (Q6) billing covers an absent physician, not a new hire. OIG has penalized billing unsupervised, uncredentialed providers' work under another NPI. Medicare's remedy is retroactive billing from the filing date.
source_title: 42 CFR 410.26 (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026); Medicare Benefit Policy Manual ch. 15 sections 60.1-60.2 (Rev. 13889); Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 26 section 10.4 Item 24J and ch. 1 section 30.2.11; HHS-OIG enforcement summary (July 2, 2018); 42 CFR 424.520-424.521
practice_impact: In a facility-based practice the workaround is mostly unavailable: no incident-to billing for hospital or SNF-stay patients, and nursing-home visits would need the physician's own initiating visit plus direct (in-person or live-video) supervision. Using another clinician's NPI otherwise is a false-claims risk.

claim: Until a provider is fully credentialed with every relevant payer, their claims cannot be submitted under their NPI.
correct_statement: Enrollment is payer by payer, not all-or-nothing. Medicare pays only enrolled providers, but once approved, billing privileges run from the application filing date (plus up to 30 days' retrospective billing), so held claims go out under the provider's own NPI. Florida Medicaid enrollment is effective on the date the application is received. Commercial plans follow their contracts.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.505, 424.520(d), 424.521(a) (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026); Fla. Stat. 409.907(9)(a) (2026); First Coast Service Options, Determining your Medicare effective date
practice_impact: A new clinician's Medicare and Medicaid facility visits are not lost while enrollment is pending: file before the first visit, hold the claims, then bill them under the clinician's own NPI after approval.

claim: Medicare: 60, 90 days from complete application submission ... The credentialing process must begin at least 90 days before a new provider sees their first patient.
correct_statement: CMS requires contractors to finish 95% of complete online (PECOS) applications in 15 days and all within 50; those needing follow-up, within 50 to 85 days. A Medicare application received over 60 days before its listed effective date may be returned. Billing privileges date from filing, plus 30 days' retrospective billing. Ninety days' lead fits commercial payers, not Medicare filing.
source_title: CMS Medicare Program Integrity Manual (Pub. 100-08) ch. 10, section 10.5 (Rev. 13717, July 8, 2026); 42 CFR 424.520(d), 424.521(a), 424.526(a)(2) (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026); First Coast Service Options, CMS-855 enrollment application processing timeframes
practice_impact: For a Medicare-dominant facility practice the costly error is filing late, not slow processing: visits more than 30 days before the filing date are unbillable, while filing 90 days early risks a returned application.

claim: Never ignore an audit letter. Non-response is treated as an admission and triggers automatic recoupment.
correct_statement: Non-response is not an admission, but it is costly. Medicare reviewers deny claims when records are not received in 45 days (30 for program-integrity contractors); the denial becomes an overpayment, recoupment can start 41 days after the demand unless appealed, and appeal rights remain. A Florida provider who ignores an insurer's overpayment claim for 140 days owes it uncontestably.
source_title: 42 CFR 405.929-405.930 and 405.373-405.379 (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026); CMS Medicare Program Integrity Manual ch. 3 sections 3.2.3.2, 3.2.3.8-3.2.3.9 (Rev. 13971, Sept. 30, 2026); Fla. Stat. 627.6131(6) (2026)
practice_impact: A missed 45-day records request turns reviewed facility visits into denials or overpayments by default; the practice keeps appeal rights, so the vendor contract must guarantee record turnaround inside that window.

claim: An RCM vendor without a current BAA is not HIPAA-compliant, and using them exposes the practice to HIPAA liability. It should be a standalone agreement, not embedded in the service contract.
correct_statement: A billing company handling patient data is a business associate, and a practice that discloses records to it without a written agreement meeting 45 CFR 164.504(e) violates HIPAA; the vendor is directly liable regardless. HIPAA does not require a standalone document: HHS says the provisions may sit inside the services agreement or in a separate one.
source_title: 45 CFR 160.103, 164.502(e), 164.504(e) (eCFR, current to Nov. 5, 2026); HHS, Standards for Privacy of Individually Identifiable Health Information, 67 FR 53182, 53264 (Aug. 14, 2002), Sample Business Associate Contract Provisions; HIPAA Omnibus Rule, 78 FR 5566 (Jan. 25, 2013)
practice_impact: The practice needs a signed, Omnibus-era agreement with its billing vendor before any records flow; whether it is a separate document or a contract exhibit does not affect compliance, so an embedded one is no reason to reject a vendor.

claim: The vendor's fee typically ranges from 4, 9% of net collections ... with the current market average tracking between 5.5% and 7.2% for full-service billing across practice types.
correct_statement: A 4-9% range roughly matches trade-press and vendor quotes, but no published survey was found for a 5.5-7.2% market average; that figure has no traceable origin. Rates track claim size: trade press put specialists at 3-8% and primary care at 8-13% (2003) or 8-10% (2010). A vendor paid a percentage may not receive Medicare payments directly.
source_title: Physicians Practice, Outsourcing Your Billing (Feb. 1, 2010); Medical Economics, Practice Pointers: Outsource billing? Here's how (May 23, 2003); 42 CFR 424.73(b)(3) and 424.80(b)(5); OIG Compliance Program Guidance for Individual and Small Group Physician Practices, 65 FR 59434 (Oct. 5, 2000). No source found for the 5.5-7.2% average.
practice_impact: Low-dollar, high-volume facility visits tend to price toward the top of the range, so a quote above 8% is not automatically above market; and Medicare receipts must land in an account the practice controls if the fee is a percentage.

claim: AR that ages past 120 days has collection probability below 40% for commercial payers and below 20% for some government payers.
correct_statement: No published source gives collection probabilities of under 40% (commercial) or under 20% (government) past 120 days; the figures have no traceable origin. Age alone does not close a claim: Medicare accepts claims for one year after service and appeals for 120 days after a denial; a Florida insurer that ignores an electronic claim for 120 days must pay it.
source_title: No traceable source for the percentages (searched MGMA, HFMA MAP Keys, AAFP and the web). Deadlines: 42 CFR 424.44 and 405.942 (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026); Fla. Stat. 627.6131 (2026); HFMA MAP Keys, Aged A/R
practice_impact: For a mostly Medicare book, many balances over 120 days are still inside the one-year filing or 120-day appeal windows; treating them as 20% assets would excuse a vendor from working recoverable money.

claim: Medicaid: 60, 120 days, with significant state variation; Commercial payers: 30, 90 days, depending on payer and network status; Hospital-based credentialing: 90, 180 days.
correct_statement: Unsourced rules of thumb, and off for Florida. AHCA says Florida Medicaid enrollment takes 60 days or less from a complete application, effective from the receipt date. UnitedHealthcare and Cigna quote about 45 to 60 days for credentialing, and UnitedHealthcare adds up to 60 days for contract loading. One teaching hospital quotes 90 days or longer for privileges.
source_title: Florida AHCA, Florida Medicaid Provider Enrollment readiness page; Fla. Stat. 409.907(9)(a) (2026); UnitedHealthcare, Join Our Network: Medical Provider FAQ; Cigna Healthcare, Credentialing; Brown University Health (Rhode Island Hospital) Medical Staff Services FAQs (all retrieved Nov. 10, 2026)
practice_impact: For a largely Medicare and Medicaid facility practice, enrollment is faster than stated and dated back to filing; the slow path is commercial and Medicare Advantage credentialing plus contract loading, which should drive the onboarding calendar.

claim: Average fully-loaded cost of replacing a billing staff member (recruiting, training, productivity gap) is 50 to 100 percent of annual salary; a biller earning $50,000 costs $25,000 to $50,000 to replace.
correct_statement: No study measures replacement cost for medical billing staff, and the vendor cites none. General estimates conflict: a review of 30 case studies put the typical cost at about 20% of salary for jobs under $50,000 (about $10,000 for a $50,000 biller); Gallup's unsourced rule of thumb is 50% to 200%.
source_title: Boushey H, Glynn SJ. There Are Significant Business Costs to Replacing Employees (Center for American Progress, 2012); Gallup, This Fixable Problem Costs U.S. Businesses $1 Trillion (2019)
practice_impact: Do not use $25,000-$50,000 per departure as a measured cost when justifying raises or retention bonuses; price the practice's own recruiting, training and backlog costs, which the best evidence suggests are nearer one fifth of salary.

claim: Medical Biller national median base pay as of 2025: $36,000, $44,000 entry (0, 2 yrs), $42,000, $52,000 mid (3, 5 yrs), $50,000, $62,000 experienced (6+ yrs).
correct_statement: BLS reports one national median for billing and posting clerks: $48,500 (2025 data; middle half $42,840-$58,290; Florida $46,540). No source publishes biller medians by experience tier, and the vendor cites none. MGMA's 2025 median for patient accounting staff with five or fewer years' experience is $48,241, above the vendor's entry band.
source_title: O*NET OnLine Local Wages, 43-3021.00 Billing and Posting Clerks (BLS OEWS 2025 data); MGMA 2026 Management and Staff Compensation Data Report
practice_impact: The vendor's $36,000-$44,000 entry band starts below the 10th percentile ($37,290) and tops out near the 25th ($42,840 nationally, $40,350 in Florida); offers in the lower part of it will lose candidates.

claim: Medical Coder, CPC national median base pay as of 2025: $42,000, $52,000 entry, $50,000, $62,000 mid, $58,000, $74,000 experienced; certification adds +5, 12% at the same experience level.
correct_statement: The bands are plausible but are not medians and carry no source. BLS's median for medical records specialists is $51,140 (2025 data; Florida $45,760). AAPC's member survey averages $67,147 for CPCs and $45,377 to $59,144 across the first nine years. AAPC reports certified staff earning 20.7% more, unadjusted; nothing supports 5-12%.
source_title: AAPC 2026 Medical Coding and Billing Salary Report; O*NET OnLine Local Wages, 29-2072.00 Medical Records Specialists (BLS OEWS 2025 data)
practice_impact: Usable only as a rough range; Florida coder pay runs about 10% below the national median in BLS data (AAPC Florida CPC average $63,513), so price offers on local data, not on the vendor's bands or its certification percentage.

claim: Medical Coder, CPC-H (hospital): key compensation factors are hospital coding complexity, DRG and APC experience; pay a +5, 12% premium for CPC, CPC-H, or CPMA certification.
correct_statement: AAPC retired the CPC-H name on January 1, 2015; the credential is COC (Certified Outpatient Coder) and covers outpatient facility coding and APCs. DRG assignment is inpatient work, tested by AAPC's CIC or AHIMA's CCS. The 5-12% premium is unsourced; AAPC's 2025 averages are $75,786 (COC), $81,591 (CPMA) and $67,147 (CPC).
source_title: AAPC, Certified Outpatient Coder (COC) and Certified Inpatient Coder (CIC) certification pages; AAPC support page on credential names; AAPC 2026 Salary Report
practice_impact: Little for a professional-fee geriatrics practice, which needs CPC-type skills (nursing-facility E/M, care management), not hospital DRG/APC coders; a job posting asking for a 'CPC-H' signals a template more than ten years out of date.

claim: Revenue Cycle Manager base pay: $62,000, $78,000 in a 1, 5 provider practice, $72,000, $90,000 at 6, 15 providers, $84,000, $105,000 at 16+ providers; Revenue Cycle Director $88,000, $110,000 in a small practice.
correct_statement: No public source reports revenue cycle manager pay by provider count; the vendor cites none and its two tables disagree ($84,000-$105,000 in one, $80,000-$100,000 in the other). Comparators: MGMA 2025 tenure-band medians of about $63,000 for supervisors and $86,680-$96,608 for general management; AAPC CPPM average $84,521; BLS medical and health services managers median $123,860.
source_title: MGMA 2026 Management and Staff Compensation Data Report; O*NET OnLine Local Wages 11-9111.00 (BLS OEWS 2025 data); AAPC 2026 Salary Report
practice_impact: Treat the bands as one vendor's opinion; a small Florida practice hiring a billing manager should benchmark against MGMA supervisor and general-management medians and local BLS data rather than these figures.

claim: For staff at market rate and meeting performance targets: cost-of-living adjustment (typically CPI-based, 3, 5%); for staff exceeding performance targets: merit increase above CPI, up to 8%.
correct_statement: CPI-based adjustments have mostly run at or below the bottom of the stated band: the Social Security COLA (CPI-W) was 2.5% for 2025, 2.8% for 2026 and 3.6% for 2027. For 2026, 64% of medical groups budgeted 1-3% base raises, 23% budgeted 4-6% and 1% budgeted 7% or more. "Up to 8%" merit is the vendor's opinion, not a benchmark.
source_title: SSA, Cost-of-Living Increase and Other Determinations for 2027, 91 FR 67380; MGMA Stat, Budgeting competitive, sustainable 2026 staff pay (Sept 10, 2025)
practice_impact: Budgeting 3-5% across-the-board raises as 'CPI' overstates inflation in two of the last three years; with the Medicare conversion factor falling about 2.3% in 2027, tie the raise pool to the actual index (3.6%) and to local Florida wage data.

claim: Geographic adjustment to national median: Tier 2 high-cost markets (Chicago, Miami, Denver, San Diego, Portland, Austin, Minneapolis) +10, 20%; Tier 4 lower-cost markets (most mid-size and smaller metros, rural), 5, 15%; fully remote roles +5, 10%.
correct_statement: BLS data contradict Miami as a +10-20% market: median pay there is about 4% below the national median for billing clerks ($46,610 vs $48,500) and medical records specialists ($49,010 vs $51,140). Austin is also near national; Denver, Minneapolis and San Diego fit. Smaller Florida metros run 10-21% below. The remote premium is unsourced.
source_title: O*NET OnLine Local Wages (BLS Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics, 2025 data), 43-3021.00 and 29-2072.00
practice_impact: Applying the vendor's Miami uplift would set billing pay roughly 14-25% above the actual South Florida median; Tampa, Orlando and Jacksonville also run 1-13% below the national median.

claim: Medical Coder strong performance: coding accuracy >=95% on audit and E&M within 10% of specialty norm; intervention needed if accuracy is below 90% or E&M distribution is significantly outside norms in either direction.
correct_statement: 95% audited accuracy is a widely used internal convention, not a CMS, OIG or AHIMA rule, and no authority sets a 90% trigger. Nothing supports "E&M within 10% of specialty norm" as a coder target: each visit's level must rest on its own documentation and medical necessity. Peer comparisons only flag records for review.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Pub. 100-04, ch. 12 s.30.6.1; OIG General Compliance Program Guidance (Nov 2023); OIG Compliance Program for Individual and Small Group Physician Practices, 65 FR 59434 (2000)
practice_impact: Rewarding coders for matching an E/M curve invites coding to the curve; a nursing-facility geriatrics panel legitimately differs from office norms (geriatric medicine bills 99309-99310 for 67% of subsequent nursing-facility visits, internal medicine 53%), so audit records, not distributions.

claim: CY 2026 Physician Fee Schedule permanently removed telehealth frequency limits for subsequent inpatient visits, subsequent nursing facility visits, and critical care consultation services; no maximum number of telehealth encounters per episode or time period.
correct_statement: H.R. 7148 became P.L. 119-75 on February 3, 2026. Section 6209 extends Medicare telehealth flexibilities (home and any geography, practitioner list, audio-only, FQHC/RHC) through December 31, 2027. The tele-mental-health in-person requirement applies to services on or after January 1, 2028, so the waiver ends December 31, 2027, one day earlier than the vendor's wording.
source_title: H.R. 7148, Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (P.L. 119-75), enrolled text, sec. 6209; CMS Telehealth FAQ updated 10/8/2026; telehealth.hhs.gov telehealth policy updates
practice_impact: Telehealth to home, assisted-living and facility patients stays billable without rural limits through 2027; from January 1, 2028, absent new law, non-behavioral telehealth again needs a rural facility site, which most Florida metro facilities are not.

claim: Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026, signed February 3, 2026, extends most Medicare telehealth flexibilities through December 31, 2027; the next potential cliff date is January 1, 2028 unless Congress acts again.
correct_statement: Correct. The CY 2026 PFS final rule (CMS-1832-F), effective January 1, 2026, permanently removed Medicare telehealth frequency limits for subsequent inpatient visits (99231-99233), subsequent nursing facility visits (99307-99310) and critical care consultations (G0508, G0509). Earlier caps were one visit every 3 days, one every 14 days and one per day.
source_title: CMS fact sheet, Calendar Year (CY) 2026 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule (CMS-1832-F)
practice_impact: High: removes the one-per-14-days cap on telehealth follow-ups for nursing facility residents; federally mandated periodic visits still must be in person under CMS manual guidance (verify current text), and POS 02 pays the facility rate.

claim: Effective January 1, 2026, CMS made permanent direct supervision of incident-to services via real-time, two-way audio-video technology under the CY 2026 PFS final rule; the supervising physician need not be physically present in the office suite.
correct_statement: Correct with a carve-out. Since January 1, 2026 (CY 2026 PFS final rule, not the 2026 appropriations act), 42 CFR 410.26(a)(2) allows direct supervision by real-time audio/video presence, not audio-only, except for services with a 010 or 090 global surgery indicator. The supervisor must remain immediately available.
source_title: eCFR, 42 CFR 410.26 (incident-to conditions; direct supervision definition); CMS fact sheet, CY 2026 PFS final rule (CMS-1832-F)
practice_impact: Limited: incident-to billing is barred in hospitals and SNFs (42 CFR 410.26(b)(1)), so this helps only office, home or assisted-living services; per the CY 2027 final rule, incident-to telehealth claims need new modifier BC from January 1, 2027.

claim: POS 10 (patient at home) is paid at the non-facility rate and POS 02 (patient not at home) at the facility rate; the difference for the same service runs roughly 10 to 25 percent depending on code and locality.
correct_statement: Correct in context. CPT deleted 99441-99443 for 2025; Medicare audio-only E/M uses 99202-99215 with modifier 93, only for patients at home. CMS gave 98000-98015 status indicator I (not valid for Medicare). The playbook omits that 98016, the brief virtual check-in that replaced G2012, is payable by Medicare.
source_title: CY 2025 Physician Fee Schedule final rule (Federal Register document 2024-25382, published December 9, 2024); telehealth.hhs.gov Medicare FFS billing page
practice_impact: Moderate: retire 99441-99443 and keep 98000-98015 off Medicare claims, but keep 98016 for virtual check-ins; audio-only E/M applies only to patients at home, not nursing facility residents.

claim: Codes 99441, 99442 and 99443 were eliminated from the CPT code set effective January 1, 2025; Medicare audio-only E&M uses 99202-99215 with modifier 93; the 98000-series codes are NOT accepted by Medicare.
correct_statement: POS 10 pays the non-facility rate and POS 02 the facility rate. In 2026 the gap for office visits is about 35-40% (99213: 2.85 vs 1.72 total RVUs; 99214: $135.61 vs $84.50) after CMS halved facility indirect practice expense; nursing facility codes differ about 12-14%.
source_title: CMS Transmittal 12671, CR 13582 (Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 26 sec. 10.5); 2026 PFS amounts via third-party fee-schedule lookups; AMA 2026 final rule summary
practice_impact: High: telehealth to a nursing facility resident is POS 02 (facility rate, about 12-14% below POS 32 in 2026, equalized for 2027); a wrong POS on home visits costs roughly 35-40%, not 10-25%. Confirm on the First Coast fee schedule.

claim: The clinical record for every audio-only claim must document audio-only delivery and the reason (patient lacked video capability or declined video); service must be to a patient at home; missing rationale leaves a paid claim vulnerable to recoupment.
correct_statement: Audio-only for non-behavioral services runs through December 31, 2027, for patients at home when the practitioner is video-capable and the patient cannot or will not use video. CMS requires modifier 93 as the attestation and stated no additional documentation is needed; a note explaining why is prudent, not a CMS requirement.
source_title: CY 2025 Physician Fee Schedule final rule (Federal Register document 2024-25382); 42 CFR 410.78(a)(3); telehealth.hhs.gov telehealth policy updates; First Coast telehealth services page
practice_impact: High: nursing facility residents are not 'at home', so audio-only visits to them are not billable telehealth; use audio-only only for patients in a private residence and keep a brief reason in the note for audit defense.

claim: CCM (99490/99491/99487/99489) and RPM (99453/99454/99457/99458) are not telehealth services in the Medicare definition; they cannot be billed using telehealth POS codes or modifiers, and doing so is incorrect coding.
correct_statement: CCM and RPM are non-face-to-face services outside the Medicare telehealth rules; no POS 02/10 or telehealth modifiers. The code lists are incomplete: CCM also uses add-ons 99439 and 99437; RPM also includes 99091 and, since January 1, 2026, 99445 (2-15 days of data) and 99470 (10-19 minutes).
source_title: CMS Telehealth FAQ (updated 10/8/2026); CY 2026 Physician Fee Schedule final rule (Federal Register document 2025-19787); CMS MLN909188 Chronic Care Management Services
practice_impact: Moderate: relevant mainly to home and assisted-living panels; a charge master built from the vendor's list would miss CCM add-ons and the 2026 RPM codes.

claim: Telehealth payment parity for fully insured commercial plans is governed by state law; more than 40 states (44 states plus D.C. as of 2026) have some form of telehealth parity law.
correct_statement: No traceable source shows that most Medicare Advantage plans require modifier 95; rules vary by plan. UnitedHealthcare MA and Humana key telehealth to POS 02/10; Florida Blue MA wants modifier 93 or 95 plus POS 02/10. CMS's claims manual itself pairs POS 02/10 with modifier 93 or 95 for Original Medicare.
source_title: UnitedHealthcare Medicare Advantage Telehealth and Telemedicine Policy, Professional; Humana Medicare telehealth FAQ; Florida Blue payment policy 20-069 Virtual Visits; Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 26 sec. 10.5
practice_impact: Verify each Florida MA plan's telehealth rule in writing (Humana, UnitedHealthcare, Florida Blue and others); a blanket 95 assumption risks denials, and Medicare adds modifiers BB and BC on January 1, 2027.

claim: Small practices - fewer than 16 clinicians in the practice's MIPS-eligible group - receive automatic reweighting ... Promoting Interoperability drops to 0%, ... Quality rises to 40% and Improvement Activities to 30%, keeping Cost at 30%.
correct_statement: A small practice is a TIN with 15 or fewer eligible clinicians (every clinician billing under the TIN in the MIPS determination period, not only MIPS-eligible ones). Its Promoting Interoperability category is automatically reweighted to 0% unless it submits PI data; weights become Quality 40%, Cost 30%, Improvement Activities 30%. The CY 2027 final rule left this unchanged.
source_title: 42 CFR 414.1305 and 414.1380(c)(2) (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026); CY 2027 PFS final rule, 91 FR 70992 (no amendment to these paragraphs)
practice_impact: A geriatrics TIN with 15 or fewer clinicians is scored Quality 40/Cost 30/IA 30 with no EHR category; submitting any PI data cancels the reweighting, and if Cost cannot be scored the split is Quality 50/IA 50.

claim: CMS has finalized 75 points as the MIPS performance threshold and will maintain it through the 2028 performance year ... Below 75, the payment adjustment scales down linearly, reaching the full -9% cap at scores of 18.75 points or lower.
correct_statement: The MIPS performance threshold is 75 points for the 2026 through 2028 performance years (2028-2030 payment years); the CY 2027 final rule published Nov. 9, 2026 did not change it. Scores of 0 to 18.75 get the full -9%. From 18.76 to 74.99 the penalty is linear, so there is a cliff: 18.76 points is about -6.75%.
source_title: 42 CFR 414.1405; CY 2026 PFS final rule, 90 FR 49918-49919 (Nov. 5, 2025); CY 2027 PFS final rule, 91 FR 70992 (Nov. 9, 2026)
practice_impact: Any MIPS-eligible clinician scoring under 75 for 2026 loses up to 9% of 2028 Medicare Part B payments; not reporting at all means the full -9%.

claim: there is no lump-sum APM bonus for the 2025 performance year or later under current law ... For CY2026, this produced a final conversion factor of $33.5675 for QPs ... versus $33.4009 for non-QPs
correct_statement: The CY 2026 conversion factors are right ($33.5675 QP, $33.4009 non-QP; CY 2027: $32.9548 and $32.6286). But the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (Feb. 3, 2026) revived the lump sum: a 3.1% APM Incentive Payment in payment year 2028 for 2026 QP performance. None is payable for 2025 performance, and none is yet enacted for 2027 performance onward.
source_title: Pub. L. 119-75 sec. 6204 (140 Stat. 646); CY 2027 PFS final rule, 91 FR 71630-71631 and 42 CFR 414.1450(b)(1)(iv); CY 2026 PFS final rule, 90 FR 49960-49961
practice_impact: If any clinician reaches QP status through an Advanced APM (for example a risk-bearing ACO track) for 2026, a 3.1% lump sum is due in 2028 and the lower 50% payment/35% patient thresholds apply; the playbook says nothing is payable.

claim: MVP registration must be completed before the performance year begins - a practice cannot retroactively elect an MVP pathway partway through the year.
correct_statement: MVP registration happens during the performance year, not before it. The window runs April 1 to November 30 of the performance year (2026 window closes 8 p.m. ET on November 30, 2026); a registration can be changed or deleted until then, and registering does not oblige the practice to report the MVP. CAHPS for MIPS registration is due June 30.
source_title: 42 CFR 414.1365(b)(1) (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026); CMS QPP 'MVP Registration' page (PY 2026); CY 2027 PFS final rule, 91 FR 71509 (traditional MIPS sunset)
practice_impact: The practice has not missed 2026: it can still register for an MVP until November 30, 2026. Under the CY 2027 final rule MVP reporting becomes mandatory from the 2031 performance year, so the registration step will matter to every MIPS practice.

claim: Improvement Activities 15% - Attestation-based; at least one high-weighted or two medium-weighted activities the practice is actually performing.
correct_statement: The 15% weight is right, but activity weights were abolished starting with the 2025 performance year. For 2025, 2026 and 2027, full credit requires attesting to 2 activities, or 1 activity for small, rural, shortage-area and non-patient-facing practices and for MVP participants. 'One high or two medium' was the pre-2025 rule, and only for special-status practices.
source_title: 42 CFR 414.1380(b)(3) and 414.1355(b); CMS QPP 'Improvement Activities: Traditional MIPS Requirements' (PY 2026)
practice_impact: A small practice needs just one activity for full Improvement Activities credit (worth 30% of its score when the EHR category is reweighted); choosing activities by 'weight' follows a retired rule.

claim: Maximum positive adjustment actually paid: +1.05% for the 2026 payment year (the lowest in the program's history); 2025 payment year +2.15%; 2023 payment year +2.34%; and an anomalous spike to +8.25% for the 2024 payment year.
correct_statement: CMS's published maximums are 2.34% (2023 payment year), 8.26% (2024), 2.15% (2025) and 1.05% (2026, the lowest through that year). The 2024 figure was no scoring anomaly: it was a 2.24% budget-neutral maximum plus up to 6.02% from the exceptional-performance bonus, which then expired. The 2027 maximum, released October 2026, was not found in a public CMS document.
source_title: CMS QPP Participation and Performance Results At-A-Glance for performance years 2021-2024 (2024 edition dated May 19, 2026); CY 2027 PFS final rule, 91 FR 71678
practice_impact: Plan on a best-case MIPS gain of roughly 1% of Part B payments; the money at risk is the 9% penalty, so avoiding a sub-75 score matters far more than chasing 100.

claim: A practice still coding to V24-era habits - documenting 'chronic kidney disease' without a stage, or 'diabetes' without a documented complication - is systematically under-capturing RAF for its MA panel
correct_statement: The CKD half holds: unstaged CKD (N18.9) maps to no payment HCC, though it never did, so it is not a V24 habit. The diabetes half is backwards: V28 pays all three diabetes HCCs the same, so E11.9 earns the same weight as diabetes with chronic complications. Extra weight comes only when the complication has its own HCC.
source_title: CMS Announcement of CY 2024 MA Capitation Rates (2024 CMS-HCC model, pp. 90-91 and relative factor table); CMS 2026 Midyear Final ICD-10-CM Mappings; CY 2027 Rate Announcement (model retained for 2027)
practice_impact: Stage every CKD patient (3a, 3b, 4, 5) because that is where the risk score is; do not push clinicians to add diabetic complication codes for score, since it adds nothing under V28 and unsupported codes are an audit exposure.

claim: CMS resumed Risk Adjustment Data Validation (RADV) audit activity under a January 27, 2026 HPMS memo, covering payment years 2018 through 2024 ... unsupported diagnoses are recouped, sometimes with extrapolated penalties across the broader patient population.
correct_statement: RADV audits never stopped: CMS began 2018 audits on Nov. 14, 2024 and 2019 audits in June 2025, and the 2018-2024 push dates from May 21, 2025; the Jan. 27, 2026 memo (not in CMS's public archive) adjusted logistics. The extrapolation rule was vacated Sept. 25, 2025 (appeal pending); CMS now collects only sampled-enrollee overpayments, from plans, not practices.
source_title: CMS, Payment Year 2024 MA Contract-Specific RADV Audit Methods and Instructions (Aug. 28, 2026); CMS RADV Announcements and Audit Schedule; CMS press release May 21, 2025; Humana Inc. v. Becerra, 801 F. Supp. 3d 624 (N.D. Tex. 2025)
practice_impact: The practice's exposure is chart requests from MA plans for dates of service 2017 onward (contracted providers must keep records 10 years) and any clawback written into its plan contracts, not a CMS penalty.

claim: Routine waiver of Medicare copays without a demonstrated financial hardship determination is a False Claims Act violation.
correct_statement: Routine waiver is unlawful in OIG's view, chiefly under the Anti-Kickback Statute and the beneficiary-inducement civil monetary penalty (up to $25,595 per item); False Claims Act liability ($14,308 to $28,619 per claim) can follow but is not automatic. Waivers are permitted if not advertised, not routine, and based on good-faith determination of financial need or on failed reasonable collection efforts.
source_title: OIG Special Fraud Alert, Routine Waiver of Copayments or Deductibles Under Medicare Part B, 59 FR 65372 (Dec 19, 1994); 42 U.S.C. 1320a-7a(a)(5), (i)(6); 42 CFR 1003.110; 45 CFR 102.3 (2025 adjustment, 91 FR 3666); 28 CFR 85.5 (90 FR 29447)
practice_impact: High relevance: nearly all patients are Medicare. Write-offs of coinsurance for facility residents need an individual documented financial-need finding or documented collection attempts; QMB dual eligibles may not be billed cost-sharing at all; Florida s. 817.234(7)(a) separately treats a general practice of waiving copays as insurance fraud.

claim: For Medicare patients, the Medicare Secondary Payer questionnaire must be completed and documented. MSP overpayment demands carry retroactive liability that can extend years into the past.
correct_statement: Physicians billing Medicare must ask the patient or representative about other coverage and keep the answers; CMS says to retain them 10 years. CMS's own questionnaire is a hospital model that may be used, not a mandatory form. Mistaken primary payments must be refunded within 60 days and can be reopened for 4 years with good cause, longer for fraud.
source_title: Medicare Secondary Payer Manual (Pub. 100-05), Chapter 3, sections 20.1-20.2.2; CMS MLN Booklet MLN006903, Medicare Secondary Payer (July 2025); Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 26 sec. 10.2 (item 11 good-faith attestation); 42 CFR 405.980(b), 411.24, 489.20(f)-(h), 401.305(f)
practice_impact: Relevant: with no front desk, MSP answers must come from the facility face sheet, the patient's representative and the Medicare eligibility (271) response, and be kept 10 years; Florida no-fault auto coverage, facility liability claims after falls and a working spouse's group plan are the likely primary payers.

claim: Balance billing a Medicaid-eligible patient for services covered by Medicaid is a compliance violation.
correct_statement: Correct for providers enrolled in Medicaid: they must accept the Medicaid payment plus any plan-authorized cost-sharing as payment in full for covered services. The rule is broader for dual eligibles: no Medicare provider, Medicaid-enrolled or not, may bill a Qualified Medicare Beneficiary for Part A or B cost-sharing, even when Medicaid pays nothing. Non-covered services are outside the rule.
source_title: 42 CFR 447.15; Florida Statutes s. 409.907(3)(j) and s. 409.908(13) (2026); Fla. Admin. Code R. 59G-1.050(2) and (9), General Medicaid Policy; CMS MLN Fact Sheet MLN7936176, Prohibition on Billing Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries (September 2025)
practice_impact: High relevance: many nursing-facility residents are dual eligibles. Florida Medicaid pays no Part B coinsurance when Medicare's payment already meets the Medicaid rate (s. 409.908(13)), and the practice still may not bill a QMB for it, so QMB status must be checked on every eligibility response.

claim: A patient enrolled in a Medicare Advantage plan cannot be billed under traditional Medicare rules; the plan's own benefit structure, authorization requirements and network restrictions govern the claim.
correct_statement: Claims for a Medicare Advantage enrollee go to the plan, and its cost-sharing, authorization and network rules apply. But traditional Medicare rules still matter: plans must follow national and local coverage determinations, non-contracted physicians are paid and limited as under Original Medicare, and once an enrollee elects hospice, Original Medicare, not the plan, pays for Part A and B services.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.101(a)-(b), 422.138, 422.214(a), 422.320(c) (eCFR current to 11/06/2026); Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 11 sec. 30.4 (hospice claims for Medicare Advantage enrollees, GV/GW modifiers)
practice_impact: High relevance: for nursing-facility and ALF patients in a Medicare Advantage plan who elect hospice, the practice must bill First Coast (Original Medicare) with hospice modifiers, not the plan; out-of-network claims are paid at Original Medicare rates; and plan denials can be challenged against Medicare's own coverage rules.

claim: Assignment of benefits and a financial responsibility acknowledgment must be signed at or before the first visit and re-signed annually; without the acknowledgment the patient has a legal argument against balance billing.
correct_statement: Signed forms are prudent, but no federal or Florida rule requires annual re-signing. Medicare's signature-on-file authorization is effective indefinitely, and participating physicians are paid directly without it. A generic financial-responsibility form does not make a Medicare patient liable for denied services (that takes a specific ABN), cannot permit billing a QMB, and does not override in-network contract limits.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), Chapter 26 sec. 10.3 (items 12-13), Chapter 1 sec. 50.1.6, Chapter 30 sec. 40.2.2; Florida Statutes s. 627.638(2) (2026)
practice_impact: Moderate: residents often cannot sign, so the practice needs one valid signature on file (patient or authorized representative, with the reason noted) rather than an annual re-signing campaign; effort is better spent on service-specific ABNs and QMB checks, which are what actually determine whether a patient can be billed.

claim: A Medicare Advantage plan that did not require authorization for office visits in January may require it in July after a mid-year policy update; MA plans update authorization requirements more frequently than commercial plans.
correct_statement: Mid-year changes are allowed: a Medicare Advantage organization may change plan rules, including authorization rules, during the year after CMS review and 30 days' notice to enrollees. The comparison with commercial plans is unsupported: the vendor cites no data, none was found, and insurers revise both together (UnitedHealthcare cut 30% of requirements for both on October 1, 2026).
source_title: 42 CFR 422.111(b)(7) and (d) (eCFR current to 11/06/2026); UnitedHealthcare provider notice, October 2026 prior authorization reductions
practice_impact: Relevant: authorization rules can change for a patient mid-year either because the plan changes them on 30 days' notice or because a nursing-facility resident switches plans (allowed in any month), so plan and authorization requirements should be re-checked at each eligibility verification rather than on a fixed quarterly cycle.

claim: Patient-responsible balances that leave the building as accounts receivable cost the practice an average of $8 to $14 per statement to bill.
correct_statement: No traceable source gives $8 to $14 per statement, and MGMA publishes no per-statement cost. The nearest figure is a 2018 Phreesia infographic: more than three statements 'costing $5 to $15 each' per balance, credited to MGMA without citation; its 2023 version drops the figure. Outsourced mailing runs about $1 per statement; one staff-inclusive anecdote is $5 to $7.
source_title: Phreesia, The Real Cost to Collect After the Visit (2018 infographic; 2023 revision); Elation Health help center, statement delivery charges; POS Professional Office Services white paper (searched: MGMA, HFMA, AAFP, CAQH sites)
practice_impact: Do not use $8 to $14 in any return-on-investment estimate; cost the practice's own statements from its vendor invoice plus staff minutes. Point-of-service collection is rarely possible in facilities anyway, so the real levers are correct secondary billing and representative contact details.

claim: Studies consistently show a substantial share of patients presenting as self-pay, commonly cited at 20 to 30 percent, have active insurance coverage they did not disclose.
correct_statement: No independent study was found. The 20 to 30 percent figure matches marketing claims by insurance-discovery vendors about hospital and ambulance self-pay accounts run through their own tools, and the claims are inconsistent: maxRTE says up to 25 percent, ZOLL more than 40 percent, while TransUnion's analysis, repeated by HFMA, found 1 to 5 percent of self-pay bad-debt accounts.
source_title: HFMA, Self Payment Collection (Feb 4, 2019), reporting TransUnion Healthcare analysis; TransUnion newsroom release; maxRTE and ZOLL Data Systems product pages (vendor marketing)
practice_impact: Little: nearly every patient of a geriatrics practice has Medicare, so true self-pay is rare; the useful version of this step is checking each eligibility response for Medicare Advantage enrollment, Medicaid or QMB status and other primary coverage, which costs nothing extra.

claim: Most states have prompt payment laws that require payers to process clean claims within defined timeframes, typically 30 to 45 days for electronic claims and 45 to 60 days for paper claims.
correct_statement: Every state has a prompt-pay law, but the typical clocks are shorter: 30 days for electronic claims in most states and 30 to 45 for paper; 60 days is rare. Florida requires payment, denial or contest within 20 days (electronic) or 40 days (paper), with 12% interest. These laws do not govern self-funded plans, Medicare or Medicare Advantage.
source_title: Fla. Stat. 627.6131 and 641.3155 (2026); 42 CFR 422.520 and 422.402; Texans for Lawsuit Reform Foundation, 'An Interstate Comparison of Healthcare Prompt-Pay Laws' (Jan. 31, 2016), Appendix A, spot-checked on Nov. 10, 2026 against current Texas, Ohio, Michigan and Arizona law; Texas Department of Insurance prompt-pay FAQ
practice_impact: Florida's clock is shorter than the playbook says, but it reaches only state-regulated insurers and HMOs (for example Medigap and commercial plans); Medicare and Medicare Advantage claims follow federal rules and contract terms.

claim: Medicare Advantage plans are not required to pay Medicare fee schedule rates. They are required to cover Medicare-covered services, but the rates at which they pay for those services are set by the plan’s contract with participating providers
correct_statement: Correct for contracted providers: the statute bars CMS from requiring a particular price structure in plan-provider contracts, and plans pay contracted providers under the contract's terms. A floor applies only without a contract: the plan must pay a non-contracted provider the Original Medicare amount, which the provider must accept as payment in full.
source_title: 42 U.S.C. 1395w-24(a)(6)(B)(iii); 42 CFR 422.520(b), 422.100(b)(2), 422.214(a) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); CMS, 'MA Payment Guide for Out of Network Payments'
practice_impact: A Medicare Advantage offer below 100% of Medicare should be weighed against the no-contract position: Original Medicare amounts for care the plan covers out of network, though HMO plans typically cover little routine out-of-network care.

claim: In the right circumstances, [out-of-network status] is a deliberate business strategy that generates higher per-service revenue, eliminates the administrative burden of network participation, and gives the practice pricing autonomy that in-network contracts do not permit.
correct_statement: Only for commercially insured or self-pay patients. For a geriatrics practice's patients, law sets the price: without a Medicare Advantage contract, physicians must accept Original Medicare amounts as payment in full; nonparticipating Medicare charges are capped at 115% of a fee schedule set 5% lower; QMB patients cannot be billed cost sharing. Opting out forfeits all Medicare and plan payment.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.214, 414.48, 414.20(b), 405.425 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); 45 CFR 149.410-149.420; Fla. Stat. 627.64194 and 641.3154 (2026); CMS Qualified Medicare Beneficiary program page (modified Mar. 16, 2026)
practice_impact: For a Florida facility-based geriatrics practice whose patients are Medicare, Medicare Advantage and dual-eligible, leaving a network buys no pricing freedom; it mainly risks HMO plans refusing to cover routine out-of-network visits.

claim: The practice has an ethical and, in most states, a legal obligation to notify patients who will be affected by the termination, patients who are currently in active treatment or who have upcoming appointments
correct_statement: The ethical duty is real, but the legal duty to notify patients generally sits with the plan, not the practice. Medicare Advantage plans must notify affected enrollees 45 days ahead for primary care terminations (30 for other specialties); federal law makes commercial plans notify continuing-care patients. Florida requires the practice to give the HMO and state regulator 60 days' notice.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.111(e) and 422.202(d)(4) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); 42 U.S.C. 300gg-113 and 300gg-138; Fla. Stat. 641.315(2) and 641.51(8) (2026); Mich. Comp. Laws 500.2212b; AMA Code of Medical Ethics Opinion 1.1.5. No statute requiring a practice to notify patients of a payer-contract termination was found; Fla. Admin. Code R. 64B8-10.002 covers physicians relocating or terminating practice.
practice_impact: If the practice drops a plan, the plan sends the legally required member notices; the practice's own legal duties are 60 days' notice to the plan and continued care on the old terms for patients in active treatment (up to six months for Florida-regulated HMO members; up to 90 days for continuing-care patients of commercial plans).

claim: For new providers, initiate credentialing with all relevant payers on the first day of employment ... Credentialing lags create revenue gaps that are not recoverable.
correct_statement: Day one is too late for commercial plans, where credentialing and enrollment can take 90-120 days and should start when the offer is accepted; Medicare applications can be filed up to 60 days before the start date. Gaps are partly recoverable: Medicare pays from the filing date plus 30 days back, Florida Medicaid from the date it receives the application.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.520(d), 424.521(a), 424.526(a)(2) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); Fla. Stat. 409.907(9)(a) (2026); AMA, 'Preparation guide for the physician credentialing process'
practice_impact: For a new geriatrics clinician, file Medicare with First Coast within the 60 days before the start date and Florida Medicaid as early as possible; start Medicare Advantage and commercial plans at offer acceptance, since those gaps depend on each contract and are often unrecoverable.

claim: Public benchmarking sources (including Milliman and the Urban Institute) show that actual commercial-to-Medicare rate ratios vary widely by state and market, national averages can range from roughly 120 percent to over 250 percent of Medicare
correct_statement: Variation is real, but the figures are mislabeled. National averages for physician services cluster near 140-147% of Medicare (Milliman 143%; MedPAC 147% for 2024). The 120-250% span matches Milliman's state range (119% Kentucky to 243% Wisconsin). Urban Institute's finding is by specialty: family medicine about 110%, internal medicine 120%, anesthesia 330%.
source_title: Milliman, 'Commercial reimbursement benchmarking' (June 19, 2024); Urban Institute, 'Commercial Health Insurance Markups over Medicare Prices for Physician Services Vary Widely by Specialty' (Oct. 2021); MedPAC, Report to the Congress (March 2026), ch. 4; HCCI (2020)
practice_impact: Geriatrics bills mostly visit codes, where commercial rates run about 110-120% of Medicare, and Florida professional prices averaged roughly 105-110% in HCCI's 2017 data; benchmarks of 150% or more should not be assumed.

claim: roughly 54 percent of eligible Medicare beneficiaries were enrolled in MA plans in 2025, rising to about 55 percent in 2026, per KFF.
correct_statement: KFF reports that 54% of eligible Medicare beneficiaries (those with both Part A and Part B) were in Medicare Advantage in 2025, 34.1 million of 62.8 million, and 55% in 2026, 35.2 million of 64.2 million. KFF notes enrollment growth slowed in 2026.
source_title: KFF, 'Medicare Advantage in 2026: Enrollment Update and Key Trends' (June 5, 2026, updated July 1, 2026); KFF, 'A Snapshot of Sources of Coverage Among Medicare Beneficiaries' (Dec. 19, 2025)
practice_impact: The figure is right, so Medicare Advantage plans are likely more than half of a Florida geriatrics practice's Medicare patients and their contract terms deserve the attention the playbook asks for.

claim: Medicare Advantage plans impose prior authorization requirements that traditional Medicare does not, for services that traditional Medicare covers without authorization.
correct_statement: True in general. Nearly all Medicare Advantage enrollees (99% in 2026) are in plans requiring prior authorization for some services; traditional Medicare generally requires none. Traditional Medicare is not authorization-free, though: it applies it to certain hospital outpatient, ambulance and equipment items, and, in Florida since January 2026, certain surgery-center procedures.
source_title: KFF, 'Medicare Advantage in 2026: Premiums, Out-of-Pocket Limits, Supplemental Benefits, and Prior Authorization' (June 5, 2026); 42 CFR 422.138; CMS, 'Prior Authorization and Pre-Claim Review Initiatives'
practice_impact: Counting authorization workload by plan, as the playbook suggests, is sound; skilled nursing stays (95% of enrollees) and home health (90%) are the services a facility-based geriatrics practice will meet most. In traditional Medicare, Florida home health agencies are under CMS's pre-claim Review Choice Demonstration.

claim: Pending prior authorizations 'typically take 7 to 14 business days' (patient script); planning guidance assumes a payer may 'consistently' take 12 to 15 days to process a request.
correct_statement: Federal rules cap standard prior authorization decisions at 7 calendar days for Medicare Advantage and Medicaid managed care since January 1, 2026 (72 hours if expedited; a 14-day extension only in limited cases) and 15 days for employer and Marketplace plans. Insurers' reported median decision time in 2025 was about one day, not 7 to 14 business days.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.568 (eCFR 2026-11-06); KFF, 'Prior Authorization Metrics Provide New Insights into Insurer Practices, but Gaps Remain' (Aug. 13, 2026); 29 CFR 2560.503-1
practice_impact: For Medicare Advantage patients a request pending past 7 calendar days is a plan violation to escalate, not a normal wait; the script would have staff and patients tolerate unlawful delays.

claim: Many payers issue authorizations with validity windows of 30 to 90 days, the specific window varies by payer and by service type.
correct_statement: Broadly right. UnitedHealthcare's imaging and cardiology authorizations are valid 45 calendar days and some delegated-group authorizations 90 days; Original Medicare's hospital outpatient affirmations last 120 days. Medicare Advantage plans must keep a course-of-treatment approval valid as long as medically necessary and may not require reauthorization for 90 days after a patient enrolls.
source_title: 2026 UnitedHealthcare Care Provider Administrative Guide (commercial and Medicare Advantage); CMS OPD Prior Authorization FAQs (Nov. 14, 2024); 42 CFR 422.112(b)(8)
practice_impact: Check the dates on each determination; for Medicare Advantage patients in an ongoing course of treatment, a plan demanding repeat authorization may be breaching 42 CFR 422.112(b)(8).

claim: When it is discovered post-service, the practice is billing for a procedure the payer may refuse to authorize retroactively, and in most cases, retroactive authorization is not available.
correct_statement: Supported for elective services at the two largest Medicare Advantage insurers. Humana says elective services not precertified beforehand are ineligible for retrospective review; UnitedHealthcare accepts retrospective requests only for urgent after-hours cases, within 2 business days for imaging. The claim is then denied and a participating provider cannot bill the patient. Emergency care needs no authorization.
source_title: Humana 2026 Provider Manual for physicians, hospitals and healthcare providers (effective March 1, 2026); 2026 UnitedHealthcare Care Provider Administrative Guide
practice_impact: A missed authorization on an elective Medicare Advantage service is usually an unrecoverable write-off the patient cannot be billed for, so authorization status must be confirmed before the service.

claim: Peer-to-peer reviews are the highest-yield appeal mechanism for clinical denials, overturn rates in practices that use them consistently are significantly higher than written appeals alone.
correct_statement: A peer-to-peer is not an appeal. For Medicare Advantage it must happen before the denial is final; afterwards only an appeal or reopening can change the decision. The comparison with written appeals has no traceable source: single-practice studies report 58% and 95% of imaging denials approved after peer-to-peer, while formal Medicare Advantage appeals overturned 67% in 2025.
source_title: 2026 UnitedHealthcare Care Provider Administrative Guide; Humana 2026 Provider Manual; KFF prior authorization metrics (Aug. 13, 2026); PubMed: Orthopedics 2023 (https://doi.org/10.3928/01477447-20231027-08), J Surg Res 2023 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jss.2023.03.013)
practice_impact: For Medicare Advantage denials, use the plan's pre-decision peer-to-peer window (24 hours at UnitedHealthcare) and otherwise file the formal appeal; relying on a post-denial phone call forfeits the route that actually overturns denials.

claim: Auth First-Pass Approval Rate target ≥80% by payer; Peer-to-Peer Overturn Rate target ≥60% per payer; Auth Expiration Rate ≤3% (stated to be CCRx's own recommended target, not an industry benchmark).
correct_statement: None of the three targets has a traceable external source; they are the vendor's own numbers. Public 2025 data put average approval at 88% in Medicare Advantage (insurer denial rates ranged 5% to 17%), 86% in Medicaid managed care and 82% in Marketplace plans, so an 80% floor is below average. No published benchmark exists for peer-to-peer overturn or expiration.
source_title: KFF, 'Prior Authorization Metrics Provide New Insights into Insurer Practices, but Gaps Remain' (Aug. 13, 2026)
practice_impact: Benchmark each Medicare Advantage plan against its own publicly posted approval rate, not a flat 80%; a practice approved only 80% of the time is doing worse than the average requester.

claim: If you don't have data on this, use 8, 12% as an industry estimate [of patient disengagement during the auth process] for procedural practices with auth wait times over 10 days.
correct_statement: No industry source gives an 8% to 12% patient drop-out rate tied to authorization waits. The AMA's 2025 survey says only that 79% of physicians see prior authorization at least sometimes lead to treatment abandonment. Narrow published figures: a dermatology survey reported 12% of authorizations delayed or abandoned treatment; one orthopedic clinic saw 12% of approved scans never completed.
source_title: 2025 AMA prior authorization physician survey (published May 2026); PubMed: Dermatol Online J 2021;27(1) (PMID 33560787), Orthopedics 2023 (https://doi.org/10.3928/01477447-20231027-08)
practice_impact: Do not plug 8-12% into the playbook's loss worksheet; count the practice's own orders that were never completed, and note that since 2026 Medicare Advantage waits beyond 7 days should be rare.

claim: Standalone tools (e.g., Infinitus, Olive, Rhyme) offer superior tracking, payer portal integration, and alert functionality.
correct_statement: Olive no longer exists: it announced its shutdown on October 31, 2023, selling its remaining businesses to Waystar and Humata Health, and oliveai.com now redirects to Waystar. Rhyme is active but serves large hospital systems. Infinitus's site could not be read. 'Superior' is an unsourced opinion; no independent comparison with EHR authorization modules is cited.
source_title: Healthcare Dive, 'Health AI startup Olive to shut down' (Nov. 1, 2023); oliveai.com redirect and Rhyme homepage (observed Nov. 10, 2026)
practice_impact: Little: one named product has been defunct for three years and another targets hospital systems, so treat the playbook's software suggestions as stale and confirm any tool still exists and fits a small practice before evaluating it.

claim: Primary Care (2, 5 providers): estimated annual staff labor cost $25K, $50K and estimated annual revenue delay/loss $15K, $40K from prior authorization, described as typical ranges, not worst-case estimates.
correct_statement: The ranges come from the vendor's unpublished experience and cannot be traced. Published figures vary widely: a measured primary care study found $2,161 to $3,430 per physician per year (2013); the AMA's 2025 survey reports 13 staff-and-physician hours weekly per physician; CAQH prices each request at $5.38 to $12.88. No public benchmark exists for revenue delay or loss.
source_title: 2025 AMA prior authorization physician survey (published May 2026); PubMed: Morley et al., J Am Board Fam Med 2013;26(1):93-5 (https://doi.org/10.3122/jabfm.2013.01.120062); 2024 CAQH Index
practice_impact: A facility-based geriatrics practice bills mostly visit codes that need no authorization, so its burden is probably well below this table; time the practice's own authorization work instead of adopting the range.

claim: Most PM systems can be configured to automatically flag claims by denial pattern, route them to the right worklist, and trigger follow-up. Hardly anyone turns this on.
correct_statement: Major practice management systems do offer denial worklists and tracking, and some generate them automatically, not as an opt-in setting. 'Hardly anyone turns this on' has no measured basis. Related data show automation is incomplete, not absent: in MGMA's February 2024 poll 36% of groups had automated under 20% of revenue cycle work, 45% between 21% and 60%, 17% more.
source_title: MGMA Stat, 'Steps toward revenue cycle automation vary across medical groups' (Feb. 27, 2024 poll); AdvancedMD 'Medical Billing Software' product sheet (copyright 2022); Experian Health 2025 State of Claims press release (Sept. 22, 2025)
practice_impact: Check whether the practice's own system already builds denial worklists by reason code before paying for setup help; the useful sort for this practice is by Medicare, Medicare Advantage and Medicaid denial type.

claim: Every PM and billing system ships configured for the average practice. Generic payer rules. Standard claim edits. Default fee schedule logic.
correct_statement: Overgeneralized. Contracted fee schedules must be loaded by each practice and edits can be customized, so defaults do need tailoring. But leading systems do not ship with only generic payer rules: athenahealth's rules engine holds payer-specific requirements updated daily, and AdvancedMD's scrubber applies Medicare, Medicaid and commercial payer edits (CCI, LCD, carrier-specific) out of the box.
source_title: athenahealth online help, 'Service Overview - athenaCollector' (accessed Nov. 10, 2026); AdvancedMD 'Claims Scrubbing' product page (accessed Nov. 10, 2026) and 'Medical Billing Software' product sheet (copyright 2022)
practice_impact: Ask the vendor which Medicare (NCCI, MUE, First Coast LCD) and Medicare Advantage edits it already maintains; the practice-specific work is place-of-service, facility and enrollment rules for nursing-facility visits plus loading contract rates.

claim: If your contracted rates aren't loaded into your system, you're billing off your chargemaster and accepting whatever the payer decides to pay; underpayments then go undetected.
correct_statement: Half right. Without expected allowed amounts loaded or audited, short payments are hard to spot, and MGMA recommends storing fee schedules and setting automated variance alerts. But billing a standard charge above contract rates is normal whether or not rates are loaded, and remittances show each payer's contractual adjustments. Florida physicians must claim underpayments within 12 months of payment.
source_title: MGMA Stat, 'Regular auditing of payer payments crucial to ensure accurate reimbursement' (Feb. 11, 2025 poll); Fla. Stat. §627.6131(19) and §641.3155(17) (2026)
practice_impact: Load the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule for the practice's Florida localities and each Medicare Advantage contract's rates, and audit at least quarterly: Florida-regulated insurers and HMOs need not accept underpayment claims filed more than 12 months after payment.

claim: Most practices find two or three high-frequency denial codes that a single configuration change eliminates ... The revenue impact shows up in 30 days.
correct_statement: No study or survey supports 'most practices find two or three' denial codes removable by one configuration change, or a 30-day payback; this is vendor assertion. Only the timing is plausible: Medicare pays clean electronic claims no sooner than day 14 and within 30 days, and Florida insurers must pay, deny or contest electronic claims within 20 days.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) Ch. 1 §80.2.1.1 and §80.2.1.2 (chapter as of Rev. 13725, 04-10-26); Fla. Stat. §627.6131(4)(b) (2026)
practice_impact: Run the top-five denial-code review on the practice's own 90-day remittance data, but do not forecast revenue from this promise; eligibility and medical-necessity denials common in facility-based geriatrics are not removed by one edit.

claim: Does your software regularly pass claims that come back denied? If the answer is yes, your claim edits are not configured for your payers.
correct_statement: Not a reliable test. Every practice has claims that pass edits and are still denied: HealthCare.gov insurers denied 19% of in-network claims in 2024, and leading causes include authorization, registration and eligibility errors, excluded services and medical necessity, which claim edits cannot fully detect. Payer-specific edits help mainly with missing or inaccurate claim data, the top cause providers cite (50%).
source_title: KFF, 'Claims Denials and Appeals in ACA Marketplace Plans in 2024' (Mar. 24, 2026); Experian Health 2025 State of Claims press release (Sept. 22, 2025); Kodiak Solutions KPI Benchmarking Report (Mar. 2026)
practice_impact: For a Medicare-heavy facility practice, post-edit denials often involve Medicare Advantage enrollment, hospice election, duplicate-visit rules and medical-necessity review; fix eligibility and documentation workflows as well as scrubber rules.

claim: Payer reserves the right to modify contract terms, including reimbursement rates, by providing written notice; with no response in the window (typically 30 to 90 days) the change is deemed accepted. 'This is legal.'
correct_statement: Notice-and-silence amendment clauses are common and usually enforceable, but legality varies by state. Texas voids preferred-provider contract terms allowing unilateral adverse material changes and requires written agreement plus 120 days; California and Ohio require 45-business-day or 90-day notice with negotiation, objection or termination rights. Florida has no general bar, but HMOs owe 30 days' prior written notice of reimbursement-schedule changes.
source_title: Tex. Ins. Code §1301.0642 (H.B. 3359, 88th Leg., eff. Sept. 1, 2023); Ohio Rev. Code §3963.04; Cal. Health & Safety Code §1375.7(b)(1); Fla. Stat. §641.315(4) and §627.6474 (2026); 42 CFR 422.202(a)(2); AMA Payor Contracting 101 (Dec. 2021)
practice_impact: In Florida amendment-by-silence is generally enforceable for commercial and Medicare Advantage agreements, so every payer notice needs a calendared response date; HMOs must give 30 days' written notice of fee-schedule changes and Medicare Advantage plans written notice before material changes.

claim: The unilateral amendment clause is in every payer contract (subhead); 'It's in almost every commercial payer contract' (body).
correct_statement: Unilateral amendment and policy-change provisions are common in commercial and Medicare Advantage agreements, but no survey quantifies them and the issue's subhead and body disagree. 'Every payer contract' is wrong: the AMA describes agreements requiring mutual written consent, Texas voids such clauses for adverse material changes in preferred-provider contracts, and Original Medicare changes payment through rulemaking, not contract amendment.
source_title: AMA Private Practice Toolkit, 'Payor Contracting 101' including sample contract language and 'Examples of Significant Payor Unilateral Policy Changes' (copyright 2021, PDF dated 12/21); Tex. Ins. Code §1301.0642
practice_impact: Read the amendment and manual-change sections of each agreement instead of assuming; Medicare fee-for-service rate changes arrive through the annual Physician Fee Schedule rule, not a letter with a response window.

claim: Payers use this clause to push through fee schedule reductions, add prior authorization requirements, change timely filing windows, and alter billing guidelines ... without a new signature.
correct_statement: Largely true: the AMA confirms payers cut rates by notice amendments and change authorization, coding and billing rules by revising manuals, often with limited notice. Limits are omitted. For Florida-regulated insurers and HMOs the six-month claim-submission period is statutory and cannot be waived or nullified by contract, and HMOs must give written notice before changing authorization procedures or reimbursement schedules.
source_title: AMA Private Practice Toolkit, 'Payor Contracting 101', section 'Examples of Significant Payor Unilateral Policy Changes' (Dec. 2021); Fla. Stat. §§627.6131(3)(b), (10); 641.3155(2)(b), (9); 641.315(4), (8) (2026)
practice_impact: Florida-regulated plans cannot shorten the six-month filing window by letter, but Medicare Advantage and self-funded plans sit outside those statutes; send every payer bulletin and manual update to one accountable owner.

claim: When the window has already closed, document the change and its revenue impact. Your next credentialing renewal is a negotiation point.
correct_statement: Documenting the change and its revenue effect is sound, but recredentialing is not a rate-negotiation event. It is a credentials review required at least every three years. Rates are reopened under the contract's term, renewal, amendment and termination-notice provisions; MGMA advises starting several months before the contract renewal date, and leverage comes from data and a credible willingness to terminate.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.204(b)(2)(ii); MGMA Stat, 'Most medical groups have gone years without a commercial payer rate increase' (Aug. 25, 2026); AMA Payor Contracting 101 (Dec. 2021)
practice_impact: Calendar each contract's anniversary and termination-notice window; tying renegotiation to the three-year recredentialing cycle could leave a rate cut in place for years.

claim: Many practices have negotiated rates back simply by responding. Payers account for silence. They do not always account for resistance.
correct_statement: No survey or study measures how often objecting to a noticed amendment restores rates. MGMA's Aug. 25, 2026 poll (203 responses) found only 29% of groups got a commercial rate increase in the past year and 50% had gone three years or longer; some respondents said simply asking worked, but payer refusal and lack of leverage were the dominant barriers.
source_title: MGMA Stat, 'Most medical groups have gone years without a commercial payer rate increase' (Aug. 25, 2026 poll; 203 responses)
practice_impact: Respond in writing to every amendment notice because it is cheap and preserves the record, but do not plan on a reversal; a small geriatrics group has limited leverage with Medicare Advantage plans.

claim: Practices with a functioning point-of-service collection program ... run 60 to 80 percent collection rates on patient responsibility.
correct_statement: No MGMA, HFMA or Kodiak benchmark ties a point-of-service program to a 60-80% patient-responsibility collection rate. Measured results vary: 1,348 athenahealth practices collected 66.7% of balances above $200 and 93.8% of small ones within a year (2015); MGMA shows 56% of copays and 39% of patient-due balances collected at time of service (2022); Kodiak's 2025 insured-patient yield was 42.4%.
source_title: MGMA Stat, 'Patient balance collection: What's moving the numbers and how to get ahead' (Oct. 22, 2025); Kodiak Solutions KPI Benchmarking Report (Mar. 2026); Chernew and Bush, Health Affairs Forefront (May 4, 2017), as reproduced by PNHP
