practice_impact: No check-in desk exists at a nursing facility and most patients are Medicare or dual eligible, so a 60-80% POS-driven target does not transfer; measure post-adjudication patient yield by payer instead.

claim: Patient balance collections were running at 34%. ... She assumed this was normal. It isn't.
correct_statement: The 34% vignette is uncheckable, and whether it is abnormal depends on the benchmark. Kodiak's large provider dataset shows commercially insured patients paid 34.4% of what they owed in 2024 and all insured patients 42.4% in 2025, so about a third is near the current norm. Older practice-only data (2015) show 66.7%-93.8% collected within 12 months.
source_title: Kodiak Solutions KPI Benchmarking Report (Mar. 2026); TechTarget RevCycle Management, 'Patient collection rate falls by over 3 percentage points' (Mar. 5, 2025); Ippolito et al., JAMA Health Forum 2025;6(8):e252284 (PubMed PMID 40779258); Chernew and Bush, Health Affairs Forefront (May 4, 2017)
practice_impact: Little direct use: do not treat 34% as proof of failure. In a Medicare-heavy facility practice, patient balances are mainly the Part B deductible and 20% coinsurance, often owed by Medigap or Medicaid instead of the patient, so benchmark by payer class.

claim: For patients with known deductible exposure, you can calculate an estimated patient responsibility before the visit. Presenting that estimate at check-in ... gives the patient the opportunity to pay ... before the claim is ever processed.
correct_statement: Estimating and requesting payment at check-in is generally allowed for commercial patients, but conditions are missing. Medicare requires amounts collected before submission to be shown on the claim and over-collections refunded; First Coast recommends not collecting deductible or coinsurance until Part B pays. QMBs may never be charged Medicare cost sharing. Eligibility responses are not final.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) Ch. 1 §30.3.1.1 and §30.3.3 (chapter as of Rev. 13725, 04-10-26); CMS MLN Fact Sheet MLN7936176, Prohibition on Billing Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries (Sept. 2025); First Coast Service Options FAQ, 'When is it acceptable to collect the deductible from the beneficiary?'; CMS Operating Rules FAQs
practice_impact: High: facility patients are mostly Original Medicare, Medicare Advantage and dual eligibles. Collecting estimated deductibles up front risks over-collection refunds and QMB violations; bill coinsurance after the remittance and screen QMB status first.

claim: Now multiply the same total by 70%. That's a conservative estimate of what a functioning POS collection program produces.
correct_statement: The arithmetic is right ($50,000 at 34% is $17,000; at 70%, $35,000), but no source supports 70% as a conservative result of a point-of-service program. MGMA reports practices collected 39% of patient-due balances at time of service in 2022; Kodiak's providers collected 42.4% of insured patient responsibility in 2025. Only older practice data reach 67%-94% within a year.
source_title: MGMA Stat, 'Patient balance collection: What's moving the numbers and how to get ahead' (Oct. 22, 2025); Kodiak Solutions KPI Benchmarking Report (Mar. 2026); HFMA, 'Patient POS collections pose a growing problem for RCM departments' (June 8, 2026)
practice_impact: Do not budget an $18,000-a-month style gain from this formula; a facility-based Medicare practice has little collectible point-of-service money, and Traditional Medicare shows the lowest POS share (15%).

claim: Eligibility verification 'you should be doing 24 to 48 hours before every appointment'; with it 'you know their deductible status, their copay, and their out-of-pocket balance'.
correct_statement: Checking one to four days ahead is common among MGMA member practices, not a formal standard. Federally adopted operating rules require plans to return base and remaining deductible, copay and coinsurance, not an out-of-pocket balance, and CMS says the response is not final. Original Medicare has 20% coinsurance, no visit copay and no out-of-pocket limit.
source_title: CMS Administrative Simplification, Operating Rules FAQs (page last modified Sept. 10, 2024); CAQH CORE Phase II 260 Eligibility & Benefits Data Content (270/271) Rule v2.1.0 (Mar. 2011) and CORE Eligibility & Benefits Data Content Rule vEB.2.1 (June 2025); MGMA, 'Pre-verifying eligibility and benefits' (Jan. 1, 2016) and 'As patients update coverage, who handles your insurance verification?' (Feb. 23, 2018); Medicare.gov costs page (2026)
practice_impact: Facility residents have no appointments: verify at admission and at the start of each month, because Medicare Advantage switches, Part A skilled stays, hospice and QMB status change who pays and what may be billed.

claim: May 12, 2026 is the CMS-R-131 transition deadline; an ABN issued that day on the old version is 'legally unenforceable' and the practice cannot bill the patient.
correct_statement: The date is right: CMS required the renewed ABN (Exp. 03/31/2029) starting May 12, 2026. The consequence is overstated: CMS says a wrong-version notice could be invalidated, leaving the practice liable, and that matters only where an ABN is mandatory. Never-covered (statutorily excluded) services can be billed to the patient with no ABN at all.
source_title: CMS MLN Connects Newsletter, March 19, 2026; Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) ch. 30 ss. 50.2.1, 50.5, 50.8
practice_impact: Any ABN signed on or after May 12, 2026 must be the Exp. 03/31/2029 version; audit ABNs issued since then, because an old-version ABN on a medical-necessity denial puts the write-off and any refund on the practice.

claim: CMS updated the ABN (CMS-R-131) in March 2026 with a 60-day transition window; the form 'did not change in any meaningful way', only readability and formatting.
correct_statement: OMB approved the renewed CMS-R-131 in March 2026 (CMS announced it March 13; expires 03/31/2029) and CMS gave 60 calendar days, to May 12, 2026. CMS describes the changes as readability and design. The layout and wording were visibly redesigned (lettered blanks A-J removed), so EHR-embedded templates must be rebuilt, not just re-dated.
source_title: CMS Beneficiary Notices Initiative page; CMS MLN Connects, March 19, 2026; ABN form and instructions (CMS files dated March 2026); Noridian JD DME notice
practice_impact: Confirm every ABN template (paper, EHR, facility packets) shows Exp. 03/31/2029 and the new layout; the old lettered-blank layout marks a superseded form.

claim: When Medicare is likely to deny a service as not medically necessary, not covered, or otherwise excluded, the practice must notify the patient first; without a valid ABN there is 'no legal mechanism to collect from the patient'.
correct_statement: An ABN is mandatory only for specific denial types, chiefly not reasonable and necessary (s.1862(a)(1)) and custodial care; without a valid one the practice cannot collect and must refund. For statutorily excluded or never-covered services an ABN is optional and the patient is liable without it (GY modifier).
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), ch. 30, ss. 50.2, 50.2.1, 50.9; First Coast Service Options, CMS beneficiary notices (Feb. 18, 2026); 42 CFR 411.404, 411.408
practice_impact: Use mandatory ABNs (GA modifier) for frequency or medical-necessity risks such as repeat visits or labs; routine foot care, dental and other excluded services can be billed to the patient without one, so do not write those off for lack of an ABN.

claim: ABNs apply to Medicare fee-for-service. They do not apply to Medicare Advantage.
correct_statement: Correct. The ABN (CMS-R-131) is only for Original Medicare (fee-for-service) beneficiaries and may not be used by Medicare Advantage plans or their contracted providers. For MA enrollees the provider must seek the plan's approval first; without the plan's own denial notice or a clear exclusion in the plan's coverage document, the enrollee is not liable.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), ch. 30, s. 50.1; CMS Parts C & D Enrollee Grievances, Organization/Coverage Determinations, and Appeals Guidance (effective July 6, 2026)
practice_impact: With a heavy MA mix, an ABN signed by an MA enrollee protects nothing; staff need the plan's pre-service organization determination before billing an MA patient for a non-covered service.

claim: The ABN must be presented before the service; a signature obtained afterward creates no valid financial liability, as 'courts and auditors have consistently held'.
correct_statement: The rule is right but its authority is CMS regulation and manual, not case law: the ABN must be delivered before the service and far enough ahead for an informed choice, and it cannot be back-dated or used for care already given. For repetitive care a late ABN works going forward only. No body of court decisions was found.
source_title: 42 CFR 411.408; Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), ch. 30, ss. 40.2.1, 50.8
practice_impact: In facility rounding, the ABN has to reach the resident or representative before the visit or test; an ABN signed after the fact shifts nothing, and emergencies never qualify.

claim: Providers win approximately 80% of Federal IDR disputes; this is 'documented CMS data from hundreds of thousands of disputes' resolved since 2022.
correct_statement: CMS public use files show providers prevailed in 77% to 88% of payment determinations in each half-year from 2023 to 2025 (85% in the second half of 2025), across about 5.8 million determinations through September 2026. That rate excludes the roughly 17 to 19% of disputes closed as ineligible, and ten filers bring about two thirds of all disputes.
source_title: CMS, Supplemental Background on the Federal IDR Public Use Files, July 1 - December 31, 2025 (as of July 22, 2026); CMS Independent Dispute Resolution Reports page
practice_impact: Little: Federal IDR covers only commercial and employer-plan out-of-network emergency care, air ambulance, and care at in-network hospitals, hospital outpatient departments and surgery centers; it does not reach Medicare, Medicare Advantage, Medicaid or nursing-facility visits.

claim: The only real question is whether the dollar amount on the claim justifies 'the $115 administrative filing fee' and the staff time to submit.
correct_statement: The $115 administrative fee applied only to disputes initiated January 22, 2024 through June 10, 2026. Since June 11, 2026 it is $15 per party per dispute, announced by CMS on June 3, before this issue. Each party also pays the arbitrator's fee ($200 to $840 single, $268 to $1,173 batched), which the loser forfeits.
source_title: 45 CFR 149.510(d) (eCFR, as amended by Federal IDR Operations final rule, 91 FR 33900, June 4, 2026); CMS No Surprises notice 'IDR Administrative Fee Update', June 3, 2026
practice_impact: Little for a Medicare, Medicare Advantage and Medicaid facility practice; for any commercial out-of-network hospital work, budget $15 plus an arbitrator fee of several hundred dollars at risk per dispute, not $115.

claim: Open negotiation is 'the 30-day window before you can file IDR' and starts from the date of the initial payment or denial; if it has passed 'you can still file' within 4 business days after it ends.
correct_statement: The periods are business days and the trigger is wrong. A party has 30 business days after the initial payment or denial to send an open negotiation notice; the 30-business-day negotiation period starts the day that notice is sent; IDR must be initiated in the 4 business days after it ends. A claim with no timely notice cannot be filed.
source_title: CMS, Federal IDR Process Guidance for Disputing Parties (December 2023 update), sections 3-4; 45 CFR 149.510(b)(1)-(2)
practice_impact: Little for this payer mix; where IDR does apply, pulling 90 days of old remittances as the issue suggests would surface claims already past the 30-business-day notice deadline and therefore ineligible.

claim: The Fifth Circuit panel upheld the QPA method, en banc review was granted, and as of June 9, 2026 no en banc decision has issued; a provider-favorable ruling 'may create retroactive adjustment opportunities' on decided disputes.
correct_statement: True on June 9, 2026, but the en banc Fifth Circuit ruled on August 11, 2026: ghost rates may not be counted in the QPA and bonus and incentive payments may not be excluded; excluding single-case agreements was upheld. The opinion does not reopen decided disputes, and IDR determinations are binding and largely unreviewable. Agencies promised guidance on August 13.
source_title: Texas Medical Association v. HHS, No. 23-40605 (5th Cir. Aug. 11, 2026) (en banc); CMS No Surprises Act notices, 'TMA III Statement', August 13, 2026
practice_impact: Little: the QPA only matters for commercial out-of-network claims under the No Surprises Act, not for Medicare, Medicare Advantage or Medicaid facility work.

claim: The 'statutory factors' that move an arbitrator above the QPA are provider training/experience/quality, 'market rate comparables', case complexity, and 'demonstration of good faith' shown by participating in open negotiation.
correct_statement: Two of the four are misstated. The listed factors are training, experience and quality; market share (not market rates); patient acuity or complexity; facility teaching status, case mix and scope; and good-faith efforts to enter network agreements plus contracted rates over the prior 4 plan years. Arbitrators may not consider usual and customary charges, billed charges or public-payer rates.
practice_impact: Little for this practice; anyone who does file should argue the real factors, since charge-based 'market comparables' are barred and good faith means network-contracting efforts, not attending open negotiation.

claim: Timely filing limits are 'set by contract, not by law. Every payer sets its own.'
correct_statement: Often set by law. Medicare's one-year limit is federal law (42 CFR 424.44); Medicaid's 12-month ceiling is federal regulation; Florida statute gives providers 6 months to bill state-regulated insurers and HMOs, including Medicaid plans, and bars waiving it by contract. Contract or plan policy controls mainly for Medicare Advantage and self-funded employer plans.
practice_impact: Medicare, Medicaid and Florida-regulated plans run on statutory clocks the practice cannot negotiate; only Medicare Advantage and self-funded plan terms need a per-payer contract table.

claim: Medicare: 12 months from date of service (with limited exceptions).
correct_statement: Correct for Original Medicare: claims must be filed within 1 calendar year after the date of service. The four exceptions are Medicare or contractor error, retroactive Medicare entitlement, retroactive entitlement with state Medicaid recoupment, and retroactive disenrollment from a Medicare Advantage or PACE plan. A timely-filing denial cannot be appealed, and the patient cannot be billed for the lapse.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.44 Time limits for filing claims; Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), ch. 1, ss. 70-70.7
practice_impact: Core payer rule: every Original Medicare visit must reach First Coast as an accepted claim within one year of service, with no appeal if missed.

claim: Medicaid: varies by state, 'ranges from 90 days to 24 months'.
correct_statement: Limits vary by state, but federal rule caps ordinary fee-for-service claims at 12 months from service, so 24 months is not a general limit; states may be shorter. Florida: 12 months for fee-for-service, 6 months by statute for Medicaid plans, and for Medicare crossovers 12 months from service or 6 months after the Medicare disposition notice, whichever is greater.
source_title: 42 CFR 447.45(d); Fla. Admin. Code r. 59G-1.052(15) (2018); AHCA Florida Medicaid Provider Reimbursement Handbook, CMS-1500 (2008), ch. 1; Fla. Stat. ss. 409.967(2)(j), 641.3155
practice_impact: Dual-eligible crossover balances get 12 months from service or 6 months after Medicare's disposition, whichever is later; the 2008 AHCA handbook's 36-month figure conflicts with the 2018 rule, so do not rely on it.

claim: Medicare Advantage: 'Set by the plan, not CMS', often 90 to 180 days, sometimes shorter.
correct_statement: Correct that CMS sets no filing deadline for contracted Medicare Advantage claims; the contract or plan manual does. The 90 to 180 day range is not a reliable rule: Humana's stated default is one year from the date of service, while a UnitedHealthcare dual plan uses 90 days for participating and 365 days for non-participating providers. Read each contract.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.520 Prompt payment by MA organization; Humana provider site, Claims Submissions; UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Manual (Dual Complete HMO SNP)
practice_impact: Medicare Advantage is a large share of facility geriatrics volume; build a per-plan limit table from each signed contract, since defaults run from 90 days to one year.

claim: The clock starts on the date of service, not on submission or rejection; 'The original submission does not preserve your timely filing. Only a clean, accepted submission does.'
correct_statement: Right for Medicare and many contracts: the clock runs from the date of service, a rejected or unprocessable submission is not a filed claim, and UnitedHealthcare applies the same limit to corrected claims. Not universal: an accepted Medicare claim later denied has separate appeal and reopening deadlines, and Florida law runs secondary and contested-claim clocks from the payer's notice.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), ch. 1, ss. 70.1, 70.2.3.2, 70.3, 80.3.1; Fla. Stat. s. 641.3155; 42 CFR 405.942, 405.980; UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide
practice_impact: Work clearinghouse and First Coast front-end rejections daily, since they never count as filed; but do not write off denied claims as untimely when an appeal, reopening or secondary-payer clock is still open.

claim: As of January 1, 2026, CMS finalized its Prior Authorization rule under the CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule
correct_statement: CMS finalized the rule (CMS-0057-F) on January 17, 2024; it was published February 8, 2024 and took effect April 8, 2024. January 1, 2026 is only the first compliance date, for the process provisions (decision timeframes, denial reasons, public metrics). The API requirements start January 1, 2027. Scope: Medicare Advantage, Medicaid/CHIP and federal-exchange plans; drugs excluded.
source_title: CMS-0057-F final rule, 89 FR 8758 (Feb. 8, 2024); CMS fact sheet on CMS-0057-F (Jan. 17, 2024)
practice_impact: The dates decide which payer duties a practice can invoke: in 2026 only decision deadlines and denial reasons apply, and only to Medicare Advantage and Medicaid plans, not Original Medicare or commercial payers.

claim: Urgent PA requests: Payers must now respond within 72 hours. Standard PA requests: Payers must respond within 7 calendar days.
correct_statement: The numbers are right but not for all payers. Since January 1, 2026 they bind Medicare Advantage, Medicaid and CHIP (managed care from rating periods starting 2026). Federal-exchange plans stay at 15 days; commercial/employer plans and Original Medicare are not covered; drugs are excluded; plans may extend up to 14 days. MA's 72-hour expedited limit predates 2026.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.568, 422.572, 438.210(d), 440.230(e) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); CMS fact sheet on CMS-0057-F
practice_impact: Usable for Medicare Advantage and Florida Medicaid plan authorizations (skilled nursing stays, therapy, equipment); no leverage against commercial payers or Original Medicare, none for drugs. A missed MA deadline is itself an appealable adverse determination (422.568(f)).

claim: Electronic PA (ePA): Covered payers must now support electronic prior authorization through standardized HL7 FHIR APIs.
correct_statement: Not yet. The FHIR Prior Authorization API is required from January 1, 2027 (Medicare Advantage and Medicaid/CHIP fee-for-service; managed care rating periods and exchange plan years starting 2027), not in 2026. CMS restated that timing on November 9, 2026. Drugs are excluded; the April 2026 proposal (CMS-0062-P) to add drugs and mandate specific implementation guides is not final.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.122(b) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule final rule, 91 FR 70992 (Nov. 9, 2026); 89 FR 8759
practice_impact: Do not expect Medicare Advantage or Medicaid plans to take FHIR-based authorizations before 2027; ask the EHR vendor about 2027 readiness. The MIPS electronic prior authorization measure is optional for 2027 and required from the 2028 performance period.

claim: CMS has a complaint mechanism, and patterns of non-compliance are being tracked.
correct_statement: True for Medicare Advantage only: since December 22, 2025 CMS has an online Provider Complaints Form whose submissions go to its Complaints Tracking Module for triage. It is not prior-authorization-specific. Medicaid plan complaints go to the state agency, exchange plans to the Marketplace call center, and commercial/employer plans are outside CMS. Plans also post annual authorization metrics.
source_title: CMS Provider Complaints Form page (last modified Feb. 18, 2026); CMS HPMS memo on Complaints Tracking Module updates (Dec. 22, 2025); 89 FR 8764-8765
practice_impact: Worth bookmarking for Medicare Advantage plans, a large share of Florida geriatric patients; for Florida Medicaid plans the complaint goes to the state agency (AHCA), not CMS, and commercial plans answer to state insurance regulators or, if self-funded, the Department of Labor.

claim: The 72-hour window only kicks in if the request is properly marked urgent.
correct_statement: Correct in substance. The 72-hour clock applies only to expedited requests. A Medicare Advantage plan must expedite when a physician states the standard timeframe could seriously jeopardize the enrollee's life, health or ability to regain maximum function; a request the plan declines to expedite moves to the standard clock. Medicaid plans must also expedite when they themselves so determine.
practice_impact: For frail facility patients, have the physician state the 'serious jeopardy' standard in the request itself; that statement obliges a Medicare Advantage plan to use the 72-hour clock. 'Time-sensitive' alone is not the regulatory test.

claim: CO (Contractual Obligation) adjustments are write-offs. PR (Patient Responsibility) codes mean the patient owes it.
correct_statement: CMS defines CO as amounts 'generally' written off and not billed to the patient, and PR as amounts that 'may be billed to the patient or insured'. PR is not always collectible: secondary insurers pay first, and Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries cannot be billed Medicare cost-sharing although remittances show PR. CO denials for fixable errors should be corrected, not written off.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) ch. 22 s.60.1; CMS memo 'QMB Program Information in Remittance Advice and Explanation of Benefits' (Apr. 3, 2018); CMS MLN Fact Sheet 'Prohibition on Billing Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries' (MLN7936176, Sept. 2025)
practice_impact: Many nursing-facility residents are dual-eligible QMBs: a PR-1 or PR-2 line carrying alert N781/N782 goes to Medicaid or is adjusted, never to the patient. Federal law bars billing QMBs for Medicare cost-sharing even when Medicaid pays nothing; violations risk sanctions.

claim: The CO-45 adjustment, Charges exceed your contractual amount, gets accepted at face value every single day.
correct_statement: The code meaning is right: reason code 45 officially reads 'Charge exceeds fee schedule/maximum allowable or contracted/legislated fee arrangement'. Per X12 the adjustment cannot equal the full charge. For Medicare the benchmark is the Physician Fee Schedule amount for the locality and place of service, not a negotiated contract. 'Every single day' is unquantified rhetoric with no data behind it.
source_title: X12 External Code Source, Claim Adjustment Reason Codes; Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 12 s.20.4.2 (site-of-service differential)
practice_impact: Check Medicare CO-45 amounts against the fee schedule for the Florida locality and setting: place of service 31 (Part A skilled stay) pays the facility rate, 32 (nursing facility) the non-facility rate, so a POS error changes the allowed amount on services with a site differential.

claim: Bundling Flags (CO-97 / CO-B15) ... CO-97 means the service is included in another allowance.
correct_statement: Correct. CO-97 means the benefit is included in the payment for another, already adjudicated service; Medicare uses B15 for the same bundle when the other service has not yet been billed or adjudicated, notably the global surgical package. Caveat: First Coast reports code-pair (NCCI) denials as CO-236, so for CO-97 check the global period and remark code first.
source_title: X12 Claim Adjustment Reason Codes; Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) ch. 12 s.40.4.D (chapter rev. May 7, 2026); First Coast Service Options top-denials guidance (July 28, 2026)
practice_impact: On Florida Medicare remittances read the remark code beside CO-97: M144 means global surgery, N70 a home health episode, M15 a bundled service. A visit bundled into a procedure's global package needs modifier 24, 25 or 57 if documented, not 59.

claim: If an unbundling modifier applies, 59, XE, XS, XU, XP, and wasn't on the claim, that's a corrected claim waiting to happen.
correct_statement: Incomplete in ways that matter. CMS treats 59 as a last resort after more specific modifiers (24, 25, 27, 57, 58, 78, 79, 91, anatomic) and bars it on visit codes. A modifier bypasses a code-pair edit only if the edit's indicator is 1 and documentation shows a distinct service. Medicare's CO-97/B15 global-package denials need global-surgery modifiers instead.
source_title: CMS MLN Booklet 'Proper Use of Modifiers 59, XE, XP, XS & XU' (MLN1783722, April 2026); Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 12 s.40.4; First Coast Service Options top-denials guidance (July 28, 2026)
practice_impact: A visit-heavy geriatrics practice will usually need modifier 25 (or 24 inside a global period) on the visit, never 59; adding 59 after a denial without documentation of a distinct service is an audit exposure, not a recovery. At First Coast resubmit only the corrected line.

claim: An EOB line with a $0.00 payment and no denial code is a data entry ghost, and payers produce them more often than you think.
correct_statement: No source supports the frequency claim; 'data entry ghost' is not a recognized term. Under the HIPAA 835 standard a remittance must balance at the service-line level, so a zero payment must carry a group code and reason code accounting for the full charge; Medicare contractors may not omit them. A code-less zero-pay line is nonconforming and should be queried.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) ch. 22 ss.30, 60, 60.1
practice_impact: little for Original Medicare remittances, which always carry group and reason codes; on paper EOBs from Medicare Advantage or commercial plans a zero-pay line with no code warrants a claim-status call.

claim: Denied Claims Nobody Appealed: The $20K/Month Math Most Practices Ignore (title) versus: The appeal program that recovers $2,500 per month does not require new staff or new software.
correct_statement: Neither figure has a traceable source; the issue never shows the math its title promises. The headline says $20K/month; the body and the vendor's blurb say $2,500/month, eight times less. The blurb's 10-20% appeal rate and 70% win rate are unsourced; CMS reports 2% of denied Original Medicare claims appealed and 48% of Part B appeals at least partly successful.
source_title: CMS, Original Medicare Claim Appeals Data - 2025 (Appeals Fact Sheets, redetermination page); vendor Issue 09 page text and archive description
practice_impact: Do not budget on either number; size the opportunity from the practice's own denial report: denied dollars by reason code, the share never worked, and the actual overturn rate by payer.

claim: If your practice submitted one claim and the payer denied it as a duplicate, the denial is a payer error... submit the appeal with the clearinghouse confirmation of single submission, and recover the payment.
correct_statement: Not automatically a payer error. First Coast says most duplicate denials mean the service was already processed and paid or exactly matches an earlier claim; others reflect a missing repeat-service modifier (76, 77, 91, 59/X). Check claim history first. In Medicare a wrongly flagged duplicate is corrected by clerical reopening; physician duplicate denials may also be appealed.
source_title: First Coast Service Options, 'Tips on how to avoid billing a duplicate claim' (Nov. 1, 2024); Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) ch. 1 s.120 and ch. 34 s.10.4
practice_impact: Repeat same-day services and refiled claims commonly produce OA-18 at First Coast; check claim status in SPOT before acting, then fix with a repeat-service modifier or clerical reopening. A clearinghouse receipt alone does not address Medicare's claims-history match.

claim: Modifier missing, wrong place of service code, procedure and diagnosis mismatch, these denials are frequently correctable on resubmission and should never be written off without a corrected claim submission.
correct_statement: Consistent with Medicare guidance. Claims returned as unprocessable (remark MA130) have no appeal rights and must be corrected and refiled within the one-year filing limit. Adjudicated denials caused by clerical errors (modifier, place of service, transposed codes) are corrected by clerical reopening, not appeal; refiling the whole claim can trigger a duplicate denial. Code changes must match the record.
source_title: First Coast Service Options, 'How to appeal a claim' (Dec. 17, 2025) and 'Before you appeal a claim or request a redetermination' (Aug. 20, 2025); Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 34 s.10.4; 42 CFR 424.44
practice_impact: For facility visits, place-of-service (31 versus 32) and modifier errors can be corrected through First Coast's SPOT portal or Reopening Gateway within one year of the determination, much faster than a written redetermination.

claim: Find the clinical practice guideline from the relevant specialty society, AMA, AAFP, ACS, specialty-specific, that supports medical necessity for the denied service.
correct_statement: A specialty-society guideline is legitimate support but not the controlling standard. Medicare Advantage plans must follow Medicare statutes, regulations and national and local coverage determinations, and may apply guideline-based criteria only where those are not fully established; Original Medicare adjudicators give substantial deference to coverage determinations. Lead with the applicable NCD or LCD. The AMA is not a specialty society.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.101(b)-(c) and 42 CFR 405.1062 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026)
practice_impact: For geriatric facility care the stronger citations are the NCD, LCD and Medicare manual provisions, then American Geriatrics Society or PALTmed (formerly AMDA) guidelines, which address nursing-facility care directly.

claim: These denials have high appeal success rates when the documentation is complete and the appeal is written in the payer's clinical language.
correct_statement: True for Medicare Advantage, not across payers; none of the public figures isolates medical-necessity denials or tests 'payer language'. Appealed Medicare Advantage authorization denials were overturned 80.7% of the time in 2024 (67% on 2025 plan-posted metrics). Original Medicare Part B redeterminations in 2025: 45% favorable, 3% partially favorable. Medicaid managed care 47%; Marketplace 43%. Few denials are appealed.
source_title: KFF, 'Medicare Advantage Insurers Made Nearly 53 Million Prior Authorization Determinations in 2024' (Jan. 28, 2026); KFF prior authorization metrics brief (Aug. 13, 2026); CMS Original Medicare Claim Appeals Data - 2025
practice_impact: Appealed Medicare Advantage authorization denials are reversed two-thirds to four-fifths of the time, Original Medicare Part B appeals about half; prioritize appeals by payer rather than on a blanket 'high success' assumption.

claim: The dispute window is typically 90 to 180 days from the payment date, check your contract.
correct_statement: Most major payers allow longer. UnitedHealthcare: 12 months from the original EOB. Florida Blue: one year from the remittance advice. Humana: 18 months. Aetna: 180 calendar days. Florida statute lets physicians claim underpayments from insurers and HMOs within 12 months of payment. Original Medicare: 120 days to appeal, one year to reopen.
source_title: Fla. Stat. 627.6131(19) and 641.3155(17) (2026); UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide ch. 10; Florida Blue Manual for Physicians and Providers; Humana 2026 Provider Manual; Aetna 'Disputes and appeals overview'; 42 CFR 405.942, 405.980
practice_impact: A 90-180 day cutoff would abandon recoverable underpayments: look back a full 12 months for Florida insurers and HMOs, and use 120 days (appeal) or one year (reopening) for Medicare.

claim: If your new contracted rate is higher than the old rate and claims from January are processing at December rates, every one of those claims is an underpayment.
correct_statement: Only for services dated on or after the day the higher rate takes effect under the contract. December services processed in January are correctly paid at the old rate. Medicare implements its fee schedule January 1 and adjusts misprocessed claims if the physician requests it. Commercial contracts may update on other dates or stay pegged to an earlier Medicare schedule.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04) ch. 23 §30.1; CMS CY 2026 Physician Fee Schedule final rule fact sheet (Oct. 31, 2025); AMA Private Practice Toolkit, 'Payor Contracting 101'
practice_impact: Audit January payments by date of service against each contract's stated effective date; CMS's 2026 practice-expense change lowered indirect cost allocations for facility-setting services, so the new rate is not always higher.

claim: Your contract may specify full payment for a 25-modifier evaluation and management service performed on the same day as a procedure. The payer's system may apply a 50 percent reduction by default.
correct_statement: Reductions of 50% tied to modifier 25 exist, but as published payer policies, not hidden system defaults. UnitedHealthcare pays 50% of a modifier-25 problem-oriented visit billed with a preventive visit unless the contract supersedes its policy. Medicare pays a modifier-25 visit in full on top of the procedure. A policy-based reduction is not automatically an underpayment.
source_title: UnitedHealthcare Commercial Reimbursement Policy 2026R0013C, Preventive Medicine and Screening Policy, Professional; Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 12 §30.6.6.B; Horizon BCBSNJ Modifier -25 policy (rev. Aug. 27, 2026)
practice_impact: Little for Medicare fee-for-service, which pays modifier-25 visits in full; for commercial and Medicare Advantage plans, read the payer's published modifier-25 policy before disputing a reduced visit.

claim: That gap is where the 3 to 7 percent leakage lives.
correct_statement: No traceable study puts payer underpayments at 3 to 7 percent of practice revenue; the issue cites none. The closest published figures: HFMA's 3-5% of hospital net revenue for all leakage (missed charges, inefficiency and underpayments), footnoted to a blog post, and the AMA's 2013 report card finding 7.1% of commercial claims processed inaccurately. Neither measures physician-practice underpayments.
source_title: HFMA, 'Why AI is such a promising tool for eliminating a hospital's revenue leakage' (Jan. 30, 2026); Medical Economics on the AMA National Health Insurer Report Card (July 10, 2013); MGMA Stat, 'Regular auditing of payer payments crucial to ensure accurate reimbursement' (Feb. 11, 2025)
practice_impact: Do not size a recovery project on 3-7% of revenue; measure the practice's own variance by auditing paid claims against contracted and Medicare fee schedule rates.

claim: Systematic errors are recoverable retroactively, often back to the date the error began.
correct_statement: Recovery reaches back only as far as the governing deadline, not to when the error began. Florida bars physician underpayment claims against insurers and HMOs more than 12 months after payment; UnitedHealthcare allows 12 months and Humana 18. Medicare corrects fee-schedule errors back to January 1 of the current year on request and reopens claims within one year.
source_title: Fla. Stat. 627.6131(19) and 641.3155(17) (2026); Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 23 §30.1; 42 CFR 405.980; UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide; Humana 2026 Provider Manual
practice_impact: Size recovery targets to the allowed look-back (12 months for Florida insurers and HMOs, one year for Medicare reopenings), and file early: each month of delay drops the oldest claims out of reach.

claim: Typical ranges: 30 days for urgent denials, 60 to 180 days for standard PA denials. Your contracts specify the exact windows.
correct_statement: Federal rules, not provider contracts, set most windows, and urgency does not shorten them. Medicare Advantage: 60 calendar days after receipt of the denial notice (65 from its date) for standard and expedited appeals. ERISA group plans: at least 180 days. Medicaid managed care: 60 days. Original Medicare: 120 days. Expedited status only speeds the plan's decision to 72 hours.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.582 and 422.584; 29 CFR 2560.503-1(h)(3)(i); 42 CFR 438.402(c)(2)(ii); 42 CFR 405.942 (eCFR, current to Nov. 5, 2026); CMS Parts C & D Appeals Guidance (eff. July 6, 2026) s. 50
practice_impact: Calendar 65 days from the notice date for every Medicare Advantage prior-auth denial, urgent or not; there is no 30-day urgent deadline, and the member's plan rules, not the practice's contract, set the window.

claim: Most payers are required to make a physician reviewer available for a peer-to-peer conversation within a defined window after a PA denial.
correct_statement: No federal rule requires a post-denial peer-to-peer. CMS calls such discussions voluntary for Medicare Advantage plans, and UnitedHealthcare and Humana require them before an MA denial; afterwards only an appeal or reopening can change it. Florida's s. 627.6141 (individual health policies) requires a physician-level appeal, by telephone if wished, for medical-necessity claim denials, answered within 15 business days.
source_title: CMS Parts C & D Enrollee Grievances, Organization/Coverage Determinations, and Appeals Guidance (eff. July 6, 2026) s. 40; UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide ch. 7; Humana 2026 Provider Manual; Fla. Stat. 627.6141 (2026)
practice_impact: For Medicare Advantage patients the peer-to-peer must happen before the denial is final (UnitedHealthcare gives a 24-hour pre-decision window); after that, file a reconsideration rather than wait for a call.

claim: appeal win rates for PA denials routinely run 40 to 70 percent at practices that have a structured process.
correct_statement: The range matches published averages for all appealed prior-authorization denials, not practices with a 'structured process': insurers' 2025 CMS-mandated metrics show 67% overturned in Medicare Advantage, 47% in Medicaid managed care and 43% on HealthCare.gov, ranging by insurer from 16% to over 90%. KFF's separate MA data show 80.7% in 2024. Neither dataset isolates practices with a structured process.
source_title: KFF, 'Prior Authorization Metrics Provide New Insights Into Insurer Practices, but Gaps Remain' (Aug. 13, 2026); KFF, 'Medicare Advantage Insurers Made Nearly 53 Million Prior Authorization Determinations in 2024' (Jan. 28, 2026)
practice_impact: Appealing Medicare Advantage prior-auth denials pays (two-thirds to four-fifths are overturned), but results swing widely by insurer; do not budget on a vendor-promised win rate.

claim: A PA denial that doesn't get appealed within the filing window is permanently closed.
correct_statement: Missing the deadline usually forfeits that appeal, but not always permanently. Medicare Advantage plans may accept a late reconsideration request for good cause, and determinations can be reopened within one year for any reason or four years for good cause. Original Medicare also allows good-cause extensions. ERISA plans may enforce their deadlines strictly, so check each denial notice.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.582(c), 422.616 and 405.942(b) (eCFR, current to Nov. 5, 2026); CMS Parts C & D Appeals Guidance (eff. July 6, 2026) ss. 50.3 and 80
practice_impact: A missed Medicare Advantage deadline is not automatically dead: file late with a written good-cause explanation or request a reopening before writing the service off.

claim: Follow-up scheduled at 14 days if no response, most payers have mandated response timelines
correct_statement: True: appeal decision deadlines are set by regulation. Medicare Advantage plans must decide standard pre-service reconsiderations within 30 calendar days (7 for Part B drugs), expedited ones within 72 hours and payment appeals within 60 days. ERISA plans: 30 days pre-service, 72 hours urgent, 60 days post-service. A 14-day follow-up is too late for expedited appeals.
practice_impact: Set follow-up by appeal type: 72 hours for expedited Medicare Advantage appeals, day 30 for standard pre-service ones; a plan that misses its deadline must send the case to the independent reviewer.

claim: CMS released the updated ICD-10-CM diagnosis code files and ICD-10-PCS procedure code files, both effective October 1, 2026.
correct_statement: The FY 2027 ICD-10-CM and ICD-10-PCS files are posted on CMS.gov and took effect October 1, 2026. ICD-10-CM is developed by CDC/NCHS, not CMS (CMS maintains PCS). CM files run through September 30, 2027; CMS labels the PCS files as valid through March 31, 2027, implying an April 2027 update.
source_title: CMS, ICD-10 Codes (2027 ICD-10-CM & PCS files)
practice_impact: Professional claims for dates of service on or after 10/1/2026 need FY 2027 ICD-10-CM codes; ICD-10-PCS is inpatient-hospital only and does not apply to physician billing.

claim: Any claim you submit on or after October 1 with a deleted code, an outdated code, or a newly invalid code combination will deny. Not pend. Not generate a soft edit. Deny.
correct_statement: There is no grace period, but validity follows the date of service or discharge, not the submission date: claims filed after October 1 for September services must still use the old codes. Medicare returns claims with discontinued diagnosis codes as unprocessable; such a claim 'is not denied', has no appeal rights, and is corrected and resubmitted.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), Chapter 23 §10.6 and Chapter 1 §80.3.1
practice_impact: Late-September facility visits billed in October must keep FY 2026 codes; switching by submission date creates rejections. Rejected claims are rebilled, not appealed, and timely filing keeps running.

claim: They come back as CO-4 (service inconsistent with code) or CO-16 (claim lacks information)
correct_statement: CARC 16 is described correctly, and Medicare Part B uses CO-16 with remark code M76 for a missing, incorrect or truncated diagnosis. CARC 4 is misdescribed: it means the procedure code is inconsistent with the modifier, not a diagnosis problem. The diagnosis-specific codes are CARC 146 (diagnosis invalid for date of service) and CARC 11.
source_title: X12 External Code Source 139, Claim Adjustment Reason Codes; Medicare Claims Processing Manual ch. 1 §80.3.2.1.2
practice_impact: Staff hunting for CO-4 will miss code-set rejections; watch CO-16 with M76/MA63/MA130, CO-146 and CO-11, plus front-end clearinghouse (277CA) rejections that never reach a remittance.

claim: CMS issued a National Coverage Determination coding-revision transmittal with an effective date of October 1 and an implementation date of October 5.
correct_statement: CMS Change Request 14464 (Transmittal 13752, May 26, 2026; rescinded and replaced by 13910 on August 14 and 13968 on September 24, 2026) carries an effective date of October 1, 2026 and implementation date of October 5, 2026. It covers NCDs 20.4, 90.2, 110.18, 110.24, 150.3 and 220.6.1; no policy changes.
source_title: CMS Transmittal 13968 (Pub 100-20), CR 14464, ICD-10 and Other Coding Revisions to NCDs, October 2026; MLN Matters MM14464
practice_impact: Little for facility-based geriatrics E/M; matters only if the practice bills bone density studies, cardiac PET, ICD implants, next-generation sequencing, aprepitant or CAR-T. No DME NCDs are in this update.

claim: When CMS updates the national code set, many commercial payers update their Local Coverage Determinations and coverage policies in the same cycle.
correct_statement: Commercial payers do not have Local Coverage Determinations. LCDs are Medicare policies issued only by Medicare Administrative Contractors (First Coast Service Options in Florida), which revise LCD billing-and-coding articles for new ICD-10 codes effective October 1, sometimes publishing weeks afterward. Commercial payers keep their own medical policies on their own schedules. Medicare Advantage plans must follow NCDs and LCDs.
source_title: 42 CFR 400.202 and 422.101(b) (eCFR, current to Nov. 5, 2026); CMS Medicare Coverage Database, First Coast article A56841, 'Billing and Coding: Vitamin D; 25 hydroxy' (rev. R5, published 10/22/2026)
practice_impact: Check First Coast's billing-and-coding articles in the Medicare Coverage Database after October 1 as well as before: its vitamin D article was revised October 22, 2026, retroactive to October 1. Commercial payers publish medical policies, not LCDs.

claim: Medicare allows one year [from the date of service to file a claim].
correct_statement: Correct for Original Medicare: a claim must be received within 1 calendar year after the date of service (the line-item 'From' date on professional claims), with narrow exceptions. An untimely-filing denial cannot be appealed. Medicare Advantage plans are not bound by this and set their own limits by contract.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.44 (eCFR, current to Nov 6, 2026); Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), ch. 1, ss. 70-70.4
practice_impact: Fee-for-service visits from late 2025 expire day by day through year-end with no appeal right; Medicare Advantage claims for the same residents follow each plan's own contract limit, often shorter, so check those first.

claim: Commercial payers typically allow 90 to 180 days from the date of service.
correct_statement: Fair as a rule of thumb: UnitedHealthcare allows participating providers at least 90 days and Humana's commercial default is 90 days, each subject to contract or state law. In Florida, statute gives providers 6 months to bill state-regulated insurers and HMOs and bars waiving it by contract; self-funded plans follow the contract.
source_title: UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide, 'Time limits for filing claims'; Humana provider site, Claims Submissions; Florida Statutes ss. 627.6131, 641.3155 (2026)
practice_impact: Little for a Medicare-heavy facility practice; where commercial or HMO coverage is primary, Florida's 6-month statutory window may rescue a claim a payer denies at 90 days.

claim: Check CAQH attestation dates, re-attestation is required every 120 days.
correct_statement: Correct: providers must re-attest their CAQH Provider Data Portal profile every 120 days (180 days in Illinois) or the profile status changes to Expired. Plans using directory confirmation prompt quarterly, so some providers attest every 90 days. CAQH rebranded as DataSpring on June 7, 2026; the portal keeps the CAQH name.
source_title: DataSpring, powered by CAQH: Resources/FAQs (Directory Management) and 'CAQH Rebrands as DataSpring' (June 7, 2026)
practice_impact: Calendar each clinician's 120-day attestation; an Expired profile stalls Medicare Advantage and commercial recredentialing for Florida plans that pull from the portal.

claim: Credentialing typically takes 60 to 90 days for Medicare and 90 to 120 days for most commercial payers.
correct_statement: Unsourced rules of thumb, and long for Medicare. CMS requires contractors to finish 95% of online initial enrollments in 15 days, or 50 days when development is needed, and all within 85. UnitedHealthcare and Cigna quote about 45 to 60 days for credentialing, plus contract loading, so 90 to 120 days end to end is plausible.
source_title: CMS Medicare Program Integrity Manual (Pub. 100-08), ch. 10, s. 10.5 (Rev. 13415, eff. 10-20-25); First Coast Service Options, 'CMS-855 enrollment application processing timeframes' (Feb 18, 2026); UnitedHealthcare 'Join our network' medical provider FAQ; Cigna Healthcare credentialing page; 42 CFR 424.520(d), 424.521(a)
practice_impact: For a new clinician, Medicare billing can start from the application receipt date with up to 30 days of back-billing, so file in PECOS before the start date; allow three to four months for each Medicare Advantage and commercial plan.

claim: Payer-specific revalidation requirements for Medicare and Medicaid ... carry hard deadlines and loss of billing privileges if missed.
correct_statement: Correct. Medicare suppliers must revalidate every 5 years by the posted due date; missing it brings a stay of enrollment (claims rejected), then deactivation back-dated to the due date, with no payment for services furnished while deactivated. States must revalidate Medicaid providers at least every 5 years and generally must terminate those that fail to submit timely information.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.515, 424.540, 424.541, 455.414, 455.416 (eCFR, current to Nov 6, 2026); First Coast Service Options, 'Revalidation overview' (Aug 24, 2026)
practice_impact: Look up every clinician and the group on the CMS Medicare Revalidation List now; a missed due date means unpaid Part B visits from that date until First Coast receives the reactivation application, and that gap cannot be billed later.

claim: In September, Oracle Health announced five AI tools aimed at catching problems before the claim goes out: prior authorization, documentation integrity, charge capture, professional fee coding and appeals.
correct_statement: Accurate. On September 23, 2026 Oracle Health announced five embedded AI capabilities for its revenue cycle products: prior authorization, clinical documentation integrity, charge capture and integrity, professional-fee coding and appeal management. They were announced as planned for release 'in the coming months', not as available, and the appeals tool works after denial.
source_title: Oracle press release, 'Oracle Health Advances Revenue Cycle Management with AI' (Oracle Health and Life Sciences Summit, Orlando, Sep 23, 2026)
practice_impact: little

claim: Ensemble, which runs revenue cycle operations for more than 200 hospitals, partnered with Penelope Health to feed payer policy rules into its workflows upstream.
correct_statement: Accurate. Ensemble announced a strategic partnership with Penelope Health on September 24, 2026 to integrate Penelope's structured payer-policy data into Ensemble's revenue cycle intelligence engine. Ensemble's release says it manages end-to-end revenue cycle operations for health systems 'including more than 200 hospitals'. The release names both companies as platform partners of the same investor, Thoreau.
source_title: Ensemble Health Partners, 'Ensemble and Penelope Health Announce Strategic Partnership' (Cincinnati and New York, Sep 24, 2026)
practice_impact: little

claim: Tanya Sanderson, senior director of denial management at Stanford Health Care, put it plainly: 'If you're not pushing for appropriate reimbursement, then, yeah, you can have a great denial rate.'
correct_statement: Accurate. Becker's reported the quote, name and title as given: Tanya Sanderson, RN, senior director of denial management at Stanford Health Care, speaking on a four-person panel at Becker's 11th Annual Health IT + Digital Health + RCM Conference, in an article published September 18, 2026.
source_title: Becker's Hospital Review, 'Revenue cycle leaders: It's time to retire denial rate as a standalone metric' (Madeline Scheetz, Sep 18, 2026), read through the publisher's public content API because the web page blocks automated readers
practice_impact: Little; it is an opinion from a hospital panel. The usable point is to read denial rate next to appeal overturn rate and net collections.

claim: Sources: Becker's Hospital Review (Scheetz, Sep 18, 2026; Marcey, Sep 18, 2026; Dyrda, Sep 23, 2026; Cass, Sep 30, 2026); TechTarget (LaPointe, Sep 24, 2026).
correct_statement: All five citations exist with matching bylines and dates. One caveat: 'Marcey' is not Becker's reporting. It is a contributed opinion article by Doug Marcey, chief technology officer of billing vendor Coronis Health, and it is the source of the newsletter's 'wave of automated denials' framing, which it offers without data.
source_title: Becker's Hospital Review articles of Sep 18, 23 and 30, 2026 (publisher's public content API); TechTarget RevCycle Management, 'Oracle Health launches 5 AI revenue cycle tools to prevent denials' (Sep 24, 2026)
practice_impact: Little; treat the issue's 'payer AI mass denial' warning as a vendor's opinion and test it against your own denial data by payer and code.

claim: As one panelist noted, many teams still assume every denial costs about $25 to work.
correct_statement: Accurately reported, but $25 is an assumption, not a measured benchmark. The speaker was Debi Lasswell, a vendor executive (Longtail), who said the assumption is not necessarily true anymore. Premier's hospital survey put the average cost of fighting a denial at $43.84 per claim in 2022 and $57.23 in 2023.
source_title: Becker's Hospital Review, 'Revenue cycle leaders: It's time to retire denial rate as a standalone metric' (Sep 18, 2026); Premier Inc., 'Claims Adjudication Costs Providers $25.7 Billion' (Feb 24, 2025)
practice_impact: Set any small-balance write-off threshold from the practice's own measured cost per appeal; batching templated appeals on repetitive low-dollar facility-visit denials can make them worth working.

claim: CMS approved an updated CMS-R-131, the Advance Beneficiary Notice of Noncoverage, on March 13, 2026. ... The transition deadline is May 12, 2026.
correct_statement: The dates hold. OMB, not CMS, approved the revised CMS-R-131 on March 10, 2026 (expires 03/31/2029); CMS announced it March 13, 2026 and made it mandatory from May 12, 2026, when the prior version expired. Today only the Exp. 03/31/2029 form is valid for Original Medicare.
source_title: CMS MLN Connects Newsletter, March 19, 2026; OMB/OIRA ICR 202511-0938-004 (control no. 0938-0566); Noridian JD DME notice 'CMS Releases Updated ABN'
practice_impact: Every ABN signed since May 12, 2026 must be the Exp. 03/31/2029 version; check paper stock, EHR templates and any facility-supplied packets, and spot-audit ABNs issued since that date.

claim: A practice that delivers a non-covered Medicare service to a beneficiary using an outdated ABN cannot bill the patient and forfeits the revenue permanently.
correct_statement: Overstated. A wrong-version ABN 'could' be invalidated, case by case, leaving the practice liable; then it cannot collect and must refund. That applies only where an ABN is mandatory (chiefly medical-necessity denials). Statutorily excluded, never-covered services can be billed to the patient with no ABN at all.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), ch. 30, ss. 50.2.1, 50.5, 50.8, 50.9
practice_impact: Old-version ABNs on medical-necessity denials (repeat visits, frequency-limited labs) put the write-off and refund on the practice; never-covered services such as routine foot care stay billable to the patient with modifier GY.

claim: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, moving through Congress as of publication, proposes Medicaid work requirements, more frequent eligibility redeterminations, restrictions on state Medicaid financing mechanisms, and removal of enhanced federal matching funds.
correct_statement: The bill was not pending in May 2026: H.R. 1 became Public Law 119-21 on July 4, 2025. It enacted work requirements and six-month renewals for expansion adults starting no later than January 1, 2027, provider-tax and state-directed-payment limits, and ended the temporary expansion-incentive match; the 90% expansion match itself remains.
source_title: Public Law 119-21 (139 Stat. 72), H.R. 1, 119th Congress, enacted July 4, 2025 (GovInfo text), Secs. 71107, 71110, 71112, 71114-71116, 71119
practice_impact: Little direct effect: Florida has not expanded Medicaid and the work and six-month-renewal rules target expansion adults, not the 65+ and dual-eligible residents a facility practice sees; watch Medicaid-pending long-term-care residents and Florida directed-payment changes instead.

claim: The Congressional Budget Office projects 11.8 to 17 million Americans losing Medicaid coverage over the next several years under the provisions as written.
correct_statement: Wrong scope and stale. CBO's 11.8 million was the rise in uninsured people by 2034 under the Senate bill, from all coverage sources; 17 million was KFF's total adding non-bill policies. For the enacted law CBO estimates 10 million more uninsured in 2034, 7.5 million of them from the Medicaid changes.
source_title: KFF, 'How Will the 2025 Reconciliation Law Affect the Uninsured Rate in Each State?' (updated Aug 20, 2025), citing CBO publication 61570; KFF Quick Take, July 1, 2025 (cbo.gov itself blocked automated access)
practice_impact: Little: the coverage losses fall mainly on working-age expansion adults, and Florida is a non-expansion state; elderly and dual-eligible nursing-facility patients are largely outside these estimates.

claim: A practice may bill claims as in-network while the plan adjudicates them as out-of-network. The difference in reimbursement can be 40 to 60 percent of contracted rate.
correct_statement: The 40 to 60 percent figure has no traceable source. By rule, a non-contracted provider treating a Medicare Advantage enrollee is owed what Original Medicare would allow, and contracted MA physician rates sit close to Medicare (about 97% in one PubMed-indexed study). The real exposures are HMO denials of unauthorized out-of-network care and higher PPO cost-sharing.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.214 (eCFR, current to Nov 6, 2026); CMS, MA Payment Guide for Out of Network Payments (4/15/2015); PubMed: Trish et al., JAMA Intern Med 2017;177(9):1287-1295, https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2017.2679
practice_impact: Verify contract status with each MA plan and pull remits by plan: out-of-network handling shows up as authorization denials or shifted cost-sharing (uncollectible from dual-eligible residents), not as a flat 40-60% rate cut.

claim: On July 5, 2026, CMS launches the ACCESS model, a voluntary, ten-year alternative payment model targeting Medicare beneficiaries with chronic conditions including hypertension, diabetes, chronic musculoskeletal pain, and depression.
correct_statement: Correct. ACCESS is a voluntary CMS Innovation Center model that began July 5, 2026 and runs through June 30, 2036. It covers Original Medicare only (not Medicare Advantage, PACE or hospice enrollees) in four tracks; heart failure, COPD, substance use and tobacco tracks are added April 1, 2027. It is not an Advanced APM.
source_title: CMS Innovation Center, ACCESS Model web page (modified Oct 28, 2026); ACCESS Request for Applications v1.1 (Feb 12, 2026), including Appendix D
practice_impact: Small: enrollment is limited to Original Medicare, and the model's required clinical exclusions remove long-term nursing home residents 66 and older, frail patients 81 and older, moderate-to-severe dementia and hospice or palliative patients, which is most of a facility-based panel.

claim: The organizations participating are not hospitals, physician groups, or health systems. They are digital health platforms... Most of them have never operated inside Medicare before.
correct_statement: Half right. CMS says most of the 160+ participants had not previously served Medicare beneficiaries. But every participant must be a Medicare Part B-enrolled provider or supplier with a physician Medical Director, and CMS's list includes ordinary physician groups, a health center and a hospital system, several in Florida. A practice may itself apply.
source_title: CMS Innovation Center, ACCESS Model Participants (last updated November 3, 2026); ACCESS Request for Applications v1.1; NPPES NPI Registry entries for the named organizations
practice_impact: The newsletter frames ACCESS only as outside competition; in fact a Florida internal medicine group serving elders (Palm Beach Elder Care) is a participant, so joining, or billing the co-management codes, is an option the newsletter hides.

claim: The ACCESS model does not prohibit practices from continuing to bill CCM for enrolled patients. (CCM codes named: 99490, 99491, 99439.)
correct_statement: Correct for a practice that is not the patient's ACCESS organization: other providers keep billing Medicare under standard rules, and CCM is not on the substitute-spend list. Exceptions: an ACCESS participant or affiliate may bill only ACCESS G-codes for its aligned patients, and may not furnish contracted care management billed through another practice for them.
source_title: CMS ACCESS Technical Frequently Asked Questions; ACCESS RFA v1.1 Appendix E; ACCESS Co-Management Payment (CMP) Billing Guidance; MLN909188 Chronic Care Management Services (June 2025)
practice_impact: CCM revenue on Original Medicare patients is not cut off by ACCESS, but a CCM vendor that is itself an ACCESS participant cannot keep doing practice-billed CCM for patients it enrolls, so ask vendors now. Co-management codes add $30 per care-update review, up to three a year per track.

claim: The Improving Seniors' Timely Access to Care Act required CMS to implement electronic prior authorization standards for MA plans by January 1, 2026, with decision times of 72 hours for urgent and 7 days for standard requests.
correct_statement: That Act is not law: H.R. 3514 was only ordered reported by Ways and Means (July 15, 2026) and S. 1816 sits in Senate Finance. The 72-hour and 7-calendar-day limits come from CMS rule CMS-0057-F, effective January 1, 2026; the electronic Prior Authorization API is not required until January 1, 2027. Drugs are excluded.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.568, 422.572 and 422.122 (eCFR, current to Nov 6, 2026); CMS-0057-F final rule, 89 FR 8758 (Feb 8, 2024); GPO govinfo bill status for S. 1816 and H.R. 3514, 119th Congress
practice_impact: Cite 42 CFR 422.568(b)(1)(ii) and 422.572(a)(1), not the unpassed Act, when a Medicare Advantage plan misses a deadline; expect real EHR-connected electronic authorization only from January 1, 2027, and the 7 days can be extended by 14.

claim: CMS Star Ratings for MA plans will be published in October 2026. Plans rated below 3.5 stars face significant financial penalties and higher risk of market exit or product consolidation.
correct_statement: The 2027 Star Ratings were published October 8, 2026 and affect 2028 payments. There is no penalty: the bonus line is 4 stars (5-point benchmark increase); below 3.5 stars the rebate share falls from 65% to 50%. CMS can terminate a contract rated under 3 stars for three consecutive years.
source_title: CMS fact sheet, 2027 Medicare Advantage and Part D Star Ratings (Oct 8, 2026); 42 CFR 422.258(d)(7), 422.266(a)(2)(ii), 422.510(a)(4)(xi) (eCFR, current to Nov 6, 2026)
practice_impact: Use the actual 2027 ratings now on Medicare Plan Finder to rank Florida plans; watch plans under 4 stars (lost bonus) as well as those under 3.5, since both squeeze benefits and provider contracts for 2028.

claim: The Improving Seniors' Timely Access to Care Act required MA plans, by January 1, 2026, to accept prior authorization requests electronically, answer urgent requests within 72 hours and standard within 7 days, and give real-time decisions for routinely approved services.
correct_statement: No such law exists; the bill is still pending in Congress, and its own text would start electronic prior authorization in plan year 2028 and only study real-time decisions. What took effect January 1, 2026 by CMS regulation is the 72-hour and 7-calendar-day decision limits and denial reasons. Electronic APIs start January 1, 2027.
source_title: S. 1816, Improving Seniors' Timely Access to Care Act of 2025 (introduced text, GPO govinfo); CMS fact sheet on CMS-0057-F; CMS Electronic Prior Authorization page (modified Oct 21, 2026)
practice_impact: Plans had no 2026 duty to take electronic requests or give real-time answers, so portal friction is not a violation; only late decisions (over 72 hours or 7 calendar days) and denials without a specific reason are complaint-worthy today.

claim: CMS will incorporate electronic prior authorization compliance into MA Star Ratings beginning with the 2027 measurement cycle; plans not meeting response time standards will face rating penalties.
correct_statement: No Star Ratings measure on electronic prior authorization exists or has been finalized. CMS instead removed the appeals-timeliness measures from Star Ratings for the 2027 measurement year (2029 ratings). The 2027 Electronic Prior Authorization measure is a MIPS Promoting Interoperability measure for clinicians: optional in 2027, required from 2028.
source_title: CMS 2027 Star Ratings Measures and Weights; 42 CFR 422.164(c); CY 2027 MA and Part D final rule, 91 FR 17384 (Apr 6, 2026); CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule final rule, 91 FR 70992 (Nov 9, 2026); CMS-0057-F, 89 FR 8758 at 8894
practice_impact: Complaints will not lower a plan's stars through any prior authorization measure. The only 2027-2028 electronic prior authorization measure sits on the clinician side (MIPS); practices of 15 or fewer clinicians are automatically reweighted out of that category.

claim: If a balance on an account opened April 2023 to December 2024, over 180 days old, traces to a service date after a Medicaid disenrollment event, it is almost certainly uncollectable and should be reviewed for write-off.
correct_statement: Reviewing these balances is sensible, but 'almost certainly uncollectable' has no source. KFF found 47% of people disenrolled in 2023 were back on Medicaid and 28% had other coverage. Re-check eligibility and other payers for the service date first; Florida's fee-for-service Medicaid accepts Medicare crossover claims for 36 months, and QMB patients cannot be billed.
source_title: KFF Survey of Medicaid Unwinding (Apr 12, 2024); Florida Medicaid Provider Reimbursement Handbook, CMS-1500 (Rule 59G-4.001); Florida MMA 1115 Special Terms and Conditions (June 25, 2025); 42 CFR 435.916, 447.45(d), 1003.110
practice_impact: For dual-eligible residents these balances are mostly Medicare coinsurance: verify Medicaid or QMB status on the service date and the 36-month crossover window before writing off, and document hardship or collection effort rather than blanket write-offs.

claim: The second audit risk is specific to practices that implemented the 2023 E/M coding changes, particularly the shift to medical decision-making as the primary documentation standard (codes cited: 99214, 99215).
correct_statement: The year is wrong for the codes cited. Office visits 99202-99215 moved to level selection by medical decision-making or total time on January 1, 2021. The January 1, 2023 changes extended that to most other families, including nursing facility (99304-99310) and home or residence (99341-99350) visits. Time is an equal alternative to MDM.
source_title: CMS Fact Sheet, PFS Payment for Office/Outpatient E/M Visits (Jan 11, 2021); MLN006764 Evaluation and Management Services (May 2026)
practice_impact: The 2023 changes are the ones that govern this practice's own codes (nursing facility and home or residence visits), which the newsletter never mentions; templates should support MDM or documented total time for 99304-99310 and 99341-99350.

claim: Compare your 12-month E/M distribution to CMS published specialty norms. If your 99215 rate is more than 15, 20 percentage points above the specialty average, your documentation needs to be airtight.
correct_statement: The 15-20 point threshold has no traceable source. CMS publishes utilization data, not 'norms'; Florida's Medicare contractor, First Coast, supplies peer E/M distribution reports on request. CMS 2025 data put 99215 at about 7.5% of established office visits for internal medicine, 4.9% family practice and 22% geriatric medicine, so that margin flags only extreme outliers.
source_title: CMS Physician/Supplier Procedure Summary, calendar year 2025 (data.cms.gov, modified Aug 11, 2026); First Coast Service Options, Requesting a comparative billing report - Part B providers (medicare.fcso.com/billing/requesting-comparative-billing-report-part-b-providers); CMS Medicare Fee-for-Service Compliance Programs page (modified Nov 2, 2026)
practice_impact: This practice bills nursing facility codes, not 99215: in 2025 the top level 99310 was about 12% of subsequent nursing facility visits for geriatric medicine, 7% internal medicine, 8% nurse practitioners (Florida: 3%, 7%, 6%). Request First Coast's E&M report per individual provider number.

claim: The CMS Medicare plan landscape data for 2027 will be published in October.
correct_statement: CMS first released the 2027 landscape file on September 22, 2026 and announced it September 28, not in October (2026 landscape: September 26, 2025). CMS said Plan Finder would show 2027 plans by October 1; open enrollment runs October 15 to December 7. The file lists plans, premiums, cost limits and star ratings by county, not provider-network changes.
source_title: CMS press release, 'Medicare Advantage and Medicare Prescription Drug Programs Expected to Remain Stable in 2027' (Sept 28, 2026); CY2027 Landscape file and ReadMe (cms.gov, updated Nov 1, 2026); CMS 2027 MA and Part D Landscape State-by-State Fact Sheets
practice_impact: Florida drops from 611 to 560 MA plans for 2027. The file has shown since late September which plans remain (12 Florida institutional SNPs by our count), but network terminations must be confirmed with each plan.

claim: Most commercial payer contracts require 90 to 180 days notice for contract modifications. A renegotiation request submitted in August positions you for January 1 effective dates.
correct_statement: No source was found for a typical 90-to-180-day notice for contract changes; terms are contract-specific. AMA's examples use 30 to 90 days for no-cause termination and 45 days for payer amendments; Florida HMO law requires 60 days for cancellation and 30 for fee-schedule changes. Agreements renew on their own term dates; no payer must grant a January 1 change.
source_title: AMA Private Practice Toolkit, 'Payor Contracting 101' (2021); Florida Statutes 641.315 (2026); 42 CFR 422.202(d)(4); UnitedHealthcare 'Join our network' FAQ
practice_impact: Read each agreement's term, renewal and notice clauses and count back from that contract's anniversary date; an August letter guarantees nothing, and Medicare and most Medicare Advantage rates are not set by negotiation.

claim: Payer contracts renew January 1, meaning rate changes, network changes, and prior authorization requirement updates all take effect simultaneously. Open enrollment runs October through December
correct_statement: Member benefit years and Medicare fee schedules reset January 1, but provider agreements renew on their own contract dates, and MA plans can change rules on 30 days' notice or end contracts on 60 days' notice year-round. Medicare open enrollment: Oct 15 to Dec 7. HealthCare.gov: Nov 1, 2026 to Jan 15, 2027. Nursing-facility residents may switch MA plans anytime.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.62, 422.111, 422.202 (eCFR current to Nov 6, 2026); CMS Plan Year 2027 Marketplace Plans and Prices Fact Sheet (Oct 30, 2026) and HealthCare.gov dates page (note: 45 CFR 155.410(e)(5) as printed still says exchange enrollment for 2027 onward must end by December 31; CMS's own 2027 announcements say January 15); AMA Payor Contracting 101 toolkit
practice_impact: High for facility-based geriatrics: long-term care residents can change MA plans in any month, so eligibility must be re-verified monthly, not just in January; contract renewal dates must be read from each agreement.

claim: The potential return, a 5 to 10 percent rate improvement across a payer that represents 15 percent of your revenue, is significant.
correct_statement: The 5-to-10-percent figure is an illustration with no source; no data on typical negotiated increases was found. On a payer worth 15 percent of revenue it equals 0.75 to 1.5 percent of total revenue. Medicare rates are not negotiable: the 2027 conversion factor falls 2.31 percent to $32.63, and Medicare Advantage physician fees track Medicare.
source_title: CMS, Calendar Year (CY) 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule fact sheet (Nov 4, 2026); via PubMed: Wang Y et al., J Gen Intern Med 2025 (https://doi.org/10.1007/s11606-025-09798-8) and Trish E et al., JAMA Intern Med 2017 (https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2017.2679); AMA Payor Contracting 101
practice_impact: For a Medicare-heavy geriatrics practice the bigger 2027 number is the 2.3 percent Medicare conversion-factor cut; a commercial renegotiation moves at most about 1 percent of revenue and small practices have little leverage.

claim: any Medicare Advantage plan where your current performance tier places you in a reimbursement category below the plan's top tier, the tier differential is quantifiable and gives you a specific dollar target
correct_statement: Medicare pays star-rating bonuses to plans, not practices, and Medicare Advantage physician fees track the Medicare fee schedule. Provider quality incentives are plan-specific add-ons earned by performance, not negotiated tiers: Wellcare's 2026 program pays the member's primary care provider of record fixed amounts per closed care gap ($25 to $100), at Wellcare's sole discretion, with no appeal.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.258(d)(7) and 422.208 (eCFR current to Nov 6, 2026); Wellcare 2026 Partnership for Quality Program Update (Centene, 2026); via PubMed: Trish E et al., JAMA Intern Med 2017 (https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2017.2679); CMS 2027 Star Ratings fact sheet (Oct 8, 2026)
practice_impact: Limited: plan quality bonuses go to the member's primary care provider of record; a facility-based practice earns them only where it is the assigned PCP (for example institutional special needs plans), and by closing gaps, not by renegotiating.

claim: For each MA plan in your network, verify the October enrollment deadline for providers who are not yet enrolled. ... A provider locked out of MA network participation for Q4 loses revenue that is not recoverable
correct_statement: No federal rule sets an October deadline or a Q4 lock-out for clinicians joining Medicare Advantage networks. Plans credential year-round and must update online directories within 30 days; October 15 is the plan's deadline to deliver directories to enrollees. PPO plans must reimburse out-of-network care, capped at Original Medicare amounts; HMO out-of-network coverage is generally limited. Any cutoff is plan-specific.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.204, 422.2267(e)(11), 422.4(a)(1)(v), 422.214 (eCFR current to Nov 6, 2026); Medicare Managed Care Manual, Chapter 6, sections 60.3 and 100
practice_impact: Do not treat October as a federal cutoff: submit each plan's application as soon as a clinician is hired, ask the plan in writing for its effective-date policy, and bill PPO patients out-of-network meanwhile.

claim: Most payers require CAQH re-attestation every 120 days. When a provider's profile expires, payers that use CAQH as their primary verification source will automatically suspend active credentialing status.
correct_statement: The 120-day cycle is right, but it is CAQH's own portal rule (180 days in Illinois); missing it only changes the portal status to Expired. No source shows automatic suspension: UnitedHealthcare and Cigna act at the three-year recredentialing, after notices and reminders, and can end participation. CAQH became DataSpring in June 2026; ProView is now the CAQH Provider Data Portal.
source_title: DataSpring (formerly CAQH) Resources FAQ; UnitedHealthcare 'Credentialing and recredentialing for health care professionals' FAQ (PCA-1-26-01522, Oct 14, 2026); Cigna Healthcare credentialing page
practice_impact: Keep every clinician's attestation current (calendar 90 days to match the quarterly directory email), but an expired profile is a recredentialing and directory risk, not an instant claims shut-off; ask each plan for its written policy.

claim: Medicare Advantage plans run on 90-day processing windows that are not negotiable. Commercial payers vary from 60 to 90 days ... Medicaid timelines vary by state, most states run 45 to 60 days
correct_statement: These are unsourced rules of thumb, not fixed windows. No CMS rule gives Medicare Advantage plans a 90-day processing period. Published standards: UnitedHealthcare 14 to 45 days once the application is complete, plus up to 60 days to load the contract; Cigna 45 to 60 days; Florida Medicaid plans 60 days; Medicare (First Coast) 15 to 50 days online.
source_title: UnitedHealthcare Credentialing FAQ (Oct 14, 2026) and State and Federal Regulatory Addendum (Rev 9/2026); Cigna Healthcare credentialing page; First Coast 'CMS-855 enrollment application processing timeframes' (Feb 18, 2026); 42 CFR 422.204; Medicare Managed Care Manual ch. 6 s. 60.3
practice_impact: Budget 60 to 120 days end to end for Medicare Advantage and commercial plans, but get each plan's posted standard in writing; Medicare and Florida Medicaid applications protect revenue from the filing date, so file those first.

claim: A location change triggers re-credentialing with many payers and re-enrollment under the new address with Medicare and Medicaid.
correct_statement: A move must be reported, but it is an update, not a new enrollment. Medicare: report a changed, added or deleted practice location within 30 days through PECOS or the CMS-855, or risk deactivation. Florida Medicaid: report changes in writing within 30 days. UnitedHealthcare treats address changes as demographic updates; Medicare Advantage rules require recredentialing only every three years.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.516 and 424.540 (eCFR current to Nov 6, 2026); First Coast Service Options, 'How to change or add a practice mailing address' (June 26, 2026); CMS-855B (12/2025) Section 4 instructions; Florida Medicaid Provider Enrollment Policy (Rule 59G-1.060, Feb 2026)
practice_impact: High: the CMS-855B tells groups to list each hospital, retirement or assisted living community and other facility where they render services; adding or dropping one must reach First Coast within 30 days, or billing privileges can be deactivated retroactively.
