claim: The revenue is not recoverable in most cases, timely filing windows expire while the enrollment is pending, and most payers will not retroactively process claims predating enrollment completion beyond a limited grace period.
correct_statement: Wrong for government payers that dominate geriatrics. Medicare billing privileges date from the application filing date (or first service date, if later), with 30 days of retroactive billing and one year to file. Florida Medicaid enrollment is effective the day the agency receives the application. UnitedHealthcare and Cigna set network effective dates at approval; earlier claims pay out-of-network or deny.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.520, 424.521, 424.44 (eCFR current to Nov 6, 2026); Florida Statutes 409.907(9)(a) and 641.3155(2)(b) (2026); First Coast, 'Determining your Medicare effective date' (Feb 18, 2026); UnitedHealthcare and Cigna credentialing pages
practice_impact: High: file the PECOS and Florida Medicaid applications before a clinician's first visit and hold the claims; that revenue is recoverable. The real exposure is Medicare Advantage and commercial plans, which pay out-of-network or deny until the effective date.

claim: CMS updates these edits every quarter. The next update, Version 32.3, takes effect October 1, 2026, under Change Request 14516, issued June 30, 2026.
correct_statement: Confirmed. CMS Transmittal 13829 (Change Request 14516, dated June 30, 2026) set NCCI procedure-to-procedure Version 32.3 effective October 1, 2026, implemented October 5. That update has passed: the next is Version 33.0, effective January 1, 2027 (Change Request 14611, Transmittal 13946, issued September 17, 2026, implementation January 4, 2027).
source_title: CMS Manual System, Pub. 100-04, Transmittal 13829, Change Request 14516 (June 30, 2026); CMS Medicare NCCI Procedure to Procedure (PTP) Edits page (last modified Sept 1, 2026); Transmittal 13946, Change Request 14611 (Sept 17, 2026)
practice_impact: The October edits are live now; confirm the claim scrubber runs Version 32.3 and will load Version 33.0 before January 1, 2027, when the annual CPT and HCPCS code changes also start.

claim: When the paired remark code is MA130, the claim has been returned as unprocessable; these claims have no appeal rights and cannot be submitted as redetermination requests. The fix is to correct and resubmit the claim.
correct_statement: Correct for Original Medicare. A claim returned as unprocessable (remark MA130) is not a denial: it has no appeal rights and, per First Coast, no reopening rights. The fix is a corrected new claim, which must still arrive within one calendar year of the date of service because a rejected claim does not count as filed.
source_title: CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), Chapter 1, sections 70.2.3 and 80.3.1-80.3.2; X12 Remittance Advice Remark Codes list; First Coast Service Options, 'What you should do with claims returned as unprocessable' (Aug 21, 2025), Part B redetermination form tutorial (Sept 25, 2026) and claims FAQ on timely filing
practice_impact: High: First Coast sends appeals filed on MA130 claims back after up to 60 days, which can push a facility visit past the one-year filing limit. Route MA130 lines to rebilling, never to appeals or the reopening gateway.

claim: A code combination billed cleanly in September can start denying on October 1 with no change on your side; when that happens, it tends to arrive as CO-97 (bundled) or CO-4 (a modifier problem).
correct_statement: The timing is right: NCCI edits apply by date of service. The codes are wrong for Original Medicare. CMS instructs contractors to deny NCCI procedure-to-procedure failures with CO-236, not CO-97 or CO-4. At First Coast, CO-97 marks status-B bundling, global surgery or home health consolidated billing, and CO-4 is an unprocessable-claim rejection for a wrong or missing modifier.
source_title: CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), Chapter 23, section 20.9.3.1; First Coast Service Options, 'Tips to prevent CARC CO 236' (Aug 25, 2026), 'CO 97' (June 18, 2026) and 'Tips to prevent RUC CO4' (Sept 16, 2026); X12 Claim Adjustment Reason Codes list
practice_impact: High: a Florida practice that pulls only CO-4 and CO-97 after a quarterly update would miss its Medicare NCCI denials entirely. Track CO-236 by date of service each quarter; Medicare Advantage and commercial plans choose their own codes.

claim: In Experian Health's 2025 State of Claims survey of 250 professionals, 41% reported denial rates of 10% or higher; missing or inaccurate data was cited by 50%, up from 46% in 2024; 90% said denials are reworked with human review.
correct_statement: The 2025 figures match Experian's release, except that 90% is the share of denials reworked with human review, not of respondents. The survey has since been superseded: the 2026 edition (October 28, 2026; 204 respondents) reports 40% with denial rates of 10% or more, and 'services not covered', not missing data, is now the top reason.
source_title: Experian plc newsroom, 'Experian Health's 3rd Annual State of Claims Survey Finds Denials Still on the Rise Amid Escalating Challenges' (Sept 22, 2025) and 'Experian Health's Annual State of Claims Survey Finds Denials Remain Elevated As Reimbursement Challenges Grow' (Oct 28, 2026)
practice_impact: Little: this is a software vendor's opinion survey of revenue-cycle staff, not a measured denial rate, and its newest edition no longer ranks missing data first. Benchmark against the practice's own denial rate by payer and code.

claim: For Medicare, a redetermination request must be filed within 120 days of receiving the initial determination.
correct_statement: Correct for Original Medicare (Parts A and B): the redetermination request must be received by the contractor within 120 calendar days of receiving the initial determination, with receipt presumed five calendar days after the notice date. It does not govern Medicare Advantage: plan reconsiderations are due 60 calendar days after receipt, and contracted providers follow their contract.
source_title: 42 CFR 405.942 and 42 CFR 422.582 (eCFR, current to November 6, 2026); First Coast Service Options, Part B redetermination request form tutorial (Sept 25, 2026)
practice_impact: First Coast tells Florida providers to count 120 days from the remittance date, so use that stricter count; and do not apply 120 days to Medicare Advantage denials, where the window is usually shorter and set by the plan.

claim: On October 1, 2026, UnitedHealthcare stopped requiring prior authorization for roughly 1,700 procedure codes, about 30% of its prior authorization requirements; Medicare Advantage and dual special needs plans: about 120 codes combined.
correct_statement: The date and the 30% figure are UnitedHealthcare's own (notice of September 1, 2026); roughly 1,700 codes is a press figure, consistent with its lists. The Medicare Advantage number is wrong: UnitedHealthcare's posted list has 70 codes for Medicare Advantage, 66 of them repeated for dual special needs plans, so 70 distinct codes, not about 120.
source_title: UnitedHealthcare Network News, 'Spend less time on approvals and more time with patients' (Sept 1, 2026) and linked list 'CPT codes no longer requiring prior authorization for UnitedHealthcare Medicare Advantage and D-SNP Plans'; Healthcare Dive, 'UnitedHealthcare cuts prior authorization from 1,700 codes' (Sept 2, 2026)
practice_impact: Almost nothing changes for facility-based geriatrics: the 70 Medicare Advantage codes are mostly surgical, plus speech and swallowing therapy (92507, 92508, 92526), chiropractic and a few equipment items. UnitedHealthcare is also adding Part B step-therapy authorizations from January 1, 2027.

claim: Already in effect since January 1, 2026: impacted payers must decide prior auth requests within 72 hours (expedited) and seven calendar days (standard), give a specific reason for every denial, and post first public metrics by March 31, 2026.
correct_statement: The dates and numbers are right, but conditions are missing. The rule excludes all drug requests, plans may extend a decision by up to 14 calendar days, Medicaid managed care plans are bound only from the first rating period starting in 2026, federal-exchange plans are exempt from the timeframes, and the 72-hour expedited limit already existed for Medicare Advantage.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.122, 422.568, 422.572 and 438.210 (eCFR, current to November 6, 2026); CMS fact sheet, CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F), January 17, 2024
practice_impact: High for a Medicare Advantage-heavy Florida practice: the 7-day clock is real leverage for non-drug requests, but do not flag drug authorizations (Part B and Part D have separate 72-hour and 24-hour clocks) or requests with a written extension notice.

claim: Due January 1, 2027: payers must have a working Prior Authorization API. On September 18, the AMA urged CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz to keep that deadline and reject broad enforcement discretion during 2027.
correct_statement: Confirmed, and still in force. The API is due January 1, 2027 for Medicare Advantage and Medicaid/CHIP fee-for-service, and from the first 2027 rating period or plan year for Medicaid managed care and federal-exchange plans; drugs are excluded. The AMA letter is dated September 18, 2026. CMS restated the deadline on October 21 and November 9; no delay was found.
source_title: 42 CFR 422.122(b) (eCFR, current to November 6, 2026); AMA letter to CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz on electronic prior authorization (Sept 18, 2026) and AMA National Advocacy Update (Sept 25, 2026); CMS CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule final rule, 91 FR 70992; CMS press release of Oct 21, 2026; CMS-0057-F page (last modified Oct 8, 2026)
practice_impact: The payer deadline stands, but it binds plans, not the practice or its EHR vendor; Original Medicare and employer plans are outside it. Ask the EHR vendor which Medicare Advantage plans will be connected on January 1, 2027 and keep the portal and fax fallback.

claim: For the 2027 MIPS performance year, clinicians attest 'yes' to sending at least one electronic prior auth request through a payer's Prior Authorization API using certified EHR data, or claim an exclusion.
correct_statement: No longer the rule. CMS proposed the change on July 16, 2026 and finalized it in the CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule rule (issued November 4, published November 9, 2026): the Electronic Prior Authorization measure is optional for 2027, worth 10 bonus points, with no exclusion and no penalty. It becomes required in 2028, alongside a new prescription-drug measure.
source_title: CMS, CY 2027 Payment Policies Under the Physician Fee Schedule final rule (CMS-1848-F), 91 FR 70992 (Nov. 9, 2026); proposed rule published July 16, 2026; original requirement in CMS-0057-F, 89 FR 8758 (Feb. 8, 2024)
practice_impact: Nothing must be attested for 2027 and a missing payer API cannot zero the Promoting Interoperability score; a yes earns 10 bonus points. Plan for mandatory reporting, including a drug measure, in the 2028 performance year.

claim: KFF's first look at publicly reported prior auth data found insurers denied at least 1 in 8 standard requests in 2025, from 12% in Medicare Advantage to 18% in marketplace plans; about two-thirds of appealed Medicare Advantage denials were overturned.
correct_statement: Accurate. KFF (August 13, 2026) found the largest insurers denied on average 12% of standard requests in Medicare Advantage, 14% in Medicaid managed care and 18% in federal-marketplace plans in 2025; 67% of appealed Medicare Advantage denials were overturned. These are enrollment-weighted averages for 14 large insurers, exclude drugs, and vary widely: 5% (Elevance) to 17% (UnitedHealth) in Medicare Advantage.
source_title: KFF, 'Prior Authorization Metrics Provide New Insights into Insurer Practices, but Gaps Remain' (published Aug 13, 2026)
practice_impact: Useful benchmark for a Medicare Advantage-heavy panel: a two-in-three overturn rate argues for appealing denials rather than writing them off, and each plan's own posted metrics show whether a given Florida plan runs above the 12% average.
